Rather, it must be that the item is worth five sela'im but its value is not fixed (קייצי), and yet the redemption is valid, proving that items of unfixed value can be used for acquisition.

The Gemara answers: actually the item is not worth five sela'im, but the case is where the priest accepted it upon himself, as in the story of Rav Kahana who took a scarf from a pidyon haben (redemption of the firstborn) and said 'this is worth five sela'im to me'.

items.text: Rav Ashi's limitation and supporting story
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's limitation and supporting story
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi limits Rav Kahana's case to a great person who needs the garment, but for ordinary people it is not valid. He cites a story where Mar bar Rav Ashi bought a garment from Rava's mother worth ten for thirteen.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi limits this to a great person like Rav Kahana who needs the scarf, but for others it is not valid, as illustrated by Mar bar Rav Ashi buying a scarf from Rava's mother worth ten for thirteen.
Rav Ashi cites a story where Mar bar Rav Ashi bought a garment from Rava's mother worth ten for thirteen, illustrating that ordinary people do not acquire through such a transaction.

items.text: קידושין במנה ונתן דינר
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's ruling on partial payment and Rav Huna's principle
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar rules that if a man says 'be betrothed to me with a maneh' and gives a dinar, she is betrothed and he must complete the payment, because it is like saying 'on condition'. Rav Huna adds that 'on condition' is like saying 'from now'.
items.desc: רבי אלעזר פוסק שאם אמר 'התקדשי לי במנה' ונתן דינר, הרי זו מקודשת וישלים, משום שזה כתנאי. רב הונא בשם רב מוסיף שהאומר 'על מנת' כאומר 'מעכשיו' דמי.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar rules that if a man says 'be betrothed to me with a maneh' and gives a dinar, she is betrothed and he must complete the payment, because it is like saying 'on condition'.
sub.desc: רבי אלעזר פוסק שהאומר 'התקדשי לי במנה' ונתן דינר – הרי זו מקודשת וישלים, משום שזה כתנאי.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna adds in the name of Rav that saying 'on condition' is equivalent to saying 'from now', reinforcing Rabbi Elazar's reasoning.
sub.desc: רב הונא בשם רב מוסיף שהאומר 'על מנת' כאומר 'מעכשיו' דמי, ומחזק את דברי רבי אלעזר.

items.text: Objection from the baraita and resolution
items.text_en: Objection from the baraita and resolution
items.desc_en: A baraita states that if a man counts out a maneh and one party retracts even on the last dinar, they may. The Gemara initially distinguishes between 'this maneh' and an unspecified maneh, but then concludes that the entire baraita refers to 'this maneh', and the seifa clarifies the reisha.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita: if a man says 'Be betrothed to me with a maneh' and counts out coins, either party may retract even on the last dinar.
The Gemara initially answers that the baraita deals with a case where he said 'this maneh', distinguishing it from an unspecified maneh.
The Gemara cites the seifa of the baraita, which explicitly uses the phrase 'this maneh', to support the distinction.
The Gemara rejects the initial distinction and concludes that both reisha and seifa refer to 'this maneh', with the seifa clarifying the reisha.
The Gemara provides a logical argument: if the reisha referred to an unspecified maneh, why would the seifa need to specify 'this maneh'?
The Gemara resolves that the seifa was taught to clarify the reisha: even with an unspecified maneh, the retraction rule applies, and betrothal is not effected.

items.text: Rav Ashi's distinction and analysis of defective coins
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's distinction and analysis of defective coins
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi distinguishes the case of counting out coins because her mind is on the entire sum. The Gemara then analyzes the cases of a copper dinar and a bad dinar, with Rav Papa defining a bad dinar as one that circulates only under pressure.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi resolves the earlier difficulty by distinguishing the case of counting out coins, because her mind is on the entire sum.
The Gemara asks about the case of a copper dinar, and answers that it applies when she received it at night or found it among other coins.
The Gemara asks about the case of a bad dinar, and Rav Papa defines it as one that circulates only under pressure.

items.text: קידושין במשכון
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on leaving a pledge
items.desc_en: Rava quotes Rav Nachman that if a man says 'be betrothed to me with a maneh' and leaves a pledge for it, she is not betrothed.
items.desc: רבא בשם רב נחמן פוסק שאם אמר 'התקדשי לי במנה' והניח משכון, אינה מקודשת.

sub.desc_en: Rava citing Rav Nachman rules: if he says 'be betrothed with a maneh' and leaves a pledge for it, she is not betrothed.
sub.desc: רבא בשם רב נחמן פוסק שאם אמר לה 'התקדשי לי במנה' והניח לה משכון על המנה, אינה מקודשת.

items.text: Betrothal with a pledge and the principle of Rabbi Yitzchak
items.text_en: Betrothal with a pledge and the principle of Rabbi Yitzchak
items.desc_en: Rava challenges Rav Nachman from a mishnah that betrothal with a pledge is valid. Rav Nachman distinguishes that the pledge belongs to others, citing Rabbi Yitzchak's principle that a creditor acquires the pledge.

sub.desc_en: Rava challenges Rav Nachman from a mishnah that betrothal with a pledge is valid, implying that a pledge itself has value.
Rav Nachman distinguishes that the mishnah refers to a pledge belonging to others, not the man's own, and invokes Rabbi Yitzchak's principle.
Rabbi Yitzchak cites a verse to prove that a creditor acquires the pledge, explaining why the pledge can serve as betrothal money.

items.text: Case of the maidservant bought with small coins
items.text_en: Case of the maidservant bought with small coins
items.desc_en: The sons of Rav Huna bar Avin bought a maidservant with small coins but did not have them, so they placed a wine vessel as a pledge. When the maidservant appreciated, Rabbi Ami ruled that since the coins were not present, the vessel is not considered payment.

sub.desc_en: The narrator recounts that the sons of Rav Huna bar Avin bought a maidservant with small coins but did not have them, so they placed a wine vessel as a pledge.
Rabbi Ami rules that since the coins were not present, the vessel is not considered payment, and the transaction is void.

items.text: Woman throws the betrothal money into the sea or fire
items.text_en: Woman throws the betrothal money into the sea or fire
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita: if a man says 'Be betrothed to me with a maneh' and she throws it into the sea or fire, she is not betrothed. The Gemara clarifies that this is not a case where she says 'Take it, I don't want it,' but rather the baraita teaches that even if she is liable for the money, she does not betroth herself because she is testing his temper.

sub.desc_en: The baraita rules that if a man says 'Be betrothed to me with a maneh' and she throws it into the sea or fire or any destructive place, she is not betrothed.
The gemara infers that if she had thrown the money before him (instead of into the sea), it would be a valid betrothal, and questions whether this holds.
The gemara rejects the inference, noting that when she throws it before him she says 'Take it, I don't want it', which shows explicit rejection.

The gemara resolves that the baraita is using a 'not only' formulation: not only in the case of throwing before him (where she verbally rejects), but even throwing into the sea (where she is liable for the money) she is not betrothed, because she is testing his temper.

items.text: Betrothal money given to father or a third party
items.text_en: Betrothal money given to father or a third party
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches: if she says 'Give them to my father and your father' she is not betrothed, but if she says 'on condition that they accept them for me' she is betrothed. The Gemara explains that the Tanna includes 'your father' to show the leniency of the first clause and 'my father' to show the stringency of the second clause. It then contrasts this with a case of 'Ploni' (a stranger), and explains why both cases are necessary.

sub.desc_en: The baraita teaches that if a man says 'Be betrothed to me with a maneh' and she says 'Give it to my father and your father,' she is not betrothed; but if she says 'on condition that they accept them for me,' she is betrothed.

The Gemara explains that the Tanna included 'my father' to demonstrate the leniency of the first clause (that even a close relative does not make her betrothed) and 'your father' to demonstrate the stringency of the second clause (that even a distant relative can make her betrothed if she conditions it).
The baraita adds a parallel case: if she says 'Give them to Ploni (a stranger),' she is not betrothed; but if she says 'on condition that he accept them for me,' she is betrothed.

The Gemara explains why both cases are necessary: from the father case alone one might think only close relatives can be agents, but from the Ploni case alone one might think only strangers cannot receive a gift, so both are needed to clarify the full halacha.

items.text: Betrothal money placed on a rock
items.text_en: Betrothal money placed on a rock
items.desc_en: A baraita: if she says 'Give them on the rock' she is not betrothed, but if the rock is hers she is betrothed. Rav Bibi raises a question about a rock belonging to both of them, which remains unresolved (תיקו).

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that if a man says 'Be betrothed to me with a maneh' and she says 'Place it on a rock,' she is not betrothed, but if the rock is hers, she is betrothed.
Rav Bibi raises an unresolved question about the status of a rock belonging to both of them.
The gemara leaves the question unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Betrothal with a loaf given to a dog
items.text_en: Betrothal with a loaf given to a dog
items.desc_en: A baraita: if she says 'Give it to a dog' she is not betrothed, but if the dog is hers she is betrothed. Rav Mari asks about a dog running after her: does she give herself because of the benefit of being saved from the dog, or can she say he is obligated to save her? This remains unresolved (תיקו).

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that if a man says 'Be betrothed to me with this loaf' and she says 'Give it to a dog,' she is not betrothed, but if the dog is hers, she is betrothed.
Rav Mari asks about a case where a dog is running after her: what is the halacha?
The gemara analyzes the two sides of the question: does she give herself because of the benefit of being saved from the dog, or can she say he is obligated to save her by Torah law?
The question remains unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Betrothal with a loaf given to a poor person
items.text_en: Betrothal with a loaf given to a poor person
items.desc_en: A baraita: if she says 'Give it to a poor person' she is not betrothed, even if the poor person is dependent on her. The reason is that she can say: just as I am obligated to support him, so are you.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that if a man says 'Be betrothed to me with this loaf' and she says 'Give it to a poor person,' she is not betrothed, even if the poor person is dependent on her.
The gemara explains the reason: she can say to him, 'Just as I am obligated to support him, so are you obligated.'

items.text: Three cases of ambiguous responses to kiddushin offers
items.text_en: Three cases of ambiguous responses to kiddushin offers
items.desc_en: Three stories are presented: a woman asks for a branch, a cup of wine, or dates; the man offers kiddushin if he gives it; she responds with a phrase like "give giving" (הבה מיהבה), "pour pouring" (אשקויי אשקיין), or "throw throwing" (שדי מישדא). Rav Hama and Rav Zevid rule that such responses are meaningless (לאו כלום הוא) and do not constitute acceptance of kiddushin.

sub.desc_en: The first story: a woman asks for a string of beads; the man offers kiddushin if he gives it; she responds 'הבה מיהבה' (give giving).
Rav Hama rules that the response 'הבה מיהבה' is meaningless and does not constitute acceptance of kiddushin.
The second story: a woman asks for a cup of wine; the man offers kiddushin; she responds 'אשקויי אשקיין' (pour pouring).
Rav Hama rules that the response 'אשקויי אשקיין' is meaningless and does not constitute acceptance of kiddushin.
The third story: a woman asks for dates; the man offers kiddushin; she responds 'שדי מישדא' (throw throwing).
Rav Zevid rules that the response 'שדי מישדא' is meaningless and does not constitute acceptance of kiddushin.

items.text: Inquiry about the imperative forms: הב, אשקי, ושדי
items.text_en: Inquiry about the imperative forms: הב, אשקי, ושדי
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: if the woman says the imperative forms "give" (הב), "pour" (אשקי), or "throw" (שדי) without the infinitive absolute, what is the law? Ravina says she is betrothed (מקודשת), while Rav Sama bar Rakta says she is not betrothed (אינה מקודשת). The halakhah follows the latter view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: if the woman says the imperative forms "give" (הב), "pour" (אשקי), or "throw" (שדי) without the infinitive absolute, what is the law?
Ravina says she is betrothed (מקודשת).
Rav Sama bar Rakta says she is not betrothed (אינה מקודשת).
The halakhah follows the latter view: she is not betrothed.

items.text: Three halakhic rulings on related matters
items.text_en: Three halakhic rulings on related matters
items.desc_en: The Gemara states three halakhot: (1) leftover items (שיראי) do not require appraisal; (2) the halakhah follows Rabbi Elazar; (3) the halakhah follows Rava quoting Rav Nachman. These rulings are given without further explanation, serving as a transition to the next topic.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara issues three halakhic rulings: leftover items (שיראי) do not require appraisal, the law follows Rabbi Elazar, and the law follows Rava citing Rav Nachman.

items.text: Baraita on betrothal by document (shtar)
items.text_en: Baraita on betrothal by document (shtar)
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches: if a man writes on paper or pottery (even if worthless) phrases like "your daughter is betrothed to me" or "your daughter is espoused to me" or "your daughter is for me as a wife," the woman is betrothed. This establishes the basic validity of a shtar erusin.

sub.desc_en: The baraita teaches the basic law of betrothal by document (שטר): if a man writes on paper or pottery, even if worthless, phrases like 'your daughter is betrothed to me' or 'your daughter is espoused to me' or 'your daughter is for me as a wife,' the woman is betrothed.

items.text: Objection and resolution regarding the wording of the shtar
items.text_en: Objection and resolution regarding the wording of the shtar
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira bar Memel objects: the shtar erusin is unlike a bill of sale, where the seller writes "my field is sold to you," but here the husband writes "your daughter is betrothed to me." Rava responds by citing verses: for sale, the Torah says "when he sells" (וּמָכַר), so the seller writes; for betrothal, the Torah says "when a man takes" (כִּי יִקַּח), so the husband writes. A further objection is raised from the verse "fields shall they buy with money" (שָׂדוֹת בַּכֶּסֶף יִקְנוּ), which is resolved by reading it as "they shall sell" (יַקְנוּ). Ultimately, Rava concludes that these are halakhot l'Moshe miSinai, and the Sages merely found scriptural support.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira bar Memel objects that the shtar erusin (betrothal document) is unlike a bill of sale, where the seller writes 'my field is sold to you,' but here the husband writes 'your daughter is betrothed to me.'

Rava answers that the difference follows the Torah's language: for sale it says 'וּמָכַר' (when he sells), so the seller writes; for betrothal it says 'כִּי יִקַּח' (when a man takes), so the husband writes.
The Gemara objects that regarding sale the verse also says 'שָׂדוֹת בַּכֶּסֶף יִקְנוּ' (fields shall they buy with money), which uses the root 'קנה' (buy) rather than 'מכר' (sell).

The Gemara answers that the verse can be read as 'יַקְנוּ' (they shall sell), and similarly for betrothal the verse 'אֶת בִּתִּי נָתַתִּי לָאִישׁ הַזֶּה' (I gave my daughter to this man) supports the father's role.

Rava concludes that these are halakhot l'Moshe miSinai (הלכות למשה מסיני), and the Sages merely found scriptural support (אסמכתא), with an alternative answer citing the verse 'וָאֶקַּח אֶת סֵפֶר הַמִּקְנָה' (I took the deed of purchase).

items.text: Rava's ruling on shtar erusin for a minor and an adult
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on shtar erusin for a minor and an adult
items.desc_en: Rava quotes Rav Nachman: if a man writes on paper or pottery phrases like "your daughter is betrothed to me" etc., whether through her father or through herself, she is betrothed with his consent (מדעתו), provided she is not a bogeret (i.e., she is a minor or na'arah). Then, a parallel case: if he writes to her directly "you are betrothed to me" etc., whether through her father or through herself, she is betrothed with her consent (מדעתה), provided she is a bogeret (an adult).

sub.desc_en: Rava quotes Rav Nachman's ruling: if a man writes a shtar erusin (betrothal document) for a minor or na'arah, using phrases like 'your daughter is betrothed to me,' whether delivered through her father or herself, she is betrothed with his consent (מדעתו), provided she has not reached bogeret (adulthood).

Rava adds the parallel case: if he writes directly to her 'you are betrothed to me,' whether through her father or herself, she is betrothed with her consent (מדעתה), provided she is a bogeret (an adult).

items.text: Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish's inquiry about a shtar not written lishmah
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish's inquiry about a shtar not written lishmah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish asks: if a shtar erusin was written not for her sake (שלא לשמה), what is the law? The Gemara begins to compare this to the requirement of lishmah in a get (bill of divorce), but the segment ends mid-sentence, leaving the question unresolved.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish asks: if a document of betrothal (שטר אירוסין) was written not for her sake (שלא לשמה), what is the law?
The Gemara begins to compare betrothal (הויה) to divorce (יציאה), but the segment ends mid-sentence, leaving the comparison incomplete.

items.text: Gemara's question and resolution on lishmah for shtar kiddushin
items.text_en: Gemara's question and resolution on lishmah for shtar kiddushin
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a betrothal document requires intent for the sake of the woman (lishmah), comparing it to money betrothal. It resolves that we derive betrothal from divorce, as the verse says 've'yatz'ah ve'hayetah'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a betrothal document requires intent for the sake of the woman (lishmah), comparing it to money betrothal.
The Gemara resolves that we derive betrothal from divorce, as the verse says 'וְיָצְאָה' (and she goes out) and 'וְהָיְתָה' (and she becomes).

items.text: Dispute on shtar written lishmah without her knowledge
items.text_en: Dispute on shtar written lishmah without her knowledge
items.desc_en: Rava and Ravina hold she is betrothed, while Rav Pappa and Rav Sherevya hold she is not. Each side derives from the hekesh of betrothal to divorce: one focuses on lishmah without knowledge, the other on the need for the giver's intent.

sub.desc_en: The gemara states a dispute: if a man wrote a bill of betrothal (שטר) for her sake (לשמה) but without her knowledge, Rava and Ravina say she is betrothed, while Rav Pappa and Rav Sherevya say she is not.

sub.text: Rav Pappa's explanation of the opposing view
sub.text_en: Rav Pappa's explanation of the opposing view
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa explains the reasoning of Rava and Ravina: the hekesh (analogy) from divorce (יציאה) to betrothal (הווייה) teaches that just as divorce requires לשמה (for her sake) but not her knowledge, so betrothal requires לשמה but not her knowledge.

sub.text: Rav Pappa's explanation of his own view
sub.text_en: Rav Pappa's explanation of his own view
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa explains his own view: the hekesh teaches that just as divorce requires the intent of the one who gives (דעת מקנה), so betrothal requires the intent of the one who gives, and here the husband did not intend to betroth her without her knowledge.

items.text: Objection from baraita and resolution via Rav Giddel
items.text_en: Objection from baraita and resolution via Rav Giddel
items.desc_en: A baraita states that betrothal documents require the knowledge of both parties. The Gemara deflects this as referring to documents of commitment (shtarei pesikata), not actual betrothal documents, citing Rav Giddel's ruling about verbal commitments.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects by citing a baraita that betrothal and marriage documents may only be written with the knowledge of both parties, implying that the woman's knowledge is required for a valid betrothal document.
The Gemara deflects the objection by explaining that the baraita refers to documents of commitment (שטרי פסיקתא), not actual betrothal documents, and cites Rav Giddel's ruling.
Rav Giddel reports in the name of Rav that verbal commitments made during betrothal negotiations are binding, supporting the distinction between commitment documents and actual betrothal documents.

items.text: Derivation of acquisition through bi'ah
items.text_en: Derivation of acquisition through bi'ah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu quotes Rabbi Yochanan that the verse 'be'ulat ba'al' teaches that a man becomes a husband through intercourse. Rabbi Zeira questions the derivation, and the Gemara explains that without this verse, one might think betrothal must precede intercourse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where do we derive that a woman is acquired through intercourse (ביאה)?
Rabbi Avahu says in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that the verse 'בְּעֻלַת בַּעַל' (a woman who has had intercourse with a husband) teaches that a man becomes a husband through intercourse.
Rabbi Zeira objects: could we not derive the same from the Mishnah's phrase 'וּבְעָלָהּ' (and he had intercourse with her) which already teaches that she is acquired through intercourse?
The Gemara resolves: from the Mishnah alone one might think that betrothal must precede intercourse, so the verse 'בְּעֻלַת בַּעַל' teaches that intercourse alone suffices for acquisition.

items.text: Challenge from the case of a betrothed na'arah
items.text_en: Challenge from the case of a betrothed na'arah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba bar Memel asks how a betrothed na'arah can be executed by stoning if intercourse alone effects betrothal. The Gemara suggests an irregular intercourse, but Abaye notes that Rabbi and the Sages dispute whether a husband's irregular intercourse renders her a be'ulah, citing a baraita.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba bar Memel challenges: if intercourse alone effects betrothal, how can a betrothed na'arah (נערה המאורסה) ever be executed by stoning, since intercourse would make her a be'ulah (בעולה) and thus subject to strangulation?
The rabbis before Abaye propose that the case is possible if the betrothed man had irregular intercourse (שלא כדרכה) with her, which does not fully render her a be'ulah.
Abaye objects: Rabbi and the Sages only dispute whether another man's irregular intercourse renders her a be'ulah, but all agree that a husband's irregular intercourse does render her a be'ulah.

The Gemara cites a baraita: if ten men had irregular intercourse with a betrothed na'arah and she remains a virgin, all are stoned; Rabbi says the first is stoned and the rest are strangled, confirming the dispute over irregular intercourse by others.

items.text: Alternative resolution by Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak
items.text_en: Alternative resolution by Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak suggests the case is where he betrothed her with a document, and since he completes the divorce, he completes the betrothal, allowing stoning.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves the difficulty by proposing the case is where he betrothed her with a document, so that since he completes the divorce (גומר ומוציא), he also completes the betrothal (גומר ומכניס), allowing stoning.

items.text: Derivation that an amah ivriyah is not acquired through bi'ah
items.text_en: Derivation that an amah ivriyah is not acquired through bi'ah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan uses the verse 'u've'alah' to teach that a woman is acquired through bi'ah, but an amah ivriyah is not, countering a potential kal vachomer from yevamah. Rabbi derives both lessons from the unusual spelling.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Rabbi Yochanan does with the verse 'וּבְעָלָהּ' (and he had relations with her), since he already derived the acquisition of a woman through bi'ah from a different verse.
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Yochanan uses the verse to teach that a woman is acquired through bi'ah, but an amah ivriyah (Hebrew maidservant) is not acquired through bi'ah.

The Gemara raises a potential kal vachomer (a fortiori argument) from yevamah (levirate widow): if a yevamah, who is not acquired through money, is acquired through bi'ah, then an amah ivriyah, who is acquired through money, should certainly be acquired through bi'ah.

The Gemara rejects the kal vachomer by noting that a yevamah is already designated (זְקוּקָה וְעוֹמֶדֶת) for the yavam, and then raises a second potential derivation from the verse 'אִם אַחֶרֶת יִקַּח לוֹ' (if he takes another wife), which compares an amah ivriyah to an ordinary woman, but the verse 'וּבְעָלָהּ' teaches that this comparison does not extend to acquisition through bi'ah.

The Gemara explains that Rabbi derives both lessons (that a woman is acquired through bi'ah and that an amah ivriyah is not) from the unusual spelling 'וּבְעָלָהּ' (with a heh suffix) instead of the simpler 'וּבָעַל' (and he had relations).

items.text: Rava's interpretation of kiddushin mesurim levi'ah
items.text_en: Rava's interpretation of kiddushin mesurim levi'ah
items.desc_en: Rava states that betrothals that are subject to intercourse are valid, but those not subject to intercourse are invalid. The Gemara notes that the verse 'u've'alah' implies all these lessons.

sub.desc_en: Rava, citing Bar Ahina, derives from the verse 'כי יקח איש אשה ובעלה' that betrothals which are subject to intercourse (קידושין המסורין לביאה) are valid, while those not subject to intercourse are invalid.
The Gemara asks what further lesson can be derived from the verse's wording.

The Gemara answers that if the verse had intended only the basic rule, it would have written 'או בעלה' (or he had intercourse); the actual wording 'ובעלה' (and he had intercourse) teaches all these additional lessons.

items.text: Derivation that a husband renders her a be'ulah irregularly, not others
items.text_en: Derivation that a husband renders her a be'ulah irregularly, not others
items.desc_en: Rabbi uses 'be'ulat ba'al' to teach that a husband renders her a be'ulah through irregular intercourse, but another does not. The Gemara questions this from a baraita where Rabbi holds the first is stoned and the rest strangled, implying others can render her a be'ulah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Rabbi does with the phrase 'be'ulat ba'al' (a woman who has been penetrated by a husband), and answers that it teaches that a husband renders her a be'ulah (penetrated woman) through irregular intercourse, but another does not.

The Gemara challenges Rabbi's position by citing a baraita where Rabbi holds that the first man who had irregular intercourse is stoned and the rest are strangled, implying that others can render her a be'ulah.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's statement and the dispute over the verse
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's statement and the dispute over the verse
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira asserts that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi agrees that all parties pay a fine in the case of seduction, distinguishing it from capital cases via the verse 'and the man who lay with her shall die alone'. The Gemara then asks how the Rabbis interpret this verse, presenting a dispute between Rabbi Oshaya and Rabbi Yonatan.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira states that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi agrees all parties pay a fine in seduction, distinguishing it from capital cases via the verse 'and the man who lay with her shall die alone'.
The Gemara asks how the Rabbis interpret the word 'alone' in the verse.
Rabbi Oshaya explains that the word 'alone' teaches that both parties must be equal in liability, citing the baraita about 'and both of them shall die'.
Rabbi Yonatan offers an alternative interpretation, that the word 'alone' teaches that only the man dies alone, not the woman.
The Gemara asks from where Rabbi Yochanan derives his reasoning.
The Gemara answers that if the verse only meant 'a man', it would have said 'a man's wife'; the extra word 'master' teaches two things.

items.text: The question of beginning vs. end of intercourse
items.text_en: The question of beginning vs. end of intercourse
items.desc_en: A dilemma is raised: does the beginning of intercourse effect acquisition (kinyan) or the end? The practical difference is a case where a woman inserts her hand and accepts kiddushin from another man after initial penetration but before completion. Amemar in the name of Rava rules that one who has intercourse intends for the completion of the act.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a dilemma: does the beginning of intercourse effect acquisition (קונה) or the end, with the practical difference being a case where a woman inserts her hand and accepts kiddushin from another man after initial penetration but before completion.

sub.text: Amemar in the name of Rava
sub.text_en: Amemar in the name of Rava
sub.desc_en: Amemar in the name of Rava rules that one who has intercourse intends for the completion of the act (גמר ביאה), thereby resolving the dilemma in favor of the end of intercourse effecting acquisition.

items.text: The question of whether intercourse effects nissuin or erusin
items.text_en: The question of whether intercourse effects nissuin or erusin
items.desc_en: Another dilemma is raised: does intercourse effect full marriage (nissuin) or only betrothal (erusin)? The practical difference involves inheritance, becoming impure for her, and annulling her vows. The Gemara leaves the question unresolved.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a dilemma: does intercourse effect full marriage (nissuin) or only betrothal (erusin), with practical differences in inheritance, impurity, and vow annulment.
The Gemara elaborates the practical consequences: if intercourse effects nissuin, he inherits, becomes impure for her, and annuls her vows; if erusin, he does none of these.
The Gemara leaves the question unresolved with the word 'מַאי' (what is the answer?).

items.text: Abaye's proof from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Abaye's proof from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Abaye brings a proof from a Mishnah that lists 'biah' (intercourse) as a mode of kiddushin and then separately mentions 'nissuah' (marriage), implying that biah effects only erusin. The Gemara deflects by saying that the term 'nissuah' refers to other modes of marriage.

sub.desc_en: Abaye cites a Mishnah that lists 'ביאה' (intercourse) as a mode of קידושין (betrothal) and then separately mentions 'נישאת' (married), implying that ביאה effects only אירוסין (betrothal), not נישואין (full marriage).

The Gemara deflects Abaye's proof by explaining that the term 'נישאת' (married) in the Mishnah refers to other modes of marriage (כסף or שטר), not to ביאה, so the Mishnah does not prove that ביאה effects only אירוסין.

items.text: Rava's proof from the law of a three-year-old girl
items.text_en: Rava's proof from the law of a three-year-old girl
items.desc_en: Rava brings a proof from a baraita that a girl of three years and one day can be betrothed through intercourse, and if a yavam has intercourse with her, he acquires her, and she is liable for adultery and impurifies her husband. This suggests that intercourse effects nissuin, as it creates full marital obligations.

sub.desc_en: Rava cites a baraita that a three-year-old girl can be betrothed through intercourse, and if a yavam has intercourse with her he acquires her, she is liable for adultery, and she impurifies her husband, proving that intercourse effects nissuin.

items.text: Opening baraita on effects of intercourse
items.text_en: Opening baraita on effects of intercourse
items.desc_en: The baraita states that a woman who has had intercourse can defile a lower couch like an upper one, and if she marries a priest she eats terumah; if she has intercourse with a forbidden relative, they are executed on her account but she is exempt; if she has intercourse with a disqualified person, she is disqualified from the priesthood.

sub.desc_en: The baraita lists four halachic effects of intercourse with a woman: she defiles a lower couch like an upper one, if married to a priest she eats terumah, if with a forbidden relative they are executed but she is exempt, and if with a disqualified person she is disqualified from the priesthood.

items.text: Gemara's question on the baraita's wording
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the baraita's wording
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the baraita uses both 'intercourse' (בִּיאָה) and 'marriage' (נִישֵּׂאת), and explains that the baraita means: if these are marriages to a priest, she eats terumah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the baraita uses both 'בִּיאָה' (intercourse) and 'נִישֵּׂאת' (married) as if they are distinct categories.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita means: if these are marriages to a priest, she eats תרומה (priestly portion).

items.text: Letter from Yochanan ben Bag Bag to Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira
items.text_en: Letter from Yochanan ben Bag Bag to Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira
items.desc_en: Yochanan ben Bag Bag writes to Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira in Netzivin, having heard that he says an arusah bat Yisrael eats terumah. Rabbi Yehuda responds with a kal vachomer from a Canaanite maidservant: if her money makes her eat terumah even though intercourse does not, then an arusah, whose intercourse does make her eat terumah, should certainly have her money make her eat terumah. However, the Sages ruled that an arusah does not eat terumah until she enters the chuppah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a letter from Yochanan ben Bag Bag to Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira, who reportedly holds that an arusah bat Yisrael eats terumah; Rabbi Yehuda challenges him to derive this from a kal vachomer.

sub.text: Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira's kal vachomer
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira's kal vachomer
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda argues via kal vachomer: if a Canaanite maidservant, whose intercourse does not permit her to eat terumah, has her money permit her, then an arusah, whose intercourse does permit her, should certainly have her money permit her.
Rabbi Yehuda concedes that despite the kal vachomer, the Sages ruled that an arusah does not eat terumah until she enters the chuppah.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the kal vachomer
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the kal vachomer
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the kal vachomer: if both intercourse and money are via chuppah, she eats in both cases; if intercourse is via chuppah and money is not, there are two factors versus one. The Gemara concludes that the case must be where both are without chuppah. It then asks: if marriage (nissuin) effects the ability to eat, it is clear that intercourse is stronger than money; but if kiddushin effects it, why is it clear here but uncertain elsewhere?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the kal vachomer works: if both intercourse and money are via chuppah, the woman eats terumah in both cases, so the kal vachomer is unnecessary.
The Gemara answers that the case must be where intercourse is via chuppah and money is not via chuppah, but then notes the imbalance of factors.

The Gemara objects: if nissuin (marriage) effects the ability to eat terumah, it is clear that intercourse is stronger than money; but if kiddushin (betrothal) effects it, why is it clear here but uncertain elsewhere?

items.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's resolution
items.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak says that the case is indeed intercourse via chuppah and money without chuppah, and the kal vachomer still stands: from a maidservant whose intercourse does not make her eat even via chuppah, but whose money makes her eat without chuppah, to an arusah whose intercourse makes her eat via chuppah, her money should make her eat without chuppah. The Sages' decree is due to 'Ulla's concern.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves that the case is intercourse via chuppah and money without chuppah, and the kal vachomer (a fortiori argument) still stands.

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's citation of the kal vachomer
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's citation of the kal vachomer
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak cites the kal vachomer sent by Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira: from a maidservant whose intercourse does not make her eat even via chuppah, but whose money makes her eat without chuppah, to an arusah whose intercourse makes her eat via chuppah, her money should make her eat without chuppah.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak concludes that the Sages' decree that an arusah does not eat terumah until she enters the chuppah is due to Ulla's concern.

items.text: Alternative explanation: Ben Bag Bag's reasoning
items.text_en: Alternative explanation: Ben Bag Bag's reasoning
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Ben Bag Bag's argument is that regarding a maidservant, there is no leftover in her acquisition (she is fully acquired), but here (with an arusah) there is a leftover (she is not fully acquired), so the kal vachomer is valid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves Ben Bag Bag's reasoning: regarding a Canaanite maidservant, her acquisition leaves no leftover (she is fully acquired), but regarding an arusah, there is a leftover (she is not fully acquired), so the kal vachomer is valid.

items.text: Ravina's interpretation and the alternative version
items.text_en: Ravina's interpretation and the alternative version
items.desc_en: Ravina says that from the Torah it was clear to him that she eats, but he sent the message regarding the rabbinic decree. The Gemara then presents an alternative version of the letter, where the concern is 'simpon' (a hidden defect), and the kal vachomer argues that just as with a maidservant we do not worry about simpon, so too with an arusah we should not worry, but the Sages decreed otherwise.

sub.desc_en: Ravina explains that from the Torah it was clear to him that she eats, but the message was sent regarding the rabbinic decree.
The Gemara presents an alternative version of the letter, where the concern is about 'simpon' (a hidden defect), and Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira challenges Yochanan ben Bag Bag with a kal vachomer.

sub.text: The kal vachomer argument in the alternative version
sub.text_en: The kal vachomer argument in the alternative version
sub.desc_en: The kal vachomer argues that just as with a maidservant we do not worry about simpon, so too with an arusah we should not worry, but the Sages decreed otherwise.

items.text: Opening statement: Until she enters the chuppah
items.text_en: Opening statement: Until she enters the chuppah
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that a woman is not fully married until she enters the chuppah, citing the reason of Ulla.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that a woman is not fully married until she enters the chuppah, citing the reason of Ulla.

items.text: Question about Ben Bag Bag and defects in slaves
items.text_en: Question about Ben Bag Bag and defects in slaves
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Ben Bag Bag's view regarding a simpon (condition) in slaves, distinguishing between visible and hidden defects, and then discusses cases of a thief or gambler.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions Ben Bag Bag's view regarding a simpon (condition) in slaves, distinguishing between visible and hidden defects, and concludes that since the buyer seeks a worker, hidden defects do not matter.

The Gemara answers that if the slave turns out to be a thief or gambler, the defect is considered to have arrived, but a notorious bandit or royal informer has a reputation that the buyer should have known.

items.text: Difference between the two opinions
items.text_en: Difference between the two opinions
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the two opinions, and answers that it lies in cases of receiving, handing over, and going.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the two opinions, given that both agree the woman does not eat terumah.
The Gemara answers that the difference lies in cases of receiving, handing over, and going.

items.text: Beit Shammai's reasoning: a dinar
items.text_en: Beit Shammai's reasoning: a dinar
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains Beit Shammai's view that betrothal requires a dinar, citing Rabbi Zeira's reason that a woman is particular about herself and will not be betrothed with less.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the reasoning behind Beit Shammai's position that betrothal requires a dinar.
Rabbi Zeira explains that a woman is particular about herself and will not be betrothed with less than a dinar.

items.text: Abaye's objection and resolution
items.text_en: Abaye's objection and resolution
items.desc_en: Abaye objects that if the reason is the woman's fastidiousness, then daughters of Rabbi Yannai who require a large sum would not be betrothed with a small coin, which is absurd. The Gemara resolves that the case is where she accepts it at night or appoints an agent.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects that if the reason for the diner minimum is the woman's fastidiousness, then the fastidious daughters of Rabbi Yannai would not be betrothed with a small coin from another man, which is absurd.
Rabbi Zeira resolves that the case is where she accepts the coin at night or appoints an agent, so her fastidiousness is not triggered.

items.text: Rav Yosef's alternative explanation
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef explains Beit Shammai's view based on Rav Yehuda quoting Rav Asi: all silver mentioned in the Torah is Tyrian silver, while rabbinic silver is provincial silver, and the Gemara questions whether this is a general rule.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef offers an alternative explanation for Beit Shammai's view, citing Rav Yehuda quoting Rav Asi that all silver mentioned in the Torah is Tyrian silver, while rabbinic silver is provincial silver.
The Gemara questions whether Rav Yehuda's statement is a general rule applicable to all contexts.

items.text: Derivation of the minimum for oath claims
items.text_en: Derivation of the minimum for oath claims
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the minimum of two silver coins for an oath claim, deriving it from the juxtaposition of "kesef" and "kelim" in the verse, where "kelim" implies two and "kesef" implies a significant item.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by citing the verse for a claim (טענה) and the Mishnah rule that the oath requires two silver coins, then asks why the Mishnah doesn't also require two vessels, given the verse's juxtaposition of 'kesef' and 'kelim'.

items.text: Derivation of the minimum for second tithe redemption
items.text_en: Derivation of the minimum for second tithe redemption
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah that one may redeem a sela of second tithe with smaller coins, deriving from the repetition of "kesef" in the verse that even a perutah suffices.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks about second tithe redemption, citing the verse 'וְצַרְתָּ הַכֶּסֶף בְּיָדְךָ' and the Mishnah that one may redeem a sela with smaller coins, and answers that the repetition of 'כֶּסֶף' and 'הַכֶּסֶף' teaches that even a perutah suffices.

items.text: Derivation of the minimum for consecrated property redemption
items.text_en: Derivation of the minimum for consecrated property redemption
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites Shmuel's ruling that consecrated property worth a maneh can be redeemed with a perutah, deriving this from a verbal analogy (gezerah shavah) between "kesef" in consecration and in tithes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises the case of consecrated property (הקדש), citing the verse 'וְנָתַן הַכֶּסֶף וְקָם לוֹ' and Shmuel's ruling that consecrated property worth a maneh can be redeemed with a perutah.
The Gemara answers that there too, the word 'כֶּסֶף' (kesef) is derived from the word 'כֶּסֶף' in the context of tithes (מעשר) via a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה), allowing redemption with a perutah.

items.text: Betrothal with a perutah and the challenge to Rav Asi
items.text_en: Betrothal with a perutah and the challenge to Rav Asi
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that betrothal is derived from the field of Ephron via a verbal analogy, and the Mishnah states Beit Hillel permits betrothal with a perutah. This challenges Rav Asi, who had earlier limited the minimum, suggesting he follows Beit Shammai.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Asi by noting that betrothal (קידושי אשה) is derived from the field of Ephron via a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה), and the Mishnah states Beit Hillel permits betrothal with a perutah (פרוטה) or its equivalent.
The Gemara objects that Rav Asi's earlier limitation of the minimum betrothal amount would align him with Beit Shammai, contradicting the Mishnah's ruling of Beit Hillel.

items.text: Rav Asi's corrected statement: distinction between Torah and rabbinic coinage
items.text_en: Rav Asi's corrected statement: distinction between Torah and rabbinic coinage
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the challenge by citing Rav Asi's actual statement: all fixed sums of money mentioned in the Torah are in Tzuri coinage, while those of rabbinic origin are in Medina coinage, which is of lesser value.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the challenge by citing Rav Asi's corrected statement: all fixed sums of money mentioned in the Torah are in Tzuri coinage, while those of rabbinic origin are in Medina coinage, which is of lesser value.

items.text: Proof from Mishnah and application to rabbinic fines
items.text_en: Proof from Mishnah and application to rabbinic fines
items.desc_en: The Gemara shows that the Mishnah already teaches that Torah sums are in holy shekels (Tzuri), so Rav Asi's novelty is that rabbinic sums are in Medina coinage, illustrated by the case of one who strikes another, where the sela is actually half a zuz (an istira).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what does this inform us? We already have a Mishnah listing five selahs for the son, thirty for the slave, fifty for the rapist and seducer, one hundred for the defamer — all in holy shekel, in Tyre maneh.
The Gemara explains that Rav Asi's novelty is that rabbinic fines are in Medina coinage, illustrated by the baraita of one who strikes another, where the sela is actually half a zuz (an istira).

items.text: Reish Lakish's explanation of Beit Shammai's reasoning
items.text_en: Reish Lakish's explanation of Beit Shammai's reasoning
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish explains Beit Shammai's position (that betrothal requires at least a dinar) based on Hezekiah's derivation from the verse regarding a maidservant: she reduces her redemption from a dinar down to a perutah, implying the initial payment must be a dinar.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish says: the reasoning of Beit Shammai is like Hezekiah's. Hezekiah said: the verse 'and he shall redeem her' teaches that she deducts from her redemption and goes out.
Hezekiah derives from the verse 'וְהֶפְדָּהּ' (and he shall redeem her) that a maidservant reduces her redemption payment and goes free.
The Gemara objects: if the master gave her a dinar, she reduces from a dinar down to a perutah, but if he gave her only a perutah, can she reduce from a perutah?
The Gemara resolves: perhaps the Torah means that if he gave her a dinar, she reduces to a perutah, but if he gave her a perutah, she does not reduce at all.

items.text: Rejection of the analogy to ייעוד
items.text_en: Rejection of the analogy to ייעוד
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the earlier attempt to derive the laws of kiddushin from the Hebrew maidservant's ייעוד (designation), arguing that the analogy fails because in ייעוד the master may choose not to designate, whereas in kiddushin the woman cannot unilaterally reduce the value.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the analogy to ייעוד (designation of a Hebrew maidservant), arguing that since the master may choose not to designate, any case where the woman cannot unilaterally reduce the value invalidates the sale analogy.

items.text: Beit Shammai's derivation from the Hebrew maidservant
items.text_en: Beit Shammai's derivation from the Hebrew maidservant
items.desc_en: Beit Shammai derive that a woman cannot be acquired with a prutah from the law of the Hebrew maidservant, who is not acquired with a prutah. The Gemara questions why they don't say half a dinar or two prutot, and answers that once removed from a prutah, the standard is a dinar.

sub.desc_en: Beit Shammai derive that a woman cannot be acquired for kiddushin with a prutah, analogizing from the Hebrew maidservant who is not acquired with a prutah.
The Gemara asks why Beit Shammai do not set the minimum at half a dinar or two prutot instead of a full dinar.
The Gemara answers that once the minimum is removed from a prutah, the standard is set at a dinar.

items.text: Rava's explanation for Beit Shammai
items.text_en: Rava's explanation for Beit Shammai
items.desc_en: Rava explains that Beit Shammai's reasoning is to prevent Jewish daughters from being treated as ownerless property, so they require a minimum of a dinar for kiddushin.

sub.desc_en: Rava explains that Beit Shammai's reasoning is to prevent Jewish daughters from being treated as ownerless property, so they require a minimum of a dinar for kiddushin.

items.text: Defining the prutah: Rav Yosef, Abaye, and the dispute over its value
items.text_en: Defining the prutah: Rav Yosef, Abaye, and the dispute over its value
items.desc_en: Beit Hillel allow kiddushin with a prutah. Rav Yosef initially thinks a prutah is any small amount, but Abaye objects citing a baraita that defines a prutah as one-eighth of an Italian issar. The Gemara then discusses conflicting traditions about the prutah's value, and a resolution is offered by an elder who corrects the text of a mishnah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by citing the Mishnah's ruling that Beit Hillel permit kiddushin with a prutah.
Rav Yosef initially thought that a prutah is any small amount (כל דהו).
Abaye objects by citing a baraita that defines a prutah as one-eighth of an Italian issar.
The Gemara raises a possible objection: perhaps the baraita's value applied only in Moses' generation, but now people consider a smaller coin a prutah.
Rav Dimi reports that Rabbi Simai in his generation measured a prutah as one-eighth of an Italian issar, supporting the baraita's value.
Ravin reports that three rabbis measured a prutah as one-sixth of an Italian issar, contradicting the baraita's value.
Rav Yosef questions how a mishnah can say 'more than two thousand' prutot in two sela'im, if the calculation yields fewer than two thousand.

An elder resolves the difficulty by correcting the mishnah's text to read 'close to two thousand' rather than 'more than two thousand', explaining that the actual count (1,536) is close to two thousand.

items.text: Reconciling the conflicting traditions on the prutah
items.text_en: Reconciling the conflicting traditions on the prutah
items.desc_en: Abaye challenges Rav Dimi and Ravin, suggesting they disagree over a tannaitic dispute between the first tanna and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel. Rav Dimi responds that both he and Ravin follow the first tanna, and the discrepancy is due to fluctuations in the value of the issar.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara restates the conflicting traditions of Rav Dimi and Ravin regarding the value of a prutah.
Abaye suggests that Rav Dimi and Ravin are disagreeing over a tannaitic dispute between the first tanna and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.
Rav Dimi responds that both he and Ravin follow the first tanna, and the discrepancy is due to fluctuations in the value of the issar.

items.text: Shmuel's ruling on kiddushin with a date
items.text_en: Shmuel's ruling on kiddushin with a date
items.desc_en: Shmuel rules that if one betroths with a date, even if a kor of dates costs a dinar, she is betrothed, because we are concerned that the date might be worth a prutah in Media. The Gemara reconciles this with the mishnah, distinguishing between definite kiddushin and doubtful kiddushin.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel rules that if one betroths with a date, even if a kor of dates costs a dinar, she is betrothed, because we are concerned that the date might be worth a prutah in Media.
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah (Beit Hillel) requires a prutah or its value, seemingly contradicting Shmuel's concern for a remote possibility.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between definite kiddushin (וודאי) where the value must be certain, and doubtful kiddushin (ספק) where we are concerned for a remote possibility.

items.text: Cases of uncertain value: Rav Shimi bar Chiya and Rav Chisda
items.text_en: Cases of uncertain value: Rav Shimi bar Chiya and Rav Chisda
items.desc_en: Two cases are presented: one where Rav Shimi bar Chiya examines a bundle of branches to see if it is worth a prutah, and another where Rav Chisda examines a kohl-stone. The Gemara notes that Rav Chisda does not accept Shmuel's concern for possible value, and a story about his mother's claim is dismissed.

sub.desc_en: A man betrothed with a bundle of branches; Rav Shimi bar Chiya examines it before Rav to determine if it is worth a פרוטה (the minimum coin).
The Gemara objects: if the bundle is not worth a פרוטה, why is the betrothal invalid? Shmuel said we must be concerned that it might be worth a פרוטה elsewhere.
The Gemara resolves: the case of Rav Shimi bar Chiya involves certain betrothal (קידושי ודאי), whereas Shmuel's statement applies to uncertain betrothal (קידושי ספק).
A man betrothed with a kohl-stone; Rav Chisda estimates its value to determine if it is worth a פרוטה.
The Gemara objects again: if the stone is not worth a פרוטה, why is the betrothal invalid? Shmuel said we must be concerned.
The Gemara explains that Rav Chisda does not accept Shmuel's concern for possible value.
The mother of the man claims the stone was worth a פרוטה on the day of betrothal, but Rav Chisda dismisses her claim, saying she cannot forbid the woman to others.

items.text: Story of Yehudit and Rabbi Chiyya
items.text_en: Story of Yehudit and Rabbi Chiyya
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts a story where Yehudit, wife of Rabbi Chiyya, suffered in childbirth and told her husband that her mother had accepted kiddushin for her when she was a minor. Rabbi Chiyya responded that her mother's action was not binding.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts the story of Yehudit, wife of Rabbi Chiyya, who suffered in childbirth and reported that her mother had accepted kiddushin for her as a minor, to which Rabbi Chiyya responded that her mother's action was not binding.

items.text: Challenge from the Rabbis and Rabbi Chanina's ruling
items.text_en: Challenge from the Rabbis and Rabbi Chanina's ruling
items.desc_en: The Rabbis asked Rav Chisda why the woman is not forbidden, given that there were witnesses who knew she was worth a perutah on that day. The Gemara then cites Rabbi Chanina's ruling that if witnesses are present, she should be forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The Rabbis ask Rav Chisda why the woman is not forbidden, given that witnesses knew she was worth a perutah on that day.

sub.text: Gemara's citation of Rabbi Chanina's ruling
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of Rabbi Chanina's ruling
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Chanina's ruling that if witnesses are present, she should be forbidden.

items.text: Abaye and Rava's objection and the conclusion
items.text_en: Abaye and Rava's objection and the conclusion
items.desc_en: Abaye and Rava did not accept Rav Chisda's reasoning, arguing that if leniency is applied to a captive woman who degrades herself, it should not be applied to a married woman. The Gemara concludes that the Sages distanced themselves from that family, not because of Shmuel's view, but because they held like Abaye and Rava.

sub.desc_en: Abaye and Rava reject Rav Chisda's reasoning, arguing that if leniency is applied to a captive woman who degrades herself, it should not be applied to a married woman.
The Gemara concludes that the Sages distanced themselves from that family not because of Shmuel's view, but because they held like Abaye and Rava.

items.text: Case of kiddushin with a myrtle twig in the market
items.text_en: Case of kiddushin with a myrtle twig in the market
items.desc_en: A man performed kiddushin with a myrtle twig in the market. Rav Acha bar Huna sent a query to Rav Yosef, who responded that the man should be flogged like Rav's ruling and required a get like Shmuel's ruling.

sub.desc_en: The gemara presents a case: a man performed kiddushin with a myrtle twig in the market, and Rav Acha bar Huna sent a query to Rav Yosef asking about the ruling.
Rav Yosef responds that the man should be flogged like Rav's ruling and required to give a get like Shmuel's ruling.

items.text: List of cases where Rav flogs
items.text_en: List of cases where Rav flogs
items.desc_en: The Gemara lists several cases where Rav would flog a person, including one who performs kiddushin in the market, one who performs kiddushin through intercourse, one who performs kiddushin without prior engagement, and others. It also discusses a case of a groom who passed by his father-in-law's house, where Rav Sheshet flogged him because his mother-in-law was living there.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara lists the first three cases where Rav flogs: one who performs kiddushin in the market, one who performs kiddushin through intercourse, and one who performs kiddushin without prior engagement.

The Gemara lists additional cases where Rav flogs: one who nullifies a get, one who gives a prior declaration about a get, one who causes distress to a rabbinic messenger, and one upon whom a ban has been in effect for thirty days.
The Gemara questions whether the rule about a groom living in his father-in-law's house applies only to dwelling but not to merely passing by.
The Gemara objects by citing a case where a groom merely passed by his father-in-law's house and Rav Sheshet flogged him.
The Gemara resolves that in that case, his mother-in-law was living there, so it was considered dwelling.

items.text: Nehardeans' alternative version
items.text_en: Nehardeans' alternative version
items.desc_en: The Nehardeans said that Rav only flogs for kiddushin through intercourse without prior engagement, and some say even with prior engagement due to licentiousness.

sub.desc_en: The Nehardeans report that Rav only flogs for kiddushin through intercourse (קידושי ביאה) without prior engagement (שידוכי).
Some say that Rav even flogs for kiddushin through intercourse with prior engagement, due to licentiousness (פריצותא).

items.text: Case of kiddushin with a chip of wood and Rava's ruling on silence
items.text_en: Case of kiddushin with a chip of wood and Rava's ruling on silence
items.desc_en: A man performed kiddushin with a chip of wood, and when told it was not worth a perutah, he said it should be sanctified with four zuz that were in it. The woman took it and was silent. Rava ruled that silence after the giving of money is meaningless, citing a baraita about a deposit and subsequent kiddushin.

sub.desc_en: A man performed kiddushin with a chip of wood; when told it was not worth a perutah, he said it should be sanctified with four zuz that were in it, and the woman took it and was silent.
Rava ruled that silence after the giving of money is meaningless, citing a baraita about a deposit and subsequent kiddushin.

Rava cites a baraita: if a man said to a woman 'deposit this sela' and later said 'be betrothed to me with it,' during the giving of money she is betrothed; after the giving, if she consented she is betrothed, if not she is not.
The Gemara asks: what does 'consented' and 'did not consent' mean in the baraita, suggesting that if it means verbal consent, then the beginning of the baraita implies something else.

items.text: Gemara's inference from the baraita about silence after money
items.text_en: Gemara's inference from the baraita about silence after money
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the baraita that if she is silent after the money is given, it is not kiddushin, because she can claim she took the money as her own. This is based on the distinction between 'willing' (saying yes) and 'not willing' (being silent).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the baraita's inference: if she says 'no' after receiving money, how could it be kiddushin? It concludes that 'willing' means saying 'yes' and 'not willing' means silence, proving that silence after money is meaningless.

items.text: Objection from Pum Nahara and resolution by Rav Aḥai
items.text_en: Objection from Pum Nahara and resolution by Rav Aḥai
items.desc_en: An objection is raised in the name of Rav Huna bar Yehoshua: in the baraita, the money was given as a deposit, so she feared liability, but here it is given as kiddushin, so if she didn't want it she would throw it away. Rav Aḥai counters that not all women know the law; she might still fear liability. Rav Aḥa bar Rav then sends a query to Ravina, who replies that they haven't heard this teaching of Rav Huna bar Yehoshua, but those who have should be concerned.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Yehoshua objects that the baraita's case of a deposit is different from kiddushin, since a woman who does not want kiddushin would simply throw the money away.
Rav Aḥai counters that not all women know the law, so she might still fear liability for the money even in kiddushin.
Rav Aḥa bar Rav sends a query to Ravina asking about the ruling in this case.
Ravina replies that they have not heard Rav Huna bar Yehoshua's teaching, but those who have should be concerned.

items.text: Story of the woman selling jewelry and Rav Naḥman's ruling
items.text_en: Story of the woman selling jewelry and Rav Naḥman's ruling
items.desc_en: A story is told of a woman selling jewelry; a man snatched a piece and said, 'If I give it to you, will you be betrothed to me?' She took it and was silent. Rav Naḥman ruled that she can say, 'Yes, I took it, but I took what is mine.'

sub.text: Story about a woman selling jewelry
sub.text_en: Story about a woman selling jewelry
sub.desc_en: A story is brought: a man snatched a jewel from a woman, and when he offered to return it as kiddushin, she was silent; Rav Nachman ruled she can claim she took it as her own.
Rav Naḥman ruled that she can say, 'Yes, I took it, but I took what is mine.'

items.text: Rava's objection from the Mishnah about robbery
items.text_en: Rava's objection from the Mishnah about robbery
items.desc_en: Rava objects to Rav Naḥman from a Mishnah: if a man betroths a woman with stolen or robbed property, or if he snatches a sela from her hand and betroths her, she is betrothed. The Gemara answers that there it is a case where he had previously courted her.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects from a baraita that says if he snatched a sela from her hand and betrothed her, she is betrothed; Rav Nachman answers that case is where he had previously courted her.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah's case is where he had previously courted her (שידך), distinguishing it from the present case.

items.text: Proof from a baraita distinguishing between courted and not courted
items.text_en: Proof from a baraita distinguishing between courted and not courted
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita to prove the distinction between a case where he courted her and where he did not. The baraita discusses a man who says to a woman, 'Take this sela which I owe you,' and then says, 'Be betrothed to me with it.' If she is silent after taking the money, she is not betrothed because she can claim she took what was hers. The Gemara then resolves the contradiction with the Mishnah about robbery by saying that case is where he courted her.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for a source that distinguishes between a case where he courted her (שדיך) and where he did not, and cites a baraita.

The Gemara questions the meaning of 'רצתה' (willing) and 'לא רצתה' (unwilling) in the baraita, arguing that if they mean verbal consent or refusal, silence would imply betrothal, contradicting the baraita.
The Gemara explains that 'רצתה' means she said 'yes', and 'לא רצתה' means she was silent, and she is not betrothed because she can claim she took what was already hers.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction with the Mishnah about robbery by concluding that the Mishnah's case is where he courted her (שדיך), while the baraita's case is where he did not court her (לא שדיך).

items.text: Rabbi Asi's teaching on acquisition of land with less than a perutah
items.text_en: Rabbi Asi's teaching on acquisition of land with less than a perutah
items.desc_en: When Rabbi Asi died, the rabbis entered to arrange his teachings. Rabbi Yaakov said in the name of Rabbi Asi quoting Rabbi Mani: Just as a woman is not acquired for less than a perutah, so too land is not acquired for less than a perutah. They objected from a baraita that says land is acquired for less than a perutah. He answered that the baraita refers to acquisition through exchange (kinyan halipin), where a vessel can acquire even if it is worth less than a perutah.

sub.desc_en: When Rabbi Asi died, the rabbis entered to arrange his teachings, and Rabbi Yaakov reported a tradition from Rabbi Asi in the name of Rabbi Mani, comparing acquisition of land to acquisition of a woman requiring at least a perutah.
The rabbis objected from a baraita that explicitly states land is acquired for less than a perutah, contradicting Rabbi Asi's statement.

Rabbi Yaakov resolves the objection by explaining that the baraita refers specifically to kinyan halipin (acquisition through exchange), where a vessel can acquire land even if it is worth less than a perutah.

items.text: Discussion on the severity of those who are not expert in gittin and kiddushin
items.text_en: Discussion on the severity of those who are not expert in gittin and kiddushin
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the statement of Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel: Whoever is not expert in the laws of gittin and kiddushin should not engage in them. Rabbi Asi in the name of Rabbi Yoḥanan says they are more severe than the generation of the flood, as it is written 'Swearing, lying, murder, stealing, and adultery have broken out, and bloodshed follows bloodshed.' The Gemara explains that this refers to those who have children from other men's wives, and the punishment extends even to the fish of the sea, unlike the flood. The Gemara then questions whether all these sins must be committed together, and answers that the land mourns because of the oath alone.

sub.text: Gemara's citation of Rav Yehuda in name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of Rav Yehuda in name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts the statement of Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel: one who is not expert in the laws of gittin and kiddushin should not engage in them.

sub.text: Rabbi Asi in the name of Rabbi Yoḥanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Asi in the name of Rabbi Yoḥanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Asi in the name of Rabbi Yoḥanan states that those who are not expert are more severe than the generation of the flood, citing the verse about oaths, lying, murder, theft, adultery, and bloodshed.
Rav Yosef explains the verse as referring to those who have children from other men's wives, adding transgression upon transgression.

sub.text: Gemara's citation of the second verse and comparison
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of the second verse and comparison
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the continuation of the verse stating that even fish of the sea perish, unlike the generation of the flood where only land creatures died.
The Gemara asks: perhaps the punishment applies only when one commits all those sins together?
The Gemara rejects that possibility, citing the verse that the land mourns because of the oath (false oath) alone.
The Gemara asks: perhaps the oath stands alone, and the other sins are separate causes for punishment?

items.text: Gemara's initial objection
items.text_en: Gemara's initial objection
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects to a previous statement by noting that the verse says "פרצו" (they broke out) not "ופרצו" (and they broke out).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the verse uses the word 'פרצו' (they broke out) without the conjunctive 'ו', not 'ופרצו' (and they broke out).

items.text: Dispute about lien being biblical or not
items.text_en: Dispute about lien being biblical or not
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel and Rabbi Asi citing Rabbi Yochanan argue whether a woman's sin-offering is brought by heirs if she died after setting it aside, reflecting a dispute about whether a lien is biblical (d'oraita) or not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a Mishnah about a woman who brought her sin-offering and died, stating that heirs bring her burnt-offering.
Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel limits the Mishnah to a case where the woman set aside the offering while alive, implying that a lien is not biblical (שיעבודא לאו דאורייתא).
Rabbi Asi citing Rabbi Yochanan disagrees, ruling that heirs bring the offering even if she did not set it aside while alive, indicating that a lien is biblical (שיעבודא דאורייתא).

items.text: Need for both disputes
items.text_en: Need for both disputes
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the same dispute appears elsewhere regarding oral loans, but explains that both cases are necessary to avoid assuming one side would concede in the other case.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the dispute about oral loans is repeated here, since Rav and Shmuel already stated one position and Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish the opposite.
The Gemara explains that both cases are necessary: without both, one might assume that Shmuel would concede to Rabbi Yochanan in the other case, or vice versa.

items.text: Rav Pappa's ruling
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's ruling
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa rules that an oral loan is collected from heirs (because the lien is biblical) but not from purchasers (because it lacks publicity).

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa rules that an oral loan is collected from heirs because the lien is biblical (שיעבודא דאורייתא), but not from purchasers because it lacks publicity (לית ליה קלא).

items.text: Derivation that death of husband acquires the wife
items.text_en: Derivation that death of husband acquires the wife
items.desc_en: The Gemara seeks a biblical source for the mishnah's statement that a wife is acquired through her husband's death. It rejects several attempts (from logic, yevama, widow to high priest) and finally proves it from the verse "פן ימות במלחמה" with a gezeirah shavah linking death to divorce.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah states that a wife is acquired (freed) by a get or by the husband's death.
The gemara notes that the get is derived from the verse, but asks: from where do we derive that the husband's death acquires the wife?
The gemara proposes a logical answer: the one who forbade her (the husband) also permits her (through death).
The gemara objects: by that logic, forbidden relations (עריות) would also be permitted by death, but they are not.
The gemara tries to derive from the yevama: a childless widow is forbidden, implying that one with children is permitted through the husband's death.
The gemara objects: perhaps a childless widow is forbidden to everyone but permitted to the yavam, while one with children is forbidden to everyone.

sub.text: Gemara's third attempted answer (widow to high priest)
sub.text_en: Gemara's third attempted answer (widow to high priest)
sub.desc_en: The gemara tries to derive from the widow to a high priest: a widow is forbidden to a high priest, implying she is permitted to a common priest through the husband's death.
The gemara objects: perhaps the widow is forbidden to a high priest by a negative commandment, but to everyone else by a positive commandment, which does not fully permit her.
Rav Ashi resolves the derivation from the verse 'פן ימות במלחמה' with a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) linking death to divorce, showing that death fully permits her like a get.

items.text: Beginning of derivation for yevama through intercourse
items.text_en: Beginning of derivation for yevama through intercourse
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to ask how a yevama is acquired through intercourse, quoting a verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks from where it is derived that a yevama (יְבָמָה) is acquired through intercourse (בִּיאָה), and begins to cite a verse.

items.text: Derivation of yibbum through bi'ah alone
items.text_en: Derivation of yibbum through bi'ah alone
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the verse 'yevamah yavo aleha' might imply that money or a document can effect yibbum like bi'ah. It rejects this by citing a baraisa that the word 'veyibmah' teaches that only bi'ah completes yibbum, not money or a document. It then suggests 'veyibmah' might mean he may force her, but concludes it teaches both.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the verse 'יְבָמָהּ יָבֹא עָלֶיהָ וּלְקָחָהּ לוֹ לְאִשָּׁה' might imply that money or a document could effect yibbum like bi'ah.
The Gemara rejects the possibility by citing a baraisa that the word 'וְיִבְּמָהּ' teaches that only bi'ah completes yibbum, not money or a document.
The Gemara suggests that 'וְיִבְּמָהּ' might mean he may force her to perform yibbum against her will.
The Gemara resolves that the extra letter in 'וְיִבְּמָהּ' teaches both that only bi'ah completes yibbum and that it is performed against her will.

items.text: Derivation of chalitzah from the verse
items.text_en: Derivation of chalitzah from the verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives chalitzah from the verse 'venikra shemo beYisrael beit chalutz hana'al', indicating that once he removes the shoe, she is permitted to all Israel. It then addresses a potential use of the word 'Yisrael' for a court of Israelites, citing a teaching of Rav Shmuel bar Yehudah and a story of Rabbi Tarfon, concluding that the word 'shemo' teaches the requirement to say 'chalutz hana'al'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks the source for חליצה (the shoe-removal ceremony) and cites the verse 'ונקרא שמו בישראל בית חלוץ הנעל' to show that once he removes the shoe, she is permitted to all Israel.

The Gemara objects that the word 'ישראל' is needed for the teaching of Rav Shmuel bar Yehudah that the ceremony must be performed in a court of Israelites, not gentiles, and resolves that two instances of 'בישראל' are written in the verse.

The Gemara further objects that the word 'ישראל' is needed for the teaching of Rabbi Yehudah about the story of Rabbi Tarfon, where the court says 'חלוץ הנעל' twice, and resolves that this requirement is derived from the word 'שמו'.

items.text: Derivation of release through yavam's death via a fortiori
items.text_en: Derivation of release through yavam's death via a fortiori
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives that the yevamah is released through the yavam's death using a kal vachomer: if an ordinary married woman, who is subject to the death penalty, is released by her husband's death, then a yevamah, who is only subject to a negative commandment, should certainly be released. It addresses an objection that an ordinary married woman can also be released by a get, but notes that a yevamah can be released by chalitzah. Rav Ashi resolves the objection by noting that in both cases, the one who forbids her also permits her.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks the source for release through the yavam's death and proposes a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument): if an ordinary married woman, who is subject to death by strangulation, is released by her husband's death, then a yevamah, who is only subject to a negative commandment, should certainly be released.

The Gemara objects that the comparison is flawed: an ordinary married woman can also be released by a גט (bill of divorce), which a yevamah cannot, but it notes that a yevamah can be released by חליצה (the shoe-removal ceremony).

Rav Ashi resolves the objection by noting that in both cases, the one who forbids her also permits her: the husband forbids and permits the married woman, and the yavam forbids and permits the yevamah.

items.text: Rejection of applying chalitzah to an ordinary married woman and get to a yevamah
items.text_en: Rejection of applying chalitzah to an ordinary married woman and get to a yevamah
items.desc_en: The Gemara proposes a kal vachomer that an ordinary married woman should be released by chalitzah, but a verse 'sefer keritut' teaches that only a document cuts her off. It then proposes that a yevamah should be released by a get, but the word 'kachah' indicates a restriction, preventing this.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument) that an ordinary married woman should be released by חליצה (chalitzah), since a יבמה (yevamah) who cannot be released by a גט (get) is released by חליצה, so an ordinary married woman who can be released by a גט should certainly be released by חליצה.
The Gemara rejects the proposal by citing the verse 'ספר כריתות' (a book of severance), which teaches that only a written document severs the marriage bond, and nothing else does.

The Gemara proposes a reciprocal kal vachomer that a יבמה (yevamah) should be released by a גט (get), since an ordinary married woman who cannot be released by חליצה is released by a גט, so a יבמה who can be released by חליצה should certainly be released by a גט.
The Gemara rejects this proposal by citing the word 'ככה' (thus), which indicates a restriction, teaching that the יבמה is released only through חליצה and not through a גט.

items.text: Challenge that a restriction does not preclude a kal vachomer
items.text_en: Challenge that a restriction does not preclude a kal vachomer
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the previous answer by noting that even where there is a restriction, a kal vachomer can be applied, as seen with Yom Kippur where the word 'chukah' is written, yet a baraisa uses a kal vachomer to teach that the lot designates the goat for a sin-offering, not the name. This shows that without the verse's exclusion, the kal vachomer would be applied despite the restriction.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the principle that a restriction (עיכובא) precludes a kal vachomer, citing Yom Kippur where the word 'חוקה' is written yet a kal vachomer is applied.
A baraita is cited establishing that the lot designates the goat as a sin-offering, not the name, implying a kal vachomer was considered.
The baraita presents the kal vachomer: if where the lot did not sanctify, the name sanctified, then where the lot sanctified, the name should certainly sanctify.
