The Gemara concludes that only because the verse explicitly excludes the kal vachomer would it not be applied, despite the restriction of 'חוקה', showing that without such exclusion, the kal vachomer would be applied.

items.text: Limitations on the shoe for chalitzah
items.text_en: Limitations on the shoe for chalitzah
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially derives from the word 'lah' that chalitzah is only with a shoe, not other items. It then addresses a potential use of 'lah' for the sake of the act itself, but notes two instances of 'lah'. It then derives from 'na'al' that only a shoe is valid, not other items. It further explains that 'na'alo' teaches that it must be his own shoe, and a baraisa expands to include any shoe, with exceptions for shoes that are too large or too small.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara initially derives from the double 'לָהּ' that the shoe is for the yevama alone, not for her co-wife.
The Gemara questions whether 'לָהּ' might instead indicate that the chalitzah must be performed for its own sake (לשמה).
The Gemara answers that two instances of 'לָהּ' are written, allowing one for each derivation.
The Gemara objects that one 'לָהּ' is still needed for לשמה (for its own sake) and the other for excluding the co-wife, leaving no room for the initial derivation.
The Gemara resolves by deriving from 'נָעַל' that only a shoe is valid for chalitzah, not other items.
The Gemara questions whether 'נָעַל' is needed for this derivation, as it might be required for a baraisa that teaches about the shoe belonging to the yavam.
The baraisa teaches that 'נַעַל' repeated includes any shoe, while 'נַעֲלוֹ' limits it to a shoe fit for the yavam, excluding those too large or too small.

items.text: Concluding remark on the previous daf's discussion
items.text_en: Concluding remark on the previous daf's discussion
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the extra letter in 'הנעל' teaches two laws: that the shoe must be of a certain type and that the ceremony applies to a footless person.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the extra letter in 'הנעל' teaches two laws: that the shoe must be of a certain type and that the ceremony applies to a footless person.

items.text: Mishnah: Acquisition and release of a Hebrew slave
items.text_en: Mishnah: Acquisition and release of a Hebrew slave
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the ways a Hebrew slave is acquired (money, document) and the ways he goes free (years, Jubilee, deduction of money). It adds that a Hebrew maidservant has an additional way to go free (signs of puberty), and a pierced slave is acquired by piercing and goes free by Jubilee or the master's death.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the methods of acquisition and release for a Hebrew slave, with special rules for a Hebrew maidservant and a pierced slave.

items.text: Derivation of acquisition by money for a Hebrew slave
items.text_en: Derivation of acquisition by money for a Hebrew slave
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source that a Hebrew slave is acquired by money. It cites a verse for a slave sold to a non-Jew, then derives for a slave sold to an Israelite by comparing a Hebrew maidservant to a Hebrew slave via a verbal analogy.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source that a Hebrew slave is acquired by money.
The Gemara cites a verse for a Hebrew slave sold to a non-Jew, showing he is acquired by money.
The Gemara derives for a Hebrew maidservant sold to an Israelite that she is acquired by money, from the verse 'והפדה'.
The Gemara derives for a Hebrew slave sold to an Israelite by comparing a Hebrew maidservant to a Hebrew slave via a verbal analogy (הקיש) from the verse 'כי ימכר לך אחיך העברי או העבריה'.

items.text: Source for a self-seller being acquired by money
items.text_en: Source for a self-seller being acquired by money
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source that one who sells himself is acquired by money. It suggests a verbal analogy 'שכיר שכיר', then notes that for those who do not use that analogy, another verse is used to teach that the upper case (self-seller) is learned from the lower case (court-seller).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source that a self-seller is acquired by money, having found the source for a court-seller.
The Gemara suggests a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) from the word 'שָׂכִיר' (hired worker) to derive the law for a self-seller.
The Gemara objects that this works only for one who accepts the verbal analogy, but what about the Tanna who does not?

The Gemara provides an alternative source: the verse 'וְכִי תַשִּׂיג' (when he becomes impoverished) adds to the earlier context, teaching that the upper case (self-seller) is learned from the lower case (court-seller).

items.text: Identifying the Tanna who does not use 'שכיר שכיר'
items.text_en: Identifying the Tanna who does not use 'שכיר שכיר'
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the Tanna who does not use the 'שכיר שכיר' analogy as the first Tanna in a beraita who distinguishes between a self-seller and a court-seller in several laws. Rabbi Elazar disagrees and equates them. The Gemara suggests that the dispute is about the use of 'שכיר שכיר'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who is the Tanna who does not use the 'שָׂכִיר' 'שָׂכִיר' analogy, and identifies him as the first Tanna in the following beraita.

The beraita lists distinctions between a self-seller and a court-seller: the self-seller is sold for six years or more, is not pierced, receives no gift, and his master does not give him a Canaanite maidservant, while the court-seller is sold only for six years, is pierced, receives a gift, and his master gives him a maidservant.
Rabbi Elazar equates the self-seller and court-seller in all these laws.
The Gemara suggests that the dispute is precisely about the use of the 'שָׂכִיר' 'שָׂכִיר' analogy: the first Tanna does not use it, while Rabbi Elazar does.

items.text: Rejection: Everyone uses 'שכיר שכיר'; dispute is over verses
items.text_en: Rejection: Everyone uses 'שכיר שכיר'; dispute is over verses
items.desc_en: Rav Tavyomi in the name of Abaye rejects the previous suggestion, stating that all agree on the 'שכיר שכיר' analogy. The dispute is over the interpretation of the verse 'ועבדך שש שנים' and other verses, which the first Tanna uses to limit the self-seller's term and piercing, while Rabbi Elazar interprets them differently.

sub.text: Rav Tavyomi in the name of Abaye
sub.text_en: Rav Tavyomi in the name of Abaye
sub.desc_en: Rav Tavyomi in the name of Abaye rejects the previous suggestion, stating that all agree on the 'שכיר שכיר' (hired worker) analogy, and the dispute is over the interpretation of a specific verse.

sub.text: Rav Tavyomi in the name of Abaye
sub.text_en: Rav Tavyomi in the name of Abaye
sub.desc_en: Explains the first Tanna's position: the verse 'ועבדך שש שנים' (and he shall serve you six years) excludes the self-seller from the six-year limit, allowing him to be sold for more than six years.

sub.text: Rav Tavyomi in the name of Abaye
sub.text_en: Rav Tavyomi in the name of Abaye
sub.desc_en: Explains Rabbi Elazar's interpretation: the word 'ועבדך' (and he shall serve you) teaches that the service is for the master, not for the master's heir.

Explains the first Tanna's position on piercing: the verse 'ורצע אדניו את אזנו במרצע' (and his master shall pierce his ear with an awl) excludes the self-seller from piercing, as it refers only to the ear of one sold by the court.

items.text: Rejection of gezerah shavah and alternative derivations
items.text_en: Rejection of gezerah shavah and alternative derivations
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the use of the gezerah shavah for the ear, and offers alternative scriptural derivations for the requirement that the ear be the right one, and for excluding a female slave from piercing.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the other Tanna (who rejects the גזירה שוה (verbal analogy)) derives that the piercing must be on the right ear, and cites Rabbi Eliezer's baraita that uses the גזירה שוה from the leper's ear.
The Gemara asks why the verse says 'אזנו' (his ear) rather than just 'אוזן' (ear), implying a specific ear.
The Gemara answers that 'אזנו' excludes a female slave from the piercing requirement.
The Gemara asks why the other Tanna does not derive the exclusion of a female slave from the verse 'ואם יאמר העבד' (the servant, not the maidservant).
The Gemara answers that the verse 'ואם יאמר העבד' is needed to teach that the piercing applies only when he is already a servant, not before.
The Gemara asks why the other Tanna does not derive the exclusion of a female slave from the repetition of 'עבד' and 'העבד'.
The Gemara answers that the other Tanna does not expound the repetition of 'עבד' and 'העבד'.

items.text: Reason of the first Tanna regarding grant for self-sold slave
items.text_en: Reason of the first Tanna regarding grant for self-sold slave
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the first Tanna holds that a self-sold slave does not receive a grant: the verse "ha'aneik ta'anik lo" excludes him. It then discusses alternative interpretations of "lo" and the opinion of Rabbi Natan.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the first Tanna holds that a self-sold slave does not receive a grant, and answers that the verse 'הַעֲנֵיק תַּעֲנִיק לוֹ' (you shall surely grant him) excludes the self-sold slave.
The Gemara objects that the word 'לוֹ' (to him) is needed to exclude heirs or creditors, not the self-sold slave, and then refines the interpretation to exclude creditors.
The Gemara cites Rabbi Natan's principle that a creditor can collect from a debtor's debtor, which supports the interpretation that 'לוֹ' excludes the self-sold slave from the grant.
The Gemara concludes that the word 'לוֹ' comes to exclude the self-sold slave, and notes that the other opinion does not accept Rabbi Natan's principle.

items.text: Reason of the first Tanna regarding the maidservant for self-sold slave
items.text_en: Reason of the first Tanna regarding the maidservant for self-sold slave
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the first Tanna holds that a self-sold slave does not receive a Canaanite maidservant: the verse "im adonav yiten lo ishah" excludes him. It then discusses alternative interpretations and the derivation from "ki mishneh sachar sachir".

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the reason of the first Tanna who holds that a self-sold slave does not receive a Canaanite maidservant.
The Gemara answers that the verse 'אִם אֲדֹנָיו יִתֶּן לוֹ אִשָּׁה' (if his master gives him a wife) excludes the self-sold slave, applying only to one sold by the court.
The Gemara objects: how does the other Tanna (who grants the maidservant to a self-sold slave) interpret this verse?
The Gemara answers that the other Tanna interprets 'לוֹ' (to him) to mean even against his will, i.e., the master may give a maidservant even to a self-sold slave against his will.

The Gemara cites a baraita that derives from the verse 'כִּי מִשְׁנֶה שְׂכַר שָׂכִיר' (for he is double the hire of a laborer) that a Hebrew slave works both day and night, implying the master provides a maidservant for companionship.
The Gemara objects: how can a Hebrew slave work both day and night, given the verse 'כִּי טוֹב לוֹ עִמָּךְ' (for it is good for him with you) implying he lives with his master?

Rabbi Yitzchak resolves that the verse 'כִּי טוֹב לוֹ עִמָּךְ' (for it is good for him with you) teaches that the master provides food and drink, and from this it is derived that the master gives him a Canaanite maidservant for companionship at night.

The Gemara concludes that the other Tanna (who grants the maidservant to a self-sold slave) learns from the verse 'אִם אֲדֹנָיו יִתֶּן לוֹ אִשָּׁה' that even against his will the master gives a maidservant, and the derivation from 'כִּי מִשְׁנֶה' would only apply voluntarily, so the verse teaches it is compulsory.

items.text: Identifying the Tanna who does not learn "sachir" "sachir"
items.text_en: Identifying the Tanna who does not learn "sachir" "sachir"
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the Tanna who does not learn the analogy of "sachir" "sachir" is Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, based on a baraita. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak objects, arguing that even one who learns the analogy needs the verse to teach that a court-sold slave is not penalized.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which Tanna does not learn the verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) of 'שכיר' 'שכיר', and suggests it is Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov based on a baraita that shows he needs a separate verse for a court-sold slave.

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak objects that even one who learns the verbal analogy needs the verse to teach that a court-sold slave, who committed a crime, is not penalized by losing the benefit of the analogy.

items.text: Exegesis of the verses regarding the pierced slave and the Jubilee
items.text_en: Exegesis of the verses regarding the pierced slave and the Jubilee
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the baraita about the pierced slave who is released by the Jubilee, deriving from the word "ish" that piercing applies only to men. It then explains why both the case of a court-sold slave and a pierced slave are written, and why both "veshavtem" and "le'olam" are needed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what baraita is referenced by the statement that the pierced slave is already mentioned, and cites the baraita that derives from the word 'איש' (man) that piercing applies only to men.
The Gemara explains why both the case of a court-sold slave and a pierced slave are written, to prevent a leniency in one case from being inferred from the other.
The Gemara explains why both 'ושבתם' (and you shall return) and 'לעולם' (forever) are needed, to teach that the pierced slave goes free at the Jubilee and not literally forever.

items.text: Identifying the Tanna as Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
items.text_en: Identifying the Tanna as Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the Tanna who does not learn the analogy of "sachir" "sachir" is Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, citing a baraita.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the Tanna who does not learn the analogy of "sachir" "sachir" is Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, citing a baraita.

items.text: Rabbi's exposition of 'in these'
items.text_en: Rabbi's exposition of 'in these'
items.desc_en: Rabbi interprets the verse 'If he is not redeemed in these' to mean that the Hebrew maidservant is redeemed only through the specified means (money or documents) and not through the six-year term. He refutes a possible kal vachomer argument that would allow redemption through the six-year term by citing the limiting word 'in these'.

sub.desc_en: רבי (Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi) states that the Hebrew slave sold to a gentile is redeemed only through relatives, not after six years.
רבי (Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi) rejects a possible קל וחומר (a fortiori inference) that would allow redemption after six years, citing the limiting phrase 'באלה' (in these).

items.text: Gemara's question and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's answer
items.text_en: Gemara's question and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Rabbi did not derive the law from a gezerah shavah of 'hired servant' from Leviticus 25:40. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak answers that the verse 'he shall redeem him' (Leviticus 25:49) indicates that redemption applies only to this specific case (the Hebrew maidservant) and not to others, thus preventing the gezerah shavah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi did not derive the law from a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) of 'שָׂכִיר' (hired worker) from Leviticus 25:40, instead using an a fortiori inference.

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak answers that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi does derive the גזירה שווה (verbal analogy), but the verse 'יִגְאָלֶנּוּ' (he shall redeem him) in Leviticus 25:49 limits redemption to this specific case and not to others, preventing the analogy from applying.

items.text: Introduction of the Tannaitic dispute
items.text_en: Introduction of the Tannaitic dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the Tannaim who disagree with Rabbi: Rabbi Yose HaGelili and Rabbi Akiva. A baraita presents their interpretations of the verse 'He shall not be redeemed in these' (Leviticus 25:50): Rabbi Yose HaGelili says 'in these' refers to freedom, but by others it leads to servitude; Rabbi Akiva says 'in these' refers to servitude, but by others it leads to freedom.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which Tanna disagrees with Rabbi, and answers that it is Rabbi Yose HaGelili and Rabbi Akiva.
A baraita is cited presenting the interpretations of Rabbi Yose HaGelili and Rabbi Akiva regarding the verse 'He shall not be redeemed in these'.
Rabbi Yose HaGelili states that 'in these' refers to freedom, but redemption by others leads to servitude.
Rabbi Akiva states that 'in these' refers to servitude, but redemption by others leads to freedom.

items.text: Scriptural basis for Rabbi Yose HaGelili and Rabbi Akiva
items.text_en: Scriptural basis for Rabbi Yose HaGelili and Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the scriptural reasoning of Rabbi Yose HaGelili and Rabbi Akiva. Rabbi Yose HaGelili reads the verse as 'If he is not redeemed in these, but by another, he shall go out in the Jubilee year,' implying that redemption by others leads to freedom. Rabbi Akiva reads it as 'If he is not redeemed, but in these, he shall go out in the Jubilee year,' implying that redemption by these (relatives) leads to freedom. The Gemara questions Rabbi Yose HaGelili's reading since the verse does not say 'but in these'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural reasoning of Rabbi Yose HaGelili, and presents his reading of the verse: 'If he is not redeemed in these' — but by another — 'he shall go out in the Jubilee year.'
Rabbi Akiva reads the verse differently: 'If he is not redeemed' — but — 'in these' — 'he shall go out in the Jubilee year,' implying that redemption by relatives leads to freedom.
The Gemara objects to Rabbi Yose HaGelili's reading, noting that the verse does not actually say 'but in these' (אֶלָּא בְּאֵלֶּה).

items.text: Dispute over the principle of 'the verse is interpreted by its context'
items.text_en: Dispute over the principle of 'the verse is interpreted by its context'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the dispute is actually based on a different verse: 'Or his uncle or his uncle's son shall redeem him' (Leviticus 25:49), which includes redemption by relatives, redemption by oneself, and redemption by others. Rabbi Yose HaGelili holds that the verse is interpreted by what precedes it, linking redemption by relatives to redemption by oneself (which leads to freedom). Rabbi Akiva holds that the verse is interpreted by what follows it, linking redemption by others to redemption by oneself (which leads to freedom).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the actual verse of dispute: Leviticus 25:49, which includes three types of redemption — by relatives, by oneself, and by others.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yose HaGelili's position
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yose HaGelili's position
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yose HaGelili holds that the verse is interpreted by its context (מקרא נדרש לפניו), linking redemption by relatives to redemption by oneself, so both lead to freedom.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Akiva's position
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Akiva's position
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva holds that the verse is interpreted by what follows it (מקרא נדרש לאחריו), linking redemption by others to redemption by oneself, so both lead to freedom.

items.text: Refinement of the dispute: the role of 'in these' and logical reasoning
items.text_en: Refinement of the dispute: the role of 'in these' and logical reasoning
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the need for the word 'in these' if the dispute is based on contextual interpretation. It then explains that without 'in these', one might think both interpretations apply, leading to all redemption being for freedom. The Gemara then clarifies that the dispute is actually based on logical reasoning: Rabbi Yose HaGelili argues that redemption by others should lead to servitude, otherwise people would refrain from redeeming him; Rabbi Akiva argues that redemption by relatives should lead to servitude, otherwise the slave would repeatedly sell himself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if the dispute is based on contextual interpretation (מקרא נדרש לפניו/לאחריו), why is the word 'באלה' (in these) needed at all? Without it, one might think both interpretations apply and all redemption leads to freedom.
The Gemara objects: if so, the original difficulty returns; therefore, the dispute is actually based on logical reasoning (סברא), not on the word 'באלה'.

The Gemara explains the logical reasoning: Rabbi Yose HaGelili holds that redemption by others leads to servitude, otherwise people would refrain from redeeming him; Rabbi Akiva holds that redemption by relatives leads to servitude, otherwise the slave would repeatedly sell himself.

items.text: The Sages' ruling and identification of the Sages as Rabbi
items.text_en: The Sages' ruling and identification of the Sages as Rabbi
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba quotes Rabbi Yochanan stating that the dispute is between Rabbi Yose HaGelili and Rabbi Akiva, but the Sages say that all redemption leads to freedom. The Gemara identifies these Sages as Rabbi himself, who uses the word 'in these' for a different exposition and interprets the verse by both its preceding and following context. The Gemara then asks what Rabbi does with the phrase 'and he shall go out in the Jubilee year', and answers that it is needed for a teaching.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that the dispute is between Rabbi Yose HaGelili and Rabbi Akiva, but the Sages say that all redemption leads to freedom.

The Gemara asks who these Sages are and answers that they are Rabbi himself, who uses the word 'in these' for a different exposition and interprets the verse by both its preceding and following context.
The Gemara asks what Rabbi does with the phrase 'and he shall go out in the Jubilee year'.
The Gemara answers that it is needed for a teaching as cited in a baraita.

items.text: Clarifying the scope of 'a gentile under your hand'
items.text_en: Clarifying the scope of 'a gentile under your hand'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the verse refers only to a gentile under one's authority, concluding that it must be so, as otherwise there is no way to act upon it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the verse refers specifically to a gentile under one's authority or to any gentile.
The Gemara answers that the verse must refer only to a gentile under one's authority, since otherwise there is no way to act upon it.

items.text: Deriving acquisition by bill of sale for a Hebrew maidservant
items.text_en: Deriving acquisition by bill of sale for a Hebrew maidservant
items.desc_en: Ulla derives that a Hebrew maidservant is acquired by a bill of sale through a comparison to a wife. The Gemara then examines the dispute between Rav Huna and Rav Chisda over who writes the bill, and Rav Acha bar Yaakov offers an alternative derivation from the verse 'she shall not go out as the slaves go out'. The Gemara weighs whether the comparison should be to a slave's acquisition by chazakah, but concludes that a bill of sale is more appropriate because it is also used for a wife.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where do we derive that a Hebrew maidservant is acquired by a bill of sale (שטר)?
Ulla answers by citing a verse: 'אִם אַחֶרֶת יִקַּח לוֹ' (If he takes another [wife]), comparing the maidservant to a wife, who is acquired by a bill of sale.
The Gemara objects: This works for Rav Huna, who says the master writes the bill, but for Rav Chisda, who says the father writes it, what can be said?

Rav Acha bar Yaakov offers an alternative derivation from the verse 'לֹא תֵצֵא כְּצֵאת הָעֲבָדִים' (she shall not go out as the slaves go out), implying she is acquired like a slave, and the acquisition method is a bill of sale.

The Gemara objects: Perhaps the acquisition method is chazakah (taking possession), but the verse 'וְהִתְנַחַלְתֶּם אֹתָם' (you shall bequeath them) teaches that chazakah applies only to Canaanite slaves, not to Hebrew maidservants.
The Gemara objects further: Perhaps the verse excludes others from a bill of sale as well, so why prefer one over the other?
The Gemara resolves: A bill of sale is more appropriate to include because it is also used for a Jewish woman (wife), and the verse 'אִם אַחֶרֶת' (if another) supports this.

items.text: Explaining the verse for Rav Huna and Rav Chisda
items.text_en: Explaining the verse for Rav Huna and Rav Chisda
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains how Rav Huna and Rav Chisda each interpret the verse 'she shall not go out as the slaves go out'—Rav Huna uses it to exclude release through loss of limbs, while Rav Chisda derives two lessons from the phrasing.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Rav Huna interprets the verse 'she shall not go out as the slaves go out'.
The Gemara explains that Rav Huna uses the verse to teach that a Hebrew maidservant does not go free through loss of limbs (ראשי איברים) like a Canaanite slave.
The Gemara asks how Rav Chisda interprets the same verse.
The Gemara explains that Rav Chisda derives two lessons from the verse's unusual phrasing 'כְּצֵאת הָעֲבָדִים' (as the going out of slaves) instead of 'כָּעֲבָדִים' (like slaves).

items.text: Modes of self-redemption for a Hebrew maidservant
items.text_en: Modes of self-redemption for a Hebrew maidservant
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists that a Hebrew maidservant can go free through years, the Jubilee year, and deduction of money. The Gemara provides scriptural sources for each, and a Tosefta adds that she can also be redeemed with money, money's worth, or a bill of sale.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a Hebrew maidservant acquires herself (goes free) through years, and the Gemara cites the scriptural source: 'Six years he shall serve, and in the seventh...'
The Gemara adds that she also goes free through the Jubilee year, citing the verse 'Until the year of the Jubilee he shall serve with you.'
Chizkiyah teaches that she also goes free through deduction of money, deriving from the verse 'והפדה' (and she shall be redeemed) that she deducts her redemption price and goes out.
A Tosefta adds that she also acquires herself through money, money's worth, and a bill of sale.

items.text: Clarifying the bill of sale for redemption and its implication
items.text_en: Clarifying the bill of sale for redemption and its implication
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the need for a bill of sale for redemption, since a verbal statement suffices. Rava concludes that this shows a Hebrew slave is truly acquired, and a master who forgives the deduction does not have it forgiven.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why a bill of sale is needed for redemption, since a verbal statement before witnesses should suffice.
Rava answers that the need for a bill of sale proves that a Hebrew slave is truly acquired (גופו קנוי), and a master who forgives the deduction does not have it forgiven.

items.text: Additional release for a Hebrew maidservant: death of the father
items.text_en: Additional release for a Hebrew maidservant: death of the father
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish argues that a Hebrew maidservant can go free through the death of her father, using a kal vachomer from signs of puberty. The Gemara challenges this from a baraita that only mentions signs, and resolves that the Tanna only lists matters with a fixed limit, while death has no fixed limit.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish opens by stating that a Hebrew maidservant (אמה העבריה) acquires her freedom through the death of her father, using a kal vachomer (קל וחומר) argument from signs of puberty.
Rav Hoshaya objects by citing a baraita that lists only signs of puberty as an additional release for the maidservant, not death of the father.

The Gemara initially answers that the Tanna omitted (שייר) death of the father, but then rejects this because death of the master is also omitted and is not considered an omission since it applies to a male Hebrew slave too.
The Gemara resolves that the Tanna only lists matters with a fixed limit (קיצבה), and death has no fixed limit, so it is omitted.
The Gemara objects that signs of puberty also have no fixed limit, yet the Tanna lists them.
Rav Safra answers that signs have no fixed upper limit (אין להם קיצבה למעלה) but they do have a fixed lower limit (אבל יש להם קיצבה), so they are included.

items.text: Opening citation of a baraita on signs of puberty
items.text_en: Opening citation of a baraita on signs of puberty
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that discusses the status of a nine-year-old who grows two pubic hairs, distinguishing between a mere 'mark' (שומא) and a definitive 'sign' (סימן) depending on age.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that distinguishes between a mere 'mark' (שומא) and a definitive 'sign' (סימן) for a nine-year-old who grows two pubic hairs, with Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda ruling it is a sign from age nine and one day onward.

items.text: Rav Sheshet's objection to Reish Lakish
items.text_en: Rav Sheshet's objection to Reish Lakish
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet cites Rabbi Shimon's statement that there are four types of slaves who receive a grant, three for a male and three for a female, implying that death of the father is not included, contradicting Reish Lakish's a fortiori argument.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheishet objects by citing Rabbi Shimon's baraita listing four types of slaves who receive a grant (הענקה), noting that three apply to a male and three to a female, and one cannot have four in one because a male lacks signs (סימנים) and a female lacks ear-boring (רציעה).

items.text: Gemara's defense and counter-arguments
items.text_en: Gemara's defense and counter-arguments
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to defend Reish Lakish by suggesting the Tanna omitted death of the father, but rejects this because the Tanna listed four items and included signs which have no fixed limit, while death of the master also has no fixed limit and was omitted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Reish Lakish by asking why the Tanna did not include death of the father among the listed items, given that the Tanna listed four items and cannot have omitted anything.
The Gemara considers the possibility that the Tanna omitted death of the father, but rejects this because the Tanna explicitly listed four items.
The Gemara suggests that the Tanna only lists items with a fixed limit, but rejects this because signs (סימנין) have no fixed limit and are listed.
The Gemara considers applying Rav Safra's principle, but notes that death of the master also has no fixed limit and is listed, so the objection stands.

items.text: Identification of the four cases and proof
items.text_en: Identification of the four cases and proof
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the four cases as years, Jubilee, Jubilee of piercing, and a Hebrew maidservant through signs, and proves from the continuation of Rabbi Shimon's statement that death of the father is not included.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the four cases as years, Jubilee, Jubilee of piercing, and a Hebrew maidservant through signs.
The Gemara proves from the continuation of Rabbi Shimon's statement that death of the father is not included, since the continuation excludes four cases in one person.

items.text: Rav Amram's objection and conclusive refutation
items.text_en: Rav Amram's objection and conclusive refutation
items.desc_en: Rav Amram cites a baraita listing those who receive a grant, including death of the master but not death of the father, and the Gemara concludes this is a conclusive refutation of Reish Lakish.

sub.desc_en: Rav Amram cites a baraita listing those who receive a grant, including death of the master but not death of the father, to challenge Reish Lakish.
The Gemara asks: if death of the father were a valid release, why is it not listed in the baraita?
The Gemara rejects the possibility that the baraita omitted items, because it uses the inclusive term 'אלו' (these are).
The Gemara considers and rejects the argument that the baraita only lists fixed-term releases, since simanim (signs of puberty) have no fixed term yet are listed.

The Gemara considers and rejects the argument that death of the father is like Rav Safra's case, since death of the master (which also has no fixed term) is listed, leading to the conclusion that Reish Lakish is conclusively refuted.

items.text: Explanation of why Reish Lakish's a fortiori argument fails
items.text_en: Explanation of why Reish Lakish's a fortiori argument fails
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Reish Lakish's a fortiori argument is refutable because signs involve a change in the body, unlike death of the father which does not.

sub.text: Gemara's challenge to Reish Lakish's kal vachomer
sub.text_en: Gemara's challenge to Reish Lakish's kal vachomer
sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Reish Lakish's argument was based on a קל וחומר (a fortiori reasoning), but this reasoning is refutable because signs involve a change in the body (שינוי הגוף), whereas death of the father does not involve a change in the body.
The Gemara explains that the a fortiori argument is refutable (פריכא) because signs involve a change in the body, unlike the death of the father which does not.

items.text: Resolution of conflicting baraitot on the grant of a Hebrew maidservant
items.text_en: Resolution of conflicting baraitot on the grant of a Hebrew maidservant
items.desc_en: Two baraitot conflict: one says the grant goes to herself, another says to her father. The Gemara initially suggests one refers to leaving through signs and the other through death of the father, but resolves that both refer to signs, distinguishing whether the father is alive.

sub.desc_en: A baraita rules that the grant of a Hebrew maidservant goes to herself, and another baraita rules that it goes to her father.
The Gemara suggests that the conflicting baraitot refer to different modes of release: one by signs of maturity, the other by the father's death.
The Gemara rejects the distinction and resolves that both baraitot refer to release by signs, distinguishing whether the father is alive or dead.

items.text: Analysis of the grant for a Hebrew slave and a maidservant
items.text_en: Analysis of the grant for a Hebrew slave and a maidservant
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the grant of a Hebrew maidservant goes to herself to exclude brothers from inheritance, and discusses the grant of a Hebrew slave, with Rav Yosef and Abaye citing different opinions about its purpose.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the grant of a Hebrew maidservant goes to herself, citing a baraita that excludes daughters from inheriting their father's rights.
The Gemara questions why the grant of a Hebrew slave to himself is stated, as it seems obvious, and Rav Yosef expresses confusion.
Abaye resolves the difficulty by citing Rav Sheshet that the baraita follows Tutai's opinion, who derives that the grant is for the slave himself and not for his creditor.

items.text: Baraita on who receives a grant and Rabbi Shimon's statement
items.text_en: Baraita on who receives a grant and Rabbi Shimon's statement
items.desc_en: A baraita lists those who receive a grant: one who leaves through years, Jubilee, death of the master, and a Hebrew maidservant through signs, but not a fugitive or one redeemed by money, with disputes between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Shimon.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by listing those who receive a grant: one who leaves through years, Jubilee, death of the master, and a Hebrew maidservant through signs.
The baraita states that a fugitive and one redeemed by money do not receive a grant, with Rabbi Meir disputing regarding the one redeemed by money.
Rabbi Shimon states that four categories receive a grant, three for a man and three for a woman, and one cannot say four for either because a man lacks signs and a woman lacks ear-piercing.

items.text: Scriptural derivation for the grant
items.text_en: Scriptural derivation for the grant
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from verses that grants apply to those who leave through years, Jubilee, death of the master, and a maidservant through signs, but excludes a fugitive and one redeemed by money, with Rabbi Meir's opinion and a baraita about a fugitive completing his term.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where are these matters (the list of those who receive a grant) derived?

A baraita teaches that one might think only the one who leaves after six years receives a grant, so the verses 'תְּשַׁלְּחֶנּוּ' and 'וְכִי תְשַׁלְּחֶנּוּ' (you shall send him forth) include the one who leaves at the Jubilee, at the master's death, and the Hebrew maidservant who leaves through signs.

The baraita continues: One might think to include a fugitive and one redeemed by money, but the verse 'וְכִי תְשַׁלְּחֶנּוּ חׇפְשִׁי מֵעִמָּךְ' (when you send him forth free from with you) excludes those whose release is not from with you; Rabbi Meir adds that a fugitive is excluded but one redeemed by money is included because his release is from with you.
A baraita explains that a fugitive must complete his term, as derived from the verse 'שֵׁשׁ שָׁנִים יַעֲבֹד' (six years he shall serve).

items.text: Illness and the slave's release
items.text_en: Illness and the slave's release
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a slave who falls ill during his six years of service still goes free in the seventh year. Rav Sheshet explains the case as one where the slave fled and the Jubilee year intervened, teaching that even then he is not granted an endowment.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a slave who falls ill during his six years of service still goes free in the seventh year, citing the verse 'and in the seventh he shall go out'.
Rav Sheshet explains that the case involves a slave who fled and the Jubilee year intervened, teaching that even then he is not granted an endowment.

items.text: Clarifying the illness case
items.text_en: Clarifying the illness case
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the earlier statement by citing a baraita: if a slave was ill for three years and worked three, he need not complete the time; if ill all six, he must complete. Rav Sheshet answers that the case is one where he did light work. The Gemara then resolves an apparent contradiction in the baraita.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the baraita's implication that illness for all six years requires completion, citing a contradictory baraita about partial illness.
Rav Sheshet resolves the contradiction by explaining that the case involves a slave who performed light work (needlework) during his illness.
The Gemara points out an internal contradiction in the baraita itself: the first clause implies four years of illness requires completion, but the second clause implies it does not.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by reinterpreting the baraita: four years of illness is treated like six full years, requiring completion.

items.text: The amount of the endowment: Tannaitic dispute
items.text_en: The amount of the endowment: Tannaitic dispute
items.desc_en: A baraita presents three opinions on how much the master must give the freed slave: Rabbi Meir says five sela from each of three types (fifteen total), Rabbi Yehuda says thirty (like the value of a slave), and Rabbi Shimon says fifty (like the valuations in the Torah).

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with the question of how much the master must give the freed slave, and presents Rabbi Meir's opinion: five sela from each of three types, totaling fifteen sela.
Rabbi Yehuda states his opinion: the endowment is thirty sela, analogous to the value of a slave.
Rabbi Shimon states his opinion: the endowment is fifty sela, analogous to the valuations in the Torah.

items.text: Rabbi Meir's reasoning
items.text_en: Rabbi Meir's reasoning
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Meir derives the amount from a verbal analogy on the word 'רֵיקָם' from the firstborn, and that the three types are each given five sela. It rejects a derivation from the 'עולת ראייה' and explains the verse 'אֲשֶׁר בֵּרַכְךָ' as the source for the amount.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the baraita's opening statement that Rabbi Meir requires five sela from each type, totaling fifteen, and explains that the point is to set a minimum, not to require equal distribution.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Meir's reasoning
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Meir's reasoning
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Meir derives the five-sela amount from a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) on the word 'רֵיקָם' from the firstborn (בכור).

The Gemara objects: perhaps the five sela should apply to all types combined, not each individually, and answers that the word 'רֵיקָם' appears at the beginning of the verse, applying separately to each type.
The Gemara rejects a possible derivation from the עולת ראייה (festival burnt-offering) by citing the verse 'אֲשֶׁר בֵּרַכְךָ' as the source for the amount.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda derives the thirty sela from a verbal analogy on 'נְתִינָה' from the slave. The Gemara objects that one could derive fifty from the valuations, but answers that when in doubt, one takes the smaller amount, and also that a slave should be derived from a slave.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda states his position that the gift is thirty sela, derived from the thirty sela of a slave via a verbal analogy on 'נְתִינָה' (giving).
The Gemara objects that one could derive fifty sela from the valuations (עֲרָכִין) using the same verbal analogy on 'נְתִינָה'.
The Gemara answers that when in doubt one takes the smaller amount, and additionally, a slave should be derived from a slave.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon's reasoning
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon's reasoning
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon derives fifty from a verbal analogy on 'נְתִינָה' from the valuations, and the verse 'אֲשֶׁר בֵּרַכְךָ' indicates the higher amount. The Gemara objects that one could derive thirty from a slave, but answers that he learns via a different analogy ('מִיכָה').

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon states that the gift to the Hebrew slave is fifty, analogous to the fifty shekels in the valuations.
The Gemara asks for the reasoning behind Rabbi Shimon's position.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Shimon derives the amount via a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) on the word 'נְתִינָה' (giving) from the valuations, where the amount is fifty.
The Gemara objects that one could instead derive the lower amount of thirty from the valuations, since the valuations have a minimum of thirty.
The Gemara rejects the objection by citing the verse 'אֲשֶׁר בֵּרַכְךָ' (which the Lord your God has blessed you), indicating that the gift must be generous, i.e., the higher amount.
The Gemara objects that one could instead derive the amount of thirty from the slave (עֶבֶד) via the same verbal analogy on 'נְתִינָה'.

The Gemara rejects the objection with two arguments: the principle of 'תָּפַשְׂתָּה מְרוּבֶּה לֹא תָּפַשְׂתָּה' (if you grasp the larger, you have not grasped it) and that a slave should be derived from a slave (i.e., the Hebrew slave from the Canaanite slave).
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Shimon actually derives the amount via a different verbal analogy on the word 'מִיכָה' (from the passage about the slave), not from the valuations.

items.text: The purpose of the three types
items.text_en: The purpose of the three types
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Torah specifies 'flock, threshing floor, and winepress' for Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon. It answers that these teach that the endowment includes only items that are typically blessed, excluding coins (Rabbi Shimon) or mules (Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov). The Gemara then explains why all three are necessary.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Torah specifies 'flock, threshing floor, and winepress' according to Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon, since they do not derive the amount from these terms.

The Gemara answers that these terms are needed for a baraita which teaches that the endowment includes only items that are typically blessed, excluding coins according to Rabbi Shimon, or mules according to Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov.
The Gemara explains why Rabbi Shimon excludes mules (they grow in body) and why Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov excludes coins (one can conduct business with them).
The Gemara explains why all three terms are necessary: 'flock' alone would exclude produce, 'threshing floor' alone would exclude animals, and 'winepress' is needed to include wine.

items.text: Clarification of the earlier dispute about the exclusion of money or mules
items.text_en: Clarification of the earlier dispute about the exclusion of money or mules
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the two earlier opinions (one excluding money, the other excluding mules) are both derived from the same verse, each according to their own interpretation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the earlier dispute by stating that one opinion excludes money (כספים) and the other excludes mules (פרדות), each derived from the same verse.

items.text: Dispute on the interpretation of the verse regarding the gift to the servant
items.text_en: Dispute on the interpretation of the verse regarding the gift to the servant
items.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma argues that the verse 'which the Lord your God has blessed you' does not limit the gift to a blessed household, but rather the amount is proportional to the blessing. Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya holds that the verse is literal: only if the household was blessed through the servant does he receive a gift, and the doubling of the verb is just a normal Hebrew expression.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma interprets the verse 'which the Lord your God has blessed you' as not limiting the gift to a blessed household, but rather the amount is proportional to the blessing.
Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya holds that the verse is literal: only if the household was blessed through the servant does he receive a gift, and the doubling of the verb is just a normal Hebrew expression.

items.text: Source that a Hebrew slave serves the son but not the daughter
items.text_en: Source that a Hebrew slave serves the son but not the daughter
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita stating that a Hebrew slave serves the son but not the daughter, while a Hebrew maidservant serves neither. It then seeks the source for the slave serving the son, deriving it from a verse that excludes an heir but includes the son. The Gemara questions why the son is preferred over the brother, and resolves that the brother's claim via levirate marriage is weaker when there is a son.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that a Hebrew slave serves the son but not the daughter, and the Gemara asks for the source.

A baraita derives from the verse 'וַעֲבָדְךָ שֵׁשׁ שָׁנִים' (and he shall serve you six years) that the slave serves you and not an heir, but the son is included from the parallel verse 'שֵׁשׁ שָׁנִים יַעֲבֹד' (six years he shall labor).
The Gemara asks why the son is included and the brother excluded, and answers that the son stands in place of the father for יִעוּד (designation) and for שְׂדֵה אֲחוּזָּה (ancestral field).

The Gemara objects that the brother should be included because he stands in place of his brother for יִבּוּם (levirate marriage), but the objection is rejected because יִבּוּם applies only when there is no son.

The Gemara questions whether without this refutation the brother would be preferred, and suggests that the son has two supporting cases (יִעוּד and שְׂדֵה אֲחוּזָּה) while the brother has only one (יִבּוּם).
The Gemara resolves that even the case of שְׂדֵה אֲחוּזָּה (ancestral field) is derived from the same refutation that יִבּוּם applies only when there is no son, so the son is preferred.

items.text: Source that a Hebrew maidservant does not serve the son or daughter
items.text_en: Source that a Hebrew maidservant does not serve the son or daughter
items.desc_en: Rabbi Peda derives from the verse 'and also to your maidservant you shall do likewise' that the maidservant is compared to the ear-pierced slave, who does not serve the son or daughter. The Gemara questions whether this verse is needed for the law of granting a gift, but resolves that the extra word 'do' teaches both laws.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where is it derived that a Hebrew maidservant does not serve the son or daughter?

רבי פדא (Rabbi Peda) answers: The verse 'וְאַף לַאֲמָתְךָ תַּעֲשֶׂה כֵּן' (and also to your maidservant you shall do likewise) juxtaposes the maidservant to the ear-pierced slave, so just as the pierced slave does not serve the son or daughter, so too the Hebrew maidservant does not serve them.
The Gemara objects: Is this verse indeed needed for that teaching? It is already required for the law of granting a severance gift, as taught in a baraita.

The Gemara clarifies: The verse could be interpreted as referring to piercing (רציעה), but since the verse 'וְאִם אָמֹר יֹאמַר הָעֶבֶד' (But if the slave shall say) specifies 'the slave' and not a maidservant, the law of piercing is already stated, leaving the verse for the severance gift.

The Gemara resolves: If the verse were only for the severance gift, it could have written 'לַאֲמָתְךָ כֵּן' (to your maidservant likewise); the extra word 'תַּעֲשֶׂה' (you shall do) teaches two things — both the severance gift and that the maidservant does not serve the son or daughter.

items.text: Source that the ear-pierced slave and one sold to a non-Jew do not serve the son or daughter
items.text_en: Source that the ear-pierced slave and one sold to a non-Jew do not serve the son or daughter
items.desc_en: The ear-pierced slave is excluded from serving the son or daughter by the verse 'and he shall serve him forever'. The one sold to a non-Jew is excluded by the verse 'and he shall reckon with his purchaser', implying not with the purchaser's heirs.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that the ear-pierced slave and the one sold to a non-Jew do not serve the son or the daughter.

sub.text: Gemara's derivation for the ear-pierced slave
sub.text_en: Gemara's derivation for the ear-pierced slave
sub.desc_en: The Gemara derives that the ear-pierced slave does not serve the son or daughter from the verse 'and he shall serve him forever'.

sub.text: Chizkiya's derivation for the one sold to a non-Jew
sub.text_en: Chizkiya's derivation for the one sold to a non-Jew
sub.desc_en: Chizkiya derives that the one sold to a non-Jew does not serve the son or daughter from the verse 'and he shall reckon with his purchaser', implying not with the purchaser's heirs.

items.text: Inheritance rights of a non-Jew and a convert
items.text_en: Inheritance rights of a non-Jew and a convert
items.desc_en: Rava states that a non-Jew inherits his father by Torah law, as implied by the verse. A convert inheriting a non-Jew is only rabbinic. The Gemara brings a mishnah about a convert and a non-Jew inheriting their non-Jewish father, where the convert may take money and the non-Jew the idolatry, but only before it enters the convert's domain. The Gemara concludes that this is a rabbinic decree to prevent the convert from backsliding, and further discusses cases where inheritance is not recognized at all.

sub.desc_en: Rava states that by Torah law a non-Jew inherits his father, but a convert inheriting a non-Jew is only rabbinic.

The Gemara cites a mishnah where a convert and a non-Jew inherit their non-Jewish father, and the convert may take money while the non-Jew takes idolatry, but only before it enters the convert's domain.
The Gemara objects that if the convert's inheritance were Torah law, even before the idolatry enters his domain he would be taking an exchange for idolatry, which is forbidden.
The Gemara resolves that the inheritance is only rabbinic, a decree to prevent the convert from backsliding, and a baraita supports this by distinguishing inheritance from partnership.

The Gemara states that a non-Jew inheriting a convert or a convert inheriting another convert is neither Torah nor rabbinic, citing a mishnah where one who repays such a loan is not favored by the sages.

The Gemara resolves an apparent contradiction between two baraitot about the sages' attitude, distinguishing between a convert whose birth and conversion were both outside holiness versus one whose birth was in holiness.

items.text: Inheritance of a Noachide and the dispute between Rava and Rav Chiyya bar Avin
items.text_en: Inheritance of a Noachide and the dispute between Rava and Rav Chiyya bar Avin
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses whether a Noachide inherits his father by Torah law. Rav Chiyya bar Avin cites verses about Esau and Lot to prove this, while Rava offers a different proof. The Gemara explains why each sage did not adopt the other's reasoning.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by noting the case of a Noachide whose conception was not in holiness but whose birth was in holiness.

sub.text: Rav Chiyya bar Avin citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rav Chiyya bar Avin citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rav Chiyya bar Avin in the name of Rabbi Yochanan asserts that a Noachide inherits his father by Torah law, citing verses about Esau and Lot.
The Gemara questions whether the proof from Esau is valid, suggesting that a Jewish apostate might be different.
The Gemara resolves the objection by citing the verse about Lot's sons as a stronger proof.
The Gemara asks why Rav Chiyya bar Avin did not adopt Rava's alternative proof from the verse about a slave's redemption.
The Gemara explains that Rav Chiyya bar Avin rejected Rava's proof because the verse does not explicitly mention heirs of the owner.
The Gemara asks why Rava did not adopt Rav Chiyya bar Avin's proof.
The Gemara explains that Rava rejected the proof because the case of Esau is exceptional due to the honor of Abraham.

items.text: Baraita: Differences between a Hebrew slave and maidservant
items.text_en: Baraita: Differences between a Hebrew slave and maidservant
items.desc_en: A baraita lists distinctions: a Hebrew slave goes free after six years, at the Jubilee, or upon the master's death, while a Hebrew maidservant does not; conversely, a maidservant goes free with signs of puberty, cannot be sold again, and is redeemed against her father's will.

sub.desc_en: The baraita lists distinctions between a Hebrew slave (עבד עברי) and a Hebrew maidservant (אמה עבריה): the slave goes free after six years, at the Jubilee, or upon the master's death, while the maidservant does not; conversely, the maidservant goes free with signs of puberty, cannot be resold, and is redeemed against her father's will.

items.text: Clarification: Maidservant goes free with signs even after designation
items.text_en: Clarification: Maidservant goes free with signs even after designation
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a maidservant can go free with signs if she has been designated (יעודה). Rav Sheshet explains the baraita refers to a case where she was not designated; the Gemara refines this, stating that even if designated, the signs still release her.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: the baraita states that a Hebrew maidservant has an advantage over a Hebrew slave in that she goes free with signs (סימנין), but another baraita says she goes free with signs — how is this a unique advantage?
Rav Sheshet resolves the contradiction by explaining that the baraita refers to a case where the master designated (יעד) the maidservant, so she would not normally go free with signs.
The Gemara objects: if she was designated (יעדה), it is obvious that she needs a bill of divorce (גט) to go free — so why would the baraita mention signs?
The Gemara explains that the baraita teaches that even after designation, the signs (סימנין) still release her, countering the notion that the halachot of signs are nullified by the designation.
The Gemara objects: if designation does not nullify the signs, why does the baraita say she goes free with signs — that is already true without designation?
The Gemara resolves: the baraita means that if the master did not designate her, she goes free even with signs — the advantage is that she goes free with signs without needing a bill of divorce.

items.text: Can a Hebrew slave be sold multiple times?
items.text_en: Can a Hebrew slave be sold multiple times?
items.desc_en: The baraita implies a Hebrew slave can be sold again, but a different baraita limits sale to once. Rava resolves the contradiction by distinguishing one theft from two thefts. Abaye disagrees, distinguishing one person from two people.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the baraita that a Hebrew maidservant cannot be sold twice, implying a Hebrew slave can, but then cites a contradictory baraita that limits sale to once.
Rava resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between one theft (sold once) and two thefts (sold again).
Abaye objects that the verse 'בִּגְנֵבָתוֹ' implies any amount, and instead distinguishes between one person (sold once) and two people (sold again).

items.text: Sale of a thief: value vs. theft amount
items.text_en: Sale of a thief: value vs. theft amount
items.desc_en: A baraita states that if a thief stole 1000 and it is worth 500, he is sold; if he stole 500 and it is worth 1000, he is not sold. Rabbi Eliezer adds a condition. Rava explains Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning: the Torah says he is sold for his theft, not for half his theft.

items.text: Redemption of a maidservant against her father's will
items.text_en: Redemption of a maidservant against her father's will
items.desc_en: The baraita states a maidservant is redeemed against her father's will. Rava thought it meant against the master's will, but Abaye objects. Abaye explains it is against the father's will due to family disgrace. The Gemara questions why a Hebrew slave is not similarly redeemed, and resolves that the maidservant cannot be resold, citing Rabbi Shimon's view.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that a Hebrew maidservant is redeemed against someone's will.
Rava thought the baraita meant against the master's will.
Abaye objects that forcing the master to accept payment is like giving him a shard instead of a pearl.
Abaye explains that the redemption is against the father's will, due to family disgrace.
The Gemara asks why a Hebrew slave is not similarly redeemed against his family's will due to family disgrace.
The Gemara answers that a Hebrew slave can go and sell himself again, so coercion is ineffective.
The Gemara objects that the father could also sell his daughter again.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita itself states she cannot be resold, citing Rabbi Shimon's view.
The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Shimon holds that a father cannot sell his daughter for servitude a second time, supporting the resolution.

items.text: Opening dispute between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Eliezer
items.text_en: Opening dispute between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Eliezer
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a disagreement: Rabbi Akiva says once a master spreads his garment over a maidservant (a symbolic act of yi'ud), he may no longer sell her; Rabbi Eliezer derives the same from the verse 'because he has dealt deceitfully with her' (בבגדו בה).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the dispute: Rabbi Akiva says once a master spreads his garment over a maidservant (symbolic yi'ud), he may no longer sell her; Rabbi Eliezer derives the same from the verse 'בבגדו בה' (because he has dealt deceitfully with her).

items.text: Gemara's explanation of the dispute's basis
items.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the dispute's basis
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Eliezer holds 'yesh em la-masoret' (the tradition is primary), while Rabbi Akiva holds 'yesh em la-mikra' (the written text is primary). Rabbi Shimon holds both are primary.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what is the fundamental point of disagreement between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Eliezer?
The Gemara explains: Rabbi Eliezer holds that the Masoretic tradition (מסורת) is primary, Rabbi Akiva holds that the biblical text (מקרא) is primary, and Rabbi Shimon holds that both are primary.

items.text: Rabba bar Avuh's question on the nature of yi'ud
items.text_en: Rabba bar Avuh's question on the nature of yi'ud
items.desc_en: Rabba bar Avuh asks whether yi'ud constitutes full marriage (nissu'in) or mere betrothal (erusin), with practical differences regarding inheritance, impurity, and annulment of vows.

sub.desc_en: Rabba bar Avuh asks: does yi'ud (designation) effect full marriage (נישואין) or only betrothal (אירוסין)? The practical difference involves inheritance, becoming impure for her, and annulling her vows.

items.text: First attempted proof from the Mishnah
items.text_en: First attempted proof from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove from the Mishnah that yi'ud creates erusin, since after the master spreads his garment, he cannot sell her but can still designate her; if it were nissu'in, the father would lose all rights over her.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove from the Mishnah that yi'ud effects betrothal (אירוסין), because if it were full marriage, the father would lose all rights over her, yet the Mishnah only prohibits selling her.

items.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's rejection of the proof
items.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's rejection of the proof
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak rejects the proof, explaining that the Mishnah refers to ordinary betrothal (not yi'ud), where the father hands her over to a husband who becomes obligated for her sustenance, clothing, and conjugal rights.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak rejects the proof: the Mishnah is discussing a general case of betrothal (קידושין דעלמא), not yi'ud, and means that once a father gives his daughter to a man who becomes obligated in her sustenance, clothing, and conjugal rights, he can no longer sell her.

items.text: Second attempted proof from a baraita
items.text_en: Second attempted proof from a baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita: one may not sell a maidservant to relatives; Rabbi Eliezer permits it. Both agree one may sell her as a widow to a High Priest, or as a divorcee or chalutzah to an ordinary priest.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita: one may not sell a maidservant to relatives; Rabbi Eliezer permits selling to relatives; and all agree one may sell her as a widow to a High Priest, or as a divorcée or חלוצה (a woman who performed חליצה) to a common priest.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the baraita
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the baraita: if the widow was betrothed by herself, why call her a widow? If her father betrothed her, he cannot sell her after marriage, as 'a person does not sell his daughter into slavery after marriage'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the baraita: how can a maidservant be a widow? If she betrothed herself, she is not a widow; if her father betrothed her, he cannot sell her after marriage (אישות).

items.text: Rav Amram's resolution: the baraita refers to yi'ud
items.text_en: Rav Amram's resolution: the baraita refers to yi'ud
items.desc_en: Rav Amram says in the name of Rabbi Yitzchak that the baraita deals with yi'ud, according to Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda who holds that the initial money was not for betrothal. If yi'ud were nissu'in, the father would lose rights after marriage.

sub.text: Rav Amram citing Rabbi Yitzchak's answer
sub.text_en: Rav Amram citing Rabbi Yitzchak's answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Amram citing Rabbi Yitzchak answers: the baraita deals with קידושי ייעוד (betrothal through yi'ud) according to Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that the initial money was not for betrothal; if yi'ud effects full marriage, the father loses rights over her.

items.text: Gemara's challenge and resolution
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: if yi'ud creates erusin, how can the father sell her after erusin? It answers that her erusin differs from her father's erusin; even if yi'ud creates nissu'in, her nissu'in differs from her father's nissu'in.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if yi'ud effects only betrothal, how can the baraita say 'all agree one may sell her as a widow'? The father cannot sell her after any marriage. The Gemara resolves: her betrothal is different from her father's betrothal, and even if yi'ud effects full marriage, her marriage is different from her father's marriage.
The Gemara answers that her erusin differs from her father's erusin; even if yi'ud creates nissu'in, her nissu'in differs from her father's nissu'in.

items.text: Gemara's further clarification
items.text_en: Gemara's further clarification
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the distinction: it is plausible that erusin differs from erusin, but how can nissu'in differ from nissu'in? This question is left unresolved.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the distinction: it is understandable that betrothal differs from betrothal, but how can marriage differ from marriage?

items.text: Resolving the contradiction for Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak
items.text_en: Resolving the contradiction for Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak, who holds that even Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda agrees the first money is for kiddushin, resolves the contradiction. He explains that Rabbi Eliezer's ruling applies only to selling her for another servitude, not for marriage.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the cases are different, challenging the resolution of the contradiction.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that Rabbi Eliezer's ruling only prohibits selling her for another servitude after servitude, but for servitude after marriage it is permitted.

items.text: Reish Lakish's inquiry about yibud for a minor son
items.text_en: Reish Lakish's inquiry about yibud for a minor son
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish asks whether a father can designate (yibud) his minor son for his Hebrew maidservant. The question is whether 'his son' includes any son or only an adult like himself.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish asks whether a father can designate (ייעד) his minor son for his Hebrew maidservant, questioning if 'his son' includes any son or only an adult like himself.

items.text: Proof from the verse about a minor's wife
items.text_en: Proof from the verse about a minor's wife
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira brings a proof: the verse 'Ish' excludes a minor, and 'eshet ish' excludes a minor's wife. If a minor could perform yibud, then a minor would have marital status. Rav Ashi explains the verse refers to a nine-year-old yavam who has a biblical relationship with his yevama, teaching that one who sleeps with her is liable for adultery.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira introduces a proof from the verse about adultery, which excludes a minor and a minor's wife.
The Gemara objects: if a minor could perform ייעוד (designation), then the verse would have found marital status for a minor, so the proof actually supports that he does not perform ייעוד.

Rav Ashi resolves the objection by explaining that the verse deals with a nine-year-old yavam who has a biblical relationship with his yevama, teaching that one who sleeps with her is liable for adultery.

items.text: Rabbi Aibu and Rabbi Yannai's ruling on yibud
items.text_en: Rabbi Aibu and Rabbi Yannai's ruling on yibud
items.desc_en: Rabbi Aibu quoting Rabbi Yannai states that yibud is only for an adult and only with consent. The Gemara clarifies that the reason is because yibud requires consent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the resolution is regarding the question of whether a minor can perform ייעוד (designation).
Rabbi Aibu in the name of Rabbi Yannai rules that ייעוד (designation) applies only to an adult and only with consent.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Aibu's statement contains two separate conditions (adult and consent), which seems redundant.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Aibu's statement is structured as a reason: the requirement of adulthood is because ייעוד requires consent.

items.text: Alternative explanation: consent of the maidservant
items.text_en: Alternative explanation: consent of the maidservant
items.desc_en: An alternative explanation is that 'da'at' refers to the maidservant's consent, derived from the verse 'asher lo ye'adah'. Abaye's son teaches that one must designate her. The Gemara explains this applies to kiddushei yi'ud according to Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda, while Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak holds that even if the first money is for kiddushin, the Torah requires a separate act of yi'ud.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative explanation that 'da'at' (consent) refers to the maidservant's own consent.
A baraita taught by Abaye's son derives from the verse 'asher lo ye'adah' that one must designate (yi'ud) the maidservant.
The Gemara explains that Abaye's son's teaching applies to kiddushei yi'ud according to Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda, who holds that the first money was not given for kiddushin.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak holds that even if the first money was given for kiddushin, the Torah requires a separate act of yi'ud.

items.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda's view on the need for time to redeem
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda's view on the need for time to redeem
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda's position: from the verse 'ye'adah vehefdah', there must be time in the day for redemption. If there is time to give a perutah, she is betrothed; otherwise not. This shows he holds the first money is not for kiddushin. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that even if it were, the Torah requires a separate redemption.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda's position is, citing a baraita that from the verse 'יְעָדָהּ, וְהֶפְדָּהּ' there must be time in the day for redemption.

sub.text: Baraita of Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda
sub.text_en: Baraita of Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda
sub.desc_en: The baraita states Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda's ruling: if there is time to give a perutah, she is betrothed; otherwise not.
The Gemara concludes that this shows Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda holds the first money was not given for kiddushin.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak objects that even if the first money were for kiddushin, the Torah's requirement of a separate redemption (וְהֶפְדָּהּ) distinguishes this case.

items.text: Rava's ruling: a father can tell his minor daughter to accept kiddushin
items.text_en: Rava's ruling: a father can tell his minor daughter to accept kiddushin
items.desc_en: Rava quoting Rav Nachman rules that a father can tell his minor daughter to accept her kiddushin, based on Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda's logic: just as there, the first money is not for kiddushin but a leftover perutah creates kiddushin, so here too.

sub.desc_en: Rava quotes Rav Nachman that a father may tell his minor daughter to accept her kiddushin, based on Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda's logic.

The Gemara explains the analogy: just as Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda holds that the first money is not for kiddushin but a leftover perutah creates kiddushin, so too here the father's instruction is valid.

items.text: Rava's ruling: kiddushin with a loan secured by collateral
items.text_en: Rava's ruling: kiddushin with a loan secured by collateral
items.desc_en: Rava quoting Rav Nachman rules that if one betroths with a loan that has a collateral, she is betrothed, based on Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda's view. The loan itself is like the first money, and the collateral is like the leftover perutah.

sub.desc_en: Rava, citing Rav Nachman, rules that if one betroths with a loan that has a collateral (משכון), the woman is betrothed, based on Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda's principle that the first money was not given for betrothal, so here the loan itself is the first money and the collateral is the leftover perutah.

items.text: Gemara's continuation of the previous sugya
items.text_en: Gemara's continuation of the previous sugya
items.desc_en: The Gemara argues that if the master leaves a perutah's worth of the purchase price and designates her, the betrothal is valid; similarly here, it should not be different.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara argues that if the master leaves a perutah's worth of the purchase price and designates her, the betrothal is valid; similarly here, it should not be different.

items.text: First baraita: the mitzvah of yibud
items.text_en: First baraita: the mitzvah of yibud
items.desc_en: The Sages teach how the mitzvah of yibud is performed: the master says to her before two witnesses 'You are betrothed to me' even at the end of the sixth year, even close to sunset. He treats her as a wife, not as a maidservant. Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda says: if there is time in the day to leave a perutah's worth with him, she is betrothed; if not, she is not.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by describing the mitzvah of yibud (designation): the master declares betrothal before two witnesses, even at the last moment, and treats her as a wife, not a maidservant.
Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda adds a condition: if there is time in the day to leave a perutah's worth with him, she is betrothed; otherwise, she is not.

items.text: Analogy to conditional betrothal and clarification
items.text_en: Analogy to conditional betrothal and clarification
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a mashal: one who says to a woman 'Be betrothed to me from now after thirty days' and another betroths her within thirty days – she is betrothed to the first. The Gemara asks: to whom does this mashal refer? It cannot be Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda, for he requires time for a perutah. Rav Acha bar Rava says: it refers to the Rabbis. The Gemara notes this is obvious, but the mashal teaches that even without saying 'from now', the betrothal is valid.

sub.desc_en: The baraita presents a mashal: one who says to a woman 'Be betrothed to me from now after thirty days' and another betroths her within thirty days – she is betrothed to the first, and then asks: to whom does this mashal refer?
The Gemara rejects the possibility that the mashal refers to Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda, because he requires time for a perutah within the day.
Rav Acha bar Rava answers that the mashal refers to the Rabbis, and the Gemara notes this is obvious.
The Gemara resolves that the mashal teaches that even without saying 'from now', the betrothal is valid.

items.text: Second baraita: selling daughter and betrothing to another
items.text_en: Second baraita: selling daughter and betrothing to another
items.desc_en: Another baraita is taught: one who sells his daughter and then goes and betroths her to another – he has mocked the master, and she is betrothed to the second, according to Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda. The Sages say: if he wishes to designate her, he may. The Gemara presents a mashal: one who says 'You are betrothed to me after thirty days' and another betroths her within thirty days – she is betrothed to the second. The Gemara asks: to whom does this refer? It cannot be the Rabbis, for they say he may designate. Rav Acha bar Rava says: it refers to Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda. The Gemara notes this is obvious, but the mashal teaches that even without saying 'after thirty days', the betrothal is valid.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: one who sells his daughter and then betroths her to another has mocked the master, and she is betrothed to the second, according to Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda.
The Sages state: if he wishes to designate her, he may do so.
A mashal is presented: one who says 'You are betrothed to me after thirty days' and another betroths her within thirty days – she is betrothed to the second.
The Gemara asks: to whom does this mashal refer?
The Gemara objects: if it refers to the Rabbis, they say he may designate her, so the mashal would not apply.
Rav Acha bar Rava answers: the mashal refers to Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda.
The Gemara objects: this is obvious.
The Gemara resolves: the mashal teaches that even without saying 'after thirty days', the betrothal is valid.

items.text: Third baraita: condition against yibud
items.text_en: Third baraita: condition against yibud
items.desc_en: Another baraita is taught: one who sells his daughter and stipulates that he will not designate her – the condition is valid, according to Rabbi Meir. The Sages say: if he wishes to designate her, he may, because he stipulated against what is written in the Torah, and any such condition is void. The Gemara objects: for Rabbi Meir, is his condition valid? But it was taught that if one says to a woman 'You are betrothed to me on condition that you have no claim of food, clothing, or conjugal rights' – she is betrothed and the condition is void, according to Rabbi Meir. Rabbi Yehuda says: in a monetary matter, the condition is valid.

sub.desc_en: A baraita presents the case of a father who sells his daughter and stipulates that he will not designate her; Rabbi Meir holds the condition is valid, while the Sages hold it is void because it contradicts Torah law.

The Gemara objects: for Rabbi Meir, is his condition valid? It cites a baraita where a man betroths a woman on condition that she has no claim of food, clothing, or conjugal rights, and Rabbi Meir rules the condition void, while Rabbi Yehuda says in a monetary matter the condition is valid.

items.text: Resolution of the contradiction regarding Rabbi Meir
items.text_en: Resolution of the contradiction regarding Rabbi Meir
items.desc_en: Chizkiya says: here it is different, because the verse says 'לְאָמָה' – sometimes he sells her only as a maidservant. The Gemara asks: what do the Rabbis do with this 'לְאָמָה'? It is needed for what was taught: 'לְאָמָה' teaches that he may sell her to invalid men (e.g., a deaf-mute or minor). A kal vachomer is presented: if he can betroth her to invalid men, should he not be able to sell her to them? The verse 'לְאָמָה' teaches that he may. Rabbi Eliezer says: if to teach that he may sell her to invalid men, it was already stated 'if she is displeasing in the eyes of her master' – that she is displeasing in marriage. What does 'לְאָמָה' teach? It teaches that he may sell her.

sub.desc_en: Chizkiya resolves the contradiction by noting that the verse 'לְאָמָה' (as a maidservant) implies that sometimes he sells her only as a maidservant, not for marriage, so a condition against designation is valid.
The Gemara asks how the Rabbis, who reject Chizkiya's interpretation, interpret the word 'לְאָמָה' (as a maidservant).
The Gemara answers that the Rabbis use the word 'לְאָמָה' (as a maidservant) to teach that a father may sell his daughter to invalid men (e.g., a deaf-mute or minor).
The baraita raises a logical inference: if a father can betroth his daughter to invalid men, should he not also be able to sell her to them?

The baraita explains that betrothal to invalid men is possible because a father can betroth his daughter even when she is a נערה (young woman), whereas he cannot sell her at that age; therefore, the verse 'לְאָמָה' (as a maidservant) is needed to teach that he may sell her to invalid men.
