Rabbi Eliezer objects that the verse 'אִם רָעָה בְּעֵינֵי אֲדֹנֶיהָ' (if she is displeasing in the eyes of her master) already implies she is displeasing in marriage, so the word 'לְאָמָה' (as a maidservant) must teach something else: that he may sell her.

items.text: Selling a maidservant to relatives
items.text_en: Selling a maidservant to relatives
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a maidservant can be sold to relatives, using a kal vachomer from selling to disqualifed individuals. It concludes that the verse "לְאָמָה" teaches that she may be sold to relatives, and explains Rabbi Meir's position.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument): if a maidservant can be sold to disqualifed individuals (פסולין), should she not also be sold to relatives (קרובים)? It then rejects the argument because selling to disqualifed individuals allows ייעוד (designation for marriage), while selling to relatives does not.
The Gemara answers that the verse 'לְאָמָה' (as a maidservant) teaches that she may be sold to relatives.

The Gemara explains that Rabbi Meir derives the law of selling to disqualifed individuals from the same source as Rabbi Eliezer, and regarding relatives, he holds like the Rabbis that she may not be sold to relatives.

items.text: Contradictory baraitot on selling to father or son
items.text_en: Contradictory baraitot on selling to father or son
items.desc_en: Two baraitot are presented: one allows selling to the father but not the son, the other forbids both. The Gemara resolves the contradiction by explaining that the Rabbis permit selling to the father when there is a possibility of ייעוד.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited stating that one may sell his daughter to her father but not to her son.
Another baraita is cited forbidding selling to either the father or the son.
The Gemara asks: the second baraita aligns with the Rabbis, but the first baraita — who is its author?
The Gemara resolves that the first baraita also follows the Rabbis, who permit selling to the father when there is a possibility of ייעוד (designation).

items.text: Interpretation of "בְּגַפּוֹ יָבֹא בְּגַפּוֹ יֵצֵא"
items.text_en: Interpretation of "בְּגַפּוֹ יָבֹא בְּגַפּוֹ יֵצֵא"
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the verse about a Hebrew slave leaving alone. Rava says it means he does not leave with severed limbs like a Canaanite slave. Abaye objects that this is derived from another verse, but the Gemara explains the necessity of this verse.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites the verse about a Hebrew slave leaving alone and presents two interpretations: the Tanna Kamma says it means he leaves with his body intact, and Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says it means he leaves alone without a family.
The Gemara asks what the Tanna Kamma's phrase 'with his body he entered, with his body he leaves' means.
Rava explains that the verse teaches that a Hebrew slave does not leave with severed limbs like a Canaanite slave.
Abaye objects that this law is already derived from the verse 'לֹא תֵצֵא כְּצֵאת הָעֲבָדִים' (she shall not go out as the slave women go out).
The Gemara resolves that without this verse, one might think the master could pay for the slave's eye and release him, so the verse teaches that he cannot.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's interpretation
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's interpretation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov interprets "יְחִידִי נִכְנַס יְחִידִי יֵצֵא" to mean that if the slave has a wife and children, the master gives him a Canaanite maidservant; if not, he does not.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's statement that a slave who entered alone leaves alone.
The Gemara asks what the phrase 'יְחִידִי יֵצֵא' (alone he shall leave) means.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov means: if the slave has a wife and children, the master gives him a Canaanite maidservant; if not, he does not.

items.text: Redemption of a Hebrew slave based on purchase price
items.text_en: Redemption of a Hebrew slave based on purchase price
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from verses that a slave redeemed by others is valued at his purchase price, not his current value. This applies to a slave sold to a non-Jew, and is extended to a slave sold to an Israelite via a גזירה שווה.

sub.desc_en: The baraita teaches that a slave sold for one hundred and then worth two hundred is redeemed only for the original purchase price, based on the verse 'מִכֶּסֶף מִקְנָתוֹ' (from the silver of his purchase).
The baraita continues: a slave sold for two hundred and then depreciated to one hundred is redeemed only for the current value, based on the verse 'כְּפִי שָׁנָיו' (according to his years).
The baraita limits this rule to a slave sold to a non-Jew, who is redeemed by relatives and therefore has the lower hand (יָדוֹ עַל הַתַּחְתּוֹנָה).
The Gemara extends the rule to a slave sold to an Israelite via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the repeated word 'שָׂכִיר' (hired laborer).

items.text: Debate on leniency in redemption
items.text_en: Debate on leniency in redemption
items.desc_en: Abaye states he is like Ben Azzai in the markets of Tiberias. A rabbi questions why the verses are interpreted leniently. The Gemara answers that the Torah is lenient with the slave, citing the baraita that one must treat the slave as an equal in food and drink.

sub.desc_en: Abaye declares himself like Ben Azzai in the markets of Tiberias, implying he will teach publicly.
A certain rabbi questions Abaye why the verses are interpreted leniently rather than strictly.
The Gemara answers that the Torah is lenient with the slave, citing the baraita that one must treat the slave as an equal in food and drink.

items.text: The severity of violating the Sabbatical year
items.text_en: The severity of violating the Sabbatical year
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina to show that violating the Sabbatical year leads to selling one's movable property, then fields, then house, then daughter, then borrowing with interest, and finally selling oneself as a slave to a non-Jew.

sub.text: Gemara's citation of Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina
sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's teaching that the dust of the Sabbatical year is severe, beginning with one who trades in seventh-year produce eventually selling movable property.

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's teaching continues
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's teaching continues
sub.desc_en: If one does not repent, he sells his fields, and if still unrepentant, he sells his house.
The Gemara questions the different phrasing 'did not feel' versus 'did not come to his hand', and resolves via Rav Huna that a repeated sin becomes permitted to the sinner.

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's teaching continues
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's teaching continues
sub.desc_en: The progression continues: one sells his daughter rather than borrow with interest, because selling a daughter is a one-time loss while interest accumulates.

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's teaching concludes
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's teaching concludes
sub.desc_en: Finally, one borrows with interest and then sells himself as a slave, first to a Jewish master and ultimately to a non-Jew or a גר תושב (resident alien).

items.text: Opening statement: the slave sold to idolatry itself
items.text_en: Opening statement: the slave sold to idolatry itself
items.desc_en: The segment introduces the case of a Hebrew slave sold to a non-Jew who is himself an idolater, setting up the context for the subsequent discussion.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces the case of a Hebrew slave sold to an idolater himself, setting the stage for the discussion.

items.text: Gemara's answer: the verse returns him
items.text_en: Gemara's answer: the verse returns him
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the verse itself provides redemption for such a slave, citing the teaching of the school of Rabbi Yishmael that the verse 'after he is sold, redemption shall be his' applies even to one who became a priest of idolatry.

sub.desc_en: The gemara responds that the verse 'אחרי נמכר גאולה תהיה לו' (after he is sold, redemption shall be his) teaches that even a slave sold to an idolater is redeemable, countering the concern that he might become a priest of idolatry.

items.text: Objection: perhaps only to prevent defilement
items.text_en: Objection: perhaps only to prevent defilement
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection: perhaps the verse only teaches that redemption is available to prevent him from becoming defiled among non-Jews, but we should be stringent regarding the actual redemption price, following Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina.

sub.text: Gemara's objection (citing Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina)
sub.text_en: Gemara's objection (citing Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina)
sub.desc_en: The gemara objects: perhaps the verse only means redemption is permitted to prevent him from becoming defiled among non-Jews, but we should be stringent regarding the actual redemption price, based on Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's principle.

items.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's resolution: two verses
items.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's resolution: two verses
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves the contradiction by noting two verses: 'if many years remain' and 'if few years remain', which teach that the redemption price depends on the slave's financial gain, not just the years. Rav Yosef praises his derivation as authoritative as Sinai.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves the contradiction by citing two verses: 'if many years remain' and 'if few years remain', explaining that the redemption price depends on the slave's financial gain, not solely on the years.
The Gemara objects that the verses might simply mean to calculate proportionally based on years worked and remaining, not on financial gain.

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak rejects the objection by noting the extra word 'בַּשָּׁנִים' (in the years) in both verses, which teaches that the calculation is based on the slave's financial gain during those years.
Rav Yosef praises Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's derivation as authoritative as if received at Sinai.

items.text: First inquiry: Hebrew slave sold to non-Jew redeemed in halves?
items.text_en: First inquiry: Hebrew slave sold to non-Jew redeemed in halves?
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Chinana asks Rav Sheishes whether a Hebrew slave sold to a non-Jew can be redeemed in halves. Rav Sheishes answers with a gezerah shavah from 'ge'ulaso' of a ancestral field, and also from the verse 'nimkar' implying the whole slave, not half.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Chinana asks Rav Sheishes whether a Hebrew slave sold to a non-Jew can be redeemed in halves.

The Gemara presents the possible reasoning: a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from 'ge'ulaso' of an ancestral field would forbid half-redemption, but perhaps the analogy is applied only leniently, not strictly.
Rav Sheishes answers that just as the verse 'נִמְכַּר' (sold) implies the whole slave, not half, so too 'נִגְאָל' (redeemed) implies the whole, not half, thus the slave cannot be redeemed in halves.

items.text: Abaye's analysis: leniency and stringency if redeemed in halves
items.text_en: Abaye's analysis: leniency and stringency if redeemed in halves
items.desc_en: Abaye explains that if we assume redemption in halves is possible, there are both lenient and stringent scenarios. He illustrates with cases of price fluctuations, showing how the calculation works differently depending on whether the slave's value increased or decreased.

sub.desc_en: Abaye opens by positing that if a Hebrew slave sold to a gentile can be redeemed in halves, there is a lenient scenario: the slave was bought for 100, paid 50, then appreciated to 200; under the halves option he pays 100 and goes free, whereas without halves he would pay 150.

The Gemara objects that the lenient scenario contradicts the principle that when the slave's value increases, redemption is based on the purchase price (מכסף מקנתו); Abaye resolves that the case involves a price that rose, fell, and rose again.

Abaye presents the stringent scenario: the slave was bought for 200, paid 100, then depreciated to 100; under the halves option he pays only 50 and goes free, whereas without halves the remaining 100 is considered a deposit and he pays the full amount.

items.text: Second inquiry: house in a walled city redeemed in halves?
items.text_en: Second inquiry: house in a walled city redeemed in halves?
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Chinana asks Rav Sheishes whether a house in a walled city can be redeemed in halves. Rav Sheishes answers from Rabbi Shimon's midrash: since the seller's power is weakened (the house is forfeited after a year), he is given the leniency of borrowing and redeeming in halves.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Chinana asks Rav Sheshet whether a house in a walled city can be partially redeemed, considering a possible גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from an ancestral field or a distinction between revealed and unrevealed cases.
Rav Sheshet answers that from Rabbi Shimon's midrash it is learned that one may borrow and redeem a house in a walled city in halves, citing the baraita on 'אם גאל יגאל' (if he will redeem).
Rabbi Shimon explains that for a seller of an ancestral field, whose power is enhanced (field returns in Jubilee), his power is weakened regarding borrowing and partial redemption.
Rabbi Shimon contrasts the consecrator, whose power is weakened (field goes to priests in Jubilee), so his power is enhanced regarding borrowing and partial redemption.

Rav Sheshet applies the same logic to a house in a walled city: since the seller's power is weakened (house is forfeited after a year), his power is enhanced to allow borrowing and partial redemption.

items.text: Objection and resolution: the baraita's logic
items.text_en: Objection and resolution: the baraita's logic
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that seems to limit borrowing and redeeming in halves to a consecrated field, not a house. The Gemara resolves that the baraita's logic is not a kal vachomer, as the house seller's power is weakened in one respect (forfeiture) but strengthened in another (immediate redemption), so the leniency of halves applies.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that cites the verse 'אִם גָּאֹל יִגְאַל' (if he will redeem) to teach that one may borrow and redeem and redeem in halves, implying this applies only to a consecrated field, not a house.

The baraita presents a kal vachomer (a fortiori inference): if a seller of an ancestral field, whose power is enhanced (field returns in Jubilee), still has diminished power (cannot borrow and redeem in halves), then a consecrator, whose power is diminished (field goes to priests in Jubilee), should certainly have diminished power (no borrowing or halves).

sub.text: Baraita's rebuttal of the a fortiori inference
sub.text_en: Baraita's rebuttal of the a fortiori inference
sub.desc_en: The baraita rejects the kal vachomer: the seller of an ancestral field has diminished power (cannot redeem immediately), but the consecrator has enhanced power (can redeem immediately), so the inference fails.
The baraita brings a counterexample: a seller of a house in a walled city has enhanced power (can redeem immediately) yet cannot borrow and redeem in halves, disproving the leniency.
The Gemara resolves that the objection is not difficult, implying the baraita's logic is not a kal vachomer and the leniency of halves applies to a house seller.

items.text: סתירה בין ברייתאות בדין גאולה לחצאין בבתי ערי חומה
items.text_en: Resolving the contradiction about borrowing and redeeming in halves
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction between two baraitot: one says one may borrow and redeem in halves, the other says one may not. It resolves the contradiction by attributing the lenient view to Rabbi Shimon and the strict view to the Rabbis.
items.desc: מובאת סתירה בין שתי ברייתאות: האחת אומרת שלווה וגואל וגואל לחצאין, והשנייה אוסרת. הגמרא מיישבת שהברייתא הראשונה כרבי שמעון והשנייה כרבנן.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that one baraita follows the Rabbis and the other follows Rabbi Shimon.
sub.desc: הגמרא מיישבת את הסתירה בין שתי הברייתות: האחת כרבנן והאחת כרבי שמעון.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents the contradiction: one baraita permits borrowing and redeeming in halves, another forbids it.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by attributing the lenient baraita to Rabbi Shimon and the strict one to the Rabbis.
The Gemara provides a mnemonic device for the names of the Sages in the following discussions.

items.text: Challenges and defense of the analogy for a consecrated field
items.text_en: Challenges and defense of the analogy for a consecrated field
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rava challenges the analogy from a seller of a house in a walled city to a consecrator, noting that the seller's power is weakened (redeemable forever) while the consecrator's is strengthened. Rav Acha Saba defends by adding the case of a seller of an ancestral field, and the common element is that both are redeemed but not in halves.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rava objects to the analogy: a seller of a house in a walled city has diminished power (cannot redeem forever), while a consecrator has enhanced power (can redeem forever), so the comparison fails.

Rav Acha Sava defends the analogy by adding the case of a seller of an ancestral field, whose power is enhanced (redeemable forever) yet he cannot borrow and redeem in halves, and the house seller proves the opposite, creating a common denominator.
The Gemara concludes that the common denominator of both cases is that they are redeemed but not in halves, and therefore the consecrator is also subject to this rule.

items.text: Further challenge and defense regarding the second year
items.text_en: Further challenge and defense regarding the second year
items.desc_en: Mar Zutra bar Rav Mari challenges the common element, noting that in the second year the power of the seller is weakened (cannot redeem) while the consecrator's is strengthened. Ravina defends by adding the case of a Hebrew slave sold to a gentile, who can redeem in the second year but not in halves.

sub.desc_en: Mar Zutra bar Rav Mari objects to the common element derivation: the common cases weaken the seller's power in the second year (cannot redeem), but the consecrator's power is strengthened (can redeem in the second year).
Ravina defends the derivation by adding the case of a Hebrew slave sold to a gentile, who can redeem in the second year yet cannot borrow and redeem or partially redeem, thus refuting the objection.

items.text: דילמה: האם בית בערי חומה נגאל לקרובים?
items.text_en: Inquiry: Is a house in a walled city redeemed by relatives?
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Chinana asks Rav Sheshet whether a house in a walled city can be redeemed by relatives. Rav Sheshet answers that it cannot, based on a possible derivation from the word 'ge'ullato' or a distinction between halves and relatives.
items.desc: רב הונא בר חנינא שואל את רב ששת האם מוכר בית בערי חומה יכול להיגאל על ידי קרוביו. רב ששת פוסק שאינו נגאל, ודוחה את האפשרות ללמוד גזירה שווה משדה אחוזה.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Chinana asks Rav Sheshet whether a house in a walled city can be redeemed by relatives.
The gemara considers a possible derivation from a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) on the word 'גאולתו' from the field of ancestral possession, which would permit redemption by relatives.
The gemara raises an alternative possibility: perhaps the word 'גאולה' is written only regarding halves, not relatives, so the analogy would not apply.
Rav Sheshet answers that a house in a walled city cannot be redeemed by relatives.

items.text: Objection from the verse 'Bekhol Ge'ullah' and the dispute between Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Eliezer
items.text_en: Objection from the verse 'Bekhol Ge'ullah' and the dispute between Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Eliezer
items.desc_en: An objection is raised from the verse 'Bekhol ge'ullah titnu' which includes houses and Hebrew slaves. The Gemara initially suggests it refers to houses in walled cities, but deflects to houses in courtyards. It then explains the dispute between Rabbi Yehoshua (redemption is optional) and Rabbi Eliezer (redemption is a duty), citing the verse as establishing it as a duty according to Rabbi Eliezer.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from the verse 'בכל גאולה תתנו' (in all redemption you shall give), which includes houses and a Hebrew slave, and initially suggests it refers to houses in walled cities, but deflects to houses in courtyards.

The Gemara objects that houses in courtyards are explicitly written in the Torah as 'על שדה הארץ יחשב' (shall be considered as the field of the land), and deflects that the verse comes to establish redemption as a duty, according to Rabbi Eliezer.

A baraita is cited: Rabbi Yehoshua interprets the verse 'וגאל את ממכר אחיו' (and he shall redeem his brother's sale) as optional, not obligatory, based on the verse 'ואיש כי לא יהיה לו גואל' (and if a man has no redeemer).

Rabbi Eliezer argues that the verse 'וגאל את ממכר אחיו' (and he shall redeem his brother's sale) is a duty, and the verse 'בכל גאולה תתנו' (in all redemption you shall give) establishes it as an obligation.

items.text: Difficulty for the one who says it includes houses in courtyards
items.text_en: Difficulty for the one who says it includes houses in courtyards
items.desc_en: The Rabbis ask Rav Ashi (or Ravina) that according to the one who says the verse includes houses in courtyards, what is the purpose of the word 'bekhol'? This remains a difficulty.

sub.desc_en: The Rabbis ask Rav Ashi (or Ravina) that according to the one who says the verse includes houses in courtyards, what is the purpose of the word 'בכל' (in all)?
The gemara concludes that this remains a difficulty (קשיא).

items.text: Another objection from the three occurrences of 'yig'alenu'
items.text_en: Another objection from the three occurrences of 'yig'alenu'
items.desc_en: Abaye objects from the three occurrences of 'yig'alenu' which include all redemptions in this order. The Gemara deflects that it refers to houses in courtyards and ancestral fields, and explains that it teaches precedence of closer relatives, as per Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects by citing the three occurrences of 'יִגְאָלֶנּוּ' (he shall redeem him) in the Torah, which he argues include all redemptions in this order, implying houses in walled cities and Hebrew slaves.
The Gemara deflects Abaye's objection by interpreting the three occurrences as referring to houses in courtyards (בתי חצרים) and ancestral fields (שדה אחוזה), not houses in walled cities.

The Gemara objects that houses in courtyards and ancestral fields are already explicitly mentioned in the verse 'עַל שְׂדֵה הָאָרֶץ יֵחָשֵׁב' (it shall be considered as part of the field of the land), so the extra occurrences seem superfluous.

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves the objection by explaining that the three occurrences teach the principle of 'לְקָרוֹב קָרוֹב קוֹדֵם' (the closer relative takes precedence in redemption), not additional categories.

items.text: Inquiry about a Hebrew slave sold to an Israelite and resolution
items.text_en: Inquiry about a Hebrew slave sold to an Israelite and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses where Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's statement was said: regarding a Hebrew slave sold to an Israelite, whether he is redeemed by relatives. The inquiry is only according to the Rabbis (not Rabbi). The Gemara attempts to resolve it from the verse 'Bekhol ge'ullah' but deflects that it refers to a slave sold to a gentile, which is explicitly stated in the Torah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks where Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's statement was said, specifying that the inquiry about a Hebrew slave sold to an Israelite being redeemed by relatives is only according to the Rabbis, not Rabbi.

The Gemara poses the dilemma: do the Rabbis derive redemption by relatives via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the word 'שָׂכִיר' (hired laborer), or do they interpret 'יִגְאָלֶנּוּ' (he shall redeem him) as applying only to this case and not to others?

The Gemara attempts to resolve the question by citing the verse 'בְּכֹל גְּאוּלָּה תִּתְּנוּ' (in all redemptions you shall give), which includes houses and a Hebrew slave, but deflects that this refers to a Hebrew slave sold to a gentile, not to an Israelite.

The Gemara objects that a Hebrew slave sold to a gentile is explicitly stated in the Torah with the verse 'אוֹ דֹדוֹ אוֹ בֶן דֹּדוֹ יִגְאָלֶנּוּ' (his uncle or his cousin shall redeem him), so the verse 'בְּכֹל גְּאוּלָּה' cannot be needed to include that case.

items.text: Gemara's question about the three 'yigalanenu' verses
items.text_en: Gemara's question about the three 'yigalanenu' verses
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the three occurrences of 'yigalanenu' include houses in walled cities and a Hebrew slave sold to an Israelite. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak answers that it refers to prioritizing the closer relative.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the verse establishes redemption as an obligation, even according to Rabbi Yehoshua.
The Gemara asks what the three occurrences of 'יִגְאָלֶנּוּ' teach.
The Gemara suggests that the verses include houses in walled cities and a Hebrew slave sold to an Israelite.
The Gemara rejects the suggestion and says it refers to houses in open areas and ancestral fields, which are already explicit.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves that the verses teach that the closer relative has priority in redemption.

items.text: Mishnah: Acquisition and release of the pierced slave
items.text_en: Mishnah: Acquisition and release of the pierced slave
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the pierced slave is acquired by piercing and frees himself at the Jubilee or upon the master's death, citing verses.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the pierced slave is acquired by piercing, citing the verse 'וְרָצַע אֲדֹנָיו אֶת אׇזְנוֹ בַּמַּרְצֵעַ'.
The Mishnah states that the pierced slave frees himself at the Jubilee or upon the master's death, citing 'וַעֲבָדוֹ' to exclude the master's children and 'לְעֹלָם' to refer to the Jubilee period.

items.text: Baraita: Materials for piercing
items.text_en: Baraita: Materials for piercing
items.desc_en: A baraita debates which materials can be used for piercing: Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda includes anything held in hand, while Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi limits it to metal, and adds a large awl.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that only an awl is explicitly mentioned, and Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda derives from 'and you shall take' that any hand-held implement is valid.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi limits piercing to metal implements by analogy to an awl, and alternatively includes a large awl from the definite article.

items.text: Debate on piercing location and hermeneutics
items.text_en: Debate on piercing location and hermeneutics
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar reports Yudan bar Ribbi's view that piercing is only in the soft part of the ear, while the Sages say a priest cannot be pierced due to a blemish. The Gemara explains the dispute as a difference between Rabbi's klal u'frat and Rabbi Yosei's ribbui u'miut methods.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar reports Yudan bar Ribbi's view that piercing is only in the soft part of the ear, while the Sages say a priest cannot be pierced due to a blemish; the Gemara asks what principle underlies the dispute.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi uses the hermeneutic of generalization and detail (כלל ופרט) to limit the piercing implement to metal.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda uses the hermeneutic of amplification and restriction (ריבוי ומיעוט) to include all implements except one.
The Gemara concludes that the amplification includes all items, and the restriction excludes only a corrosive substance (סם).

items.text: Explanation of 'the awl' as the large one
items.text_en: Explanation of 'the awl' as the large one
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that 'the awl' means the unique one among awls, similar to Rava's interpretation of 'the thigh'.

sub.desc_en: Mar states that 'the awl' includes the large awl, and the Gemara explains that this is derived from the definite article, similar to Rava's interpretation of 'the thigh'.

items.text: Reiteration and resolution: priest and piercing
items.text_en: Reiteration and resolution: priest and piercing
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar repeats Yudan bar Ribbi's view and the Sages' objection. Rabba bar Rav Sheila resolves that the verse 'and he shall return to his family' means to the honored family member, so a priest cannot be pierced.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar reports that Yudan bar Ribbi taught that piercing is done only on the earlobe.
The Sages object that a Hebrew slave who is a priest is not pierced because it would render him blemished.
The Gemara questions why a priest cannot be pierced even if it makes him blemished.
Rabba bar Rav Sheila resolves that the verse 'and he shall return to his family' means to the honored family member, so a priest cannot be pierced.

items.text: Inquiry: Can a priest's master give him a Canaanite maidservant?
items.text_en: Inquiry: Can a priest's master give him a Canaanite maidservant?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a priest who is a Hebrew slave can be given a Canaanite maidservant. Rav permits it, Shmuel forbids it. Rav Nachman challenges Rav Anan for not citing the baraita that a priest is not pierced, implying he cannot have a maidservant.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a dilemma: may a master give a Canaanite maidservant to a Hebrew slave who is a priest, considering the novelty of the permission?
Rav permits and Shmuel prohibits a master giving a Canaanite maidservant to a priest-slave.
Rav Nachman challenges Rav Anan for not citing the baraita that a priest-slave is not pierced because it makes him blemished, implying he cannot have a maidservant.
Rav Nachman explains that if a priest cannot have a maidservant, he cannot declare love for his wife and children, so the baraita's reason (blemish) proves he can have one.

items.text: Inquiry: May a priest marry a captive woman (yefat to'ar)?
items.text_en: Inquiry: May a priest marry a captive woman (yefat to'ar)?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a priest may marry a captive woman. Rav permits it, Shmuel forbids it. The dispute is analyzed: whether it concerns the first or second act of intercourse, with different versions of the debate.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a dilemma: may a priest engage in intercourse with a captive woman (יפת תואר), given the novelty of the permission and the additional mitzvot for priests?
Rav rules that a priest is permitted to engage in intercourse with a captive woman.
Shmuel rules that a priest is prohibited from engaging in intercourse with a captive woman.
According to the first version, everyone agrees that the first act of intercourse is permitted because the Torah spoke only against the evil inclination.
The dispute concerns the second act of intercourse: Rav permits it because once permitted, it remains permitted; Shmuel prohibits it because she becomes a convert, unfit for a priest.

According to the second version, everyone agrees the second act is prohibited; the dispute is about the first act: Rav permits it due to the evil inclination, Shmuel prohibits it because if he cannot bring her home, he cannot take her initially.

items.text: Baraita on yefat to'ar
items.text_en: Baraita on yefat to'ar
items.desc_en: A baraita expounds the verses on the captive woman, stating that the Torah speaks against the evil inclination, and it is better for Israelites to eat meat.

sub.desc_en: The baraita expounds the verses on the captive woman, stating that the Torah speaks against the evil inclination, and it is better for Israelites to eat meat.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Derashot on the verses of the Hebrew slave
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Derashot on the verses of the Hebrew slave
items.desc_en: The Mishnah expounds the verses regarding the Hebrew slave who wishes to remain, deriving that he must be pierced only if he declares his love at the right time, and that he cannot take multiple wives for himself and his family. It also teaches that he should not be oppressed in war.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah expounds the verses regarding the captive woman, deriving that she is permitted only after proper slaughter, that desire alone suffices even if she is unattractive, that she is taken alone and not with a companion, that the master acquires her exclusively for himself and not for his father or son, and that he must not oppress her in war.

items.text: Baraita: The requirement to declare at the beginning and end of the sixth year
items.text_en: Baraita: The requirement to declare at the beginning and end of the sixth year
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that the slave must declare his love both at the beginning and at the end of the sixth year. If he only declares at the beginning, he is not pierced, as the verse says 'I will not go out free'—implying at the time of going out. If he only declares at the end, he is not pierced, as the verse says 'If the slave shall say'—implying while he is still a slave.

sub.desc_en: The baraita teaches that the slave must declare his love twice—at the beginning and end of the sixth year—and derives from verses that each declaration is required at a specific time.

items.text: Gemara's question and Rava's resolution on the timing of the declaration
items.text_en: Gemara's question and Rava's resolution on the timing of the declaration
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the baraita: why does the first case derive from 'I will not go out free' rather than from the requirement of 'I love my master'? And why does the second case need a verse, since at the end of the sixth year he is still a slave? Rava explains that 'beginning of the sixth' means the beginning of the last perutah, and 'end of the sixth' means the end of the last perutah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the first case of the baraita derives the invalidity from 'I will not go out free' rather than from the requirement of 'I love my master', which is absent.
The Gemara further questions why the second case needs a verse, since at the end of the sixth year the slave is still a slave.

Rava resolves the questions by explaining that 'beginning of the sixth' refers to the beginning of the last perutah (monetary unit) of the sixth year, and 'end of the sixth' refers to the end of that last perutah.

items.text: Baraita: Conditions of mutual love and benefit between slave and master
items.text_en: Baraita: Conditions of mutual love and benefit between slave and master
items.desc_en: A baraita lists conditions for the slave to be pierced: he must have a wife and children, and his master must also have a wife and children; the slave must love his master and be loved by him; both must be healthy. If any condition is missing, he is not pierced.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that if the slave has a wife and children but the master does not, or vice versa, the slave is not pierced.
The baraita continues listing conditions: mutual love, mutual health, and if any condition is missing, the slave is not pierced.

items.text: Rav Beivai's query: both are sick
items.text_en: Rav Beivai's query: both are sick
items.desc_en: Rav Beivai bar Abaye asks: if both the slave and the master are sick, what is the law? Do we require 'with you' (which exists) or 'for it is good for him with you' (which may not be good)? The question remains unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: Rav Beivai bar Abaye asks: if both the slave and the master are sick, is the slave eligible for ear-boring? Do we require the word 'עִמָּךְ' (with you), which exists, or the phrase 'כִּי טוֹב לוֹ עִמָּךְ' (for it is good for him with you), which may not be fulfilled?
The question remains unresolved (תיקו, let it stand).

items.text: Baraita: The master must provide equal living conditions
items.text_en: Baraita: The master must provide equal living conditions
items.desc_en: A baraita expounds 'for it is good for him with you' to mean that the master must provide the slave with the same quality of food, drink, and bedding as himself. From here they said: one who acquires a Hebrew slave acquires a master for himself.

sub.desc_en: The baraita expounds the verse 'כי טוב לו עמך' to require the master to provide equal food, drink, and bedding, concluding that acquiring a Hebrew slave is like acquiring a master for oneself.

items.text: Baraita and Gemara: Master's obligation to support the slave's family
items.text_en: Baraita and Gemara: Master's obligation to support the slave's family
items.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi Shimon who derives from the verses that the master is obligated to support the slave's children and wife. The Gemara explains that both derivations are necessary: for children, one might think they are not obligated because they cannot work, but for the wife, one might think she should work and eat; and vice versa.

sub.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi Shimon who derives from the verses that the master is obligated to support the slave's children and wife.
The Gemara explains that the derivation for children is necessary because one might think they are not obligated since they cannot work, but for the wife one might think she should work and eat.

The Gemara adds that the derivation for the wife is necessary because one might think children are not obligated since they are accustomed to being supported, but the wife is not; therefore both derivations are needed.

items.text: Beginning of a new baraita
items.text_en: Beginning of a new baraita
items.desc_en: The text begins a new baraita, but the content is not provided in this segment.

sub.desc_en: The baraita begins with the standard formula 'תנו רבנן' (the rabbis taught), introducing a new teaching.

items.text: Gemara's clarification of the piercing verse
items.text_en: Gemara's clarification of the piercing verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara refines the interpretation of the verse about piercing the slave's ear. It first considers a hypothetical reading that would require piercing the ear against the door, then corrects this by citing the verse that explicitly mentions both ear and door, concluding that the piercing must go through the ear into the door.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes a hypothetical reading of the verse that would require piercing the ear against the door, then objects that the verse already mentions piercing the ear.

The Gemara corrects the interpretation: one might think to pierce the ear externally and then press it against the door, but the verse 'in his ear and in the door' teaches that one pierces through the ear until reaching the door.

items.text: Requirement that the door be standing
items.text_en: Requirement that the door be standing
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from the word 'door' that it must be standing, not detached, by comparing it to 'doorpost' which is always standing.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a possible interpretation: from the word 'door' one might think it applies whether the door is standing or detached.
The Gemara resolves the ambiguity by invoking a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) with 'doorpost' (מזוזה), which is always standing, thus the door must also be standing.

items.text: Homiletical interpretations of the piercing
items.text_en: Homiletical interpretations of the piercing
items.desc_en: Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai and Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi each offer homiletical interpretations of why the ear and door are specifically chosen for the piercing ritual, connecting them to the Exodus and the principle that Israelites are servants only to God.

sub.desc_en: Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai interprets the piercing of the ear homiletically: the ear that heard God's declaration at Sinai that Israelites are servants only to Him is pierced because this slave acquired a master for himself.

Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi offers a complementary homily: the door and doorpost, which witnessed the Passover in Egypt and the liberation of Israel, testify against the slave who re-enslaves himself, so he is pierced before them.

items.text: Mishnah: Acquisition and release of a Canaanite slave
items.text_en: Mishnah: Acquisition and release of a Canaanite slave
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a Canaanite slave is acquired through money, document, or hazakah, and can be freed through money via others or a document via himself according to Rabbi Meir, while the Sages say money via himself and document via others, provided the money is from others.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the modes of acquisition and release for a Canaanite slave, with a dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages.

items.text: Gemara: Source for acquisition modes
items.text_en: Gemara: Source for acquisition modes
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives the modes of acquisition for a Canaanite slave from a biblical analogy to a field, but rejects the comparison regarding return in the Jubilee year, citing the verse that they are to be slaves forever.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of the Mishnah's acquisition modes for a Canaanite slave and answers by citing the verse 'וְהִתְנַחַלְתֶּם אֹתָם לִבְנֵיכֶם' (and you shall bequeath them to your children), drawing an analogy to a field (שדה אחוזה) which is acquired by money, document, and possession.

The Gemara objects that if the analogy to a field were complete, the slave would return to the owner in the Jubilee year, but the verse 'לְעֹלָם בָּהֶם תַּעֲבֹדוּ' (you shall work them forever) teaches that the slave does not return.

items.text: Discussion of acquisition by exchange and meshikhah
items.text_en: Discussion of acquisition by exchange and meshikhah
items.desc_en: A baraisa adds acquisition by exchange (halipin). The Gemara explains why our Tanna did not list it, and then discusses Shmuel's statement that a slave is acquired by meshikhah (pulling), and why meshikhah is not listed in the Mishnah.

sub.desc_en: A baraita adds that a Canaanite slave is also acquired by exchange (חליפין).
The Gemara asks why our Tanna (of the Mishnah) did not list exchange as a mode of acquisition.
The Gemara answers that our Tanna only lists modes that apply to both land and movables; exchange applies only to movables, not land, so he omitted it.

items.text: Clarification of meshikhah and comparison to animal
items.text_en: Clarification of meshikhah and comparison to animal
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Shmuel's distinction between grabbing and calling, citing a baraisa that for an animal, calling it is a valid meshikhah. The resolution is that an animal goes by its owner's intent, while a slave goes by his own intent, except for a minor slave who is like an animal.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel states that a Canaanite slave is acquired through meshikhah (pulling), specifying that grabbing the slave and bringing him acquires him, but calling him does not.

The Gemara questions why the Tanna of our Mishnah omitted meshikhah from the modes of acquisition, and explains that he only listed modes common to both land and movables, not meshikhah which applies only to movables.
The Gemara objects to Shmuel's distinction, citing a baraisa that for an animal, calling it is a valid meshikhah.
The baraisa details how meshikhah works for an animal, including calling it, and Rabbi Asi (or Rabbi Acha) adds that it must walk a full body length.

sub.text: Resolution by the Sages and Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Resolution by the Sages and Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the objection: an animal goes by its owner's intent, while a slave goes by his own intent, except for a minor slave who is like an animal, as stated by Rav Ashi.

items.text: Discussion of hazakah and acquisition by lifting
items.text_en: Discussion of hazakah and acquisition by lifting
items.desc_en: The baraisa details acts of hazakah that acquire a slave. Rabbi Shimon comments that hazakah should not be greater than hagbahah (lifting), which acquires everywhere. Rav Ashi explains that if the slave lifts his master, he is acquired, but not if the master lifts him. The Gemara then questions whether a maidservant could be acquired through sexual relations, and discusses the difference between normal and abnormal relations.

sub.desc_en: The baraita lists acts of hazakah (taking possession) that acquire a Canaanite slave, including lifting him.
Rabbi Shimon objects that hazakah should not be greater than hagbahah (lifting), which acquires everywhere.
The Gemara asks what Rabbi Shimon means by his statement.
Rav Ashi explains that if the slave lifts his master, he is acquired, but not if the master lifts him, and Rabbi Shimon's point is that hazakah cannot be more effective than hagbahah.
The Gemara asks whether a maidservant could be acquired through sexual relations, given the logic of acquisition by benefit.
The Gemara answers that in the case of a maidservant, both parties benefit, unlike the slave who suffers when lifted.
The Gemara asks what about abnormal sexual relations, where there is no mutual pleasure.
Rav Achai bar Adda answers that both parties may still derive pleasure, and the verse 'משכבי אשה' (the lying of a woman) equates normal and abnormal relations.

items.text: Story of Rabbi Yehuda Hindua'a and Mar Zutra
items.text_en: Story of Rabbi Yehuda Hindua'a and Mar Zutra
items.desc_en: A story is told about Rabbi Yehuda Hindua'a, a convert with no heirs, who was ill. Mar Zutra visited him and, seeing he was very ill, instructed his slave to remove his shoes and bring them home, possibly as a means of acquisition.

sub.desc_en: The gemara tells a story about Rabbi Yehuda Hindua'a, a convert with no heirs, who fell ill; Mar Zutra visited him, saw his condition was grave, and instructed his slave to remove his shoes and bring them home, with some saying the slave was an adult.

items.text: Opening Mishnah citation
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah citation
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a slave can acquire his freedom through money via others, implying not by himself, and through a document by himself, implying not via others.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that a slave can acquire freedom through money via others, implying not by himself, and through a document by himself, implying not via others.

items.text: Alternative version and baraita about a convert's slaves
items.text_en: Alternative version and baraita about a convert's slaves
items.desc_en: An alternative version of the Mishnah is presented, and a baraita is cited regarding a convert who died and whose slaves were taken by Israelites, with Abba Shaul distinguishing between adult and minor slaves.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents an alternative version of the Mishnah, stating that the slave was a minor, and that this version does not follow Abba Shaul.
A baraita is cited about a convert who died and whose property was seized by Israelites, where the Tanna Kamma rules that both adult and minor slaves acquire themselves as free men.
Abba Shaul distinguishes between adult slaves, who acquire themselves as free men, and minor slaves, who are acquired by whoever takes possession of them.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's first clause
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's first clause
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling that a slave acquires freedom through money via others but not by himself, considering whether it is with or without his knowledge. It concludes that it must be with his knowledge, teaching that a slave has no acquisition without his master.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's ruling that a slave acquires freedom through money via others but not by himself refers to a case without his knowledge, citing Rabbi Meir's principle that it is a detriment (חוב) to leave the master, and the rule that one cannot act to someone's detriment in their absence.

The Gemara resolves that the case must be with the slave's knowledge, and the Mishnah teaches that a slave has no acquisition (קניין) without his master, so others can acquire for him but he cannot acquire for himself.

items.text: Contradiction from the Mishnah's second clause
items.text_en: Contradiction from the Mishnah's second clause
items.desc_en: The Gemara points out a contradiction: if the first clause is with his knowledge, then the second clause (document by himself, not via others) is problematic because via others should also work. The suggestion that 'by himself' means 'even by himself' is rejected by citing a baraita of Rabbi Meir.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: if the first clause is with his knowledge, then the second clause (document by himself, not via others) is problematic because via others should also work.
The Gemara suggests that 'by himself' means 'even by himself', but rejects this by citing a baraita of Rabbi Meir that explicitly states 'by himself and not via others'.

items.text: Abaye's resolution: money is different because it can be acquired against the slave's will
items.text_en: Abaye's resolution: money is different because it can be acquired against the slave's will
items.desc_en: Abaye argues that the Mishnah deals with a case without the slave's knowledge, and money is unique because the master can acquire it for the slave against his will, unlike a document. The Gemara objects that a document also has this quality, but Abaye distinguishes between types of documents; however, the Gemara notes that money is a single type, so the distinction fails.

sub.desc_en: Abaye resolves the difficulty by asserting that the Mishnah deals with a case without the slave's knowledge, and money is unique because the master can acquire it for the slave against his will.
The Gemara objects that a document also can be acquired against the slave's will, but Abaye distinguishes between types of documents.
The Gemara rejects Abaye's distinction, noting that money is a single type, so the distinction between types of documents does not apply.

items.text: Rava's alternative explanation
items.text_en: Rava's alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Rava explains that money works because the master's acceptance causes the acquisition, while a document requires acceptance by others, so the Mishnah's distinction stands.

sub.desc_en: Rava explains that money works because the master's acceptance causes the acquisition, while a document requires acceptance by others, so the Mishnah's distinction stands.

items.text: Analysis of the Sages' opinion and identification of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
items.text_en: Analysis of the Sages' opinion and identification of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
items.desc_en: The Gemara examines the Sages' ruling that a slave acquires freedom through money by himself but not via others, and through a document via others but not by himself. It resolves the contradictions by identifying the source as Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, who holds that a document must be given to a domain not his own, and concludes there are three disputes on the matter.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah cites the Sages' ruling that a slave acquires freedom through money by himself but not via others, and through a document via others but not by himself.
The Gemara questions why the Sages restrict money acquisition to the slave himself, given that receiving money on his behalf without his knowledge should be a זכות (benefit) and thus valid.
The Gemara objects that if the phrase 'by himself' includes even via others, then the document clause contradicts the principle that a slave's hand and his get (שטר) come together.
The Gemara objects that if the document clause includes even via others, then the Mishnah should have combined both acquisition methods into a single general statement.

The Gemara resolves that the Sages' opinion actually holds that money works both by himself and via others, while the document restriction is attributed to Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, yielding three disputes on the matter.

items.text: Rabbah's derivation and a query
items.text_en: Rabbah's derivation and a query
items.desc_en: Rabbah explains Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's reasoning by a verbal analogy from a woman: just as a woman requires a get to be given to a domain not her own, so too a slave requires a document to be given to a domain not his own. The daf ends with a query from Rabbah.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah explains Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's reasoning by deriving a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the word 'לה' (to her) used for both a woman and a slave: just as a woman requires a גט (bill of divorce) to be given to a domain not her own, so too a slave requires a document of emancipation to be given to a domain not his own.
Rabbah raises a query (בעיא) that is left unresolved at the end of the daf.

items.text: Question about a slave as an agent for his own get
items.text_en: Question about a slave as an agent for his own get
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question regarding Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar: can a Canaanite slave appoint an agent to receive his bill of manumission from his master? It compares the slave to a woman via a verbal analogy, but questions whether the slave's inability to receive his own get prevents him from appointing an agent. The Gemara resolves that the analogy holds.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question regarding Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar: can a Canaanite slave appoint an agent to receive his bill of manumission from his master, given the verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) from a woman?
The Gemara resolves the question: after raising it, it concludes that the verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) from a woman applies, so the slave can appoint an agent.

items.text: Challenge from Rav Huna's statement about priests
items.text_en: Challenge from Rav Huna's statement about priests
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rav Huna's statement that priests are agents of God, not of Israel, and questions whether there is anything Israel cannot do that priests can. It objects with the case of a slave, who cannot receive his own get but can appoint an agent. The Gemara distinguishes: Israelites have no involvement in the Torah of sacrifices, while slaves are involved in gittin, as a baraita shows a slave can receive another slave's get.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rav Huna's statement that priests are agents of God, not of Israel, and challenges that if they were our agents, there would be nothing we cannot do that they can.
The Gemara objects with the case of a slave, who cannot receive his own get but can appoint an agent.

The Gemara distinguishes: Israelites have no involvement in the Torah of sacrifices, while slaves are involved in gittin, as a baraita shows a slave can receive another slave's get from his master but not from his own master.

items.text: Initial framing of the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis
items.text_en: Initial framing of the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the dispute in a baraita about a slave acquiring money on condition of freedom hinges on whether a slave has acquisition without his master (Rabbi Meir says no, the Rabbis say yes).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the dispute in the baraita about a slave acquiring money on condition of freedom hinges on whether a slave has acquisition without his master (Rabbi Meir says no, the Rabbis say yes).

items.text: Rabbah's interpretation: condition that the master has no rights
items.text_en: Rabbah's interpretation: condition that the master has no rights
items.desc_en: Rabbah says all agree a slave has no acquisition without his master; the dispute is about a gift given on condition that the master has no rights. Rabbi Meir holds the condition is ineffective because the slave's acquisition automatically goes to the master, while the Rabbis hold the condition is valid.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah in the name of Rav Sheishet establishes that all agree a slave has no acquisition without his master, and frames the dispute as a case where a third party gives the slave a coin on condition that the master has no rights over it.

Rabbah explains that Rabbi Meir holds the condition is ineffective because the slave's acquisition automatically transfers to the master, while the Rabbis hold the condition is valid and the slave acquires the coin for himself.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's alternative interpretation: condition of freedom
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's alternative interpretation: condition of freedom
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar says all agree the slave acquires and the master acquires; the dispute is about a gift given on condition that the slave go free. Rabbi Meir again says the condition is ineffective, while the Rabbis say the condition prevents the master from acquiring because the gift is not given to the slave for his own benefit.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar introduces an alternative interpretation: everyone agrees that the slave acquires and the master acquires, and the dispute is about a gift given on condition that the slave go free.
Rabbi Meir maintains that when the giver says 'acquire', the slave acquires and the master acquires, and the condition 'on condition' is ineffective.

The Rabbis maintain that the giver does not transfer the money to the slave himself, since he only said 'on condition that you are emancipated with it', so the condition is valid and the slave is emancipated.

items.text: Introduction of contradictions within Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis
items.text_en: Introduction of contradictions within Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Meir's and the Rabbis' positions in this dispute seem to contradict their own views elsewhere, and introduces a baraita to examine this.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction between Rabbi Meir's position here and his position elsewhere, and similarly for the Rabbis, introducing a baraita to examine this.

items.text: Opening Mishnah and initial question
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and initial question
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a woman does not redeem second tithe without adding a fifth, but Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says in the name of Rabbi Meir that she does. The Gemara questions how this is possible: if she uses her husband's money for his tithe, she acts as his agent; if she uses her own money for his tithe, the Torah says 'a man' not 'a woman'.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute: the Tanna Kamma rules that a woman does not redeem second tithe without adding a fifth, while Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar in the name of Rabbi Meir rules that she does.

The Gemara questions how Rabbi Meir's position is possible: if the woman uses her husband's money for his tithe, she acts as his agent and must add a fifth; if she uses her own money, the Torah says 'איש' (a man) not 'אשה' (a woman), implying she cannot redeem his tithe at all.
The Gemara considers the alternative scenario: if she uses her own money for his tithe, the Torah's phrase 'איש' excludes a woman from redeeming another's tithe.

The Gemara proposes a scenario where another person gives the woman a sum of money specifically for redeeming the husband's tithe, but then notes that this would reverse the positions of the Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Meir.

Abaye says to reverse the Mishnah's positions, while Rava says not to reverse, explaining that the case involves tithe that came from a woman's property, and Rabbi Meir holds that second tithe is ממון הקדש (sacred property) which the husband does not acquire.
Rava explains that the Rabbis (Tanna Kamma) hold that second tithe is ממון הדיוט (ordinary property) which the husband acquires, so the woman acts as his agent and must add a fifth.

items.text: Second possibility rejected
items.text_en: Second possibility rejected
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the possibility that she uses her own money for his tithe, because the Torah says 'a man' (איש) and not 'a woman'.

items.text: Third scenario proposed
items.text_en: Third scenario proposed
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests a scenario where another person gives her a sum of money on condition that she redeem the tithe with it, and notes that the opinions seem reversed.

items.text: Abaye and Rava's resolution
items.text_en: Abaye and Rava's resolution
items.desc_en: Abaye says to reverse the opinions. Rava says not to reverse, explaining that the case involves tithe that came from a woman's property (בי נשא), and Rabbi Meir holds that tithe is sacred property (ממון הקדש) so the husband does not acquire it, while the Rabbis hold it is ordinary property (ממון הדיוט) so the husband acquires it, and she acts as his agent.

sub.desc_en: Abaye proposes reversing the opinions in the Mishnah to resolve the contradiction.

Rava rejects reversal and explains that the case involves tithe from the wife's property (בי נשא), where Rabbi Meir holds tithe is ממון הקדש (sacred property) so the husband does not acquire it, while the Rabbis hold it is ממון הדיוט (ordinary property) so the husband acquires it and she acts as his agent.

items.text: Derivation for limbs that do not regrow
items.text_en: Derivation for limbs that do not regrow
items.desc_en: A Tanna taught that a slave goes free for tooth, eye, and other limbs that do not regrow. The Gemara explains that tooth and eye are explicitly written, and other limbs are derived by analogy: like tooth and eye, they are visible and permanent defects.

sub.desc_en: A Tanna taught that a slave goes free for tooth, eye, and other limbs that do not regrow.
The Gemara asks: Granted, tooth and eye are explicitly written, but from where do we derive other limbs?
The Gemara answers: They are derived by analogy to tooth and eye — like tooth and eye, they are visible and permanent defects.

items.text: Objection and defense of the derivation
items.text_en: Objection and defense of the derivation
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that tooth and eye might be two verses that come as one (שני כתובים הבאים כאחד) which do not teach a general rule. It then explains why they are necessary: if only 'tooth' were written, one might think even a tooth that regrows is included.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that tooth and eye might be two verses that come as one (שני כתובים הבאים כאחד) which do not teach a general rule.
The Gemara explains why both verses are necessary: if only 'tooth' were written, one might think even a tooth that regrows is included.

items.text: Derivation of which limbs qualify for freedom
items.text_en: Derivation of which limbs qualify for freedom
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why both 'eye' and 'tooth' are written in the Torah, and then uses a כלל ופרט וכלל (generalization, specification, and generalization) to derive that any permanent, visible, and disabling blemish qualifies. It then addresses a challenge from a baraita about a tooth that is dislodged but not completely lost, and another about a hand that is crushed but will heal, showing that the verse 'לחפשי ישלחנו' is a ריבוי (amplification) that includes some cases but not others.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that both 'eye' and 'tooth' are written to exclude a milk tooth, which regenerates.
The Gemara raises an objection: perhaps the verses should be interpreted as a generalization and a detail, limiting freedom only to eye and tooth.

The Gemara answers that the verse 'to freedom shall he send him' is a second generalization, forming a כלל ופרט וכלל (generalization, specification, and generalization), which includes any permanent, visible blemish.

The Gemara objects that a stricter limitation would require the blemish to also disable the limb, but a baraita about pulling out a beard shows that the verse is an amplification (ריבוי) including non-disabling blemishes.
The Gemara resolves that the amplification does not include temporary injuries, as the explicit examples of tooth and eye exclude them.

items.text: Dispute about the need for a writ of manumission
items.text_en: Dispute about the need for a writ of manumission
items.desc_en: A baraita records a dispute among Tannaim: Rabbi Shimon, Rabbi Eliezer, and Rabbi Akiva hold that a slave who loses a limb needs a writ of manumission (גט שחרור), while Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Tarfon hold he does not. The Gemara explains Rabbi Shimon's reasoning, deriving from a גזירה שוה (verbal analogy) with divorce, and then explains Rabbi Meir's position based on the placement of the word 'חפשי' in the verse.

sub.desc_en: A baraita records a dispute among Tannaim: Rabbi Shimon, Rabbi Eliezer, and Rabbi Akiva hold that a slave who loses a limb needs a writ of manumission (גט שחרור), while Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Tarfon hold he does not.

The deciders before the Sages propose a compromise: Rabbi Tarfon's view applies to tooth and eye (explicit in Torah), Rabbi Akiva's to other limbs (a rabbinic interpretation). The Gemara questions and clarifies that it is a rabbinic midrash, not a penalty.

The Gemara explains Rabbi Shimon's reasoning: a גזירה שוה (verbal analogy) from divorce requires a document. Rabbi Meir argues that the verse's wording 'to freedom shall he send him' implies freedom from the start, no document needed.

items.text: Damage by sound and the liability of a frightener
items.text_en: Damage by sound and the liability of a frightener
items.desc_en: A baraita states that if a master strikes his slave's eye and blinds it, or his ear and deafens it, the slave goes free, but if he merely shouts near his eye or ear without contact, the slave does not go free. Rav Shemen questions this, citing cases where sound causes damage (e.g., a rooster breaking glass, a horse or donkey breaking vessels). Rav Ashi distinguishes humans because they are sentient and can be held liable for frightening, citing a baraita that one who frightens another is exempt from human courts but liable in heavenly courts, and only if he holds him and shouts is he liable.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that striking the eye or ear directly frees the slave, but shouting near them does not.
Rav Shemen questions whether sound is considered nothing, given that it can cause damage.
Rami bar Yeḥezkel cites a baraita that a rooster's crow breaking glass requires full payment, showing sound can cause damage.

sub.text: Rav Yosef citing the Sages of Rav's study hall
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef citing the Sages of Rav's study hall
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef adds that a horse's neigh or donkey's bray breaking vessels requires half damages, further supporting that sound can cause damage.
Rav Ashi distinguishes humans because they are sentient and frighten themselves, so the sound alone is not the direct cause.
A baraita supports that one who frightens another is exempt from human courts unless he physically holds him, showing that mere sound does not create liability for the frightener.

items.text: Diminished vision or loose tooth
items.text_en: Diminished vision or loose tooth
items.desc_en: Two baraitot discuss cases where the eye was already dim or the tooth already loose before the master's blow. The first baraita says that if the slave can still use the limb, he does not go free; if not, he does. The second baraita says that if the limb was already impaired and the master completely destroyed it, the slave goes free if he could previously use it, but not if he could not. The Gemara explains why both baraitot are necessary.

sub.desc_en: First baraita: if master struck a healthy eye/tooth and weakened it, slave goes free only if he can no longer use it.
Second baraita: if the limb was already impaired and master completely destroyed it, slave goes free only if he could previously use it.
Gemara explains why both baraitot are necessary: each teaches a case the other might have excluded.

items.text: Master as physician and intent to destroy
items.text_en: Master as physician and intent to destroy
items.desc_en: A baraita states that if the master is a physician and the slave asks him to treat his eye or tooth, and the master accidentally destroys it, the slave goes free. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel requires intent to destroy, based on the word 'ושחתה'. The Gemara explains that the Rabbis use this word to exempt one who accidentally destroys a fetus while performing surgery on a maidservant, as taught by Rabbi Elazar. The other opinion derives this from a different reading.

sub.desc_en: The baraita presents a case where the master is a physician and the slave asks for treatment, but the master accidentally destroys the eye or tooth; the slave is emancipated.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel requires intent to destroy, based on the verse 'ושחתה' (and destroys it).
The Gemara asks what the Rabbis (who disagree with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel) derive from the word 'ושחתה'.
The Gemara answers that the Rabbis use the word to exempt one who accidentally destroys a fetus while performing surgery on a maidservant, as taught by Rabbi Elazar.
The Gemara notes that the other opinion (Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel) derives the same halakha from the difference between 'ושחת' and 'ושחתה', while the Rabbis do not expound that difference.

items.text: Blind eye and a digression to bird offerings
items.text_en: Blind eye and a digression to bird offerings
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet rules that if a slave's eye was already blind and the master gouged it out, the slave goes free because he is now missing a limb. The Gemara then digresses to a baraita about bird offerings, stating that the laws of תמות וזכרות (unblemished and male) apply to animals but not to birds, and that if a bird's wing withered, leg was cut off, or eye was gouged out, it is invalid, derived from the verse 'מן העוף'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet rules that if a slave's eye was already blind and the master gouged it out, the slave goes free because he is now missing a limb.
A baraita states that the laws of תמות וזכרות (unblemished and male) apply to animal offerings but not to bird offerings.

The Gemara derives from the verse 'מן העוף' that a bird with a withered wing, severed leg, or gouged-out eye is invalid as an offering, supporting the principle that loss of a limb is a significant blemish.

sub.text: Rav Chiyya bar Ashi citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Chiyya bar Ashi citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Chiyya bar Ashi begins a statement in the name of Rav, but the text is cut off, likely continuing a related halakha.

items.text: Opening Mishnah and Rav Huna's qualification
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and Rav Huna's qualification
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a slave's extra limb is cut off, he goes free. Rav Huna qualifies that this applies only if the limb is counted on the back of the hand.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a slave's extra limb is cut off, he goes free.
Rav Huna qualifies that this applies only if the limb is counted on the back of the hand.

items.text: Story of the elders of Nezonia and Rav Hamnuna
items.text_en: Story of the elders of Nezonia and Rav Hamnuna
items.desc_en: The elders of Nezonia did not attend Rav Chisda's lecture. Rav Chisda sent Rav Hamnuna to rebuke them. They asked Rav Hamnuna about a slave castrated in the testicles, but he could not answer, and they mocked him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports that the elders of Nezonia did not attend Rav Chisda's lecture, so Rav Chisda sent Rav Hamnuna to rebuke them.

sub.text: Rav Hamnuna's question to the elders
sub.text_en: Rav Hamnuna's question to the elders
sub.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna asks the elders why they did not come, and they reply that they had asked Rav Chisda a question and he could not answer.
Rav Hamnuna boasts that he can answer any question they might ask.
The elders ask Rav Hamnuna whether a slave castrated in the testicles is considered to have a visible blemish (כְּמוּם שֶׁבַּגָּלוּי) or not.
Rav Hamnuna does not know the answer.
The elders mock Rav Hamnuna by calling him 'Karnuna' (horned one) instead of Hamnuna.

items.text: Rav Chisda cites the baraita of twenty-four limb-tips
items.text_en: Rav Chisda cites the baraita of twenty-four limb-tips
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda tells Rav Hamnuna that the elders asked him from a baraita listing twenty-four limb-tips that do not transmit impurity as a 'living' (michyah). The baraita adds that a slave goes free through any of them, and Rabbi adds castration, Ben Azzai adds the tongue.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda tells Rav Hamnuna that the elders asked him from a baraita.
The baraita lists twenty-four limb-tips that do not transmit impurity as a 'living' (מחיה).
Rabbi Yehuda adds the tips of a man's breasts to the list.
The baraita rules that a slave goes free through any of these limb-tips.
Rabbi adds castration to the list of limb-tips that free a slave.
Ben Azzai adds the tongue to the list of limb-tips that free a slave.

items.text: Gemara's question: What castration does Rabbi mean?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: What castration does Rabbi mean?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what castration does Rabbi refer to? If it is castration of the tendon, that is already included in 'the head of the membrum'. Therefore, it must be castration of the testicles.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what type of castration Rabbi refers to, concluding it must be castration of the testicles.

items.text: Contradiction regarding Rabbi's view on the tongue
items.text_en: Contradiction regarding Rabbi's view on the tongue
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi adds castration but not the tongue, yet a baraita seems to contradict this regarding sprinkling on the mouth. The Gemara initially deflects by saying it was on the lips, but then cites another baraita explicitly saying 'on his tongue' and a case of most of the tongue being removed, where Rabbi considers it a speaking organ.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Rabbi adds castration but not the tongue, citing a baraita where Rabbi rules that sprinkling on the mouth is effective, implying the tongue is considered a visible organ.
The Gemara deflects by suggesting the baraita refers to the lips, not the tongue, and explains that the teaching is needed to counter a possible assumption about lip closure.
The Gemara objects by citing another baraita that explicitly says 'on his tongue' and a case where most of the tongue was removed, with Rabbi considering it a speaking organ.

items.text: Resolution: Rabbi and Ben Azzai disagree, and the Tanna's order
items.text_en: Resolution: Rabbi and Ben Azzai disagree, and the Tanna's order
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that Rabbi only adds castration, not the tongue, while Ben Azzai adds the tongue but not castration. The 'af' in the baraita refers to the earlier list. The Gemara questions why Ben Azzai is listed after Rabbi, and explains that the Tanna heard both and fixed them in the order he heard, and the Mishnah does not move from its place.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that Rabbi only adds castration (סירוס) and does not need to mention the tongue, while Ben Azzai adds the tongue but not castration.
The Gemara explains that the word 'af' (also) in the baraita refers to the earlier list of twenty-four limbs, not to the immediately preceding opinion.
The Gemara questions why Ben Azzai's opinion is listed after Rabbi's, since logically it should come first.
The Gemara explains that the Tanna heard Rabbi's statement first and fixed it, then heard Ben Azzai's and taught it, and the Mishnah does not move from its place.

items.text: Ulla's distinction: tongue for impurity, immersion, and sprinkling
items.text_en: Ulla's distinction: tongue for impurity, immersion, and sprinkling
items.desc_en: Ulla states that everyone agrees the tongue is considered exposed for impurity from a creeping thing, but hidden for immersion. The dispute between Rabbi and the Rabbis is only regarding sprinkling: Rabbi compares it to impurity, the Rabbis to immersion. Both derive their positions from the verse about sprinkling.

sub.desc_en: Ulla opens by stating that everyone agrees the tongue is considered exposed (גלוי) for impurity from a creeping thing, because the verse 'אשר יגע בו' (which touches it) applies to anything that can be touched.

Ulla continues that for immersion (טבילה), the tongue is considered hidden (כטָמוּן), because the verse 'ורחץ בשרו במים' (and he shall wash his flesh in water) requires water to reach the external surface of the body, and the tongue is internal.
Ulla concludes that the dispute between Rabbi and the Rabbis is only regarding sprinkling (הזאה): Rabbi compares it to impurity, while the Rabbis compare it to immersion.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of the scriptural basis
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the scriptural basis
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that both Rabbi and the Rabbis derive their positions from the same verse about sprinkling: Rabbi focuses on the phrase 'וחטאו' (and he shall purify him), while the Rabbis focus on the subsequent phrase 'וכבס בגדיו ורחץ במים' (and he shall wash his clothes and bathe in water).

The Gemara objects: why don't the Rabbis compare sprinkling to impurity? It answers that they derive purity from purity (טהרה מטהרה). And why doesn't Rabbi compare it to immersion? Because the phrase 'וכבס בגדיו' (and he shall wash his clothes) interrupts the context, separating sprinkling from immersion.

items.text: Challenge to Rabbi's view on immersion from a maidservant incident
items.text_en: Challenge to Rabbi's view on immersion from a maidservant incident
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi's view that the tongue is considered hidden for immersion, citing a case where Rabbi required a maidservant to immerse again because a bone was between her teeth. The Gemara resolves that while the water need not actually enter, the place must be fit for water to enter, as per Rabbi Zeira's principle about kneading.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi's view that the tongue is considered hidden (כטָמוּן) for immersion, citing a case where Rabbi required a maidservant to immerse again because a bone was between her teeth.
The Gemara resolves that while actual entry of water is not required, the place must be fit for water to enter.
The Gemara supports the resolution with Rabbi Zeira's principle that anything fit for kneading (בִּילָּה) does not require actual kneading, but something unfit for kneading requires it.

items.text: Tannaitic dispute on the location of blemishes
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute on the location of blemishes
items.desc_en: The Tannaim debate whether the terms 'crushed, bruised, torn, cut' refer to the testicles (ביצים) or the penis (גיד). Rabbi Yehuda says all refer to the testicles, Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says all refer to the penis, and Rabbi Yosei distinguishes between the terms.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a Tannaitic dispute: the terms 'crushed, bruised, torn, cut' all refer to the testicles, according to Rabbi Yehuda.
The gemara objects: does Rabbi Yehuda mean the terms apply only to the testicles and not to the penis?
The gemara resolves: Rabbi Yehuda means the terms apply also to the testicles (in addition to the penis).
Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov states that all four terms refer exclusively to the penis.
Rabbi Yosei distinguishes: 'crushed and bruised' apply also to the testicles, but 'torn and cut' apply only to the penis, not the testicles.

items.text: Mishnah: modes of acquisition for animals
items.text_en: Mishnah: modes of acquisition for animals
