items.text: Can a father or rabbi waive their honor?
items.text_en: Can a father or rabbi waive their honor?
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda says a father can waive his honor, but a rabbi cannot. Rav Yosef disagrees, arguing that even a rabbi can, citing God walking before Israel. Rava objects that God owns the world and Torah, so the analogy is imperfect.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda rules that a father who waives his honor is honored as waived, but a rabbi who waives his honor is not.
Rav Yosef objects, arguing that even a rabbi's waiver is effective, citing the verse that God walked before Israel as a precedent.
Rava rejects the analogy, noting that God owns the world and the Torah, so He can waive His honor, unlike a human rabbi.

items.text: Rava's retraction and the story of the wedding feast
items.text_en: Rava's retraction and the story of the wedding feast
items.desc_en: Rava initially says a Torah scholar's Torah is his own, but then retracts. A story is told where Rava was serving drinks at his son's wedding; some rabbis stood for him and others did not, causing him to be upset. The Gemara questions whether this contradicts the principle that a scholar may waive his honor.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rava's initial statement that a Torah scholar's Torah is his own, asking how that can be.
Rava retracts and affirms that a Torah scholar's Torah is indeed his own, citing the verse 'and in His Torah he meditates day and night'.
The Gemara objects with a story: at Rava's son's wedding, Rava served drinks; some rabbis stood for him and others did not, and Rava was upset, calling the latter not true rabbis.
A further story: Rav Papa served at his son's wedding and was upset when Rabbi Yitzchak did not stand for him, showing that even if a scholar waives honor, honor should still be shown.

items.text: Rav Ashi's distinction: Nasi vs. ordinary scholar
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's distinction: Nasi vs. ordinary scholar
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi states that even according to the view that a scholar may waive his honor, a Nasi may not. A baraita is brought as a challenge: Rabban Gamliel served drinks at a feast, and Rabbi Eliezer objected, but Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Tzadok defended him, showing that a Nasi may serve others.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi states that even according to the view that a rabbi may waive his honor, a Nasi may not.
The Gemara raises an objection from a story where Rabban Gamliel, a Nasi, served drinks, and Rabbi Eliezer objected to the honor being waived.
Rabbi Yehoshua defends Rabban Gamliel's action by citing Abraham, who served guests who appeared as Arabs, implying that a Nasi may waive honor.
Rabbi Tzadok adds a proof from God's own service to creatures, further supporting that a Nasi may waive honor.

items.text: Revised version of Rav Ashi's statement: King vs. Nasi
items.text_en: Revised version of Rav Ashi's statement: King vs. Nasi
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the previous version and presents a corrected statement by Rav Ashi: even according to the view that a Nasi may waive his honor, a king may not, as the Torah commands that his awe be upon you.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi revises his earlier statement: even according to the view that a Nasi may waive his honor, a king may not, because the Torah commands that his awe be upon you.

items.text: Baraita on the definition of 'zaken' and the nature of honor
items.text_en: Baraita on the definition of 'zaken' and the nature of honor
items.desc_en: A baraita expounds the verse 'Mipnei seivah takum' (rise before the elderly). It defines 'zaken' as a wise person, not merely an old ignoramus. It further limits the obligation to rise to a place of respect, excludes financial expenditure, and requires genuine fear of God, not feigned ignorance.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by expounding the verse 'Mipnei seivah takum' (rise before the elderly), asking whether it applies even to an ignorant old man (זָקֵן אַשְׁמַאי), and answers that 'zaken' means only a wise person, citing the verse about the seventy elders.
Rabbi Yosei HaGelili adds that 'zaken' specifically refers to one who has acquired wisdom (קָנָה חׇכְמָה), citing the verse 'ה׳ קָנָנִי' (the Lord acquired me).
The baraita asks whether one must rise from a distance, and answers that the verse 'תָּקוּם וְהָדַרְתָּ' (rise and honor) limits the obligation to a place where honor is appropriate.
The baraita asks whether one may honor the elder with money, and answers that just as rising involves no financial loss, so too honor must be without financial expenditure.
The baraita asks whether one must rise from a bathroom or bathhouse, and answers that the verse limits rising to a place where honor is appropriate.

The baraita asks whether one may close his eyes as if he did not see the elder, and answers that the verse 'וְיָרֵאתָ' (and you shall fear) applies to matters of the heart, requiring genuine fear of God.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar derives from the juxtaposition of 'zaken' and 'yareta' that an elder should not impose himself (יַטְרִיחַ) on others.
Isi ben Yehuda interprets the verse 'Mipnei seivah takum' to include any elderly person, regardless of wisdom.
The gemara asks whether Rabbi Yosei HaGelili's position is identical to the first Tanna, and answers that the difference between them is a young wise person (יַנִּיק וְחַכִּים).
The gemara explains that the first Tanna excludes a young wise person, while Rabbi Yosei HaGelili includes even a young wise person.

The gemara asks for Rabbi Yosei HaGelili's reasoning, and he argues that if the first Tanna were correct, the Torah would have written 'Mipnei seivah zaken takum' (from before old age and a wise person you shall rise).
Rabbi Yosei HaGelili argues that the Torah separated 'seivah' and 'zaken' to indicate that each term has its own distinct meaning, implying that even a young wise person is included.

The gemara explains that the first Tanna separates 'seivah' and 'zaken' in order to juxtapose 'zaken' with 'yareta' (fear), and then asks for the first Tanna's own reasoning, beginning a new argument.

items.text: Dispute between Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Yosei HaGelili about a young sage
items.text_en: Dispute between Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Yosei HaGelili about a young sage
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Yosei HaGelili's statement seems identical to the Tanna Kamma. It explains the difference: a young sage. The Tanna Kamma holds that a young sage does not qualify as 'zaken', while Rabbi Yosei HaGelili holds that he does. The Gemara provides scriptural reasoning for both positions.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's derivation that an elder should not trouble others, and Isi ben Yehuda's opinion that any hoary head is included.
The Gemara asks whether Rabbi Yosei HaGelili's view is identical to the first tanna, and answers that the difference lies in the case of a young sage.
The Gemara explains that the first tanna excludes a young sage, while Rabbi Yosei HaGelili includes him.

sub.text: Gemara's reasoning for Rabbi Yosei HaGelili
sub.text_en: Gemara's reasoning for Rabbi Yosei HaGelili
sub.desc_en: The Gemara provides Rabbi Yosei HaGelili's scriptural proof: the separation of 'hoary head' and 'elder' in the verse indicates that even a young sage is included.
The Gemara explains that the first tanna separates the terms to juxtapose 'elder' with 'fear', and then asks for his own scriptural reasoning.

items.text: Opening derivation of the single command
items.text_en: Opening derivation of the single command
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the verse 'from before old age you shall rise and honor' uses both 'rise' and 'honor' without a conjunction, implying they are one and the same command.

items.text: Deriving honor without financial loss and without work interruption
items.text_en: Deriving honor without financial loss and without work interruption
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially suggests that honor must be without financial loss, but objects that rising itself can cause loss. It resolves by comparing rising to honor: honor must be without work interruption, and rising must be without financial loss, leading to the rule that craftsmen need not rise while working.

items.text: Contradiction from a mishnah and resolution
items.text_en: Contradiction from a mishnah and resolution
items.desc_en: A mishnah states that all craftsmen stand before them (the dignitaries), but Rabbi Yochanan distinguishes: they stand before them (the dignitaries), but not before Torah scholars. Rabbi Yosei bar Avin praises the mitzvah at its time, but the Gemara suggests a different reason: to avoid causing them to stumble in the future.

items.text: Standing in bathhouse and bathroom
items.text_en: Standing in bathhouse and bathroom
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether one must stand in a bathhouse or bathroom, citing incidents where Rabbi Chiyya and Bar Kappara did not stand for Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi, who complained. The father suggested they were sitting and reflecting. The Gemara distinguishes between inner and outer rooms, and supports this with Rabbi Yochanan's statement that reflection is permitted everywhere except bathhouse and bathroom, though it suggests the case might be different due to duress.

items.text: Closing eyes to avoid obligation
items.text_en: Closing eyes to avoid obligation
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the idea of closing eyes as if not seeing, since that would be wicked. Instead, it suggests closing eyes before the time of obligation arrives, so that when the time comes, one does not see the elder standing. The verse 'rise and fear' teaches otherwise.

items.text: Distance for standing and Abaye's practice
items.text_en: Distance for standing and Abaye's practice
items.desc_en: A baraita defines the distance for rising as four cubits. Abaye limits this to a non-prominent rabbi, but for a prominent rabbi, one must rise as soon as seen. Abaye would stand upon seeing the ear of Rav Yosef's donkey. In another incident, Abaye rode by Rav Mesharshiya and the rabbis who did not stand, and they excused themselves saying they were not aware.

items.text: Elder not to impose, and honor for all elderly
items.text_en: Elder not to impose, and honor for all elderly
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar derives that an elder should not impose. Abaye and Rabbi Zeira would go around. Ravina rebuked a man who passed without covering his head, but was told he might be from a place where rabbis are familiar. Isi ben Yehuda includes all old age, and Rabbi Yochanan rules accordingly, standing before elderly non-Jews. Various practices of honoring the elderly are recounted.

items.text: Introduction of a new statement
items.text_en: Introduction of a new statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins a new statement from Rabbi Aivu quoting Rabbi Yannai, which likely continues the discussion.

items.text: The Mishnah and its challenge
items.text_en: The Mishnah and its challenge
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a student may only stand before his teacher in the morning and evening, so as not to exceed the honor due to Heaven. A baraita is brought that seems to contradict this, implying that an elder should not be burdened at all. The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah means only morning and evening, but even then, the student should minimize the burden as much as possible.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's teaching on standing and its derivation
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's teaching on standing and its derivation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar states that a student who does not stand before his teacher is called wicked, will not live long, and will forget his learning. He derives this from a verse, using a verbal analogy to connect 'fear' to 'standing'.

items.text: Question: Standing before a father who is also one's teacher
items.text_en: Question: Standing before a father who is also one's teacher
items.desc_en: A question is raised: if one's son is also his teacher, must one stand before him? A proof is brought from Shmuel telling Rav Yehuda to stand before his father, Rav Yechzekel. The Gemara deflects this, saying Rav Yechzekel was a man of good deeds, and then explains that Shmuel was actually telling Rav Yehuda to stand when his father came from behind, without concern for Shmuel's own honor.

items.text: Question: Standing before a son who is one's teacher
items.text_en: Question: Standing before a son who is one's teacher
items.desc_en: Another question is raised: if one's son is his teacher, must the father stand before him? Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says he is not worthy of standing before his son, but does so only because of the honor of the Patriarchate. The Gemara clarifies that even if the son is his teacher, the father is not obligated to stand, but in this case, he does so for the honor of the Patriarchate.

items.text: Question: Is a rider considered a walker?
items.text_en: Question: Is a rider considered a walker?
items.desc_en: A question is raised whether a rider is considered a walker for the purpose of standing. Abaye brings a proof from the laws of impurity under a tree, where a rider is considered like a walker. Rav Nachman bar Kohen confirms this.

items.text: Question: Standing before a Torah scroll
items.text_en: Question: Standing before a Torah scroll
items.desc_en: A question is raised whether one must stand before a Torah scroll. Rabbi Chilkiyah, Rabbi Simon, and Rabbi Elazar say it is a kal vachomer: if one stands before those who study it, certainly one should stand before it itself. A story is told about Rabbi Il'ai and Rabbi Yaakov bar Zavdi who stood before Rabbi Shimon bar Abba, who rebuked them, holding like Rabbi Elazar that a student should not stand before his teacher while engaged in Torah study. Abaye cursed this opinion.

items.text: The verse about Moses and the laws of standing for a sage, court head, and patriarch
items.text_en: The verse about Moses and the laws of standing for a sage, court head, and patriarch
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the verse 'And they looked after Moses until he entered the Tent of Meeting,' with a dispute between Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha whether this was for disgrace or praise. It then cites a baraita detailing the laws of standing: for a sage, one stands four cubits; for a court head, one stands as far as the eye can see; for a patriarch, one stands as far as the eye can see and does not sit until he sits in his place.

items.text: Beginning of the next Mishnah: Time-bound positive commandments
items.text_en: Beginning of the next Mishnah: Time-bound positive commandments
items.desc_en: The Mishnah begins listing time-bound positive commandments, such as sukkah, lulav, shofar, and tzitzit.

items.text: Opening Mishnah excerpt and definition
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah excerpt and definition
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists tefillin as a time-bound positive commandment from which women are exempt, and defines non-time-bound positive commandments such as mezuzah, maakeh, returning a lost object, and shiluach haken.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists tefillin as a time-bound positive commandment from which women are exempt, and defines non-time-bound positive commandments such as mezuzah, maakeh, returning a lost object, and shiluach haken.

items.text: Gemara's challenge to the general rule
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge to the general rule
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the general principle by noting exceptions: matzah, simchah, and hakhel are time-bound yet women are obligated; Torah study, procreation, and pidyon haben are not time-bound yet women are exempt.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the general rule by citing exceptions: matzah, simchah, and hakhel are time-bound yet women are obligated; Torah study, procreation, and pidyon haben are not time-bound yet women are exempt.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's principle about general rules
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's principle about general rules
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that one cannot derive laws from general rules, even when the rule explicitly says 'except'. He supports this with a Mishnah about eruv that lists exceptions but omits other items, proving the rule is not exhaustive.

sub.desc_en: רבי יוחנן (Rabbi Yochanan) states that one cannot derive laws from general rules, even when the rule explicitly says 'except'.
The Gemara supports this with a Mishnah about עירוב (eruv) that lists exceptions but omits truffles and mushrooms, proving the rule is not exhaustive.

items.text: Derivation of the rule from tefillin
items.text_en: Derivation of the rule from tefillin
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives that women are exempt from all positive time-bound commandments by a gezeirah shavah from tefillin, and tefillin itself is derived from Torah study via a scriptural juxtaposition.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks from where we derive that women are exempt from positive, time-bound commandments.
It is derived by a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from תפילין (phylacteries): just as women are exempt from תפילין, so too they are exempt from all positive, time-bound commandments.
The Gemara asks how the exemption of women from תפילין itself is derived.
תפילין is derived from תלמוד תורה (Torah study) by scriptural juxtaposition: just as women are exempt from תלמוד תורה, so too they are exempt from תפילין.

items.text: Objection and resolution regarding mezuzah
items.text_en: Objection and resolution regarding mezuzah
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that tefillin could be compared to mezuzah instead of Torah study, but answers that tefillin is juxtaposed to Torah study in both first and second paragraphs, while to mezuzah only in the second. It then rejects comparing mezuzah to Torah study because the verse's blessing of long life applies to men who need life, not women.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that tefillin could be compared to mezuzah instead of Torah study, potentially exempting women from tefillin.
The Gemara answers that tefillin is juxtaposed to Torah study in both paragraphs, while to mezuzah only in the second, so the comparison to Torah study is stronger.
The Gemara objects that mezuzah could be compared to Torah study, potentially exempting women from mezuzah.
The Gemara rejects the comparison because the verse's blessing of long life applies to men who need life, not women, so mezuzah remains obligatory for women.

items.text: Challenge from sukkah and Abaye's resolution
items.text_en: Challenge from sukkah and Abaye's resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that sukkah is a time-bound commandment yet the Torah needed to explicitly exclude women with 'ha'ezrach', implying they would otherwise be obligated. Abaye explains that otherwise one might think sukkah is like a dwelling where husband and wife live together, so the verse excludes women.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the general principle by noting that sukkah is a time-bound commandment, yet the Torah needed to explicitly exclude women with the word 'הָאֶזְרָח' (the native-born), implying they would otherwise be obligated.
Abaye explains that the exclusion was necessary because one might otherwise think sukkah is like a dwelling (דירה) where husband and wife live together, so the verse explicitly excludes women.

items.text: Rava's alternative explanation
items.text_en: Rava's alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Rava begins his own explanation regarding the sukkah exemption, but the text cuts off at this point.

sub.desc_en: Rava begins his alternative explanation regarding the sukkah exemption, but the text cuts off at this point.

items.text: Need for the verse regarding matzah
items.text_en: Need for the verse regarding matzah
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that a special verse is needed to exempt women from matzah, as one might have derived an obligation from the parallel of 'fifteen' in the Festival of Matzot.

items.text: Challenge from the commandment of appearance (Re'iyah)
items.text_en: Challenge from the commandment of appearance (Re'iyah)
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that appearance (Re'iyah) is a positive time-bound commandment, and women would be obligated were it not for the verse 'your males' excluding them.

items.text: Derivation from the assembly (Hakhel) and Abaye's answer
items.text_en: Derivation from the assembly (Hakhel) and Abaye's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests deriving obligation from the assembly (Hakhel), but Abaye answers that a married woman is made happy by her husband, and a widow is considered as dwelling with him.

items.text: Matzah and Hakhel as two verses that come as one
items.text_en: Matzah and Hakhel as two verses that come as one
items.desc_en: The Gemara argues that matzah and Hakhel are two verses that come as one, and therefore they do not teach a general rule.

items.text: Tefillin and Re'iyah as two verses that come as one
items.text_en: Tefillin and Re'iyah as two verses that come as one
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why tefillin and Re'iyah are not also considered two verses that come as one, and explains that each is necessary individually to prevent a mistaken derivation.

items.text: Necessity of both matzah and Hakhel
items.text_en: Necessity of both matzah and Hakhel
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why both matzah and Hakhel are necessary: without Hakhel, one might have derived from Sukkot; without matzah, one might have thought children are obligated and women certainly.

items.text: Alternative view and derivation from fear (Mora)
items.text_en: Alternative view and derivation from fear (Mora)
items.desc_en: The Gemara addresses the view that two verses do teach, and derives women's obligation in non-time-bound positive commandments from the fear of parents (Mora), rejecting a derivation from Torah study because it and procreation are two verses that come as one.

items.text: Addressing Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka's view on 'two verses that come as one'
items.text_en: Addressing Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka's view on 'two verses that come as one'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka, who holds that 'Be fruitful and multiply' applies to women, would explain the exemption of women from Torah study and redemption of the firstborn. It suggests these are two verses that come as one and thus do not teach a general principle. The Gemara then raises a difficulty: if 'Be fruitful and multiply' and 'Reverence' are also two verses that come as one, they too should not teach. The Gemara resolves that both verses are necessary to derive the exemption of women from each commandment individually.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka, who holds that 'Be fruitful and multiply' applies to women, would explain the exemption of women from Torah study and redemption of the firstborn, suggesting these are two verses that come as one and thus do not teach a general principle.
The Gemara objects that if 'Be fruitful and multiply' and 'Reverence' are also two verses that come as one, they too should not teach the exemption of women.
The Gemara resolves that both verses are necessary to derive the exemption of women from each commandment individually, so they are not redundant and do teach.

items.text: Rava's answer via the Papuna'im: the analogy from tefillin
items.text_en: Rava's answer via the Papuna'im: the analogy from tefillin
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what can be said according to the view that 'two verses that come as one' do teach a general principle. Rava reports that the Papuna'im, identified as Rav Acha bar Yaakov, know the reasoning: the verse 'And it shall be for a sign upon your hand...' likens the entire Torah to tefillin. Just as tefillin is a positive time-bound commandment from which women are exempt, so too all positive time-bound commandments exempt women. This implies that non-time-bound positive commandments are obligatory for women.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what can be said for the position that two verses that come as one do teach a general principle.
Rava states that the Paphunaeans know the reasoning for this matter.
Rabbi Acha bar Yaakov derives from the verse that all Torah is compared to tefillin, so women are exempt from time-bound positive commandments but obligated in non-time-bound ones.

items.text: Addressing Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda on tefillin and 'two verses'
items.text_en: Addressing Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda on tefillin and 'two verses'
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the previous answer works for those who consider tefillin a time-bound commandment. For Rabbi Meir, who considers tefillin non-time-bound, he holds that 'two verses that come as one' do not teach, so the exemption of women from time-bound commandments is derived from the two verses of Torah study and redemption of the firstborn. For Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that 'two verses that come as one' do teach and that tefillin is non-time-bound, the Gemara explains that matzah, joy, and assembly are three verses that come as one, and three such verses do not teach a general principle.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: the previous answer works for one who holds tefillin is a time-bound commandment, but for one who holds it is not time-bound, what can be said?

The Gemara answers: Rabbi Meir holds tefillin is non-time-bound, and he holds that 'two verses that come as one' do not teach a general principle, so the exemption of women from time-bound commandments is derived from the two verses of Torah study and redemption of the firstborn.

The Gemara explains: for Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that 'two verses that come as one' do teach and that tefillin is non-time-bound, the exemption is derived because matzah, joy, and assembly are three verses that come as one, and three such verses do not teach a general principle.

items.text: Source for women being obligated in all negative commandments
items.text_en: Source for women being obligated in all negative commandments
items.desc_en: The Gemara turns to the Mishnah's statement that women are obligated in all negative commandments. It cites three derivations: from the verse 'If a man or a woman commits any of the sins of mankind' (Rav Yehuda citing Rav and the school of Rabbi Yishmael) equating women to men for all penalties; from the school of Rabbi Eliezer citing 'which you shall set before them' equating women for all laws; and from the school of Chizkiyah citing 'and he kills a man or a woman' equating women for all capital punishments. The Gemara explains that all three are necessary, as each addresses a potential leniency: for penalties one might think women are exempt due to divine mercy, for laws one might think women are exempt as they are not involved in business, and for capital punishment one might think women are exempt because it is their livelihood.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source that women are obligated in all negative commandments.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda citing Rav and the school of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda citing Rav and the school of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Rav and the school of Rabbi Yishmael derives from the verse that the Torah equates a woman to a man for all penalties.
The school of Rabbi Eliezer teaches that the verse equates a woman to a man for all laws.
The school of Chizkiya teaches that the verse equates a woman to a man for all capital punishments.

The Gemara explains that all three derivations are necessary, as each addresses a different potential exclusion: penalties might be lenient due to atonement, laws might exclude women from business dealings, and capital punishment might be limited to men.

items.text: Conclusion of previous derivation
items.text_en: Conclusion of previous derivation
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the three cases (saving a life, returning a lost object, and sending away the mother bird) are all necessary to teach, because each has a unique aspect that might have led to a different ruling.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the three cases (saving a life, returning a lost object, and sending away the mother bird) are all necessary to teach, because each has a unique aspect that might have led to a different ruling.

items.text: Deriving women's exemption from בל תקיף and בל תשחית
items.text_en: Deriving women's exemption from בל תקיף and בל תשחית
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we know women are exempt from the prohibitions of rounding the head and marring the beard. It answers that the verse connects these two commandments: whoever is subject to השחתה (marring) is subject to הקפה (rounding). Since women have no beard, they are not subject to השחתה, and therefore not to הקפה. Two proofs are offered: a logical one (they have no beard) and a scriptural one (the verse says 'your beard' in the masculine singular, excluding a woman's beard).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we know that women are exempt from the prohibitions of rounding the head (בל תקיף) and marring the beard (בל תשחית), given that the exemption from impurity for priests is derived from the verse 'בני אהרן' (sons of Aaron, not daughters).

The Gemara answers that the verse connects the two prohibitions: whoever is subject to השחתה (marring the beard) is subject to הקפה (rounding the head); since women have no beard, they are exempt from both.
The Gemara offers a logical proof that women are not subject to השחתה: they simply have no beard.

The Gemara offers a scriptural proof: the verse says 'זְקָנֶךָ' (your beard, masculine singular) rather than 'זְקַנְכֶם' (your beards, plural), implying the prohibition applies only to a man's beard, not a woman's.

items.text: Challenge from a baraita about a woman's beard
items.text_en: Challenge from a baraita about a woman's beard
items.desc_en: A baraita states that a woman's beard and a eunuch's beard are considered a beard for all purposes. The Gemara initially assumes this includes the prohibition of השחתה. Abaye rejects this, arguing that a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the priests (בני אהרן) teaches that women are exempt from השחתה, just as they are exempt from the priestly prohibitions.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the exemption of women from השחתה by citing a baraita that a woman's beard is considered a beard for all purposes, implying it includes the prohibition of השחתה.
Abaye rejects the challenge, arguing that a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the priests (בני אהרן) teaches that women are exempt from השחתה, just as they are exempt from the priestly prohibitions.

items.text: Discussion of the גזירה שווה and its necessity
items.text_en: Discussion of the גזירה שווה and its necessity
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why a גזירה שווה is needed; perhaps the verse 'בני אהרן' applies to the entire context, and a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument) would suffice. It then explains that without the גזירה שווה, one might think the topic is interrupted. The Gemara then shows that the גזירה שווה is actually needed for another teaching: to define the prohibited act of shaving as that which involves destruction (תער). Finally, it notes that the verse's wording 'פאת זקנך' teaches two things: the prohibition of marring and the exclusion of women.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) is needed, proposing that if the verse 'בני אהרן' applies to the entire context, a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument) could exempt all Israelites from the prohibitions.
The Gemara answers that without the גזירה שווה, one might think the topic is interrupted, so the analogy is necessary to connect the prohibitions.
The Gemara objects that even now, one might still claim the topic is interrupted, questioning the necessity of the גזירה שווה.
The Gemara explains that the גזירה שווה is actually needed for another teaching: to define the prohibited act of shaving as that which involves destruction (תער), as taught in a baraita.
The Gemara concludes that the verse's wording 'פאת זקנך' teaches two things: the prohibition of marring and the exclusion of women.

items.text: Resolving the baraita about a woman's beard
items.text_en: Resolving the baraita about a woman's beard
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the baraita about a woman's beard coming for all purposes actually teaches. Mar Zutra says it is for the impurity of negaim (skin afflictions). The Gemara objects that the Torah explicitly mentions a woman's beard in that context. Mar Zutra then clarifies it is for the purification of negaim. The Gemara further questions that if she is susceptible to impurity, she is obviously susceptible to purification. The answer is that one might have thought the verse 'איש או אשה' applies separately, so the teaching is necessary.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for what halachic purpose the baraita equates a woman's beard to a man's beard for all matters.
Mar Zutra answers that the baraita applies to the impurity of negaim (skin afflictions).
The Gemara objects that the Torah explicitly mentions a woman's beard in the context of negaim impurity, so the baraita is unnecessary.
Mar Zutra clarifies that the baraita applies to the purification of negaim, not their impurity.
The Gemara objects that if a woman is susceptible to impurity from negaim, she is obviously susceptible to purification, so the baraita is still unnecessary.

The Gemara resolves that the baraita is necessary because one might have thought the verse 'איש או אשה' applies separately to each clause, so the teaching clarifies that a woman's beard is treated like a man's for purification.

items.text: Isi's teaching: women exempt from בל יקרחו
items.text_en: Isi's teaching: women exempt from בל יקרחו
items.desc_en: Isi teaches that women are also exempt from the prohibition of making a bald spot (בל יקרחו). He derives this from the verse 'בנים אתם לה׳ אלהיכם', interpreting 'בנים' (sons) to exclude daughters. The Gemara analyzes his reasoning, explaining that the verse 'כי עם קדוש אתה' already addresses the prohibition of גידידה (cutting), so 'בנים ולא בנות' must apply to קרחה. It then questions why not apply the exclusion to both, and explains that Isi holds that the verse about 'עם קדוש' refers to שריטה (scratching), not גידידה.

sub.desc_en: Isi teaches that women are exempt from the prohibition of making a bald spot (בל יקרחו), deriving it from the verse 'בנים אתם לה׳ אלהיכם' — 'בנים' (sons) excludes daughters, applying specifically to קרחה.

The Gemara questions whether the exclusion 'בנים ולא בנות' applies to קרחה (bald spot) or to גדידה (cutting), and resolves that since the verse 'כי עם קדוש אתה' already addresses גדידה, the exclusion must apply to קרחה.

The Gemara asks why the exclusion is applied specifically to קרחה rather than to גדידה, and answers that גדידה applies both where hair grows and where it does not, while קרחה applies only where hair grows, so the exclusion is more logically applied to the narrower prohibition.

The Gemara objects that perhaps the exclusion should apply to both קרחה and גדידה, and that the verse 'כי עם קדוש אתה' refers to שריטה (scratching) rather than to גדידה, but concludes that Isi holds that שריטה and גדידה are the same prohibition.

items.text: Opening statement: 'It is one'
items.text_en: Opening statement: 'It is one'
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the topic with the phrase 'אחת היא' (it is one), setting the stage for the discussion about the prohibition of making a bald spot.

items.text: Abaye's explanation of Isi's ruling
items.text_en: Abaye's explanation of Isi's ruling
items.desc_en: Abaye explains that Isi's ruling that women are exempt from the prohibition of making a bald spot is derived from a verbal analogy (גזרה שוה) between 'קרחה' here and in the context of the sons of Aaron. He argues that without this analogy, one might think the verse is interrupted and women would be exempt via a kal vachomer. The Gemara then uses the verbal analogy to derive other laws, such as liability for each bald spot and for the entire head, and applies them to Israelites.

items.text: Rava's alternative explanation and debate with Abaye
items.text_en: Rava's alternative explanation and debate with Abaye
items.desc_en: Rava offers a different reason for Isi's ruling, deriving the exemption of women from the phrase 'between your eyes' (בין עיניכם) in the context of tefillin, where women are exempt. The Gemara then explains why each sage rejects the other's derivation: Rava does not accept the verbal analogy from 'קרחה', while Abaye argues that the tefillin derivation itself comes from the same verse about the bald spot.

items.text: Interpretation of 'You are children' and the debate between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Meir
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'You are children' and the debate between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Meir
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how both Abaye and Rava interpret the verse 'בנים אתם לה' אלהיכם' (You are children to the Lord your God). It cites a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda says that only when Israelites act like children are they called children, while Rabbi Meir argues they are always called children, citing multiple verses to prove that even sinful Israelites are still called children.

items.text: Mishnah: List of rites performed only by men
items.text_en: Mishnah: List of rites performed only by men
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists several sacrificial rites (semichah, tenufah, hagashah, kemitzah, haktarah, melikah, kabbalah, and hazayah) that are performed only by men, except for the meal-offering of a sotah and a nazirite woman, which involve waving (tenufah).

items.text: Gemara: Scriptural sources for each rite's exclusion of women
items.text_en: Gemara: Scriptural sources for each rite's exclusion of women
items.desc_en: The Gemara provides scriptural derivations for each rite listed in the Mishnah, showing that the Torah uses masculine terms (בני ישראל, בני אהרן) to exclude women. For semichah and tenufah, the verse 'דבר אל בני ישראל' implies only sons of Israel. For hagashah, kemitzah, haktarah, and kabbalah, the phrase 'בני אהרן' excludes daughters. For melikah, it is linked to haktarah. The Gemara begins to discuss kabbalah with a citation from Mar.

items.text: Derivation of priestly sprinkling for the bird offering
items.text_en: Derivation of priestly sprinkling for the bird offering
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins by interpreting the verse 'and they shall offer' as referring to the receiving of the blood. It then questions which sprinkling is meant, rejecting the red heifer (where Elazar is specified) and the inner sprinklings (where the anointed priest is specified). It concludes that it refers to the sprinkling of the bird offering, derived via a קל וחומר from the lamb offering: just as the lamb, which does not require a priest for slaughter, requires a priest for sprinkling, so too the bird, which requires a priest for pinching, should certainly require a priest for sprinkling.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara interprets the verse 'וְהִקְרִיבוּ' (and they shall offer) as referring to the receiving of the blood.
The Gemara asks which sprinkling is meant, rejecting the red heifer (where Elazar is specified) and the inner sprinklings (where the anointed priest is specified).
The Gemara concludes that it refers to the sprinkling of the bird offering, derived via a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument) from the lamb offering.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's question about the sotah meal-offering
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's question about the sotah meal-offering
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar asks Rabbi Yoshiya of his generation: from where do we derive that the meal-offering of a sotah requires waving? He immediately notes that the requirement is explicit in the verse itself, so he clarifies: from where do we derive that the waving must be performed by the owners?

sub.text: Rabbi Elazar's question to Rabbi Yoshiya
sub.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's question to Rabbi Yoshiya
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar asks Rabbi Yoshiya from where we derive that the meal-offering of a sotah requires waving, then immediately clarifies that the waving by the owners is the real question, since the verse itself mandates waving.

items.text: Derivation of owner's waving from peace-offering
items.text_en: Derivation of owner's waving from peace-offering
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers by deriving the requirement from the peace-offering using a verbal analogy of 'hand'. The verse here says 'from the hand of the woman' and there it says 'his hands shall bring it'. Just as there a priest is involved, so too here a priest is involved; just as there the owners perform the waving, so too here the owners perform it. The practical outcome is that the priest places his hand under the hand of the owner and waves.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara derives the requirement for owner's waving in the sotah meal-offering from the peace-offering using a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) on the word 'יד' (hand), concluding that the priest places his hand under the owner's hand and waves.

items.text: Derivation for the nazirite meal-offering
items.text_en: Derivation for the nazirite meal-offering
items.desc_en: Having found the source for the sotah, the Gemara asks: from where do we derive the same requirement for the nazirite? It answers using a verbal analogy of 'hand' (or 'palm') from the sotah offering.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: having found the source for the sotah meal-offering requiring waving, from where do we derive the same requirement for the nazirite meal-offering?
The Gemara answers: it is derived by a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) of 'כַּף' (palm/hand) from the sotah offering.

items.text: Mishnah: Land-dependent vs. non-land-dependent commandments
items.text_en: Mishnah: Land-dependent vs. non-land-dependent commandments
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states a general principle: any commandment that is dependent on the land (of Israel) is practiced only in the land, and any commandment that is not dependent on the land is practiced both in the land and outside the land.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the general principle that land-dependent commandments apply only in the land of Israel, while non-land-dependent commandments apply both in and outside the land.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists exceptions to the rule that commandments dependent on the land apply only in the Land of Israel: orlah and kilayim apply even outside the land; Rabbi Eliezer adds the new grain offering (chadash).

items.text: Gemara's initial question and Rav Yehuda's clarification
items.text_en: Gemara's initial question and Rav Yehuda's clarification
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'dependent' and 'not dependent' mean, initially suggesting it refers to whether the verse mentions 'coming into the land'. Rav Yehuda rejects this, explaining that the distinction is between bodily obligations (chovat haguf) and land obligations (chovat karka).

items.text: Derivation from the verse and the baraita
items.text_en: Derivation from the verse and the baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that derives from the verse 'These are the statutes... in the land' that all commandments might be limited to the land, but the verse 'all the days' teaches they apply everywhere. The baraita then uses a kal vachomer from idolatry to establish that bodily obligations apply both in and outside the land.

items.text: The dilemma about Rabbi Eliezer's position
items.text_en: The dilemma about Rabbi Eliezer's position
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a dilemma: does Rabbi Eliezer argue leniently or stringently regarding the new grain offering?

items.text: First possibility: Rabbi Eliezer argues stringently
items.text_en: First possibility: Rabbi Eliezer argues stringently
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the first possibility: the first tanna says only orlah and kilayim apply outside the land due to halakha le-Moshe mi-Sinai, but chadash does not. Rabbi Eliezer argues stringently that chadash also applies outside the land, interpreting 'moshav' as any place you dwell.

items.text: Second possibility: Rabbi Eliezer argues leniently
items.text_en: Second possibility: Rabbi Eliezer argues leniently
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents the alternative: the first tanna includes chadash as well, and Rabbi Eliezer argues leniently that chadash applies only in the land, interpreting 'moshav' as after inheritance and settlement. The word 'af' in the Mishnah refers to the first clause.

items.text: Proof from Abaye's statement
items.text_en: Proof from Abaye's statement
items.desc_en: Abaye identifies the tanna who disagrees with Rabbi Eliezer as Rabbi Yishmael, who holds that 'moshav' always means after inheritance and settlement. Rabbi Akiva objects with Shabbat, which uses 'moshavot' yet applies everywhere, but Rabbi Yishmael responds with a kal vachomer. The Gemara concludes that this proves Rabbi Eliezer argues stringently.

items.text: Transition to the next topic
items.text_en: Transition to the next topic
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to examine the context of Rabbi Yishmael's statement, noting it was said regarding libations (nesakhim), and starts to analyze that topic.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva on 'bia' and 'moshav'
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva on 'bia' and 'moshav'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael explains that 'bia' and 'moshav' in the Torah always come after inheritance and settlement. Rabbi Akiva objects using the example of Shabbat, where 'moshavot' is written, and Rabbi Yishmael responds that Shabbat is a fortiori.

items.text: The underlying dispute: libation offerings in the wilderness
items.text_en: The underlying dispute: libation offerings in the wilderness
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the dispute between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva is about whether libation offerings were brought in the wilderness. Rabbi Yishmael holds they were not, while Rabbi Akiva holds they were.

items.text: Abaye's observation and the baraitot of the school of Rabbi Yishmael
items.text_en: Abaye's observation and the baraitot of the school of Rabbi Yishmael
items.desc_en: Abaye notes a contradiction between two baraitot from the school of Rabbi Yishmael. One baraita derives that all 'bia' commands are after inheritance and settlement, while another baraita argues that king and first fruits are two verses that come as one and thus do not teach. The Gemara then explains why both verses are necessary and why one could not be derived from the other.

items.text: The necessity of 'moshav' for Shabbat, forbidden fats and blood, and matzah and maror
items.text_en: The necessity of 'moshav' for Shabbat, forbidden fats and blood, and matzah and maror
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the word 'moshav' is written regarding Shabbat, forbidden fats and blood, and matzah and maror. For each, it was necessary to teach that the commandment applies even outside the Land or even when there is no Temple or Paschal lamb.

items.text: The necessity of 'bia' for tefillin and firstborn donkey
items.text_en: The necessity of 'bia' for tefillin and firstborn donkey
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the word 'bia' regarding tefillin and the firstborn donkey is used to teach that one should perform these commandments in order to enter the Land.

items.text: Proof from the verse about eating from the produce of the land
items.text_en: Proof from the verse about eating from the produce of the land
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a proof for the opinion that 'moshav' means wherever you dwell, citing the verse that the Israelites ate from the produce of the land only after the Passover, implying that before that they did not eat from it.

items.text: Opening statement about the omer and eating
items.text_en: Opening statement about the omer and eating
items.desc_en: The Gemara quotes a statement that the omer is brought first and then one may eat the new grain.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the omer is brought first and then one may eat the new grain.

items.text: Question and answer about the timing of eating after inheritance and settlement
items.text_en: Question and answer about the timing of eating after inheritance and settlement
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how one could eat immediately according to the opinion that the new grain is permitted after inheritance and settlement, and answers with a verse showing that the manna continued until the 16th of Nisan.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: according to the opinion that the new grain was permitted only after inheritance and settlement, why could they not eat immediately upon entering the land?
The Gemara answers with a scriptural derivation: the manna continued until the sixteenth of Nisan, so the new grain was not needed immediately.

items.text: Baraita about the taste of manna in the cakes from Egypt
items.text_en: Baraita about the taste of manna in the cakes from Egypt
items.desc_en: A baraita explains that the verse 'forty years' includes the taste of manna in the cakes they brought from Egypt.

sub.desc_en: A baraita clarifies that the forty years of manna included the taste of manna in the cakes brought from Egypt.

items.text: Baraita about Moses' death and birth on the 7th of Adar
items.text_en: Baraita about Moses' death and birth on the 7th of Adar
items.desc_en: A baraita proves that Moses died on the 7th of Adar through scriptural calculations, and also that he was born on the same date, as God completes the years of the righteous exactly.

sub.desc_en: The baraita proves through scriptural calculations that Moses died on the 7th of Adar.
The baraita proves that Moses was born on the 7th of Adar, as God completes the years of the righteous exactly.

items.text: Baraita of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai about three commandments
items.text_en: Baraita of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai about three commandments
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai states that three commandments were given upon entering the Land, and a kal vachomer is made to extend them outside the Land, with a distinction regarding kilayim and orlah.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai states that three commandments were given to Israel upon entering the land and apply both in the land and outside it.
The Gemara explains that the rule applies to a prohibition that is not permanent, not a prohibition of benefit, and has a permitted alternative, and applies both in the land and outside it.
The Gemara argues that kilayim, whose prohibition is permanent and includes benefit, should logically apply both in the land and outside, and the same applies to orlah in two respects.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon's statement
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon's statement
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon begins his own statement, which is cut off.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon begins his statement (the content is cut off).

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that mitzvot given before entering the Land of Israel apply both in and outside the land, while those given after entering apply only in the land, except for remission of debts and release of slaves which apply everywhere.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the general rule that mitzvot given before entering the Land apply everywhere, while those given after entering apply only in the Land, with exceptions for remission of debts and release of slaves.

items.text: Gemara's question on remission of debts
items.text_en: Gemara's question on remission of debts
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why remission of debts is considered a bodily obligation, and explains that it is derived from a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi links it to the sabbatical year of land, but a verse teaches it applies everywhere.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why remission of debts (שמיטת כספים) is considered a bodily obligation (חובת הגוף), implying it should apply everywhere.
The Gemara answers that the statement was needed only to introduce a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi links remission of debts to the sabbatical year of land.
The Gemara objects that the baraita could be interpreted as limiting remission of debts to the land of Israel only, not everywhere.
The Gemara resolves by citing the verse 'כי קרא שמיטה לה׳' (for it is a sabbatical to the Lord) to teach that remission of debts applies everywhere.

items.text: Gemara's discussion on release of slaves
items.text_en: Gemara's discussion on release of slaves
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that release of slaves is a bodily obligation, and though one might think it applies only in the land from the verse 'proclaim liberty in the land', another verse teaches it applies everywhere, but only when the Jubilee is observed in the land.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why release of slaves is listed as an exception, since it is a bodily obligation and should apply everywhere regardless of land.
The Gemara explains that one might have thought from the verse 'וּקְרָאתֶם דְּרוֹר בָּאָרֶץ' that release applies only in the land, but the verse 'יוֹבֵל הִיא' teaches it applies everywhere.
The Gemara resolves that the word 'בָּאָרֶץ' teaches that release of slaves applies outside the land only when the Jubilee year is observed in the land.

items.text: Introduction of orlah and kilayim
items.text_en: Introduction of orlah and kilayim
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah stating that new grain is forbidden everywhere by Torah law, orlah is a halakhah, and kilayim is rabbinic. It then records a dispute between Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel and Ulla in the name of Rabbi Yochanan about the nature of this halakhah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah stating that new grain is forbidden by Torah law everywhere, orlah is a halakhah, and kilayim is rabbinic.
The Gemara asks what the term 'halakhah' in the Mishnah means.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel answers that it is a local custom (הלכתא מדינה).

sub.text: Ulla in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Ulla in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Ulla in the name of Rabbi Yochanan answers that it is a law from Moses at Sinai (הלכה למשה מסיני).

items.text: Ulla's argument for his position
items.text_en: Ulla's argument for his position
items.desc_en: Ulla argues that his view (halakhah le-Moshe mi-Sinai) explains the difference between orlah and kilayim in cases of doubt: for orlah, there is a leniency outside the land, while for kilayim, the leniency is even greater, as one may pick and buy without seeing.

sub.desc_en: Ulla opens his argument to Rav Yehuda, stating that according to his own view (הלכה למשה מסיני), the distinction between doubt regarding orlah and kilayim is well explained.

Ulla cites the Mishnah regarding doubt about orlah: in the Land of Israel it is forbidden, in Syria it is permitted, and outside the Land one may descend and buy, provided he does not see the gatherer.

Ulla cites the Mishnah regarding kilayim: in the Land it is forbidden, in Syria it is permitted, and outside the Land one may descend and pick, provided he does not pick by hand, showing a greater leniency than orlah.

items.text: Beginning of Rav Yehuda's response
items.text_en: Beginning of Rav Yehuda's response
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins Rav Yehuda's response to Ulla, challenging his position.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda begins his response to Ulla, challenging Ulla's position by saying 'but according to you'.

items.text: Opening dispute on the wording of the mishnah
items.text_en: Opening dispute on the wording of the mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the mishnah's phrasing, suggesting alternative formulations. Shmuel instructs Rav Anan to teach either 'yored veloke'ach' or 'yored veloket', while Mar bar Ravna teaches a lenient version: 'yored veloket, provided he does not pick by hand'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the mishnah's phrasing, suggesting alternative formulations: 'yored veloke'ach' or 'yored veloket'.
Shmuel instructs Rav Anan to teach either formulation, leaving the choice open.
Mar bar Ravna teaches a lenient version: 'yored veloket, provided he does not pick by hand'.

items.text: Stories of lenient practice and the statement of the sharp ones of Pumbedita
items.text_en: Stories of lenient practice and the statement of the sharp ones of Pumbedita
items.desc_en: Levi asks Shmuel to provide him with fruit from outside the Land, and Rav Avya and Rabbah bar Rav Chanan supply each other. The sharp ones of Pumbedita declare: 'There is no orlah outside the Land'.

sub.desc_en: Levi asks Shmuel to supply him with fruit from outside the Land for him to eat.

sub.text: Narrative of Rav Avya and Rabbah bar Rav Chanan
sub.text_en: Narrative of Rav Avya and Rabbah bar Rav Chanan
sub.desc_en: Rav Avya and Rabbah bar Rav Chanan supply each other with fruit from outside the Land.
The sharp ones of Pumbedita declare that the prohibition of ערלה (orlah) does not apply outside the Land of Israel.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's stringent response
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's stringent response
items.desc_en: Rav Yehudah sends a query to Rabbi Yochanan, who responds with a strict ruling: seal its doubt, destroy its certainty, and declare that their fruits require burial. He curses anyone who says there is no orlah outside the Land.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehudah sends a query to Rabbi Yochanan regarding the status of orlah outside the Land.
Rabbi Yochanan responds with a strict ruling: seal its doubt, destroy its certainty, declare their fruits require burial, and curses anyone who denies orlah outside the Land.

items.text: Chain of tradition supporting the lenient view
items.text_en: Chain of tradition supporting the lenient view
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: With whom did the sharp ones of Pumbedita hold? It cites a baraita where Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yosei reports a chain from Rabbi Yosei ben Dormaskit to Rabbi Yosei HaGelili to Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri to Rabbi Eliezer HaGadol, all stating: 'There is no orlah outside the Land'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: With whom did the sharp ones of Pumbedita hold when they ruled that there is no orlah outside the Land?

The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yosei reports a chain of tradition from Rabbi Yosei ben Dormaskit through Rabbi Yosei HaGelili and Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri to Rabbi Eliezer HaGadol, all stating: 'There is no orlah outside the Land'.

items.text: Reconciliation of conflicting traditions
items.text_en: Reconciliation of conflicting traditions
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: Did Rabbi Eliezer not say 'even the new'? It explains that the mishnah refers to 'chadash' (new grain). Rabbi Asi quotes Rabbi Yochanan: Orlah outside the Land is a halachah leMoshe miSinai. Rabbi Zeira challenges this with a baraita allowing doubtful orlah outside the Land. Rabbi Asi, stunned, clarifies: Its doubt is permitted, its certainty is forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: Did Rabbi Eliezer not say 'even the new grain' in the Mishnah, contradicting the baraita that he holds no orlah outside the Land?
The Gemara resolves: Teach that the Mishnah refers to 'chadash' (new grain) of the Land of Israel, not orlah outside the Land.
Rabbi Asi quotes Rabbi Yochanan: The prohibition of orlah outside the Land is a halachah leMoshe miSinai (a law transmitted to Moses at Sinai).
Rabbi Zeira challenges Rabbi Asi with a baraita that permits doubtful orlah outside the Land, contradicting the stringency of a halachah leMoshe miSinai.
Rabbi Asi clarifies: The halachah leMoshe miSinai means its certainty is forbidden, but its doubt is permitted, reconciling the baraita.

items.text: Kilayim outside the Land: Torah law or rabbinic?
items.text_en: Kilayim outside the Land: Torah law or rabbinic?
items.desc_en: Rabbi Asi quotes Rabbi Yochanan: One is lashed for kilayim by Torah law. Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yosei objects: We learned that kilayim is from the words of the Scribes! The Gemara resolves: Here it refers to kilayim of the vineyard, there to grafting trees. Shmuel derives from a verse that kilayim applies both in and outside the Land, but 'your field' excludes seeds outside the Land.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Asi quotes Rabbi Yochanan stating that one is lashed for kilayim by Torah law.
Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yosei objects that the Mishnah teaches kilayim is from the words of the Scribes, not Torah law.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: here (Rabbi Yochanan) refers to kilayim of the vineyard (כלאי הכרם), there (the Mishnah) refers to grafting trees (הרכבת האילן), which is rabbinic.
Shmuel derives from the verse 'את חקתי תשמרו' that the prohibition of kilayim applies both in the Land and outside the Land, by analogy from בהמתך (your animal) which applies everywhere.
The Gemara resolves the apparent contradiction from the word 'שדך' (your field): it excludes seeds (זרעים) outside the Land from the Torah prohibition, but kilayim of the vineyard remains Torah law.

items.text: Stories of Rav Chanan and Rav Anan regarding kilayim
items.text_en: Stories of Rav Chanan and Rav Anan regarding kilayim
items.desc_en: Rav Chanan and Rav Anan see a man planting mixed seeds and consider excommunicating him, but refrain because they did not warn him. They later see a man planting wheat and barley among vines, and again refrain, citing Rabbi Yoshiyah's requirement that the act be done simultaneously.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chanan and Rav Anan are walking and see a man planting mixed seeds together.
Rav Chanan suggests excommunicating the man for violating the prohibition of kilayim.
Rav Anan rejects the proposal because they did not warn the man first.
They later see a man planting wheat and barley among vines.
Rav Chanan again suggests excommunicating the man.
Rav Anan rejects again, citing Rabbi Yoshiyah's requirement that the act be done simultaneously with a single hand motion.

items.text: Rav Yosef's practice and Abaye's challenge
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's practice and Abaye's challenge
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef mixes seeds and plants them. Abaye objects: We learned that kilayim is from the words of the Scribes! Rav Yosef distinguishes: Kilayim of the vineyard, which is prohibited for benefit in the Land, the Sages decreed outside the Land; kilayim of seeds, not prohibited for benefit, they did not decree. Rav Yosef later retracts, citing Rav's practice of mixing seeds in his garden, implying it was permitted.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef mixes seeds and plants them, establishing the initial scenario.
Abaye objects that the Mishnah teaches kilayim is from the words of the Scribes, implying it applies even outside the Land.
Rav Yosef distinguishes: kilayim of the vineyard, prohibited for benefit in the Land, the Sages decreed outside the Land; kilayim of seeds, not prohibited for benefit, they did not decree.
Rav Yosef retracts his earlier answer, citing Rav's practice of mixing seeds in his garden as evidence that it was permitted, and Abaye begins to challenge this new claim.

items.text: Transition from previous sugya
items.text_en: Transition from previous sugya
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the previous discussion about planting patterns in a garden bed, explaining that the arrangement of four on each side and one in the middle is acceptable due to aesthetic reasons or to avoid extra work for the watchman.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the arrangement of four plants on each side and one in the middle of the garden bed is acceptable either for aesthetic reasons or to avoid extra work for the watchman.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that anyone who performs a single mitzvah is treated well, has their days lengthened, and inherits the land; conversely, one who does not perform a single mitzvah does not receive these benefits.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who performs a single מצוה (commandment) is rewarded with good and long life and inherits the land, while one who does not perform even one is not rewarded.

items.text: Gemara's first question and resolution
items.text_en: Gemara's first question and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from a Baraita that lists specific mitzvot whose fruits are enjoyed in this world, implying not all mitzvot have immediate reward. Rav Yehuda resolves that the Mishnah refers to one who has one extra mitzvah over their merits, and Rav Shemaya adds that this applies when the scales are balanced.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from a Baraita listing specific mitzvot whose fruits are enjoyed in this world, implying not all mitzvot have immediate reward.
Rav Yehuda resolves that the Mishnah refers to one who has one extra mitzvah over their merits.
Rav Shemaya adds that this applies when the scales are balanced.

items.text: Second contradiction and two resolutions
items.text_en: Second contradiction and two resolutions
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises another contradiction from a Baraita that says one with more merits is treated badly, and one with more sins is treated well. Abaye resolves that the Mishnah refers to a day of good and a day of bad. Rava says the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yaakov, who holds there is no reward for mitzvot in this world.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from a Baraita that says one with more merits is treated badly, and one with more sins is treated well.
Abaye resolves that the Mishnah refers to a day of good and a day of bad.
Rava says the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yaakov, who holds there is no reward for mitzvot in this world.

items.text: Rabbi Yaakov's proof from the story of the son and the nest
items.text_en: Rabbi Yaakov's proof from the story of the son and the nest
items.desc_en: A Baraita cites Rabbi Yaakov who argues that reward for mitzvot is not in this world, using the example of a son who fulfills both honoring his father and sending away the mother bird, yet dies upon returning. The verses promising good and long days refer to the World to Come.

sub.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi Yaakov's proof from the story of a son who died while fulfilling the commandments of honoring parents and sending away the mother bird, showing that the promised good and long days refer to the world to come.

Rabbi Yaakov tells the story of a son who fulfills both mitzvot of honoring his father and sending away the mother bird, yet dies upon returning, proving that the promised good and long days refer to the World to Come.

items.text: Defense of the story's validity
items.text_en: Defense of the story's validity
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the story actually happened, suggesting the son might have had sinful thoughts. It counters that evil thoughts are not joined to action, except for idolatry. Rabbi Yaakov's point is that if reward existed in this world, the mitzvot would have protected him from such thoughts.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the story of the son who died while fulfilling both mitzvot actually happened as described.
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Yaakov actually witnessed the event, so it is historically reliable.
The Gemara objects that perhaps the son had sinful thoughts, which caused his death despite the mitzvot.
The Gemara rejects the objection, stating that the Holy One, blessed be He, does not join evil thoughts to action (for punishment).
The Gemara objects further that perhaps the son had thoughts of idolatry, which are an exception to the rule that thoughts are not joined to action.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yaakov's point is precisely that if reward existed in this world, the mitzvot would have protected the son from even coming to such thoughts.

items.text: Reconciliation with the principle that messengers of mitzvot are unharmed
items.text_en: Reconciliation with the principle that messengers of mitzvot are unharmed
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Elazar said messengers of a mitzvah are not harmed, but distinguishes between going and returning. When challenged that Rabbi Elazar said both directions, it answers that the ladder was unstable, a fixed danger, and one does not rely on miracles in such cases, citing Samuel's concern.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rabbi Elazar stated that messengers of a mitzvah are not harmed, contradicting the story where the boy died while fulfilling a mitzvah.
The Gemara answers that the principle applies only on the way to perform the mitzvah, not on the return, distinguishing the boy's death on his return.
The Gemara objects further that Rabbi Elazar explicitly said messengers of a mitzvah are not harmed either on the way or on the return.
The Gemara resolves that the ladder was unstable, a fixed danger, and one does not rely on a miracle in such cases, citing Samuel's fear of Saul as a precedent.

items.text: Acher's downfall and the story of the ladder
items.text_en: Acher's downfall and the story of the ladder
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef says that if Acher (Elisha ben Avuya) had interpreted the verse like Rabbi Yaakov, he would not have sinned. Some say Acher saw a similar incident; others say he saw the tongue of Chutzpit the Meturgeman being dragged by a pig, leading him to heresy.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef states that if Acher had interpreted the verse like Rabbi Yaakov, he would not have sinned.
The Gemara asks: What was the incident with Acher?
Some say Acher saw an incident similar to the one described by Rabbi Yaakov.
Others say Acher saw the tongue of Chutzpit the Meturgeman being dragged by a pig, which led him to heresy.

items.text: Contradiction about reward for refraining from sin
items.text_en: Contradiction about reward for refraining from sin
items.desc_en: Rav Tovi bar Rav Kisma raises a contradiction: the Mishnah implies reward only for doing a mitzvah, but another source says one who sits and does not sin is rewarded as if they performed a mitzvah. Rava resolves that it refers to one who was tempted by a sin and refrained, illustrated by the story of Rabbi Chanina bar Papi who was saved from a matron through miraculous means.

sub.text: Rav Tovi bar Rav Kisma's question
sub.text_en: Rav Tovi bar Rav Kisma's question
sub.desc_en: Rav Tovi bar Rav Kisma raises a contradiction: the Mishnah implies reward only for doing a mitzvah, but another source says one who sits and does not sin is rewarded as if they performed a mitzvah.
Rava resolves that the second source refers to one who was tempted by a sin and refrained.

sub.text: Supporting story of Rabbi Chanina bar Papi
sub.text_en: Supporting story of Rabbi Chanina bar Papi
sub.desc_en: The gemara illustrates Rava's answer with the story of Rabbi Chanina bar Papi who was saved from a matron through miraculous means.

items.text: Stories of rabbis saved from temptation
items.text_en: Stories of rabbis saved from temptation
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts how Rabbi Tzadok and Rav Kahana were each approached by a Roman matron and miraculously saved from sin. Rabbi Tzadok pretended to be weak and then sat in an oven, while Rav Kahana jumped from a roof and was caught by Elijah. These stories illustrate the principle that one who is saved from a forbidden sexual encounter is worthy of a miracle.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by recounting that Caesar's officers guarded Rabbi Tzadok all night and asked if he was saved from a forbidden sexual encounter, citing the principle that one saved from such a sin is worthy of a miracle.
The Gemara tells how a Roman matron propositioned Rabbi Tzadok; he feigned weakness, asked for food, and when she baked bread in an oven, he sat inside it, demonstrating his resolve to avoid sin.
The Gemara tells how a Roman matron propositioned Rav Kahana; he said he would prepare himself, jumped from a roof, and was caught by Elijah, who gave him a purse of dinars.

items.text: The Mishnah on mitzvot with fruits in this world
items.text_en: The Mishnah on mitzvot with fruits in this world
items.desc_en: Rava cites the Mishnah listing mitzvot whose fruits are enjoyed in this world while the principal remains for the World to Come: honoring parents, gemilut chasadim, bringing peace, and Torah study which is equivalent to all. The Gemara provides scriptural support for each, with Rabbi Abahu deriving a gezerah shavah for peace.

sub.desc_en: Rava cites the Mishnah listing mitzvot whose fruits are enjoyed in this world while the principal remains for the World to Come.

sub.text: Gemara's scriptural support for honoring parents and gemilut chasadim
sub.text_en: Gemara's scriptural support for honoring parents and gemilut chasadim
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites verses for honoring parents (long life) and gemilut chasadim (finds life and honor).

sub.text: Rabbi Abahu's gezerah shavah for peace and Torah study
sub.text_en: Rabbi Abahu's gezerah shavah for peace and Torah study
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abahu derives a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from 'רדיפה' (pursuit) to link peace with gemilut chasadim, and cites the verse for Torah study as life and length of days.

items.text: Objection: Why not include shiluach haken?
items.text_en: Objection: Why not include shiluach haken?
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the mitzvah of shiluach haken also has the reward of long life, so it should have been included in the Mishnah. The answer is that the Tanna taught and omitted some items, but this is challenged because the Mishnah says 'these are the things' implying an exhaustive list.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the mitzvah of shiluach haken also has the reward of long life, so it should have been included in the Mishnah.
The Gemara answers that the Tanna taught and omitted some items.
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah says 'these are the things,' implying an exhaustive list, so the answer of omission is invalid.

items.text: Rava's explanation: Merit has principal and fruits
items.text_en: Rava's explanation: Merit has principal and fruits
items.desc_en: Rava explains that merit has both principal and fruits, as derived from the verse about the righteous. Sin has principal but no fruits, except for sins that produce fruits. This resolves the objection by showing that the Mishnah only includes mitzvot whose fruits are explicitly mentioned in the Torah.

sub.desc_en: Rava introduces that Rav Idi explained to him the distinction between a righteous person who is good to Heaven and people versus one who is only good to Heaven.
Rava draws a parallel analogy for the wicked, distinguishing between one who is bad to Heaven and people versus one who is only bad to Heaven.
Rava concludes that merit has both principal and fruits, while sin has principal but no fruits, citing verses for each.
Rava qualifies that a sin which produces fruits does have fruits, but one that does not produce fruits has none.

items.text: Good and bad thoughts are joined to action
items.text_en: Good and bad thoughts are joined to action
items.desc_en: The Gemara teaches that a good thought is joined to action by God, even if not fulfilled due to circumstances. A bad thought is not joined to action unless it produces fruit, except for idolatry, where even a thought is considered severe, as taught by Rav Acha bar Yaakov.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that a good thought is joined to action, citing a verse and Rav Asi's explanation that even if one intended a מצוה (commandment) but was prevented, it is credited as if performed.
The Gemara asks about bad thoughts, stating that God does not join them to action, citing a verse, and then questions a contradictory verse about bringing 'fruit of their thoughts'.
The Gemara resolves that a bad thought that produces fruit (leads to action) is joined to action, but one without fruit is not.
The Gemara objects with a verse that seems to punish mere thoughts of idolatry, contradicting the principle that bad thoughts without fruit are not joined.
Rav Acha bar Yaakov answers that the verse refers specifically to עבודה זרה (idolatry), which is uniquely severe, as denying it is like affirming the entire Torah.

items.text: Sin in private vs. public desecration of God's name
items.text_en: Sin in private vs. public desecration of God's name
items.desc_en: Ulla cites Rav Huna that repeating a sin makes it permissible, but the Gemara corrects that it becomes like permissible. Rabbi Abahu and Rabbi Ilai rule that it is better to sin in private than to publicly desecrate God's name. A contradiction is raised about one who does not care for God's honor, and resolved: if one can overcome his inclination, he must not sin even in private; if not, he may sin in private.

sub.desc_en: Ulla cites Rav Huna's principle that repeating a sin makes it seem permissible, but the Gemara corrects that it only becomes like permissible.

sub.text: Rabbi Abahu in the name of Rabbi Chanina
sub.text_en: Rabbi Abahu in the name of Rabbi Chanina
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abahu cites Rabbi Chanina that it is better to sin in private than to publicly desecrate God's name, citing a verse.
Rabbi Ilai the Elder advises that one overcome by his inclination should go to an unrecognized place and sin privately rather than desecrate God's name publicly.
The Gemara objects by citing a baraita that one who does not care for God's honor should not have been born, with Rabbah and Rav Yosef defining this as one who sins in private.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: if one can overcome his inclination, he must not sin even in private; if not, he may sin in private to avoid public desecration.

items.text: The principle of no leniency for chillul Hashem
items.text_en: The principle of no leniency for chillul Hashem
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that there is no 'surrounding' for chillul Hashem, meaning one cannot treat it leniently. Mar Zutra explains it means one does not act like a storekeeper (who gives a little extra), while Mar bar Ravina says it means if a person's merits and sins are balanced, the sin of chillul Hashem tips the scale to guilt.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that there is no 'surrounding' (leniency) for chillul Hashem, whether unintentional or intentional.
The Gemara asks what 'אין מקיפין' (no surrounding) means in this context.
Mar Zutra explains that 'אין מקיפין' means one does not act like a storekeeper (who gives a little extra), i.e., no lenient calculation.
Mar bar Ravina explains that 'אין מקיפין' means if a person's merits and sins are balanced, the sin of chillul Hashem tips the scale to guilt.
The Sages taught a baraita that begins with 'לעולם' (always), providing further support for the severity of chillul Hashem.

items.text: Opening Tannaic statement and Rabbi Elazar's expansion
items.text_en: Opening Tannaic statement and Rabbi Elazar's expansion
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that a person should see themselves as half guilty and half innocent; one mitzvah tips the scale to merit, one sin to guilt. Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon expands this to say the world is judged by its majority, so one action can tip the entire world.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a person should view themselves as half guilty and half innocent, and that one mitzvah or sin tips the scale, citing the verse 'one sinner destroys much good'.
Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon expands the Mishnah's principle, teaching that since the world is judged by its majority, one action can tip not only the individual but the entire world to merit or guilt.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's view and Resh Lakish's resolution
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's view and Resh Lakish's resolution
