items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai argues that even a completely righteous person who rebels at the end loses all previous merit, and a complete sinner who repents is no longer reminded of his wickedness. The Gemara questions how this fits with the half-half model, and Resh Lakish answers that it refers to one who is confounded about his earlier deeds.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai states that even a completely righteous person who rebels at the end loses all previous merit, and a complete sinner who repents is no longer reminded of his wickedness.
The Gemara questions how Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's view fits with the half-half model of judgment.
Resh Lakish answers that it refers to one who is confounded about his earlier deeds, so the half-half model does not apply.

items.text: Mishnah: The threefold cord
items.text_en: Mishnah: The threefold cord
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who is engaged in Scripture, Mishnah, and proper conduct (דרך ארץ) will not sin quickly, citing the verse about a threefold cord not being quickly broken. One lacking all three is not part of civilized society.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one engaged in Scripture, Mishnah, and proper conduct (דרך ארץ) will not sin quickly, citing the verse about a threefold cord, and that one lacking all three is not part of civilized society.

items.text: Gemara: Parable of the tree for righteous and wicked
items.text_en: Gemara: Parable of the tree for righteous and wicked
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok compares the righteous to a tree whose trunk is in a pure place but branches extend to impurity; when branches are cut, the whole is pure, so God brings suffering to the righteous to secure their share in the World to Come. The wicked are like a tree whose trunk is in impurity but branches extend to purity; when branches are cut, the whole is impure, so God gives them good in this world to lead them to the lowest level.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok compares the righteous to a tree whose trunk is in a pure place but branches extend to impurity; when branches are cut, the whole is pure, so God brings suffering to the righteous to secure their share in the World to Come.

Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok compares the wicked to a tree whose trunk is in impurity but branches extend to purity; when branches are cut, the whole is impure, so God gives them good in this world to lead them to the lowest level.

items.text: Debate: Is study or action greater?
items.text_en: Debate: Is study or action greater?
items.desc_en: The elders in the attic of Beit Nitzah in Lod were asked whether study or action is greater. Rabbi Tarfon said action is greater, Rabbi Akiva said study is greater, and all concluded that study is greater because it leads to action.

sub.desc_en: The narrative sets the scene: Rabbi Tarfon and the elders were gathered in the attic of Beit Nitzah in Lod, and a question was posed to them: is study (תלמוד) or action (מעשה) greater?
Rabbi Tarfon answers that action (מעשה) is greater.
Rabbi Akiva answers that study (תלמוד) is greater.
All the elders conclude that study (תלמוד) is greater because it leads to action (מעשה).

items.text: Rabbi Yose: Study precedes practice in time and judgment
items.text_en: Rabbi Yose: Study precedes practice in time and judgment
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yose states that study preceded the practice of various agricultural commandments by many years. The Gemara clarifies a calculation about the Jubilee year. It then derives that just as study precedes action, so judgment on Torah study precedes judgment on actions, and reward for study precedes reward for actions, citing verses.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yose states that Torah study preceded the practice of various agricultural commandments by many years, listing specific intervals.
The Gemara questions the calculation, noting that the interval for Jubilee should be 104 years, not 103.
The Gemara resolves the discrepancy by explaining that Rabbi Yose holds that the Jubilee year itself counts as a Sabbatical year from its beginning, reducing the total by one.
The Gemara cites Rav Hamnuna to derive that just as study precedes action, so judgment on Torah study precedes judgment on actions, supported by a verse.
The Gemara concludes that just as judgment precedes action, so reward for study precedes reward for action, citing a verse about inheriting lands for keeping God's laws.

items.text: Disqualification for testimony and Bar Kappara's teaching
items.text_en: Disqualification for testimony and Bar Kappara's teaching
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan says one who lacks Scripture, Mishnah, and proper conduct is disqualified from testimony. A baraita compares one who eats in the market to a dog, and some say such a person is disqualified from testimony; Rabbi Idi bar Avin rules in favor of the latter. Bar Kappara begins a teaching about an angry person.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who lacks Scripture and Mishnah is not part of civilized society.
Rabbi Yochanan rules that such a person is disqualified from giving testimony.
A baraita compares one who eats in the market to a dog.
Some say such a person is disqualified from testimony.
Rabbi Idi bar Avin rules that the halacha follows the opinion that disqualifies such a person from testimony.
Bar Kappara begins a teaching about an angry person.

items.text: Closing statement of the previous chapter
items.text_en: Closing statement of the previous chapter
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that one who does not engage in Torah, Mishnah, and proper conduct is a disgrace, citing a verse about the seat of scoffers.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that one who does not engage in Torah, Mishnah, and proper conduct is a disgrace, citing the verse about the seat of scoffers.

items.text: Return to the Mishnah
items.text_en: Return to the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The text returns to the Mishnah's discussion of betrothal.

sub.desc_en: The gemara signals a return to the Mishnah's discussion of betrothal.

items.text: Mishnah: Betrothal through oneself or agent
items.text_en: Mishnah: Betrothal through oneself or agent
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a man may betroth through himself or his agent, and a woman may be betrothed through herself or her agent; a father may betroth his minor daughter through himself or his agent.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule that a man may betroth through himself or his agent, and similarly a woman may be betrothed through herself or her agent, and a father may betroth his minor daughter through himself or his agent.

items.text: Gemara's question and Rav Yosef's answer about the man
items.text_en: Gemara's question and Rav Yosef's answer about the man
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah mentions agency when self-betrothal is obvious. Rav Yosef explains that it teaches a mitzvah to perform betrothal personally rather than through an agent, citing examples of rabbis preparing food themselves. Another version adds a prohibition based on Rav Yehuda's statement that one must see the woman before betrothal to avoid finding something repulsive.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah mentions that a man can betroth through an agent, since betrothing himself is more obvious.
Rav Yosef answers that it is a מצוה (commandment) to perform betrothal personally rather than through an agent.
The Gemara cites examples of Rav Safra roasting a head and Rava salting a fish to show that rabbis personally prepare food rather than delegating.
An alternative version adds that there is also a prohibition involved in betrothing through an agent.
Rav Yehuda citing Rav states that a man is forbidden to betroth a woman until he sees her, lest he find something repulsive and violate the commandment to love one's neighbor as oneself.

items.text: Rav Yosef's answer applied to the woman, and Reish Lakish's view
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's answer applied to the woman, and Reish Lakish's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rav Yosef's statement was actually said regarding the woman's case: it is a mitzvah for her to be betrothed personally. However, there is no prohibition for her, as Reish Lakish says it is better to live with a husband than to be a widow.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that Rav Yosef's statement about a mitzvah to perform the act personally was actually said regarding the woman's case in the Mishnah.
The Gemara concludes that for the woman there is no prohibition against using a shaliach, citing Reish Lakish's principle that it is better to live with a husband than to be a widow.

items.text: Father's betrothal of his daughter: only when she is a נערה
items.text_en: Father's betrothal of his daughter: only when she is a נערה
items.desc_en: The Mishnah specifies that a father may betroth his daughter when she is a נערה (adolescent), implying not when she is a קטנה (minor). This supports Rav's statement that one should not betroth his minor daughter until she grows up and expresses her preference.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a father may betroth his daughter when she is a נערה (adolescent), implying not when she is a קטנה (minor).
The Gemara notes that this supports Rav's statement, as cited by Rav Yehuda or Rabbi Elazar, that one should not betroth his minor daughter until she grows up and expresses her preference.

items.text: Derivation of agency for betrothal from divorce
items.text_en: Derivation of agency for betrothal from divorce
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives agency for divorce from the verses 'ושלח' and 'ושלחה', teaching that a husband and wife can appoint agents, and an agent can appoint another agent. For betrothal, it is derived by analogy from divorce using the verses 'ויצאה' and 'והיתה', equating betrothal (הויה) to divorce (יציאה).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where do we derive the principle of agency (שליחות) for betrothal? It cites a baraita that derives from the verse 'ושלח' that a husband can appoint an agent for divorce.
The baraita continues: from 'ושלחה' we learn that the wife can appoint an agent, and from the repetition of 'ושלח' and 'ושלחה' we learn that an agent can appoint another agent.
The Gemara asks: we found agency for divorce, but from where do we derive it for betrothal? It raises an objection: perhaps divorce is unique because it can be performed against the wife's will.

The Gemara answers: the verse 'ויצאה' (and she departs) and 'והיתה' (and she becomes) equate betrothal (הויה) to divorce (יציאה), teaching that just as divorce allows agency, so too betrothal allows agency.

items.text: Digression: Agency in terumah
items.text_en: Digression: Agency in terumah
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah about an agent for terumah, who must act according to the homeowner's intent, and if unknown, gives an average amount (one-fiftieth).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah about an agent for תרומה (priestly portion), who must act according to the homeowner's intent, and if unknown, gives an average amount (one-fiftieth).

items.text: Opening Mishnah and derivation of agency for terumah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and derivation of agency for terumah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one reduces or increases the measure by ten, his terumah is valid. The Gemara asks for the source, considering a possible derivation from gittin, but rejects it because gittin applies to non-sacred matters. Instead, the verse 'atem' and 'gam atem' includes the agent.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one reduces or increases the measure by ten, his תרומה (priestly portion) is valid.
The Gemara asks for the source of agency for תרומה, and considers deriving it from גיטין (bills of divorce), but rejects this because גיטין apply to non-sacred matters.
The Gemara answers that the verse 'אַתֶּם' and 'גַּם אַתֶּם' includes the agent for תרומה.

items.text: Objection: Why not write only in terumah and derive others?
items.text_en: Objection: Why not write only in terumah and derive others?
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: why not write the law only in terumah and derive gittin and kodashim from it? It answers that terumah has a unique aspect (involves intent) that would prevent derivation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: why not write the law of agency only in the context of תרומה (priestly portion) and derive the other cases (גיטין and קדשים) from it?
The Gemara answers: because one can refute the derivation, since תרומה (priestly portion) has a unique aspect — it involves מחשבה (intent), which the other cases lack.

items.text: Derivation of agency from kodashim (Passover offering)
items.text_en: Derivation of agency from kodashim (Passover offering)
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah about a group that lost its Passover offering and appointed an agent. It asks for the source, considering derivation from terumah or gittin, but rejects because those are non-sacred relative to kodashim. It then derives from Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha's teaching that an agent is like the person himself, based on the verse 'and they shall slaughter it'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah about a group that lost its Passover offering and appointed an agent, detailing the ruling when the agent slaughters first.
The Gemara asks for the source of agency in kodashim, and rejects deriving it from terumah or gittin because those are non-sacred (חול) relative to kodashim.
The Gemara derives agency from Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha's teaching, based on the verse 'וְשָׁחֲטוּ אֹתוֹ' (and they shall slaughter it), showing that one agent acts for the entire community.

items.text: Objection: Why not write only in kodashim?
items.text_en: Objection: Why not write only in kodashim?
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: why not write the law only in kodashim and derive others? It answers that kodashim has a unique aspect (most actions are done through an agent) that would prevent derivation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Torah should not write the law of agency only in the context of kodashim (sacred offerings) and derive the other cases from there.

The Gemara rejects the proposal because kodashim has a unique feature — most of their actions are performed through an agent — which would prevent deriving other cases via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy).

items.text: Attempt to derive one from two, and final resolution
items.text_en: Attempt to derive one from two, and final resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers deriving one law from the other two, but each proposed derivation fails due to unique aspects. It concludes that the law for terumah is written explicitly, and the others are derived from it, but the verse 'atem' and 'gam atem' is still needed for other purposes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: since one law cannot be derived from another, can we derive one from the other two together?

The Gemara rejects deriving the law of קדשים (sacrifices) from the other two, and also rejects deriving גירושין (divorce) from the other two, because each has a unique feature not shared by the others.

The Gemara concludes that the law for תרומה (priestly portion) is written explicitly in the verse, and the other two are derived from it, but the verse 'אתם' and 'גם אתם' is still needed for other purposes.

items.text: Purpose of 'atem' and 'gam atem' for Rabbi Yannai
items.text_en: Purpose of 'atem' and 'gam atem' for Rabbi Yannai
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the extra words 'atem' and 'gam atem' are needed for Rabbi Yannai's teaching that the agent must be a member of the covenant (a Jew). This excludes a slave, who cannot be an agent for a get, and a gentile, who might be thought eligible because he can separate terumah for himself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the extra words 'atem' and 'gam atem' are needed in the verse about terumah.
Rabbi Yannai explains that 'gam atem' teaches that just as you (the principals) are members of the covenant (בני ברית), so too your agents must be members of the covenant.

The Gemara objects that this principle is already derived from Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba quoting Rabbi Yochanan, who rules that a slave cannot be an agent for a get because he is not subject to the laws of gittin and kiddushin.

The Gemara resolves that the verse is still needed: one might have thought that a slave, who is entirely excluded from the realm of marriage and divorce, is disqualified, but a gentile, who can separate terumah for himself, might be considered eligible as an agent; therefore the verse teaches that a gentile is also excluded.

items.text: Purpose for Rabbi Shimon who exempts gentile's terumah
items.text_en: Purpose for Rabbi Shimon who exempts gentile's terumah
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: for Rabbi Shimon, who exempts gentile's terumah from the laws of me'ilah, why is 'atem' and 'gam atem' needed? It answers that one might think the verse excludes agents entirely, so the extra words include them.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: for Rabbi Shimon, who exempts gentile's terumah from the laws of me'ilah, why are the words 'atem' and 'gam atem' needed?
The Gemara answers: the extra words are necessary, because one might think the verse excludes agents entirely, so the extra words include them.

items.text: Source for Rabbi Yonatan who uses the verse differently
items.text_en: Source for Rabbi Yonatan who uses the verse differently
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: for Rabbi Yonatan, who expounds the verse for another teaching, what is the source for agency? It begins to cite a baraita where Rabbi Yonatan derives that all of Israel go out (to war) from the verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: for Rabbi Yonatan, who expounds this verse for another teaching, what is the source for agency?
The Gemara begins to cite a baraita where Rabbi Yonatan derives that all of Israel go out (to war) from the verse.

items.text: Deriving agency for sacrifices from the paschal lamb
items.text_en: Deriving agency for sacrifices from the paschal lamb
items.desc_en: The Gemara seeks a source for the principle that a person's agent is like himself in sacrificial matters. It first suggests the verse about the paschal lamb, where all of Israel are considered to slaughter one lamb, implying agency, but rejects it because each person has a share in the lamb. It then proposes a verse about taking a lamb for each household, but again rejects it for the same reason, concluding that the two verses together teach agency even where one has no share.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where is the principle of agency in sacrificial matters derived, given that the verse about the paschal lamb implies agency but each person has a share in the lamb?
The Gemara tentatively answers that the source is from that very verse, but immediately objects that the paschal lamb is different because each person has a share in it.
The Gemara proposes another verse about taking a lamb for each household, but again objects that each person has a share in it.
The Gemara concludes that the two verses together teach agency even where one has no share in the offering.

items.text: Rejecting the derivation due to Rabbi Yitzchak's teaching
items.text_en: Rejecting the derivation due to Rabbi Yitzchak's teaching
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the verse is needed for Rabbi Yitzchak's teaching that an adult acquires for the household, not a minor. It responds that this is derived from another verse. The Gemara further objects that the verse is needed to teach that the paschal lamb may be slaughtered for an individual, but the Gemara holds like the one who says it is not slaughtered for an individual.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the verse is needed for Rabbi Yitzchak's teaching that an adult acquires for the household, not a minor.
The Gemara responds that Rabbi Yitzchak's teaching is derived from another verse, not this one.
The Gemara further objects that the verse is needed to teach that the paschal lamb may be slaughtered for an individual.
The Gemara resolves that the derivation holds because it follows the opinion that the paschal lamb is not slaughtered for an individual.

items.text: Rav Giddel's derivation of agency from the princes
items.text_en: Rav Giddel's derivation of agency from the princes
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rav Giddel quoting Rav who derives the principle that a person's agent is like himself from the verse about the princes taking for the land. The Gemara questions why this is needed, and then notes that the verse deals with minors who are not capable of agency.

sub.desc_en: Rav Giddel quotes Rav, asking from where we derive that a person's agent is like himself, citing the verse about the princes taking for the land.
The Gemara objects: why not derive agency from this verse directly, and questions whether this is really about agency.
The Gemara rejects the derivation because the verse deals with minors who are not capable of agency.

items.text: Rava bar Rav Huna's derivation of acquisition for a person not present
items.text_en: Rava bar Rav Huna's derivation of acquisition for a person not present
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rava bar Rav Huna quoting Rav Giddel quoting Rav that the verse teaches that one can acquire benefit for a person not in his presence. The Gemara objects that this is not always a benefit, as some prefer mountains and others valleys.

sub.text: Rava bar Rav Huna quoting Rav Giddel quoting Rav
sub.text_en: Rava bar Rav Huna quoting Rav Giddel quoting Rav
sub.desc_en: Rava bar Rav Huna quotes Rav Giddel quoting Rav that the verse 'וְנָשִׂיא אֶחָד נָשִׂיא אֶחָד' teaches that one can acquire benefit (זכין) for a person not in his presence.
The Gemara objects that this is not always a benefit (זכות), since some prefer mountains and others valleys, so the acquisition could be a detriment (חובה).

items.text: Rava bar Rav Huna's derivation for orphans and court-appointed guardians
items.text_en: Rava bar Rav Huna's derivation for orphans and court-appointed guardians
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a version of Rava bar Rav Huna's teaching that the verse teaches that for orphans dividing their father's estate, the court appoints a guardian to both obligate and acquire for them. The Gemara clarifies that the guardian obligates with the intent to acquire, and cites the verse as the source.

sub.text: Gemara's citation of Rava bar Rav Huna
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of Rava bar Rav Huna
sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces Rava bar Rav Huna's teaching that the court appoints a guardian for orphans dividing their father's estate to obligate and acquire for them.
The Gemara questions why the guardian would need to 'obligate' the orphans, since obligation is detrimental.
The Gemara clarifies that the guardian obligates with the intent to acquire (לָחוּב עַל מְנָת לִזְכּוֹת), and cites the verse as the source.

items.text: Rav Nachman and Shmuel's dispute about orphans' right to protest
items.text_en: Rav Nachman and Shmuel's dispute about orphans' right to protest
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman quotes Shmuel that the court appoints a guardian for orphans and selects a good portion, but when the orphans grow up they can protest the division. Rav Nachman himself says they cannot protest, because otherwise the court's power is undermined.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman cites Shmuel's ruling that when orphans come to divide their father's estate, the court appoints a guardian and selects a good portion, but when the orphans grow up they can protest the division.
Rav Nachman states his own view that the orphans cannot protest after growing up, because otherwise the court's authority (כוח בית דין) would be undermined.

items.text: Objection from the Mishnah about court assessments and resolution
items.text_en: Objection from the Mishnah about court assessments and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rav Nachman's principle of 'the power of the court' seems contradicted by a Mishnah where Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel uses that phrase but the Sages disagree, and Rav Nachman rules like the Sages. The Gemara resolves that there is no contradiction.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rav Nachman holds the principle of 'the power of the court' (מה כוח בית דין יפה), given a Mishnah where Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel uses that phrase but the Sages disagree.
The Gemara cites a Mishnah about court assessments where Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says 'if so, what power of the court is there?' (אם כן מה כוח בית דין יפה), implying the principle.

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Chinana citing Rav Nachman
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Chinana citing Rav Nachman
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Chinana reports that Rav Nachman rules the הלכה (binding law) follows the Sages, who reject Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's use of 'the power of the court' principle.
The Gemara resolves that there is no contradiction between Rav Nachman's position and the Mishnah.

items.text: Distinction between cases where agents can and cannot protest
items.text_en: Distinction between cases where agents can and cannot protest
items.desc_en: The Gemara distinguishes between a case where the agent was mistaken (can protest) and where he was not (cannot protest). It explains that even if not mistaken, they can protest about the wind (i.e., a trivial matter).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara distinguishes between a case where the agent was mistaken (can protest) and where he was not (cannot protest), and clarifies that even when not mistaken, they can protest about trivial matters like the wind.

items.text: Rav Nachman's ruling on brothers dividing property
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's ruling on brothers dividing property
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman states that brothers who divide inherited property are considered like buyers. If the division is off by less than a sixth, the transaction stands; if more than a sixth, it is void; if exactly a sixth, the transaction stands but the overcharge must be returned.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman rules that brothers dividing inherited property are treated as buyers, with specific laws of אונאה (overcharge) applying: less than a sixth stands, more than a sixth is void, exactly a sixth stands with return of the overcharge.

items.text: Rava's qualifications to Rav Nachman's ruling
items.text_en: Rava's qualifications to Rav Nachman's ruling
items.desc_en: Rava qualifies each part of Rav Nachman's ruling: the rule about less than a sixth applies only when the brother did not appoint an agent; the rule about more than a sixth applies only when they did not agree to a court valuation; the rule about exactly a sixth applies only to movable property, not land, and even for land if the division was by measure, weight, or count, the transaction is void even for less than a sixth.

sub.desc_en: Rava qualifies Rav Nachman's ruling about less than a sixth: it applies only when the brother did not appoint an agent, because an agent is sent to correct, not to distort.
Rava qualifies the rule about more than a sixth: it applies only when they did not agree to a court valuation, but if they did, the sale stands, citing a baraita about court valuations.

Rava qualifies the rule about exactly a sixth: it applies only to movable property, not land, and even for land, if divided by measure, weight, or count, the transaction is void even for less than a sixth, citing Rabba's principle.

items.text: Mishnah on sending a fire through an agent and the principle of no agency for sin
items.text_en: Mishnah on sending a fire through an agent and the principle of no agency for sin
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a mishnah about one who sends a fire through a deaf-mute, imbecile, or minor – he is exempt from human judgment but liable to Heaven; if sent through a competent adult, the adult is liable. The Gemara asks why the sender is not liable via the principle of agency, and answers that there is no agency for sin (ein shaliach lidvar aveirah).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a mishnah about one who sends a fire through a deaf-mute, imbecile, or minor – exempt from human judgment but liable to Heaven; if sent through a competent adult, the adult is liable.
The Gemara asks why the sender is not liable via the principle of agency (שלוחו של אדם כמותו).
The Gemara answers that there is no agency for sin (אין שליח לדבר עבירה), since the words of the master and the words of the student – whose words are heeded?

items.text: Challenge from the law of me'ilah (misuse of consecrated property)
items.text_en: Challenge from the law of me'ilah (misuse of consecrated property)
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the principle of no agency for sin from a baraita about me'ilah: if an agent did not carry out his mission, the agent is liable; if he did, the owner is liable. This seems to show agency exists for a sin. The Gemara answers that me'ilah is different because it is derived via a verbal analogy (gezeirah shavah) from terumah, which establishes agency.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita on me'ilah (misuse of consecrated property): if the agent did not carry out his mission, the agent is liable; if he did, the owner is liable.
The Gemara challenges: why does the owner become liable through the agent's action, given the principle that there is no agency for sin (אין שליח לדבר עבירה)?
The Gemara answers that me'ilah is different because it is derived via a verbal analogy (גזירה שוה) from terumah, which establishes agency.

items.text: Rejection of learning from me'ilah due to two verses as one
items.text_en: Rejection of learning from me'ilah due to two verses as one
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects learning from me'ilah because me'ilah and the law of shlichut yad (sending a hand) are two verses that come as one (shenei ketuvim haba'im ke'echad) and thus cannot teach other cases. It then explains the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel regarding shlichut yad, where Beit Shammai holds one is liable for mere intent, while Beit Hillel requires a physical act. The verses are reconciled to include agency.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why we cannot learn the principle of agency from the law of me'ilah (misuse of sacred property), and answers that me'ilah and shlichut yad (the law of an agent who steals) are two verses that come as one (שני כתובים הבאים כאחד) and thus cannot teach other cases.
The Gemara asks what the verse regarding shlichut yad (sending a hand) is, which serves as the second verse that comes as one.

The Gemara cites a baraita that records the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel regarding the verse 'על כל דבר פשע' (for any matter of trespass): Beit Shammai holds that one is liable for mere intent (מחשבה כמעשה), while Beit Hillel requires a physical act of sending a hand (שליחות יד).

sub.text: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel's debate
sub.text_en: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel's debate
sub.desc_en: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel debate the interpretation of the verses: Beit Shammai argues from 'על כל דבר פשע' that intent alone suffices, Beit Hillel counters with 'אם לא שלח ידו' requiring a physical act, and Beit Shammai then explains that the verse 'על כל דבר פשע' teaches that agency (shlichut) applies to one's servant or agent.

items.text: Conclusion for Beit Shammai's interpretation
items.text_en: Conclusion for Beit Shammai's interpretation
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that for Beit Shammai, who interpret the verse about intent, the derivation of agency from the verse is straightforward.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that for Beit Shammai, who interpret the verse about intent, the derivation of agency from the verse is straightforward.

items.text: Rejecting derivation from me'ilah and tevichah u-mekhirah as two verses that come as one
items.text_en: Rejecting derivation from me'ilah and tevichah u-mekhirah as two verses that come as one
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the attempt to derive that an agent is liable from the laws of me'ilah and tevichah u-mekhirah, because these are two verses that come as one and thus cannot teach a general rule. It then explains the derivation from tevichah u-mekhirah and cites the derivations from the schools of Rabbi Yishmael and Chizkiyah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes to derive the agent's liability from me'ilah and tevichah u-mekhirah, but rejects it because these are two verses that come as one and thus cannot teach a general rule.
The Gemara explains the derivation from tevichah u-mekhirah: just as sale is through another, so too slaughter is through another.
The school of Rabbi Yishmael teaches that the word 'אוֹ' (or) comes to include the agent.
The school of Chizkiyah teaches that the word 'תַּחַת' (instead) comes to include the agent.

items.text: Deriving the rule from shechutei chutz and the verse 've-nichrat ha-ish ha-hu'
items.text_en: Deriving the rule from shechutei chutz and the verse 've-nichrat ha-ish ha-hu'
items.desc_en: For those who hold that two verses that come as one do teach, the Gemara cites the derivation from shechutei chutz. It then asks how we derive the rule for the entire Torah, and answers that the verse 've-nichrat ha-ish ha-hu' is written to teach this principle for the entire Torah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the previous derivation works for the view that two verses that come as one do not teach, but asks what can be said for the opposing view.
The Gemara answers that the Torah revealed in the case of shechutei chutz (slaughter outside the Temple) that the verse 'דם יחשב לאיש ההוא דם שפך' teaches 'he' and not his agent.
The Gemara asks: we found the rule for shechutei chutz, but from where do we derive it for the entire Torah?
The Gemara answers that we would learn from shechutei chutz, but then the verse 'ונכרת האיש ההוא' is written to apply the principle to the entire Torah.

items.text: Exposition of 'hu' and 'ha-hu' for those who hold two verses do not teach
items.text_en: Exposition of 'hu' and 'ha-hu' for those who hold two verses do not teach
items.desc_en: For those who hold that two verses that come as one do not teach, the Gemara explains that the extra 'hu' and 'ha-hu' verses are used to exclude cases of two people holding a knife, an unwilling person, an unwitting person, and a misled person. The other opinion does not expound 'hu' and 'ha-hu'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: For the one who holds that two verses that come as one do not teach, what does he expound from these 'ha-hu' verses?
The Gemara answers: One verse excludes two people holding a knife and slaughtering, and the other 'hu' excludes an unwilling person, an unwitting person, and a misled person.
The Gemara asks: And the other opinion (who holds that two verses do teach) — what does he do with these verses?
The Gemara answers: The other opinion derives the exclusions from 'hu' and 'ha-hu' themselves, and does not expound the extra 'hu' and 'ha-hu' verses.

items.text: Dispute between Shammai the Elder and Tanna Kamma regarding the agent's liability in murder
items.text_en: Dispute between Shammai the Elder and Tanna Kamma regarding the agent's liability in murder
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who sends an agent to kill is liable while the agent is exempt. Shammai the Elder, citing Chaggai the prophet, holds the agent liable, based on the verse 'Oto haragta be-cherev bnei Ammon'. The Gemara explains that Shammai holds that two verses that come as one teach, and does not expound 'hu' and 'ha-hu'. Alternatively, Shammai's liability is only in the eyes of Heaven. The Gemara also discusses the case of Uriah the Hittite.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who sends an agent to kill is liable while the agent is exempt; Shammai the Elder, citing Chaggai the prophet, holds the agent liable based on the verse 'אֹתוֹ הָרַגְתָּ בְּחֶרֶב בְּנֵי עַמּוֹן'.
The Gemara explains that Shammai holds that two verses that come as one teach, and does not expound 'הוּא' and 'הַהוּא'; alternatively, Shammai's liability is only in the eyes of Heaven.

The Gemara objects that if Shammai's liability is only in the eyes of Heaven, then the Tanna Kamma would hold the agent exempt even from Heaven, which is impossible; the Gemara resolves that the dispute is about a major and minor judgment.
The Gemara offers an alternative explanation: the case of Uriah is different because the verse 'אֹתוֹ הָרַגְתָּ בְּחֶרֶב בְּנֵי עַמּוֹן' explicitly indicates liability.

The Gemara rejects this, explaining that the verse compares Uriah to the sword of Ammon, meaning just as one is not punished for the sword, so too one is not punished for Uriah, because he was a rebel against the kingdom.

items.text: Rava's ruling on agency for forbidden acts like bestiality and eating chelev
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on agency for forbidden acts like bestiality and eating chelev
items.desc_en: Rava states that even if Shammai holds that two verses teach and does not expound 'hu' and 'ha-hu', he would agree that in cases of bestiality or eating chelev, the sender is liable and the agent is exempt, because we never find in the entire Torah that one benefits while another is liable.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that even if Shammai holds that two verses teach and does not expound 'hu' and 'ha-hu', he would agree that in cases of bestiality or eating chelev, the sender is liable and the agent is exempt, because we never find in the entire Torah that one benefits while another is liable.

items.text: Dispute between Rav and the school of Rabbi Sheila about whether an agent becomes a witness
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and the school of Rabbi Sheila about whether an agent becomes a witness
items.desc_en: Rav holds that an agent becomes a witness, while the school of Rabbi Sheila holds he does not. The Gemara explains the reasoning: the school of Rabbi Sheila argues that since the agent is like the person himself, he cannot be a witness. A baraita is brought from Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel regarding three people sent to betroth a woman. The Gemara concludes that the halakha is that an agent becomes a witness.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute: Rav holds that an agent becomes a witness, while the school of Rabbi Sheila holds that an agent does not become a witness.
The Gemara asks what the reasoning of the school of Rabbi Sheila is, and rejects a possible answer that it is because the principal did not explicitly say 'be my witness'.

The Gemara explains: Rav holds that the agent is empowered to strengthen the transaction, while the school of Rabbi Sheila holds that since the agent is like the person himself, he cannot serve as a witness.

sub.text: Supporting baraita (Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel)
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita (Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel)
sub.desc_en: A baraita is brought: if one told three people to betroth a woman, Beit Shammai says one is an agent and two are witnesses, while Beit Hillel says all are agents and an agent does not become a witness; the Gemara notes that the dispute is only about three, but with two all agree.
The Gemara resolves that Rav follows the Tanna Rabbi Natan's version of the dispute, and concludes that the halakha (הלכה) is that an agent becomes a witness.

items.text: Rava in the name of Rav Nachman: two agents are also witnesses for betrothal and divorce
items.text_en: Rava in the name of Rav Nachman: two agents are also witnesses for betrothal and divorce
items.desc_en: Rava quotes Rav Nachman that if one says to two people 'Go and betroth a woman for me,' they are both his agents and his witnesses. The same applies to divorce.

sub.desc_en: Rava states in the name of Rav Nachman that when one tells two people to go betroth a woman for him, they serve both as his agents and as witnesses, and the same rule applies to divorce.

items.text: Opening Mishnah and Gemara's first question
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and Gemara's first question
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a betrothed woman and her father receive her get together. Rabbi Yehuda says only the father receives it. The Gemara asks: why is this rule needed for kiddushin? Because the father might restrict her; for divorce, perhaps he gave her his eye? And for money, they might dispute.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the same rule applies to monetary cases.
The Gemara asks why the Mishnah needs to list both kiddushin and divorce cases, explaining that each case alone might have been insufficient to teach the rule.

items.text: Gemara's first answer: witnesses needed for repayment
items.text_en: Gemara's first answer: witnesses needed for repayment
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially assumes that a lender who lends with witnesses must repay with witnesses, so the witnesses' testimony that they saw repayment would be relevant. But if the lender says 'I didn't repay' and the witnesses say 'they did repay', they contradict each other, so the lender's oath would be needed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the lender's assumption is: if he assumes that a loan with witnesses requires repayment with witnesses, then the witnesses are interested parties because they could be sued for repayment if they say they didn't repay.

items.text: Gemara's revised answer: no witnesses needed for repayment
items.text_en: Gemara's revised answer: no witnesses needed for repayment
items.desc_en: The Gemara revises: a lender who lends with witnesses does NOT need to repay with witnesses. So the witnesses can say 'we returned the loan to the lender' and the lender can say 'I didn't receive it', and they don't contradict. But the lender's oath (heiset) is instituted to prevent fraud.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara revises its position: a lender who lends with witnesses does not need to repay with witnesses, so the witnesses can claim they repaid the lender, and the lender's denial does not contradict them.

items.text: Gemara's conclusion: oath instituted for lenders
items.text_en: Gemara's conclusion: oath instituted for lenders
items.desc_en: Since the rabbis instituted the heiset oath for lenders, the witnesses now swear they gave the money, and the lender swears he didn't receive it, and the borrower repays the lender.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that now that the rabbis instituted the heiset oath (שבועת היסת), the witnesses swear they gave the money, the lender swears he did not receive it, and the borrower repays the lender.

items.text: Mishnah: woman and father receive get together
items.text_en: Mishnah: woman and father receive get together
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states: a betrothed woman and her father receive her get. Rabbi Yehuda says only the father receives it. And any woman who cannot guard her get cannot divorce.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a betrothed girl and her father receive her get together, but Rabbi Yehuda says only the father receives it, and any girl who cannot guard her get cannot be divorced.

items.text: Resh Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan dispute on kiddushin
items.text_en: Resh Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan dispute on kiddushin
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish says the dispute over who receives the get extends to kiddushin: the father or the woman. Rabbi Yochanan says the dispute is only for divorce; for kiddushin, all agree the father betroths, not the woman.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish says the dispute between the Sages and Rabbi Yehuda applies equally to divorce and kiddushin, while Rabbi Yochanan says it applies only to divorce, but for kiddushin all agree the father alone acts.
Rabbi Yochanan counters that the dispute applies only to divorce; for kiddushin, all agree that the father betroths the daughter, not the woman herself.

items.text: Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina explains Rabbi Yochanan's reasoning
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina explains Rabbi Yochanan's reasoning
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina explains: for divorce, the woman enters her father's domain, so both she and father are involved. For kiddushin, she leaves her father's domain, so only the father acts.

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's explanation
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's explanation
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina explains Rabbi Yochanan's reasoning: for divorce, which returns the girl to her father's authority, both she and her father can receive it; for kiddushin, which removes her from her father's authority, only the father can act.

items.text: Gemara cites a maamar (statement) supporting the distinction
items.text_en: Gemara cites a maamar (statement) supporting the distinction
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a maamar that says: for kiddushin, which removes the woman from her father's domain, the father betroths, not the woman. This supports Rabbi Yochanan's view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the case of מאמר (a yavam's declaration of betrothal) also removes the girl from her father's authority, yet a Mishnah teaches otherwise, challenging Rabbi Yochanan's distinction.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a minor girl from betrothal (i.e., a yevamah who is a minor) cannot receive ma'amar without her father's consent, while a נערה (adolescent) can consent either herself or through her father, unlike in regular kiddushin.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a minor girl from betrothal cannot receive ma'amar without her father's consent, while a נערה (adolescent) can consent either herself or through her father, unlike in regular kiddushin.

items.text: Gemara's resolution of Rabbi Yochanan's position
items.text_en: Gemara's resolution of Rabbi Yochanan's position
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina explains Rabbi Yochanan's reasoning: in kiddushin, which requires consent, only the father acts; in divorce, which is against her will, both she and her father act. The Gemara objects that ma'amar is also with consent, yet the Mishnah says both she and her father. The Gemara answers that the Mishnah refers to ma'amar against her will, and follows Rabbi's opinion that ma'amar can be done against her will, derived from yibum. The dispute between Rabbi and the Sages is whether to derive from yibum or kiddushin.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a corrected version of Rabbi Yochanan's statement.

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's explanation
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's explanation
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina explains Rabbi Yochanan's reasoning: in kiddushin, which requires consent, only the father acts; in divorce, which is against her will, both she and her father act.
The Gemara objects that ma'amar is also with consent, yet the Mishnah says both she and her father.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah refers to ma'amar against her will, and follows Rabbi's opinion that ma'amar can be done against her will, citing a baraita.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi derives ma'amar from yibum (against her will), while the Sages derive it from kiddushin (with consent).
The Gemara concludes that the dispute between Rabbi and the Sages is whether to derive from yibum or kiddushin.

items.text: Support for Rabbi Yochanan and refutation of Resh Lakish
items.text_en: Support for Rabbi Yochanan and refutation of Resh Lakish
items.desc_en: The Gemara finds support for Rabbi Yochanan from the Mishnah's phrase 'unlike in kiddushin,' which would be a refutation of Resh Lakish. Resh Lakish deflects by attributing the Mishnah to Rabbi Yehudah, who holds that two hands cannot acquire simultaneously. The Gemara questions why the Mishnah says 'unlike in kiddushin' rather than 'unlike in divorce,' and answers that since ma'amar resembles kiddushin, the Mishnah used that term. The Gemara then explains that ma'amar is different because the yevamah is already 'bound' (זקוקה ועומדת), resolving both the original question and Rabbi Yochanan's difficulty.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara finds support for Rabbi Yochanan's resolution from the Mishnah's phrase 'unlike in kiddushin,' and suggests this refutes Resh Lakish.
Resh Lakish deflects the refutation by attributing the Mishnah to Rabbi Yehudah, who holds that two hands cannot acquire simultaneously.
The Gemara questions why the Mishnah says 'unlike in kiddushin' rather than 'unlike in divorce,' given Rabbi Yehudah's position.
The Gemara answers that since ma'amar (the act of yibbum) resembles kiddushin, the Mishnah used the term 'kiddushin' rather than 'divorce.'
The Gemara explains that ma'amar is different from kiddushin because the yevamah is already 'bound' (זקוקה ועומדת), resolving both the original question and Rabbi Yochanan's difficulty.

items.text: Refutation of Resh Lakish from a Mishnah about a father's agency
items.text_en: Refutation of Resh Lakish from a Mishnah about a father's agency
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah stating that a man can betroth his daughter when she is a נערה through himself or his agent, but not through her or her agent, which contradicts Resh Lakish's position. Resh Lakish responds that this Mishnah also follows Rabbi Yehudah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah stating that a man can betroth his daughter when she is a נערה through himself or his agent, but not through her or her agent, which contradicts Resh Lakish's position.
Resh Lakish responds that this Mishnah also follows Rabbi Yehudah's position.

items.text: Analysis of the Mishnah's attribution: Rabbi Yehudah or Rabbi Shimon?
items.text_en: Analysis of the Mishnah's attribution: Rabbi Yehudah or Rabbi Shimon?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah can be attributed to Rabbi Yehudah, given that its later clause about 'hitkadshi li' follows Rabbi Shimon's view that one must say 'shevuah' to each. The Gemara considers that the entire Mishnah might be Rabbi Shimon, who holds like Rabbi Yehudah regarding agency. It concludes that the entire Mishnah is Rabbi Shimon, and he holds like Rabbi Yehudah regarding agency.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah can be attributed to Rabbi Yehudah, given that the later clause about 'hitkadshi li' requires a separate declaration for each item.
Rabbah answers that the Mishnah's clause follows Rabbi Shimon, who requires a separate oath for each item.
The Gemara objects that if the entire Mishnah were Rabbi Yehudah, he would have to hold like Rabbi Shimon on this specific point, which is unlikely.
A baraita is cited showing that Rabbi Yehudah holds one is liable for each separate oath only when the word 'shevuah' is repeated, unlike Rabbi Shimon who requires 'shevuah' for each.
The Gemara concludes that the entire Mishnah is Rabbi Shimon, who holds like Rabbi Yehudah regarding agency.

items.text: Anecdote about Rabbi Asi and the academy's ruling
items.text_en: Anecdote about Rabbi Asi and the academy's ruling
items.desc_en: Rabbi Asi did not enter the academy; he asked Rabbi Zeira what was said. Rabbi Zeira reported that Rabbi Avin said the entire academy follows Rabbi Yochanan, and Resh Lakish cried out in vain. Rabbi Avin is identified as a reliable authority. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak clarifies which Rabbi Avin is meant.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Asi did not enter the academy and asked Rabbi Zeira what was said there.
Rabbi Zeira reported that he also did not enter, but Rabbi Avin said the entire academy follows Rabbi Yochanan, and Resh Lakish cried out in vain.
Rabbi Asi asked whether the Rabbi Avin mentioned is the one who is a reliable authority (בר סמכא).
Rabbi Zeira confirmed that he is indeed a reliable authority, comparing him to the sea for frying pans.

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak clarifies that the Rabbi Avin referred to is neither the son of Rabbi Chiyya nor the son of Kahana, but the anonymous Rabbi Avin, which matters for reconciling his own statements.

items.text: Transition to next topic
items.text_en: Transition to next topic
items.desc_en: Rava asks a question of Rav Nachman, beginning a new discussion.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks a question of Rav Nachman, initiating a new discussion.

items.text: Rava's question about a נערה making an agent
items.text_en: Rava's question about a נערה making an agent
items.desc_en: Rava asks whether a נערה can appoint an agent to receive her get, comparing her status to her father's hand (like her father, she can appoint an agent) or her father's courtyard (the get only takes effect when it reaches her hand).

sub.desc_en: Rava asks whether a נערה (minor girl who has reached puberty) can appoint an agent to receive her get, comparing her status to her father's hand (like her father, she can appoint an agent) or her father's courtyard (the get only takes effect when it reaches her hand).

items.text: Gemara's objection from Rava's own ruling
items.text_en: Gemara's objection from Rava's own ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: Does Rava really have a doubt? He himself ruled that if a get is placed in the hand of a sleeping slave who guards it, it is valid, but if the slave is awake, it is not. If a נערה were like her father's courtyard, even when the get reaches her hand it would not be valid, since it would be a courtyard not guarded with her father's knowledge.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: How can Rava be uncertain? He himself ruled that if a get is placed in the hand of her sleeping slave who guards it, it is a valid get, implying she has her own courtyard; if she were like her father's courtyard, the get would not take effect even when it reaches her hand, because it would be a courtyard guarded without the father's knowledge.

items.text: Resolution: Rava's question is about agency, not courtyard
items.text_en: Resolution: Rava's question is about agency, not courtyard
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that Rava is certain a נערה is like her father's hand, but his question is whether her hand is as strong as her father's to appoint an agent. Rava answers that she cannot appoint an agent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves: Rava is certain she is like her father's hand; his question is whether her power is as strong as her father's to appoint an agent herself, and the answer is that she cannot appoint an agent.
Rava answers that a נערה (minor girl) cannot appoint an agent to receive her גט (bill of divorce).

items.text: Challenge from a Mishnah and resolution
items.text_en: Challenge from a Mishnah and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rava's answer from a Mishnah: a קטנה who says 'accept my get' – it is not a get until it reaches her hand, implying a נערה's get is valid. The Gemara initially deflects by saying the case is where she has no father, but then resolves by emending the Mishnah to distinguish between a קטנה and a נערה, and between cases with and without a father.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rava's ruling by citing a Mishnah: a קטנה (minor girl) who says 'accept my get' – it is not a get until it reaches her hand, implying that a נערה (adolescent girl) can appoint an agent and her get is valid.
The Gemara initially deflects by suggesting the Mishnah's case is where the girl has no father, so the distinction between קטנה and נערה applies only when there is no father to receive the get.
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah's later clause mentions the father, proving that the first clause also deals with a case where the girl has a father, contradicting the deflection.

The Gemara resolves by emending the Mishnah: it teaches that a קטנה cannot appoint an agent, but a נערה can; this applies when she has no father, but when she has a father and he appoints an agent, the husband cannot retract.

items.text: Dispute about a קטנה betrothed without father's knowledge
items.text_en: Dispute about a קטנה betrothed without father's knowledge
items.desc_en: The Gemara reports a dispute: Shmuel says a קטנה who accepted betrothal without her father's knowledge needs both a get and mi'un. Karna objects: if a get is needed, why mi'un? If mi'un, why a get?

sub.desc_en: It was stated: A קטנה (minor girl) who was betrothed without her father's knowledge — Shmuel says she needs both a get and מיאון (refusal); Karna objects: if she needs a get, why מיאון? If she needs מיאון, why a get?
Karna objects: if a גט is needed, why מיאון? If מיאון suffices, why a גט? The two remedies seem contradictory.

items.text: Rav's ruling and oath
items.text_en: Rav's ruling and oath
items.desc_en: The case is sent to Rav, who swears that she needs both a get and mi'un, and says that Abba bar Abba's descendant (Shmuel) would not say otherwise.

sub.text: Narrative of Mar Ukva's court and Rav's ruling
sub.text_en: Narrative of Mar Ukva's court and Rav's ruling
sub.desc_en: They told him: Mar Ukva and his court in Kafri reversed the case and sent it to Rav, who swore that she needs both a get and מיאון, and it is unthinkable that the descendant of Abba bar Abba would say otherwise.

items.text: Reason for the dual requirement
items.text_en: Reason for the dual requirement
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika explains: she needs a get in case the father was appeased by the betrothal, and mi'un in case he was not, to prevent people from saying that betrothal does not take effect on her sister. Rav Nachman adds that this applies only if the father had arranged a match (שידוכין).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the reason for the dual requirement of a get and mi'un.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika's answer
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika's answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika explains: she needs a get in case the father was appeased by the betrothal, and mi'un in case he was not, to prevent people from saying that betrothal does not take effect on her sister.
Rav Nachman adds that this applies only if the father had arranged a match (שידוכין).

items.text: Ulla's lenient opinion
items.text_en: Ulla's lenient opinion
items.desc_en: Ulla says she does not even need mi'un. The Gemara notes a dispute about whether this applies even when there were שידוכין, and records two versions of Ulla's statement.

sub.desc_en: Ulla says she does not even need מיאון, and there is a dispute about whether this applies even when a match was arranged.
The Gemara asks whether Ulla's lenient opinion applies even when there were prior שידוכין (matchmaking negotiations).
The Gemara resolves that there are two versions of Ulla's statement: one who teaches the lenient version does not teach the version about שידוכין, and vice versa.
An alternative version records Ulla's statement without any mention of שידוכין, simply stating that a minor betrothed without her father's knowledge needs no mi'un.

items.text: Challenge from a Mishnah about sisters and resolution
items.text_en: Challenge from a Mishnah about sisters and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana challenges Ulla from a Mishnah that says if a woman dies, mi'uns, or divorces, her co-wives are permitted. The Gemara infers this refers to a case where she betrothed herself, and she needs mi'un. Rav Kahana resolves that the case is where she was treated as an orphan during her father's lifetime (e.g., he was unavailable).

sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana challenges from a Mishnah listing cases where co-wives are permitted, including mi'un (refusal).
The Gemara infers that the Mishnah must refer to a case where the girl betrothed herself, since if her father betrothed her, she would need a full get, not just mi'un.
Rav Kahana resolves the challenge by explaining that the case involves a girl treated as an orphan during her father's lifetime (e.g., he was unavailable), so her betrothal is valid only with mi'un.

items.text: A tangential ruling about selling to relatives
items.text_en: A tangential ruling about selling to relatives
items.desc_en: The Gemara briefly records a dispute: one opinion says a father cannot sell his minor daughter to relatives, while Rabbi Elazar says he may.

sub.text: Rav Hamnuna's objection from a baraita
sub.text_en: Rav Hamnuna's objection from a baraita
sub.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna objects from a baraita: One may not sell her (the minor's property) to relatives; but in the name of Rabbi Elazar they said one may sell to relatives.
In the name of Rabbi Elazar, the baraita concludes that he may sell her to relatives.

items.text: Opening question on the Mishnah's case of a widow sold as a maidservant
items.text_en: Opening question on the Mishnah's case of a widow sold as a maidservant
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a girl can be called a widow if she was sold by her father after betrothal, since a father cannot sell his daughter after marriage. It concludes that she must have betrothed herself, making her a widow.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the Mishnah can call the girl a widow (אלמנה) if she was sold by her father after betrothal, since a father cannot sell his daughter after marriage, concluding that she must have betrothed herself.

items.text: Rav Amram's answer: the case involves kiddushei yi'ud
items.text_en: Rav Amram's answer: the case involves kiddushei yi'ud
items.desc_en: Rav Amram citing Rabbi Yitzchak explains that the Mishnah refers to kiddushei yi'ud, and follows Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda who holds that the first money given for a maidservant is not for betrothal.

sub.desc_en: Rav Amram in the name of Rabbi Yitzchak answers that the case involves קידושי ייעוד (betrothal through designation) and follows Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that the initial money given for the maidservant was not for betrothal purposes.

items.text: Rav Huna's ruling on mi'un for a yevamah who was betrothed twice
items.text_en: Rav Huna's ruling on mi'un for a yevamah who was betrothed twice
items.desc_en: Rav Huna citing Rav states that a girl who falls to yibbum can perform mi'un to annul the ma'amar but not the zikah. The case is when a father betrothed her to two men and may have been appeased by one.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a case where a girl's husband died and she fell to יבום (levirate marriage), and Rav Huna citing Rav rules that she may perform מיאון (refusal) against the מאמר (levirate betrothal) but not against the זיקה (levirate bond), requiring a גט (divorce document), חליצה (release ceremony), and מיאון.

items.text: Explanation of the three requirements: get, chalitzah, and mi'un
items.text_en: Explanation of the three requirements: get, chalitzah, and mi'un
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why each requirement is needed: a get in case the father was appeased by the second betrothal, chalitzah in case he was appeased by the first, and mi'un in case he was not appeased at all, to prevent people from thinking that betrothal of a sister is permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains the reasons for each requirement: a גט (divorce document) in case the father consented to the second betrothal, חליצה (release ceremony) in case he consented to the first, and מיאון (refusal) in case he consented to neither, to prevent people from saying that betrothal does not take effect with the sister.

items.text: Case without ma'amar: only chalitzah is needed
items.text_en: Case without ma'amar: only chalitzah is needed
items.desc_en: If the yavam did not perform ma'amar, only chalitzah is required. The Gemara asks why mi'un is not needed to prevent people from thinking that betrothal of a sister is permitted, and answers that everyone knows that a sister of a chalutzah is only prohibited by rabbinic law, as Reish Lakish taught.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that if the brother did not perform מאמר (levirate betrothal), she only needs חליצה (release ceremony), and addresses the concern about people saying betrothal does not take effect with the sister by citing Reish Lakish that a חלוצה (released woman) is prohibited to her sister only by rabbinic law, so no such concern arises.
The Gemara asks why mi'un is not also required to prevent people from thinking that betrothal of a sister is permitted.
The Gemara answers that everyone knows that the sister of a chalutzah is only prohibited by rabbinic law, citing Reish Lakish's teaching.
Reish Lakish teaches that the sister of a gerushah is prohibited by Torah law, but the sister of a chalutzah is only prohibited by rabbinic decree.

items.text: Ravina's ruling on a case of drinking wine under a palm tree
items.text_en: Ravina's ruling on a case of drinking wine under a palm tree
items.desc_en: Ravina discusses a case where two men were drinking wine, and one gave a cup to the other and said his daughter is betrothed to the other's son. Ravina rules that even according to the one who is concerned that the father may have been appeased, in this case there is no concern.

sub.desc_en: Ravina relates a story of two men drinking wine under a palm tree in Babylonia, where one gave a cup to the other and said his daughter is betrothed to the other's son, and Ravina comments that even according to the one who is concerned that the father might have consented, this case is different.
Ravina rules that even according to the one who is concerned that the father may have been appeased, in this case there is no such concern.

items.text: Gemara's discussion of the possibility of the son's consent
items.text_en: Gemara's discussion of the possibility of the son's consent
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers whether we suspect the son was appeased, and the rabbis ask Ravina if the father might have appointed the son as his agent. Ravina rejects this, and Rabba bar Shimi confirms that the master explicitly rejected the view of Rav and Shmuel.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that we do not suspect the son was appeased.
The rabbis ask Ravina whether perhaps the father appointed the son as his agent.
Ravina rejects the possibility, saying a person is not brazen enough to appoint his father as an agent.
The rabbis ask whether perhaps the son appeased the father.
Rabba bar Shimi confirms that the master explicitly rejected the view of Rav and Shmuel.

items.text: Case of betrothal with a bundle of vegetables in the market
items.text_en: Case of betrothal with a bundle of vegetables in the market
items.desc_en: Ravina rules that even one who suspects the father was appeased would not apply that concern when the betrothal is done in a degrading manner. Rav Acha from Difti asks whether the degradation is due to the vegetables or the market, and Ravina responds that both are degrading.

sub.desc_en: Ravina rules that when a man betroths a woman with a bundle of vegetables in the market, even one who suspects the father was appeased would not apply that concern because the act is degrading, unlike a dignified betrothal.
Rav Acha from Difti asks Ravina whether the degradation is due to the vegetables or the market, and what the ruling would be if only one factor applies.
Ravina responds that both the vegetables and the market are degrading, so either factor alone suffices to preclude concern about the father's consent.

items.text: Case of a man who betrothed his relative after coercion
items.text_en: Case of a man who betrothed his relative after coercion
items.desc_en: A man said to his relative (a woman) that she should be betrothed to his relative, and she said to his relative. He coerced her until she said 'be to his relative.' While they were eating and drinking, his relative came and betrothed her. Abaye and Rava debate whether we assume the betrothal is valid based on the principle that the remnant of Israel does not act deceitfully, or that a person does not prepare a feast and then ruin it.

sub.desc_en: The gemara presents a case: a man said to his relative (a woman) that she should be betrothed to his relative, and she said to his relative; he coerced her until she said 'be to his relative,' and while they were eating and drinking, his relative came and betrothed her.
Abaye argues that the betrothal is valid, citing the verse that the remnant of Israel does not act deceitfully, implying she truly consented.
Rava argues that the betrothal is valid based on the principle that a person does not prepare a feast and then ruin it, so the relative would not have betrothed her without her genuine consent.
The gemara asks what practical difference exists between Abaye's and Rava's positions, and answers that it is a case where the relative did not exert effort (i.e., did not prepare the feast).

items.text: Betrothal with father's knowledge, father went overseas
items.text_en: Betrothal with father's knowledge, father went overseas
items.desc_en: If a daughter was betrothed with her father's knowledge and then he went overseas, and she married, Rav says she may eat terumah until her father returns and objects. Rav Asi says she may not, lest the father object retroactively. The ruling followed Rav Asi. Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak adds that Rav agrees that if she dies, he does not inherit her.

sub.desc_en: Presents the case: a daughter betrothed with her father's knowledge, then the father went overseas, and she married.
Rav rules that she may eat תרומה (priestly portion) until her father returns and objects.
Rav Asi rules that she may not eat, lest the father object retroactively and she be found to have eaten תרומה (priestly portion) as a non-priestess.
The incident occurred and Rav deferred to Rav Asi's position in practice.

sub.text: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak's addition
sub.text_en: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak's addition
sub.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak adds that Rav concedes that if she dies, he does not inherit her.
The gemara explains the principle: money remains in the possession of its owner (the father).

items.text: Betrothal with father's knowledge, marriage without, father present
items.text_en: Betrothal with father's knowledge, marriage without, father present
items.desc_en: If she was betrothed with her father's knowledge but married without his knowledge, and her father is present, Rav Huna says she does not eat terumah, reasoning that the father's silence is due to anger. Rav Yirmeya bar Abba says she does eat, reasoning that the father's silence indicates acquiescence.

sub.desc_en: The gemara presents a case: a woman betrothed with her father's knowledge but married without it, while her father is present, and records the opposing positions of Rav Huna (she does not eat terumah) and Rav Yirmeya bar Abba (she does eat).
Rav Huna explains his position: even according to Rav, who permits eating when the father is absent, here the father's silence is due to anger (רתח), not acquiescence.

Rav Yirmeya bar Abba explains his position: even according to Rav Asi, who prohibits eating when the father might later object, here the father's silence indicates acquiescence (איתנוחי), so she may eat.

items.text: Betrothal and marriage both without father's knowledge, father present
items.text_en: Betrothal and marriage both without father's knowledge, father present
items.desc_en: If she was betrothed and married without her father's knowledge, and her father is present, Rav Huna says she eats terumah, while Rav Yirmeya bar Abba says she does not. Ulla criticizes Rav Huna's position, arguing that if in the previous case (where betrothal was with knowledge) she does not eat, here (where betrothal was without knowledge) she certainly should not eat.

sub.desc_en: The gemara presents a case: a woman was betrothed and married without her father's knowledge, while her father is present.
Rav Huna rules that she eats תרומה (the priestly portion).
Rav Yirmeya bar Abba rules that she does not eat תרומה (the priestly portion).

Ulla sharply criticizes Rav Huna's ruling, arguing by a קל וחומר (a fortiori) that if in the previous case (betrothal with knowledge) she does not eat, here (betrothal without knowledge) she certainly should not eat.

items.text: Rava explains Rav Huna's reasoning
items.text_en: Rava explains Rav Huna's reasoning
items.desc_en: Rava explains Rav Huna's reasoning for his earlier ruling: because the father's act of betrothing his minor daughter is like an act of an orphan during the father's lifetime (i.e., the daughter has no say).

sub.desc_en: Rava explains Rav Huna's reasoning: because the father's act of betrothing his minor daughter is like an act of an orphan during the father's lifetime.

items.text: Dispute about a minor girl betrothed without her father's knowledge
items.text_en: Dispute about a minor girl betrothed without her father's knowledge
items.desc_en: Rav and Rav Asi dispute whether a minor girl betrothed without her father's knowledge can retract. Rav holds both she and her father can retract; Rav Asi holds only the father can. Rav Huna (or Chiyya bar Rav) cites a verse to challenge Rav Asi, who deflects by saying the verse refers to seduction not for marriage. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains the verse teaches that the seducer pays a fine. Rav Yosef and Abaye further clarify the need for kiddushin with the father's consent.

sub.desc_en: The gemara states the dispute: Rav holds that both a minor girl betrothed without her father's knowledge and her father can retract, while Rav Asi holds only the father can retract.

sub.text: Rav Huna (or Chiyya bar Rav) challenges Rav Asi
sub.text_en: Rav Huna (or Chiyya bar Rav) challenges Rav Asi
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna (or Chiyya bar Rav) challenges Rav Asi by citing the verse 'אם מאן ימאן אביה' (if her father refuses), arguing that the repetition implies the girl herself can also refuse.
Rav tells the challengers not to follow the objection, as Rav Asi can deflect by saying the verse refers to a case where he seduced her not for the sake of marriage.
The gemara objects: does the verse really need to address a case of seduction not for marriage?
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that the verse teaches that the seducer pays a fine like a seducer (מפתה).
Rav Yosef asks: if so, the Mishnah's requirement of kiddushin (קידושין) for a seduced woman is redundant if he seduced her for marriage.
Abaye answers that the kiddushin (קידושין) is needed with the father's consent, even if the seduction was for marriage.

items.text: Mishnah: Betrothal with dates
items.text_en: Mishnah: Betrothal with dates
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents cases of betrothal with multiple dates: if one says 'be betrothed to me with this date' and then 'with this one,' if any has value of a perutah she is betrothed; if he says 'with this and this and this,' only if the total equals a perutah. If she eats each one immediately, she is not betrothed unless one has a perutah's worth.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents three cases of betrothal with dates: sequential offers requiring one date worth a perutah, a combined offer requiring total value of a perutah, and immediate consumption requiring one date worth a perutah.

items.text: Gemara identifies the Tanna of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara identifies the Tanna of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rabba identifies the Tanna of the Mishnah's first case as Rabbi Shimon, who requires an explicit statement for each item (like in oaths).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who is the Tanna of the Mishnah that uses the repeated phrase 'הִתְקַדְּשִׁי' (be betrothed to me) for each date.
Rabba identifies the Tanna as Rabbi Shimon, who requires a separate oath statement for each item, analogous to the Mishnah's requirement for each date.

items.text: Analysis of the Mishnah's second case: eating dates
items.text_en: Analysis of the Mishnah's second case: eating dates
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions which part of the Mishnah the case of eating refers to. It suggests it cannot be the first clause (where he says 'with this' each time) because even if she eats, she should be betrothed if there's value. It must be the latter clause. Rabbi Yochanan despairs of understanding. Rav and Shmuel explain it is a 'not necessary' statement: even in the first case, eating might lead her to acquire herself, so the Mishnah teaches otherwise. Rabbi Ammi says it refers to the latter clause, meaning the last date must have a perutah's worth.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which clause of the Mishnah the case of eating dates refers to, and rejects the possibility that it refers to the first clause because even if she eats, she should be betrothed if there is value, concluding it must refer to the latter clause.
The Gemara objects that even in the first date, the betrothal is a loan (מלוה) and thus invalid, and Rabbi Yochanan despairs of finding a resolution.

Rav and Shmuel explain that the Mishnah is a 'not necessary' statement: even in the first clause, eating might lead her to acquire herself, so the Mishnah teaches that she is not betrothed unless there is a perutah's worth.
Rabbi Ammi says the case refers to the latter clause, and the Mishnah's phrase 'עד שיהא באחת מהן שוה פרוטה' means the last date must have a perutah's worth.

items.text: Rava derives three principles from Rabbi Ammi
items.text_en: Rava derives three principles from Rabbi Ammi
items.desc_en: Rava infers three halakhot from Rabbi Ammi's statement: betrothal with a loan is not valid; betrothal with a loan and a perutah, her intent is on the perutah.

sub.desc_en: Rava derives three halakhot from Rabbi Ammi's statement: betrothal with a loan is not valid; betrothal with a loan and a perutah, her intent is on the perutah.

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on money given for invalid betrothal
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on money given for invalid betrothal
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from a previous statement that money given for an invalid betrothal is returned. It then cites a dispute: Rav says the money is returned because the giver intended it as a deposit, while Shmuel says it is a gift because the giver intended it as a gift, though he did not say so explicitly due to embarrassment.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from a previous statement that money given for an invalid betrothal is returned.
The Gemara cites a dispute: Rav says money given for betrothing one's sister is returned, while Shmuel says it is a gift.
Rav explains that the giver knows betrothal does not take effect with his sister, so he intended the money as a deposit, but he did not explicitly say so because she would not accept it.
Shmuel explains that the giver knows betrothal does not take effect, so he intended the money as a gift, but he did not say so explicitly because it would embarrass her.

items.text: Ravina's objection from the case of challah from flour
items.text_en: Ravina's objection from the case of challah from flour
items.desc_en: Ravina objects: If one separates challah from flour, it is invalid and the flour is considered stolen in the priest's hand. Why not say the person intended it as a gift? The Gemara distinguishes: there is a concern that the priest might mix the flour with other flour and mistakenly eat untithed dough.

sub.desc_en: Ravina objects from the case of separating challah from flour: the flour is considered stolen in the priest's hand, yet one could argue the person gave it as a gift, analogous to the sister case.
The Gemara distinguishes: there is a concern that the priest might mix the flour with other flour and mistakenly eat untithed dough, so the gift is invalid.

items.text: Gemara's challenge and resolution: partial knowledge
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge and resolution: partial knowledge
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: But the person knows challah is not separated from flour! It answers: He knows and does not know—he knows the rule but thinks the reason is merely the priest's inconvenience, which he is willing to forgo. The Gemara then asks why the challah cannot be treated as terumah and eaten after separating challah from elsewhere, citing a mishnah about produce from a perforated pot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: But you said that a person knows that one does not separate חלה (challah) from flour, so why would the priest think it is a gift?
