Rabbi Yochanan explains they derive from the same verse: 'This shall be yours from the most holy things from the fire' – Rabbi Yehuda reads 'yours' for all needs, Rabbi Yosei compares it to fire, for consumption only.

sub.desc_en: The baraita recounts that after Rabbi Meir's death, Rabbi Yehuda forbade Rabbi Meir's students from entering, accusing them of being contentious and seeking to undermine him.
Sumchus forced his way in and reported Rabbi Meir's ruling that one who betroths with his priestly portion of sacrifices, whether most holy or lesser holy, has not effected betrothal.
Rabbi Yehuda became angry, repeated his warning, and objected: how could a woman be in the Temple courtyard to receive betrothal?
Rabbi Yosei defended the need to preserve Torah, arguing that a woman could be in the courtyard to receive betrothal or send an agent, and if she forced her way in, what then?

A baraita records the dispute: Rabbi Yehuda says she is betrothed, Rabbi Yosei says not; Rabbi Yochanan explains they derive from the same verse 'זה יהיה לך מקדש הקדשים מן האש' — Rabbi Yehuda reads 'לך' (for you) for all needs, Rabbi Yosei compares it to fire, for consumption only.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's statement (fragment)
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's statement (fragment)
items.desc_en: The daf ends with Rabbi Yochanan beginning a statement, which is cut off.

sub.desc_en: A baraita records the dispute: Rabbi Yehuda holds she is betrothed, Rabbi Yosei holds she is not betrothed.

רבי יוחנן (Rabbi Yochanan) explains that both sages derive their positions from the same verse: 'זה יהיה לך מקודש הקודשים מן האש' (This shall be yours of the most holy things, reserved from the fire). Rabbi Yehuda interprets 'לך' (to you) as for all your needs, while Rabbi Yosei compares it to fire, which is only for consumption.
The daf ends with Rabbi Yochanan beginning a statement that is cut off.

items.text: Conclusion of the dispute and Abaye's support for Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Conclusion of the dispute and Abaye's support for Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that the Sages concluded that one who betroths with his priestly portion of sacrifices, whether most sacred or less sacred, has not effected betrothal. Rav maintains it is still a dispute. Abaye says the opinion of Rabbi Yochanan is more reasonable.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports that the Sages concluded that one who betroths with his priestly portion of sacrifices, whether most sacred or less sacred, has not effected betrothal.
Rav maintains that the dispute remains unresolved.
Abaye says that the opinion of Rabbi Yochanan is more reasonable.

items.text: Baraita on dividing meal-offerings and its implication
items.text_en: Baraita on dividing meal-offerings and its implication
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that derives from verses that meal-offerings cannot be divided against animal sacrifices, birds, or other meal-offerings of different types. The baraita concludes that just as one cannot divide most sacred offerings, so too less sacred offerings cannot be divided. The Gemara identifies this baraita as following Rabbi Yehuda, who holds there is no division at all.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by citing a verse to prove that meal-offerings cannot be divided against animal sacrifices.
The baraita raises a possible distinction: perhaps meal-offerings may be divided against bird-offerings, since birds replace meal-offerings in cases of poverty, but a verse refutes this.
The baraita raises another possible distinction: perhaps bird-offerings may be divided against animal sacrifices, since both involve blood, but a verse refutes this.
The baraita raises a further possible distinction: perhaps meal-offerings may be divided against other meal-offerings of the same type, but a verse refutes this.
The baraita raises a final possible distinction: perhaps different types of meal-offering pans may be divided against each other if they share the same texture, but a verse refutes this.
The baraita concludes by extending the prohibition from most sacred offerings to less sacred offerings, using the verse 'אִישׁ כְּאָחִיו' and the adjacent verse about the thanksgiving offering.
The baraita adds that every adult male, even a blemished priest, may receive a portion, but a minor may not, even if unblemished.
The Gemara identifies the anonymous baraita as following Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that there is no division at all, and concludes that this supports Rabbi Yochanan's position.

items.text: Rava's challenge and the story of the greedy ones
items.text_en: Rava's challenge and the story of the greedy ones
items.desc_en: Rava asks whether a baraita does not support Rav as well, citing a baraita about modest priests withdrawing their hands and greedy ones dividing. The Gemara explains that 'dividing' means snatching, as illustrated by a story of one who snatched his portion and his fellow's, called 'Ben Chamtzan'. The verse about 'chametz' (violence) is cited.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks whether a baraita does not also support Rav's position, citing a baraita about modest priests withdrawing their hands and greedy ones dividing.
The Gemara explains that 'dividing' in the baraita means snatching, as illustrated by a story of one who snatched his portion and his fellow's, called 'Ben Chamtzan'.
Rabbah bar Rav Sheila cites a verse (Psalms 71:4) that uses the word 'חוֹמֵץ' (violent one) to connect the nickname 'Ben Chamtzan' to the concept of violence.
Rabbah offers an alternative verse (Isaiah 1:17) that uses the word 'חָמוֹץ' (the violent one) to further support the connection.

items.text: Betrothal with second tithe
items.text_en: Betrothal with second tithe
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who betroths with second tithe, whether unintentionally or intentionally, has not effected betrothal according to Rabbi Meir. Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes: unintentionally not, intentionally yes. The Gemara asks for the source and cites a verse: 'for the Lord it is holy' – it is for the Lord, not to betroth a woman.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the dispute: Rabbi Meir says betrothal with second tithe is invalid in all cases; Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes between unintentional (invalid) and intentional (valid).
The Gemara asks for the scriptural source of this ruling.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Rava in the name of the Gemara
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Rava in the name of the Gemara
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rava cites the verse 'לַה׳ הוּא קֹדֶשׁ לַה׳' (it is holy to the Lord) to prove that second tithe is designated for the Lord, not for betrothing a woman.

items.text: Challenges from other consecrated items
items.text_en: Challenges from other consecrated items
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the derivation from second tithe by noting that terumat ma'aser, challah, shevi'it, and terumah all have similar language yet betrothal with them is valid. It answers that each lacks either the word 'laShem' or 'kodesh' in the specific context, or the verse applies to Israelites, not priests.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the derivation from second tithe by citing terumat ma'aser, which has the phrase 'תרומת ה (a portion for the Lord)', yet betrothal with terumah is valid.
The Gemara answers that terumat ma'aser lacks the word 'לה (to the Lord)' in the specific context of the verse used for the derivation.
The Gemara challenges further by citing challah, which has the phrase 'תתנו לה (you shall give to the Lord)', yet betrothal with challah is valid.
The Gemara answers that challah lacks the word 'קדש (holy)' in the verse.
The Gemara challenges by citing shevi'it, which has the phrase 'קדש תהיה לכם (it shall be holy to you)', yet betrothal with shevi'it produce is valid.
The Gemara answers that shevi'it lacks the word 'לה (to the Lord)' in the verse.
The Gemara challenges by citing terumah, which has both 'קדש (holy)' and 'לה (to the Lord)', yet betrothal with terumah is valid.
The Gemara answers that the verse for terumah is written regarding Israelites, not priests, so it does not apply to the priestly context of the derivation.

items.text: Derivation from the verse
items.text_en: Derivation from the verse
items.desc_en: Ravin Saba explains before Rav that the verse 'hu' teaches that a consecrated item remains in its state of sanctity, implying that betrothal with it is ineffective unless done intentionally.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the matter is not self-evident from the verse.
Ravin Saba explains before Rav that the verse 'הוּא' teaches that a consecrated item remains in its state of sanctity, implying that betrothal with it is ineffective unless done intentionally.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that with consecrated items, if done intentionally, betrothal is valid according to Rabbi Meir, but not if done unintentionally; Rabbi Yehuda holds the opposite. Rabbi Yaakov reports hearing from Rabbi Yochanan two rulings: unintentional betrothal with ma'aser (tithe) according to Rabbi Yehuda, and unintentional betrothal with hekdesh according to Rabbi Meir, both invalid.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda regarding betrothal with consecrated items: Rabbi Meir rules that intentional betrothal is valid and unintentional is not, while Rabbi Yehuda rules the opposite.

Rabbi Yaakov reports hearing from Rabbi Yochanan two rulings: unintentional betrothal with ma'aser (tithe) according to Rabbi Yehuda, and unintentional betrothal with hekdesh according to Rabbi Meir, both invalid.

items.text: Reasoning for the two rulings
items.text_en: Reasoning for the two rulings
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that one ruling is because the woman does not want the betrothal, and the other because neither party wants it. Rabbi Yirmeya attempts to determine which applies to which case: with ma'aser, the woman dislikes the travel burden, but the man wants to acquire a wife; with hekdesh, both dislike causing desecration.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that one ruling is because the woman does not want the betrothal, and the other because neither party wants it, but it is unknown which applies to which case.
Rabbi Yirmeya proposes that with ma'aser, the woman dislikes the travel burden but the man wants to acquire a wife, while with hekdesh, both dislike causing desecration.

items.text: Rabbi Yaakov's counter-reasoning
items.text_en: Rabbi Yaakov's counter-reasoning
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yaakov argues the opposite: with ma'aser, the man also dislikes the travel burden, so both are unwilling; with hekdesh, the woman dislikes desecration, but the man wants to acquire a wife, so only she is unwilling.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yaakov argues the opposite: with ma'aser, the man also dislikes the travel burden, so both are unwilling; with hekdesh, the woman dislikes desecration, but the man wants to acquire a wife, so only she is unwilling.

items.text: Rava's question about the money
items.text_en: Rava's question about the money
items.desc_en: Rava asks Rav Chisda: if the woman is not betrothed, do the consecrated coins become non-sacred? Rav Chisda responds that if the woman is not betrothed, how could the coins become non-sacred?

sub.desc_en: Rava asks Rav Chisda: if the woman is not betrothed, do the consecrated coins become non-sacred?
Rav Chisda responds rhetorically: if the woman is not betrothed, how could the coins become non-sacred?

items.text: Question about sale
items.text_en: Question about sale
items.desc_en: Rav Chiya bar Avin asks Rav Chisda about the law in a case of sale with consecrated items. Rav Chisda answers that even in a sale, the buyer does not acquire the item.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chiya bar Avin asks Rav Chisda about the law in a case of sale with consecrated items.
Rav Chisda answers that even in a sale, the buyer does not acquire the item.

items.text: Objection from the Mishnah about a shopkeeper
items.text_en: Objection from the Mishnah about a shopkeeper
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a Mishnah where Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda dispute whether a shopkeeper is like a homeowner (liable for misuse) or like a money-changer (not liable). The Gemara explains that both agree that if the shopkeeper took the money, he misused it, but Rabbi Meir argues that according to Rabbi Yehuda's own logic, the shopkeeper should be like a homeowner, yet Rabbi Yehuda rejects this.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a Mishnah where Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda dispute whether a shopkeeper is like a homeowner (liable for misuse) or like a money-changer (not liable).

The Gemara explains that both agree that if the shopkeeper took the money, he misused it, but Rabbi Meir argues that according to Rabbi Yehuda's own logic, the shopkeeper should be like a homeowner, yet Rabbi Yehuda rejects this.

items.text: Rav's statement
items.text_en: Rav's statement
items.desc_en: The daf ends with 'Amar Rav', introducing a new statement by Rav, but the content is cut off.

sub.desc_en: Rav begins a new statement, but the content is cut off at the end of the daf.

items.text: Gemara's initial difficulty with Rabbi Meir's position
items.text_en: Gemara's initial difficulty with Rabbi Meir's position
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that it has examined all aspects of Rabbi Meir's view and found no case where an unintentional act desacralizes hekdesh but an intentional act does. It explains that the Mishnah's case of priestly garments that did not wear out is different because they were permitted for benefit, as the Torah was not given to ministering angels.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara announces that it has examined all aspects of Rabbi Meir's view and found no case where an unintentional act desacralizes hekdesh but an intentional act does not.
The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's case of priestly garments that did not wear out is different because they were permitted for benefit, as the Torah was not given to ministering angels.

items.text: First attempted proof from priestly garments
items.text_en: First attempted proof from priestly garments
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita: Rabbi Meir says that worn-out priestly garments are subject to me'ilah. The Gemara asks whether this implies even if they are not worn out, but concludes that it specifically means worn-out garments.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita where Rabbi Meir rules that worn-out priestly garments are subject to מְעִילָה (misappropriation of sacred property), attempting to prove that even non-worn garments might be included.
The Gemara asks whether the baraita implies that even non-worn-out garments are subject to מְעִילָה.
The Gemara rejects the proof, clarifying that the baraita specifically refers only to worn-out garments, not to new ones.

items.text: Second proof and its rejection
items.text_en: Second proof and its rejection
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings another baraita: Rabbi Yehuda says me'ilah applies to new priestly garments but not old ones; Rabbi Meir says me'ilah applies even to old ones, including remnants of the chamber. The Gemara objects: why should remnants of the chamber be subject to me'ilah, given that they were permitted for benefit? It then suggests that the statement should be attributed to Rabbi Yehuda, not Rabbi Meir.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita: Rabbi Yehuda says me'ilah applies to new priestly garments but not old ones; Rabbi Meir says me'ilah applies even to old ones, including remnants of the chamber.
The Gemara objects: why should remnants of the chamber be subject to me'ilah, given that they were permitted for benefit, as the city wall and towers come from those remnants?
The Gemara resolves the difficulty by reattributing the statement to Rabbi Yehuda instead of Rabbi Meir.

items.text: Third proof and its rejection
items.text_en: Third proof and its rejection
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita from Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yitzchak: Rabbi Meir says that stones of Jerusalem that fell are subject to me'ilah. The Gemara again suggests that this should be attributed to Rabbi Yehuda, not Rabbi Meir.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita from Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yitzchak stating that Rabbi Meir holds stones of Jerusalem that fell are subject to me'ilah (מעילה), as a third proof that Rabbi Meir's position is consistent.
The Gemara rejects the proof by reinterpreting the baraita: do not say it is Rabbi Meir, but rather say it is Rabbi Yehuda, thereby aligning the ruling with the established pattern.

items.text: Objection to attributing to Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Objection to attributing to Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if it is Rabbi Yehuda, does he hold that Jerusalem is consecrated? It cites a Mishnah where Rabbi Yehuda says that one who says 'Jerusalem' has said nothing, and a baraita where he says that one who says 'like Jerusalem' has said nothing unless he vows by something offered in Jerusalem.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the attributed opinion is Rabbi Yehuda's, does he hold that Jerusalem is consecrated? It cites a Mishnah where Rabbi Yehuda rules that one who vows by 'Jerusalem' has said nothing.

The Gemara rejects the objection by citing a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda says that even one who says 'like Jerusalem' has said nothing unless he vows by something offered in Jerusalem, implying that Jerusalem itself is consecrated for offerings.

items.text: Bar Padda's two versions of Rabbi Meir's opinion
items.text_en: Bar Padda's two versions of Rabbi Meir's opinion
items.desc_en: Ulla and Ravin each report Bar Padda's statement that Rabbi Meir held: hekdesh is desacralized intentionally but not unintentionally, except that the unintentional case is considered desacralized for the purpose of a sacrifice (Ulla) or for eating (Ravin). The Gemara questions how one could be liable for a sacrifice if it is not desacralized.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces that there are two versions of Bar Padda's statement, both aligned with Rabbi Yehuda's position.

Ulla reports Bar Padda's version that Rabbi Meir said hekdesh is desacralized intentionally but not unintentionally, except that the unintentional case is considered desacralized only for the purpose of a sacrifice.
The Gemara questions how one could be liable for a sacrifice if the hekdesh is not desacralized.
Ravin clarifies Bar Padda's statement: Rabbi Meir held that the unintentional case is considered desacralized only for eating, not for a sacrifice, resolving the earlier question.

items.text: Rav Nachman's ruling on halakha
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's ruling on halakha
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Ada bar Ahava states that the halakha follows Rabbi Meir regarding ma'aser because an anonymous mishna supports him, and follows Rabbi Yehuda regarding hekdesh because an anonymous mishna supports him.

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Ada bar Ahava
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Ada bar Ahava
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Ada bar Ahava rules that the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Meir regarding מעשר (tithe) because an anonymous mishna supports him, and follows Rabbi Yehuda regarding הקדש (consecrated property) because an anonymous mishna supports him.

items.text: Proof for Rabbi Meir regarding ma'aser from neta revai
items.text_en: Proof for Rabbi Meir regarding ma'aser from neta revai
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a mishna about neta revai where Beit Hillel rules it has the added fifth and bi'ur, like ma'aser. The Gemara deduces that Beit Hillel must follow Rabbi Meir (who considers ma'aser sacred property), not Rabbi Yehuda (who considers it owner's property), because otherwise they would not compare it to ma'aser.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the proof is that Rabbi Meir's view on ma'aser is supported, and cites a mishna about neta revai where Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel dispute whether it has the added fifth and bi'ur.
The mishna continues: Beit Shammai says neta revai has peret and olelot (gleanings), while Beit Hillel says all goes to the winepress.
The Gemara explains that Beit Hillel derives the laws of neta revai from ma'aser via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) on the word 'קֹדֶשׁ', while Beit Shammai does not make this derivation.

The Gemara deduces that Beit Hillel, who compare neta revai to ma'aser, must follow Rabbi Meir (who considers ma'aser sacred property), not Rabbi Yehuda (who considers it owner's property), because otherwise they would not rule that all goes to the winepress.

items.text: Proof for Rabbi Yehuda regarding hekdesh from a mishna
items.text_en: Proof for Rabbi Yehuda regarding hekdesh from a mishna
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a mishna about a deaf-mute who sends a sacrifice with a hearing person, where the storekeeper is liable for me'ilah only when he takes the money. This is consistent with Rabbi Yehuda's view that hekdesh is not desacralized unintentionally. The Gemara then questions whether there is also a mishna supporting Rabbi Yehuda regarding ma'aser, and cites one about redeeming ma'aser sheini with an added fifth, which seems to follow Rabbi Yehuda.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a mishna about a deaf-mute who sends a sacrifice with a hearing person, where the storekeeper is liable for me'ilah only when he takes the money, consistent with Rabbi Yehuda's view that hekdesh is not desacralized unintentionally.
The Gemara questions whether there is also a mishna supporting Rabbi Yehuda regarding ma'aser, and cites one about redeeming ma'aser sheini with an added fifth, which seems to follow Rabbi Yehuda.

items.text: Rejection: the mishna can follow Rabbi Meir if given before tithing
items.text_en: Rejection: the mishna can follow Rabbi Meir if given before tithing
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the proof, explaining that the mishna could follow Rabbi Meir if the gift was given while the produce was still untithed (טבל), since Rabbi Meir holds that gifts not yet separated are considered as if not separated.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the proof, explaining that the mishna can follow Rabbi Meir if the gift was given while the produce was still untithed (טבל), since Rabbi Meir holds that gifts not yet separated are considered as if not separated.

items.text: Second attempt: proof from neta revai redemption
items.text_en: Second attempt: proof from neta revai redemption
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a mishna about redeeming neta revai with an added fifth, which seems to follow Rabbi Yehuda. The Gemara rejects this, explaining it could follow Rabbi Meir if the redemption was when the fruit was in the smadar stage (unripe), and not according to Rabbi Yosei who considers smadar forbidden as fruit.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes a proof from a mishna about redeeming neta revai (fourth-year vineyard fruit) with an added fifth, which seems to follow Rabbi Yehuda's view that maaser sheni is ordinary property.

The Gemara rejects the proof, explaining that the mishna could follow Rabbi Meir if the redemption occurred when the fruit was in the smadar (unripe) stage, and not according to Rabbi Yosei who considers smadar forbidden as fruit.

items.text: Third attempt and conclusion: the halakha follows Rabbi Meir due to a choice mishna
items.text_en: Third attempt and conclusion: the halakha follows Rabbi Meir due to a choice mishna
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a mishna about redeeming ma'aser that appreciated in value, which seems to follow Rabbi Yehuda. The Gemara initially distinguishes between one anonymous mishna and two, but Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak concludes that the halakha follows Rabbi Meir because a 'choice' mishna (בחירתא) supports him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about redeeming ma'aser that appreciated in value, and asks whether it follows Rabbi Yehuda, since it allows the buyer to profit, which would contradict Rabbi Meir's view that ma'aser is ממון גבוה (sacred property).

The Gemara answers that the baraita indeed follows Rabbi Yehuda, and distinguishes between one anonymous mishna (חד סתמא) and two (תרי סתמי) to explain why the halakha follows Rabbi Meir for ma'aser despite this baraita.
The Gemara objects that if an anonymous mishna is decisive, there should be no difference between one and two such mishnayot.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak concludes that the halakha follows Rabbi Meir because a 'choice' mishna (בחירתא) — a preferred, authoritative mishna — supports him, overriding the earlier distinction.

items.text: Opening Mishnah citation
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah citation
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that animals found in the area from Jerusalem to Migdal Eder are considered burnt offerings if male and peace offerings if female.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that animals found from Jerusalem to Migdal Eder are classified as burnt offerings if male and peace offerings if female.

items.text: Gemara's question and Rabbi Oshaya's answer
items.text_en: Gemara's question and Rabbi Oshaya's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why males are only burnt offerings and not peace offerings. Rabbi Oshaya explains that the Mishnah deals with a case where one comes to be liable for their value, and it follows Rabbi Meir who holds that consecrated property can be desecrated intentionally.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why males are exclusively burnt offerings and not also peace offerings.

Rabbi Oshaya explains that the Mishnah deals with a case where one comes to redeem the animals with their monetary value, and follows Rabbi Meir's view that intentional desacralization (הקדש במזיד מתחלל) is effective.

items.text: Objection from the law of me'ilah
items.text_en: Objection from the law of me'ilah
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that consecrated objects of intrinsic sanctity cannot be desecrated, citing a Mishnah that only animals and service vessels can be subject to multiple acts of me'ilah. It distinguishes between Rabbi Yehuda's view (unintentional desecration) and Rabbi Meir's view (intentional desecration).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: can consecrated objects of intrinsic sanctity (קדושת הגוף) be desecrated at all? It cites a Mishnah that only a consecrated animal or service vessel can be subject to multiple acts of me'ilah (מעילה), implying that other consecrated objects cannot be desecrated.

The Mishnah elaborates: if one person rides a consecrated animal, then another rides it, and another, each commits me'ilah; similarly with a gold cup, showing that only these items can be desecrated multiple times.

The Gemara resolves: that Mishnah about me'ilah reflects Rabbi Yehuda's view, but the case here follows Rabbi Meir's view, who holds that intentional desecration (הקדש במזיד מתחלל) applies even to קדושת הגוף.

items.text: Distinction between unintentional and intentional desecration
items.text_en: Distinction between unintentional and intentional desecration
items.desc_en: The Gemara argues that from Rabbi Yehuda's view we can infer that even Rabbi Meir, who allows intentional desecration, does not allow desecration of intrinsic sanctity. The distinction is that in the me'ilah case one does not intend to remove the object from sanctity, while here one does intend to do so.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara argues by inference from Rabbi Yehuda to Rabbi Meir: just as Rabbi Yehuda holds that sanctity of the body is not desacralized even in unintentional cases, so too Rabbi Meir should hold that it is not desacralized in intentional cases.

The Gemara distinguishes: there (in the baraita) one does not intend to remove the animal to non-sacred status, but here (in the Mishnah) one does intend to redeem it, so desacralization is effective.

items.text: Question about lesser sanctity and a kal vachomer
items.text_en: Question about lesser sanctity and a kal vachomer
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Meir's view applies to lesser sanctity objects. A certain rabbi named Rabbi Yaakov responds with a kal vachomer: if objects of the highest sanctity can be desecrated, certainly those of lesser sanctity can.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Meir's view applies only to קדשי קדשים (most sacred offerings) or also to קדשים קלים (lesser sacred offerings).
Rabbi Yaakov answers with a קל וחומר (a fortiori) argument: if קדשי קדשים are desacralized, then קדשים קלים certainly are.

items.text: Supporting tradition from Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina
items.text_en: Supporting tradition from Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina
items.desc_en: A tradition is cited in the name of Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina that Rabbi Meir indeed held that intentional desecration applies to both highest and lesser sanctity objects, using the same kal vachomer.

sub.desc_en: A supporting tradition from Rabbi Chama bar Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina confirms that Rabbi Meir held intentional desacralization applies to both קדשי קדשים and קדשים קלים, using the same קל וחומר argument.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's solution for uncertain designation
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's solution for uncertain designation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan objects to the idea of sinning to gain merit, and instead proposes waiting until the animal develops a blemish, then bringing two animals and stipulating that one is for the intended sacrifice.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan objects to the idea of sinning to gain merit, asking whether one tells a person to sin for the sake of reward.
Rabbi Yochanan proposes waiting until the animal develops a blemish, then bringing two animals and stipulating that one is for the intended sacrifice.

items.text: Challenges regarding male animals
items.text_en: Challenges regarding male animals
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises potential problems: the animal might be a todah (requiring bread), an asham (which must be two years old), an asham metzora or nazir (uncommon), or a pesach (which has time-specific rules). Each is addressed with a solution or dismissal.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by noting that male animals are designated as עולות (burnt offerings), and raises the concern that the animal might be a תודה (thanksgiving offering) which requires bread, but answers that bread can be brought along.

The Gemara questions whether the animal might be an אשם (guilt offering), which must be a בן שנתיים (two-year-old), but finds it is a בן שנה (one-year-old); it then dismisses the possibilities of אשם מצורע (guilt offering of a leper) or אשם נזיר (guilt offering of a nazirite) as uncommon.

The Gemara questions whether the animal might be a פסח (Passover offering), but answers that in its proper time people are careful about it, and outside its time it is treated as a שלמים (peace offering).
The Gemara questions whether the animals might be בכור (firstborn) or מעשר (tithe), but answers that for the purpose of eating them with a blemish (במומן), they are indeed eaten that way.

items.text: Challenges regarding female animals
items.text_en: Challenges regarding female animals
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises similar issues for female animals: they might be a todah (requiring bread) or a chatat (which must be a year old). The todah problem is solved by bringing bread; the chatat problem is dismissed as uncommon.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that female animals brought with second-tithe money are designated as שלמים (peace offerings).
The Gemara raises the concern that the animal might be a תודה (thanksgiving offering), which requires bread, and answers that one can bring bread alongside it.
The Gemara raises the concern that the animal might be a חטאת (sin offering), which must be a year old, and dismisses the possibility of an overdue sin offering as uncommon.

items.text: Case of a year-old female found
items.text_en: Case of a year-old female found
items.desc_en: If the female animal turns out to be a year old, it might be a chatat. Chananya ben Chakinay says a year-old goat is for a chatat, but Abaye explains that it is treated like a chatat: confined to a pen and left to die.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what is the law if the female animal turns out to be a year old (בת שנתה)?
A baraita is cited: Chananya ben Chakinay says a year-old female goat is designated for a חטאת (sin-offering).
The Gemara objects: can it really be brought as a חטאת (sin-offering)?
Abaye resolves: it is treated like a חטאת (sin-offering) — confined to a pen (כיפה) and left to die on its own.

items.text: Beginning of a new baraita
items.text_en: Beginning of a new baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a baraita stating that one may not purchase an animal with second-tithe money, setting up the next discussion.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that one may not purchase an animal with second-tithe money.

items.text: Opening Mishnah and Rabbi Yehuda's qualification
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and Rabbi Yehuda's qualification
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one inadvertently purchased an animal with second-tithe money, the money returns to its place; if intentionally, the animal must be brought and eaten in Jerusalem. Rabbi Yehuda qualifies this, saying the rule applies only when one intended to buy a peace-offering, but if one intended to redeem the money for non-sacred use, whether inadvertent or intentional, the money returns.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the basic rule: if one inadvertently purchased an animal with second-tithe money, the money returns to its place; if intentionally, the animal must be brought and eaten in Jerusalem.

Rabbi Yehuda qualifies the Mishnah: the distinction between inadvertent and intentional applies only when one intended to buy a peace-offering; if one intended to redeem the money for non-sacred use, whether inadvertent or intentional, the money returns.

items.text: Gemara's question and Rabbi Elazar's answer
items.text_en: Gemara's question and Rabbi Elazar's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: But we learned in a Mishnah that Rabbi Yehuda says that if one intentionally uses second-tithe money for a purchase, the money is consecrated (and the animal becomes a peace-offering). How does this reconcile with his statement here? Rabbi Elazar answers: A woman (who buys the animal) knows that second-tithe money cannot be redeemed through her, so she will go up and eat it in Jerusalem.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Yehuda's position in the Mishnah by citing a contradictory Mishnah where Rabbi Yehuda rules that intentional use of second-tithe money consecrates the purchase.
Rabbi Elazar resolves the contradiction by explaining that a woman knows second-tithe money cannot be redeemed through her, so she will go up and eat the animal in Jerusalem.

items.text: Rabbi Yirmeya's objection
items.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's objection
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya objects: Consider an unclean animal, slaves, and land, which a person knows cannot be purchased with second-tithe money, yet the Mishnah teaches that if one bought them, he must eat corresponding food (i.e., the money is not returned). This contradicts Rabbi Elazar's reasoning.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya objects that an unclean animal, slaves, and land, which people know cannot be purchased with second-tithe money, still require eating corresponding food if bought, contradicting Rabbi Elazar's reasoning.

items.text: Resolution: dealing with a knowledgeable woman
items.text_en: Resolution: dealing with a knowledgeable woman
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves: Here we are dealing with a woman who is a chaverah (trustworthy in tithes), who knows the law. Therefore, her purchase is considered intentional and the animal becomes consecrated.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the difficulty by explaining that the case involves a woman who is a chaverah (trustworthy in tithes) and knows the law, so her purchase is intentional and consecrates the animal.

items.text: Question on the Mishnah's ruling
items.text_en: Question on the Mishnah's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: The Master said in the Mishnah that if one bought an unclean animal, he eats corresponding food. But why? Let the money return to its place, as in the case of the woman?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah rules that one who bought an unclean animal with second tithe money eats corresponding food, arguing that the money should return to its place as in the case of the woman.

items.text: Shmuel's statement (begins)
items.text_en: Shmuel's statement (begins)
items.desc_en: Shmuel begins to speak, presumably to answer the previous question, but the text cuts off here.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel begins to speak, presumably to answer the previous question, but the text cuts off here.

items.text: Continuation of the previous sugya: why the seller is penalized
items.text_en: Continuation of the previous sugya: why the seller is penalized
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the seller is penalized only when he fled, implying that if he did not flee, he is not penalized. It then questions why the buyer is not penalized, and answers that the mouse is not the thief, but the hole is the thief, meaning the prohibition is where the issur lies.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the seller is penalized only when he fled, implying that if he did not flee, he is not penalized.
The Gemara asks why the buyer is not penalized, and answers that the mouse is not the thief, but the hole is the thief.
The Gemara explains that the prohibition is where the issur lies, so the seller is penalized there.

items.text: Mishnah: items that cannot be used for kiddushin
items.text_en: Mishnah: items that cannot be used for kiddushin
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists items that cannot be used for kiddushin: orlah, kilayim of the vineyard, a stoned ox, the heifer whose neck is broken, birds of the metzora, hair of a nazirite, a firstborn donkey, meat in milk, and unconsecrated animals slaughtered in the Temple courtyard. If one sold these and used the proceeds for kiddushin, the kiddushin is valid.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists items that cannot be used for kiddushin, but if sold and the proceeds used, the kiddushin is valid.

items.text: Source for orlah: prohibition of benefit
items.text_en: Source for orlah: prohibition of benefit
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source that orlah is prohibited for benefit. It cites a baraisa that derives from the verse "וַעֲרַלְתֶּם אֶת עׇרְלָתוֹ" that all forms of benefit are prohibited.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source that orlah (ערלה, fruit of a tree in its first three years) is prohibited for benefit (הנאה).

A baraisa (תניא) is cited, deriving from the verse 'וַעֲרַלְתֶּם אֶת עׇרְלָתוֹ' (and you shall treat its fruit as orlah) that all forms of benefit from orlah are prohibited, beyond the explicit prohibition of eating.

items.text: Source for kilayim of the vineyard: prohibition of benefit
items.text_en: Source for kilayim of the vineyard: prohibition of benefit
items.desc_en: Chizkiyah derives from the verse "פֶּן תִּקְדַּשׁ" that kilayim is burned. Rav Ashi suggests a different derivation from "פֶּן יִהְיֶה קֹדֶשׁ", but the Gemara concludes that Chizkiyah's derivation is correct.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where do we derive the prohibition of benefit from kilayim of the vineyard?
Chizkiyah derives from the verse 'פֶּן תִּקְדַּשׁ' that kilayim is burned, implying prohibition of benefit.
Rav Ashi suggests a different derivation from 'פֶּן יִהְיֶה קֹדֶשׁ', comparing kilayim to consecrated property that can be redeemed.
The Gemara concludes that Chizkiyah's derivation is the correct one, rejecting Rav Ashi's alternative.

items.text: Source for a stoned ox: prohibition of eating and benefit
items.text_en: Source for a stoned ox: prohibition of eating and benefit
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source that a stoned ox is prohibited. A baraisa teaches that the verse "לֹא יֵאָכֵל אֶת בְּשָׂרוֹ" teaches that if one slaughtered it after its verdict, it is prohibited for eating. For benefit, the verse "וּבַעַל הַשּׁוֹר נָקִי" is expounded by Shimon ben Zoma to mean the owner is free from any benefit from it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source that a stoned ox is prohibited, and cites a baraisa that derives from the verse 'לֹא יֵאָכֵל אֶת בְּשָׂרוֹ' that slaughtering it after the verdict prohibits it for eating.
Shimon ben Zoma expounds the verse 'וּבַעַל הַשּׁוֹר נָקִי' to teach that the owner is free from any benefit from the ox, prohibiting benefit from it.

items.text: Analysis: the verse "לֹא יֵאָכֵל" applies to slaughter after verdict
items.text_en: Analysis: the verse "לֹא יֵאָכֵל" applies to slaughter after verdict
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the verse "לֹא יֵאָכֵל" applies to slaughter after the verdict or to stoning itself. It cites Rabbi Avahu in the name of Rabbi Elazar that wherever "לֹא יֹאכַל" is stated, it includes both eating and benefit unless specified otherwise. The Gemara then argues that here, since the prohibition of eating is derived from "סָקוֹל יִסָּקֵל", the verse "לֹא יֵאָכֵל" must come for benefit. It also notes that the word "אֶת בְּשָׂרוֹ" teaches that even if slaughtered in a manner resembling meat, it is prohibited.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the verse 'לֹא יֵאָכֵל אֶת בְּשָׂרוֹ' applies to slaughter after the verdict or to stoning itself, citing Rabbi Avahu in the name of Rabbi Elazar.

Rabbi Avahu in the name of Rabbi Elazar states that wherever the Torah says 'לֹא יֹאכַל' (do not eat), it includes both eating and benefit unless the text specifies otherwise, as it does for נְבֵילָה (carcass).

The Gemara answers that the rule of Rabbi Elazar applies only where the prohibition of eating comes from 'לֹא יֹאכַל', but here the prohibition of eating comes from 'סָקוֹל יִסָּקֵל', so 'לֹא יֵאָכֵל' must come for benefit, otherwise the verse would have said 'לֹא יֵהָנֶה'.
The Gemara further argues that the word 'אֶת בְּשָׂרוֹ' (its flesh) teaches that even if the ox is slaughtered in a manner resembling meat (i.e., with a knife), it is still prohibited.

items.text: Mar Zutra's objection and resolution
items.text_en: Mar Zutra's objection and resolution
items.desc_en: Mar Zutra objects that perhaps the prohibition applies only when slaughtered with a stone, resembling stoning, but not with a knife. The Gemara dismisses this, noting that the Torah does not specify a knife, and a baraisa states that one may slaughter with anything, including a stone.

sub.desc_en: Mar Zutra objects that perhaps the prohibition of eating the gored ox applies only when slaughtered with a stone, resembling stoning, but not with a knife.
The Gemara rejects the objection, noting that the Torah does not specify a knife, and a baraisa states that one may slaughter with anything, including a stone, glass, or a reed sliver.

items.text: The verse "וּבַעַל הַשּׁוֹר נָקִי" teaches prohibition of the hide
items.text_en: The verse "וּבַעַל הַשּׁוֹר נָקִי" teaches prohibition of the hide
items.desc_en: Now that both eating and benefit are derived from "לֹא יֵאָכֵל", the verse "וּבַעַל הַשּׁוֹר נָקִי" comes to prohibit benefit from the hide. The Gemara then asks how other tannaim who use this verse for other laws derive the prohibition of the hide, and answers that they derive it from "אֶת בְּשָׂרוֹ" – including what is attached to its flesh.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that now that both the prohibition of eating and the prohibition of benefit are derived from 'לֹא יֵאָכֵל' (it shall not be eaten), the verse 'וּבַעַל הַשּׁוֹר נָקִי' (the owner of the ox is clear) comes to prohibit benefit from the hide, since one might have thought that only the flesh is forbidden but the hide is permitted.

The Gemara asks: For those Tannaim who use the verse 'וּבַעַל הַשּׁוֹר נָקִי' for other laws (half of the ransom and the value of offspring), from where do they derive the prohibition of benefit from the hide?
The Gemara answers that they derive it from the word 'אֶת בְּשָׂרוֹ' (its flesh), which includes what is attached to its flesh, i.e., the hide.

items.text: Shimon HaAmsoni's exegesis of 'et' and Rabbi Akiva's addition
items.text_en: Shimon HaAmsoni's exegesis of 'et' and Rabbi Akiva's addition
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces Shimon HaAmsoni (or Nechemya HaAmsoni) who used to expound every 'et' in the Torah, but when he reached 'et Hashem Elokecha tira' he refrained. His students asked what would become of his previous expositions, and he said he received reward for both. Rabbi Akiva later taught that 'et' includes talmidei chachamim.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces Shimon HaAmsoni (or Nechemya HaAmsoni) who expounded every 'et' in the Torah but refrained when reaching 'et Hashem Elokecha tira'.
The students ask what will become of all his previous expositions of 'et'.
Shimon HaAmsoni replies that he received reward both for the exposition and for the refraining.
Rabbi Akiva later taught that 'et' in 'et Hashem Elokecha tira' includes talmidei chachamim.

items.text: Derivation for the heifer and the birds of the metzora
items.text_en: Derivation for the heifer and the birds of the metzora
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks the source for the prohibition of the heifer whose neck is broken, citing the school of Rabbi Yannai that 'kapara' is written regarding it, like sacrifices. For the birds of the metzora, the school of Rabbi Yishmael derives from a verbal analogy: just as with inner offerings the preparer (the bird) is like the atoner (the sacrifice), so too with outer offerings.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks the source for the prohibition of the heifer whose neck is broken (עגלה ערופה), and the school of Rabbi Yannai answers that the word 'כפרה' (atonement) is written regarding it, like sacrifices.

The Gemara asks the source for the birds of the metzora (ציפורי מצורע), and the school of Rabbi Yishmael derives from a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) that just as with inner offerings the preparer (the bird) is like the atoner (the sacrifice), so too with outer offerings.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish on when the birds become forbidden
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish on when the birds become forbidden
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan says the birds of the metzora are forbidden from the time of slaughter, while Resh Lakish says from the time of taking. Resh Lakish derives from the heifer: just as the heifer is forbidden from life (when taken), so too the birds. Rabbi Yannai says he heard a boundary for the heifer but forgot, and the colleagues say its descent to the harsh valley forbids it. The Gemara questions the analogy.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents the dispute: Rabbi Yochanan says the birds of the metzora are forbidden from the time of slaughter, Resh Lakish says from the time of taking.
Rabbi Yochanan explains that slaughter itself is what prohibits the birds.
Resh Lakish derives from the heifer (עגלה ערופה) that just as the heifer is forbidden from life (when taken), so too the birds are forbidden from life (when taken).
The Gemara asks when the heifer itself becomes forbidden, and Rabbi Yannai says he heard a boundary but forgot.
The colleagues say that the heifer's descent to the harsh valley (נחל איתן) is what forbids it.

The Gemara objects: if the heifer is not forbidden from the time of taking (but only later), then the analogy would suggest the birds are also not forbidden from the time of taking; but the Gemara rejects this, noting that the heifer has another boundary (descent to the valley) while the birds have no other boundary.

items.text: First objection from a baraita and resolution
items.text_en: First objection from a baraita and resolution
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan objects to Resh Lakish from a baraita that includes the sent-away bird as permitted and the slaughtered bird as forbidden. If the bird were forbidden from life, why would slaughter be needed? Resh Lakish answers that it might have been thought that since it was consecrated, slaughter permits it, so the verse teaches otherwise. A second objection from a baraita about a bird found to be a treifah: the first bird is permitted. Resh Lakish answers that the case is where the treifah was found in its innards, so sanctity never applied.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan objects to Resh Lakish from a baraita that includes the sent-away bird as permitted and the slaughtered bird as forbidden, arguing that if the bird were forbidden from life, the verse would not need to teach about the slaughtered bird.
Resh Lakish answers that the verse is needed to counter a possible inference that since the bird was consecrated, slaughter would permit it, so the verse teaches otherwise.
A second objection is raised from a baraita about a bird found to be a טריפה (ritually unfit): the first bird is permitted in benefit, contradicting Resh Lakish's view that it is forbidden from life.
Resh Lakish answers that the case is where the טריפה (ritually unfit condition) was found in its innards, so sanctity never applied to it.

items.text: Third objection from a baraita about improper slaughter
items.text_en: Third objection from a baraita about improper slaughter
items.desc_en: A baraita states: if one slaughtered the bird without hyssop, cedar wood, or crimson wool, Rabbi Yaakov says it is forbidden because it was designated for its mitzvah, Rabbi Shimon says it is permitted because it was slaughtered not according to its mitzvah. The Gemara explains they disagree about whether an improper slaughter is considered slaughter, but both agree it is not forbidden from life.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita: if one slaughtered the bird without hyssop, cedar wood, or crimson wool, Rabbi Yaakov forbids it because it was designated for its mitzvah, and Rabbi Shimon permits it because it was slaughtered not according to its mitzvah.

The Gemara explains that the dispute is only about whether an improper slaughter is considered slaughter (שחיטה שאינה ראויה – שמה שחיטה), but both agree that the bird is not forbidden from life (מחיים לא מיתסרא).

items.text: Support for Resh Lakish from the school of Rabbi Yishmael
items.text_en: Support for Resh Lakish from the school of Rabbi Yishmael
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the dispute is between Tanna'im, citing the school of Rabbi Yishmael's verbal analogy: just as with inner offerings the preparer is like the atoner, so too with outer offerings. This implies the birds are forbidden from life, supporting Resh Lakish.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the dispute as being between Tanna'im, citing the school of Rabbi Yishmael's teaching about a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) between inner and outer offerings.

The baraita completes the verbal analogy: just as with inner offerings the preparer (מכשיר) is treated like the atoner (מכפר), so too with outer offerings, implying the birds are forbidden from life, supporting Resh Lakish.

items.text: Clarification of the baraita and a challenge
items.text_en: Clarification of the baraita and a challenge
items.desc_en: The Gemara revisits the baraita about the sent-away and slaughtered birds, and Rabbi Yochanan says in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai that we do not find living creatures that are forbidden. Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak challenges this, but the text is cut off.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the baraita that the verse 'כל צפור טהורה תאכלו' (every clean bird you may eat) includes the sent-away bird, and 'וזה אשר לא תאכלו מהם' (and this you shall not eat from them) includes the slaughtered bird.
The Gemara asks: Could we reverse the interpretation (i.e., the sent-away bird is forbidden and the slaughtered one is permitted)?

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan says in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai that we do not find living creatures that are forbidden, so the sent-away bird (which remains alive) cannot be forbidden.

sub.text: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak's challenge
sub.text_en: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak's challenge
sub.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak challenges this, but the text is cut off.

items.text: Rejection of the objection from מוקצה and נעבד
items.text_en: Rejection of the objection from מוקצה and נעבד
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the objection that מוקצה and נעבד, which are living animals, are forbidden in benefit. It explains that they are forbidden only for the Most High (sacrifice), but for a common person they are permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that מוקצה and נעבד, which are living animals, are forbidden in benefit.
The Gemara answers that they are forbidden only for the Most High (sacrifice), but for a common person they are permitted.

items.text: Rabbi Yirmeya's objection from a rove'a and nirba
items.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's objection from a rove'a and nirba
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya objects that a rove'a (an animal that copulated with a human) and nirba (an animal that was copulated with) are living animals and are forbidden. Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai answers that we have not found a majority of living animals that are forbidden.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya objects that a rove'a (an animal that copulated with a human) and nirba (an animal that was copulated with) are living animals and are forbidden, challenging the earlier principle.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan answers in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai that we have not found a majority of living animals that are forbidden, so the objection is not a majority-based challenge.

items.text: Derivation from the verse about the sent-away bird
items.text_en: Derivation from the verse about the sent-away bird
items.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Yishmael derives from the verse 'and he shall send it upon the face of the field' that the sent-away bird is permitted like a field. The Gemara questions this derivation, noting that the word 'field' is needed for another teaching. It concludes that the extra word 'the field' teaches both.

sub.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Yishmael cites a verse to derive that the sent-away bird is permitted like a field.
The Gemara objects that the word 'field' is needed for a different teaching about how to send the bird.
The Gemara resolves that the extra word 'the field' teaches both the permission and the manner of sending.

items.text: Rava's alternative explanation
items.text_en: Rava's alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Rava says that the Torah did not say 'send' for a stumbling block; the sent-away bird is permitted because it is not a source of prohibition.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves the difficulty by stating that the Torah did not intend the command 'send' to create a prohibition; the sent-away bird is permitted because it is not a source of stumbling.

items.text: The hair of a nazirite
items.text_en: The hair of a nazirite
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives that the hair of a nazirite is forbidden in benefit from the verse 'holy shall he be, he shall let the locks of the hair of his head grow'. It rejects the comparison to consecrated property because the verse says 'holy' (kadosh) not 'sacred' (kodesh).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where is it derived that the hair of a nazirite is forbidden in benefit? It answers by citing the verse 'קָדֹשׁ יִהְיֶה גַּדֵּל פֶּרַע שְׂעַר רֹאשׁוֹ' (holy shall he be, he shall let the locks of the hair of his head grow), interpreting that his growth shall be holy.

The Gemara objects: If the word 'קָדוֹשׁ' were read as 'קֹדֶשׁ' (sacred), it would imply that the hair, like consecrated property, can be redeemed and its value used for non-sacred purposes, which is not the case.
The Gemara resolves: We read the word as 'קָדוֹשׁ' (holy), not 'קֹדֶשׁ' (sacred), so the comparison to consecrated property is rejected, and the hair remains forbidden in benefit.

items.text: The firstborn donkey
items.text_en: The firstborn donkey
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah seems to disagree with Rabbi Shimon, who permits benefit from a firstborn donkey. Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar Avuah explains that the Mishnah refers to after decapitation, and all agree it is forbidden then.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's ruling on a firstborn donkey (פטר חמור) aligns with Rabbi Shimon, citing a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda forbids benefit and Rabbi Shimon permits it.

sub.text: Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar Avuah
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar Avuah
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuah explains that the Mishnah refers to after decapitation (עריפה), and in that case all agree it is forbidden.

items.text: Meat in milk
items.text_en: Meat in milk
items.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Yishmael derives three prohibitions from the three occurrences of 'you shall not cook a kid in its mother's milk': eating, benefit, and cooking. The Gemara notes that the Mishnah disagrees with Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda, who permits benefit from meat in milk.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where do we derive the prohibition of meat in milk?
The school of Rabbi Yishmael teaches that the three occurrences of 'you shall not cook a kid in its mother's milk' indicate prohibitions of eating, benefit, and cooking.
The Gemara notes that the Mishnah does not align with this Tanna.
Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda holds that meat in milk is forbidden for eating but permitted for benefit, citing a verbal analogy from the verse 'for you are a holy people'.

items.text: Non-sacred animals slaughtered in the Temple courtyard
items.text_en: Non-sacred animals slaughtered in the Temple courtyard
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Meir derives the prohibition from a kal vachomer: just as sacred animals slaughtered outside are forbidden, so non-sacred animals slaughtered inside are forbidden. The Gemara rejects this and Abaye offers a different derivation from three extra verses, which exclude blemished animals, undomesticated animals, and birds, and also teach that if one slaughters, the meat is forbidden to eat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where are these matters (the prohibition of non-sacred animals slaughtered in the Temple courtyard) derived?

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Meir
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Meir
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Meir derives the prohibition via a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument): just as sacred animals slaughtered outside are forbidden, so non-sacred animals slaughtered inside are forbidden.
The Gemara objects: just as sacred animals slaughtered outside are punishable by כרת (excision), so too non-sacred animals slaughtered inside would be punishable by כרת — but that is not the case.
The Gemara answers: the verse limits the punishment of כרת to a קרבן (sacrifice), not to non-sacred animals slaughtered in the courtyard.
The Gemara objects further: the קל וחומר can be refuted because the case of sacred animals outside has the unique stringency of כרת punishment.
Abaye offers a different derivation from three extra verses: 'וּשְׁחָטוֹ', 'וְשָׁחַט אֹתוֹ', 'וְשָׁחַט אֹתוֹ'.

Abaye explains: the verse 'כִּי יִרְחַק... וְזָבַחְתָּ' teaches that you may slaughter only in a distant place, not in the nearby place (the Temple courtyard), excluding non-sacred animals from being slaughtered there.
Abaye expands: the three extra verses include blemished animals, undomesticated animals, and birds in the prohibition.
Abaye concludes: the verse 'וְאָכַלְתָּ' teaches that if one slaughters non-sacred animals in the courtyard, the meat is forbidden to eat.

items.text: Opening baraita: animals slaughtered in the courtyard
items.text_en: Opening baraita: animals slaughtered in the courtyard
items.desc_en: The baraita derives from verses that animals unfit for the altar, including blemished animals, undomesticated animals, and birds, may be slaughtered in the Temple courtyard, but their meat is not to be thrown to dogs; rather, it is forbidden to throw non-sacred meat slaughtered in the courtyard to dogs.

sub.desc_en: The baraita derives from verses that blemished animals, undomesticated animals, and birds may be slaughtered in the Temple courtyard, and concludes that non-sacred meat slaughtered there may not be thrown to dogs.

items.text: Mar Yehuda's question and contradiction
items.text_en: Mar Yehuda's question and contradiction
items.desc_en: Mar Yehuda asks Rav Yosef and Rav Shmuel about a baraita where Rabbi Shimon rules that one who betroths with non-sacred meat slaughtered in the courtyard is betrothed, implying it is not biblically forbidden. They then raise a contradiction from another baraita where Rabbi Shimon says such meat must be burned.

sub.text: Mar Yehuda's question to Rav Yosef and Rav Shmuel
sub.text_en: Mar Yehuda's question to Rav Yosef and Rav Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Mar Yehuda presents a baraita where Rabbi Shimon rules that one who betroths with non-sacred meat slaughtered in the courtyard is betrothed, implying the prohibition is not biblical.
Mar Yehuda raises a contradiction from another baraita where Rabbi Shimon rules that such meat must be burned, and the rabbis remain silent.

items.text: Rabbah's resolution: the case of a tereifah
items.text_en: Rabbah's resolution: the case of a tereifah
items.desc_en: Rabbah resolves the contradiction by explaining that the baraita deals with an animal that was slaughtered and found to be a tereifah. Rabbi Shimon, consistent with his view, permits benefit from such meat, while the Sages forbid it.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah resolves the contradiction by explaining that the case involves an animal found to be טריפה (a terefah), and Rabbi Shimon follows his own view that a terefah slaughtered in the courtyard is permitted in benefit.
A baraita is cited: one who slaughters a tereifah or slaughters and finds it a tereifah — Rabbi Shimon permits benefit, while the Sages forbid it.

items.text: Derivation from idolatry: proceeds of forbidden items
items.text_en: Derivation from idolatry: proceeds of forbidden items
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives that if one sells forbidden items and betroths with their proceeds, the betrothal is valid, based on the verse regarding idolatry. However, one cannot learn from idolatry alone because it and the Sabbatical year are two verses that come as one and do not teach a general rule.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source that betrothal with proceeds of forbidden items is valid, and answers that it is derived from idolatry, where the verse 'וְהָיִיתָ חֵרֶם כָּמֹהוּ' teaches that anything derived from it is like it, implying other prohibitions are permitted.
The Gemara objects that one could learn from idolatry alone, but rejects this because idolatry and the Sabbatical year are two verses that come as one and do not teach a general rule.

items.text: Sabbatical year and its unique law
items.text_en: Sabbatical year and its unique law
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the law of the Sabbatical year: its produce is sanctified and its money value is also sanctified, but unlike sacred items, the sanctity remains in the last item purchased, and the original produce remains forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the source is for the Sabbatical year's produce having sanctity that transfers to its monetary value.
The Gemara cites the verse 'יובל היא קדש תהיה לכם' (it is a Jubilee, it shall be holy to you) to derive that the Sabbatical year, like sacred items, seizes the value of its produce.
The Gemara objects that if the analogy to sacred items were complete, the Sabbatical year's sanctity would also transfer to the purchased item and release the original produce, which is not the case.

The Gemara resolves by citing the word 'תִּהְיֶה' (it shall be) to teach that the sanctity remains in its current state, i.e., the original produce stays forbidden and the sanctity does not exit to חולין (non-sacred status).

A baraita illustrates the rule: when one purchases meat with Sabbatical produce, both are subject to biur (removal); the last item purchased retains the sanctity, while the original produce remains forbidden.

items.text: Alternative derivation for those who learn from two verses
items.text_en: Alternative derivation for those who learn from two verses
items.desc_en: For those who hold that two verses that come as one do teach a general rule, the Gemara notes that there are two exclusions: 'for it is a cherem' and 'it is a jubilee', limiting the rule to those specific cases.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative resolution for those who hold that two verses coming as one do teach: two exclusions are written, limiting the rule to idolatry and the Sabbatical year alone.
The Gemara answers: two exclusions are written — 'for it is a cherem' and 'it is a jubilee' — limiting the rule to those specific cases.

items.text: Mishnah: betrothal with terumot and gifts
items.text_en: Mishnah: betrothal with terumot and gifts
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who betroths with terumot, tithes, priestly gifts, purification water, or purification ash is betrothed, even if he is an Israelite.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who betroths with תרומה (priestly portions), מעשרות (tithes), מתנות (gifts), מי חטאת (water of purification), or אפר חטאת (ashes of purification) effects betrothal, even if he is an Israelite.

items.text: Gemara: Ulla's statement and the dispute over tovat hana'ah
items.text_en: Gemara: Ulla's statement and the dispute over tovat hana'ah
items.desc_en: Ulla states that the benefit of priestly gifts is not considered money. Rabbi Abba challenges him with the Mishnah. Ulla answers that it refers to an Israelite who inherited untithed produce from his priestly mother's father, and holds that gifts not yet separated are considered as separated. Rabbi Chiyya bar Avin then asks Rav Huna the same question, who cites the Mishnah, and is answered with the same resolution.

sub.desc_en: Ulla states that the benefit of priestly gifts (טובת הנאה) is not considered money.
Rabbi Abba challenges Ulla by citing the Mishnah which says that one who betroths with priestly gifts is betrothed, implying that the benefit is money.
Ulla answers that the Mishnah refers to an Israelite who inherited untithed produce from his priestly mother's father, and holds that gifts not yet separated are considered as already separated.
Rabbi Chiyya bar Avin asks Rav Huna whether the benefit of priestly gifts is considered money or not.
Rav Huna answers by citing the same Mishnah, implying that the benefit is money.
Rabbi Chiyya bar Avin resolves the difficulty by noting that the Mishnah was already explained as referring to an Israelite who inherited untithed produce from his priestly mother's father.

items.text: Rav Asi's position clarified
items.text_en: Rav Asi's position clarified
items.desc_en: Rav Asi, who was embarrassed by Rav's earlier statement, is told that Rav was actually supporting his view by citing Rav Asi's own teaching about hutzal.

sub.desc_en: Rav tells Rav Asi that his earlier statement about hutzal was actually supporting Rav Asi's own position, relieving Rav Asi's embarrassment.

items.text: Tannaitic dispute about tovat hana'ah
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute about tovat hana'ah
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that a dispute between Rabbi and Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda about whether a thief of tevel pays for the value of the tevel or only the value of the non-sacred portion hinges on whether tovat hana'ah is considered money.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the dispute between Rabbi and Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda about a thief of tevel hinges on whether טובת הנאה (the benefit of designating the priestly gifts) is considered money.

items.text: First rejection: dispute about inherited tevel
items.text_en: First rejection: dispute about inherited tevel
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the suggestion, explaining that both agree tovat hana'ah is not money, and the dispute is about whether tevel that fell to a priest from his mother's father is considered as if terumah was already separated.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the proposed interpretation of the dispute, asserting that both sides agree טובת הנאה (the right to designate the priest) is not money, and the real dispute is whether tevel inherited from a priestly grandfather is treated as if terumah was already separated.

items.text: Second explanation: dispute about Shmuel's principle
items.text_en: Second explanation: dispute about Shmuel's principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative: both agree the tevel is considered as if separated and tovat hana'ah is not money, but they dispute whether Shmuel's ruling that a single wheat kernel exempts the entire pile applies.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes an alternative: both agree that the tevel is considered as if separated and that tovat hana'ah is not money.
The Gemara frames the dispute as revolving around Shmuel's principle that a single wheat kernel exempts the entire pile.
The Gemara resolves: Rabbi accepts Shmuel's principle, while Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda rejects it.

items.text: Third explanation: rabbinic penalty on the thief
items.text_en: Third explanation: rabbinic penalty on the thief
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that both reject Shmuel's ruling, and Rabbi's position is that the Sages penalized the thief by making him pay the full value.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers a third explanation: both Tannaim reject Shmuel's ruling, and Rabbi's position is that the Sages penalized the thief by making him pay the full value.

items.text: Fourth explanation: rabbinic penalty on the owner
items.text_en: Fourth explanation: rabbinic penalty on the owner
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers another alternative: both accept Shmuel's ruling, and Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda's position is that the Sages penalized the owner for delaying the separation of terumot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that both Rabbi and Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda accept Shmuel's ruling, and the dispute is about whether the Sages penalized the owner for delaying the separation of tithes.

items.text: Contradiction about payment for mitzvot resolved
items.text_en: Contradiction about payment for mitzvot resolved
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction between the Mishnah allowing kiddushin with mei chatat and efer parah and a baraita invalidating such acts if payment is taken. Abaye resolves it by distinguishing between payment for bringing the water and filling the vessel (permitted) versus payment for the actual sprinkling and sanctification (forbidden).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who betroths with terumot, ma'asrot, matanot, mei chatat, or efer parah effects valid kiddushin even though the recipient is an Israelite.
The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita that invalidates any act done for payment, including sprinkling and sanctifying, rendering the water and ashes invalid.
Abaye resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between payment for bringing and filling the vessel (permitted) and payment for the actual sprinkling and sanctification (forbidden).

The Gemara notes that the language of the Mishnah and baraita supports Abaye's distinction, as the Mishnah mentions 'mei chatat and efer parah' while the baraita mentions 'to sprinkle and to sanctify'.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara on agency and conditional kiddushin
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on agency and conditional kiddushin
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents cases of an agent who betroths a woman for himself instead of for the sender, and conditional kiddushin with a time delay. The Gemara explains that the agent acted deceitfully, and the Mishnah's phrasing 'went' implies he went with deceit.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the case of an agent who betroths a woman for himself instead of for the sender, and the case of conditional kiddushin with a time delay.
The Mishnah details the rulings for the agent who betrothed for himself and for conditional kiddushin with a time delay.
A baraita teaches that the agent's action is valid, but he acted deceitfully.
The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's phrasing 'went' implies he went with deceit.
The Gemara asks why the Mishnah uses the phrase 'one who says to his fellow' here.

items.text: Why the Mishnah teaches both 'to his messenger' and 'to his friend'
items.text_en: Why the Mishnah teaches both 'to his messenger' and 'to his friend'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that both cases teach a novelty: in the case of a messenger, one might think only a messenger is considered a deceiver because he relies on his agency, but a friend is not; in the case of a friend, one might think only a friend's kiddushin in a different location is invalid because he wouldn't bother, but a messenger who bothered would be considered as showing the place. The Mishnah teaches otherwise.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the mishnah in the previous chapter uses the term 'to his agent' while the mishnah here uses 'to another'.
The Gemara answers that the mishnah here teaches a novelty: one might think only an agent is considered a deceiver because he relies on his agency, but a friend is not; the mishnah teaches otherwise.

The Gemara adds that the mishnah there also teaches a novelty: one might think only a friend's betrothal in a different place is invalid because he wouldn't bother, but an agent who bothered would be considered as showing the place; the mishnah teaches otherwise.

items.text: Stories of agents who acted for themselves: Ravin Ḥasida and Rabba bar bar Ḥana
items.text_en: Stories of agents who acted for themselves: Ravin Ḥasida and Rabba bar bar Ḥana
items.desc_en: Two stories illustrate the principle that an agent who betrays his trust and acts for himself is considered a deceiver, yet his action is valid. Ravin Ḥasida went to betroth a woman for his son but betrothed her for himself; Rabba bar bar Ḥana was given money to buy land but bought it for himself. In both cases, the action is upheld but the agent is criticized for deceit.

sub.desc_en: Ravin Ḥasida goes to betroth a woman for his son but betroths her to himself.
The Gemara objects that the baraita teaches such an agent's action is valid but he is a deceiver, questioning how a pious man could act this way.
The Gemara explains that the woman's family would not give her to the son, only to the father.
The Gemara objects that Ravin should have informed his son before betrothing her.
The Gemara explains that Ravin feared someone else would betroth her in the meantime.

sub.text: Story of Rabba bar bar Ḥana
sub.text_en: Story of Rabba bar bar Ḥana
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Ḥana gives money to Rav to buy land, but Rav buys it for himself.
The Gemara objects that the baraita teaches such an agent's action is valid but he is a deceiver.
The Gemara explains that the land was in a valley of violent men who respected Rav but not Rabba bar bar Ḥana.
The Gemara objects that Rav should have informed Rabba bar bar Ḥana.
The Gemara explains that Rav feared someone else would purchase the land in the meantime.

items.text: The story of Rav Giddel and Rabbi Abba: the poor man turning a loaf
items.text_en: The story of Rav Giddel and Rabbi Abba: the poor man turning a loaf
items.desc_en: Rav Giddel was negotiating to buy a field, and Rabbi Abba bought it from under him. Rav Giddel complained to Rabbi Zeira, who brought the case to Rav Yitzḥak Nappaḥa. Rav Yitzḥak ruled that one who takes a livelihood from a poor man is called wicked. Rabbi Abba offered to give the field as a gift, but Rav Giddel refused gifts, and neither took it, so it became known as 'the Rabbis' field'.

sub.desc_en: The gemara narrates that Rav Giddel was negotiating to buy a field, Rabbi Abba bought it, Rav Giddel complained to Rabbi Zeira, who brought the case to Rav Yitzḥak Nappaḥa, who asked: 'A poor man turns over a loaf and another comes and takes it — what is the law?'
Rav Yitzḥak Nappaḥa rules that such a person is called wicked; Rabbi Abba explains he did not know, offers to give the field as a gift, but Rav Giddel refuses gifts.
Neither Rav Giddel nor Rabbi Abba takes the field, so it becomes known as 'the Rabbis' field'.

items.text: If another betroths her within thirty days: Rav and Shmuel's ruling
items.text_en: If another betroths her within thirty days: Rav and Shmuel's ruling
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses a case where a man says 'Be betrothed to me after thirty days' and another betroths her within that period. Rav and Shmuel both rule she is betrothed to the second, even if the money was consumed. The Gemara explains that these coins are neither like a loan nor a deposit: unlike a deposit, they are consumed in her domain; unlike a loan, they were given for kiddushin.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the case of a man who says 'Be betrothed to me after thirty days' and another betroths her within that period, asking what the halacha is.
Rav and Shmuel both rule that she is betrothed to the second man, even if the money was consumed.
The Gemara asks for the reason behind Rav and Shmuel's ruling.
The Gemara explains that these coins are neither like a loan nor a deposit: unlike a deposit, they are consumed in her domain; unlike a loan, they were given for kiddushin.

items.text: If she retracts within thirty days: dispute between Rabbi Yoḥanan and Reish Lakish
items.text_en: If she retracts within thirty days: dispute between Rabbi Yoḥanan and Reish Lakish
items.desc_en: If no other man betrothed her and she retracts, Rabbi Yoḥanan rules she can retract because speech can nullify speech, while Reish Lakish rules she cannot because speech cannot nullify an action (the giving of money). Rabbi Yoḥanan brings a proof from terumah where speech nullifies speech, but Reish Lakish distinguishes because giving money is like an action. Rabbi Yoḥanan then brings a proof from a bill of divorce where the husband can nullify the agency, and the Gemara explains that there too, as long as the get hasn't reached her hand, it is speech nullifying speech.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: If no other man betrothed her and she retracts her consent within thirty days, what is the halakha?
Rabbi Yoḥanan rules that she can retract, because a later statement comes and nullifies the earlier statement.
Reish Lakish rules that she cannot retract, because a later statement does not come and nullify the earlier statement.

sub.text: Rabbi Yoḥanan's objection to Reish Lakish
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yoḥanan's objection to Reish Lakish
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yoḥanan raises an objection from a mishna about teruma: if one cancels the agency before the agent separates teruma, the teruma is invalid, showing that speech can nullify speech.
Reish Lakish rejects the objection, distinguishing that giving money to a woman is like an action, and speech cannot nullify an action.

Rabbi Yoḥanan raises another objection from a baraita about a bill of divorce: the husband can nullify the agency by speech even after giving the get to the agent, which is like giving money to a woman.
Reish Lakish resolves the objection: there too, as long as the get has not reached the woman's hand, it is speech nullifying speech, not an action.

items.text: Reish Lakish's counter-objection from vessels and impurity
items.text_en: Reish Lakish's counter-objection from vessels and impurity
