items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel disagree about whether we coerce or merely request a man to give a get when he claims kiddushin and she denies it. The Gemara clarifies that the dispute applies to the latter part of the Mishnah, and resolves that Shmuel says we request a get, and Rav says if he gives it voluntarily, we coerce him to give a ketubah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports a dispute: Rav says the court forces the man to give a גט (bill of divorce), and Shmuel says the court merely requests it.
The Gemara asks to which case of the Mishnah this dispute applies, and concludes it cannot be the first clause, so it must be the latter clause.
The Gemara objects: granted that the court may request a גט (bill of divorce), but why should it force him, since he can claim he does not want to be forbidden to her relatives?
The Gemara resolves: the statements were said independently — Shmuel says we request a גט (bill of divorce), and Rav says if he gives it voluntarily, we force him to give a כתובה (marriage contract).

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Adda quoting Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Adda quoting Rav
sub.desc_en: A supporting tradition from Rav Acha bar Adda quoting Rav (or Rav Hamnuna quoting Rav) states: we request and force, and the Gemara explains that this means we request a גט (bill of divorce) and if he gives it voluntarily, we force him to give a כתובה (marriage contract).

items.text: Kiddushin with one witness
items.text_en: Kiddushin with one witness
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda rules that one who betroths with a single witness is not suspected of valid kiddushin. The Gemara asks about a case where both agree, and Rav Nachman in the name of Shmuel says even then it is not valid. Rava challenges from the Mishnah, and the Gemara resolves that the Mishnah deals with a case where the witnesses went overseas.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda rules that one who betroths with a single witness is not suspected of valid kiddushin.
The Gemara asks Rav Yehuda: if both parties agree, what is the halakha?
Rav Yehuda gives an unclear answer, leaving the matter unresolved.
Rav Nachman in the name of Shmuel rules that even if both parties agree, the betrothal is not valid.
Rava challenges Rav Nachman from the Mishnah, arguing that the case must involve one witness.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah deals with a case where the witnesses went overseas, not with one witness.

items.text: Challenge from the divorce and inn case
items.text_en: Challenge from the divorce and inn case
items.desc_en: Rava challenges Rav Nachman from a Mishnah about a divorced woman who stays overnight with her ex-husband, where Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel disagree. The Gemara initially suggests it involves one witness, but then rejects this and explains that the case involves witnesses to seclusion but not to intercourse, and Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel disagree about whether seclusion alone creates a presumption of intercourse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects with a baraita about a divorced woman who stayed overnight with her ex-husband: if there are witnesses, why do Beit Shammai say no second get is needed? If no witnesses, why do Beit Hillel require one? This implies a single witness is effective.
The Gemara further objects: if a single witness is believed, why does the baraita distinguish between betrothal and marriage? This shows the case is not about a single witness.

The Gemara answers that the baraita deals with a case where there are witnesses to seclusion but no witnesses to intercourse, and Beit Shammai hold that seclusion does not create a presumption of intercourse.

items.text: Opening dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
items.text_en: Opening dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a dispute about whether the same witnesses for yichud (seclusion) serve as witnesses for bi'ah (sexual intercourse). Beit Hillel agrees that this applies only when the woman is not divorced from betrothal, because the husband is not familiar with her.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel regarding whether the same witnesses for seclusion (יִחוּד) serve as witnesses for intercourse (בִיאָה), with Beit Hillel conceding this does not apply when the woman is divorced from betrothal because the husband is not familiar with her.

items.text: Rav's ruling on kiddushin with one witness
items.text_en: Rav's ruling on kiddushin with one witness
items.desc_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Shmuel bar Marta quotes Rav: one who betroths with a single witness is not suspected of valid kiddushin, even if both parties admit. Rabbah bar Rav Huna attributes this to the Great Court, identified as Rav or Rabbi.

sub.text: Rav Yitzchak bar Shmuel bar Marta in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Shmuel bar Marta in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Shmuel bar Marta quotes Rav: one who betroths with a single witness is not suspected of valid kiddushin, even if both parties admit.
Rabbah bar Rav Huna attributes the same ruling to the Great Court, identified as Rav.
An alternative version states that Rabbah bar Rav Huna said in the name of Rav that the Great Court, identified as Rabbi, ruled this.

items.text: Objection from a baraita about two men and a woman
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita about two men and a woman
items.desc_en: Rav Achadvoi bar Ami raises an objection from a baraita where two men claim a woman as their wife, and she claims they are her slaves. The baraita requires two bills of divorce, implying that a single witness suffices for her claim, contradicting Rav.

sub.desc_en: Rav Achadvoi bar Ami raises an objection by citing a baraita about two men and a woman with a bundle, where each man claims the woman as his wife and the woman claims both men as her slaves.

The Gemara analyzes the baraita: if each man had multiple witnesses, the woman could not claim them as slaves, so it must be that each man has only one witness, implying a single witness suffices for kiddushin, contradicting Rav.

items.text: Rejection of the objection and reinterpretation
items.text_en: Rejection of the objection and reinterpretation
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the objection: a single witness is not believed in a contradictory claim. Instead, the baraita is about permitting the woman to the world, and the requirement for two bills of divorce is only to collect her ketubah from the bundle, following Rabbi Meir's view that movable property is liened for ketubah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the objection by arguing that a single witness is not believed when contradicted, and instead reinterprets the baraita as permitting the woman to the world.
The Gemara resolves that the requirement for two bills of divorce is only to collect her ketubah from the bundle, following Rabbi Meir's view that movable property is liened for ketubah.

items.text: Dispute between Rav Kahana and Rav Pappa on the matter
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav Kahana and Rav Pappa on the matter
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana says we do not suspect kiddushin with one witness; Rav Pappa says we do. Rav Ashi asks Rav Kahana if he derives this from a gezeirah shavah of 'davar' from monetary law, where admission of a litigant is like a hundred witnesses. Rav Kahana responds that there the litigant does not obligate others, but here he does.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the ruling is, and presents the dispute: Rav Kahana says we do not suspect kiddushin with one witness, Rav Pappa says we do.

sub.text: Rav Ashi's question to Rav Kahana
sub.text_en: Rav Ashi's question to Rav Kahana
sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi asks Rav Kahana if he derives his position from a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) of 'דבר' (matter) from monetary law.
Rav Ashi objects that just as in monetary law the litigant's admission is like a hundred witnesses, so too here the admission of the couple should be like a hundred witnesses.
Rav Kahana answers that in monetary law the litigant does not obligate others, but here the admission would obligate others (the woman's future children), so the analogy does not apply.

items.text: Case of Mar Zutra and Rav Adda Saba about witnesses
items.text_en: Case of Mar Zutra and Rav Adda Saba about witnesses
items.desc_en: Mar Zutra and Rav Adda Saba divided property and came before Rav Ashi, asking whether the Torah's requirement of two witnesses means they cannot retract, or whether the matter is only established with witnesses. Rav Ashi answered that witnesses were only created to lie, implying that their testimony is not absolute.

sub.desc_en: Mar Zutra and Rav Adda Saba divided their property between themselves.

sub.text: Mar Zutra and Rav Adda Saba's question to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Mar Zutra and Rav Adda Saba's question to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: They came before Rav Ashi and asked whether the Torah's requirement of two witnesses means they cannot retract their division.
They posed an alternative: perhaps the matter is only established with witnesses, meaning they could retract.
Rav Ashi answered that witnesses were only created to lie, implying that their testimony is not absolute and they can retract.

items.text: Abaye's rulings on a single witness and silence
items.text_en: Abaye's rulings on a single witness and silence
items.desc_en: Abaye states that if a single witness says 'you ate chelev' and the person is silent, the witness is believed. A baraita supports this: if the person denies it, he is exempt, implying that silence is admission. Similarly for 'your pure items became impure'.

sub.desc_en: Abaye states that if a single witness says 'you ate חלב (forbidden fat)' and the person is silent, the witness is believed.
A baraita supports this: if the person denies it, he is exempt, implying that silence is admission.
Abaye states that if a single witness says 'your טהרות (pure items) became טמא (impure)' and the person is silent, the witness is believed.
A baraita supports this: if the person denies it, he is exempt, implying that silence is admission.

items.text: Opening Mishnah and Gemara's analysis of silence as admission
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and Gemara's analysis of silence as admission
items.desc_en: The Gemara examines the Mishnah's rule that if one says 'your ox was mounted' and the owner is silent, the witness is believed. It compares this to a baraita about an animal that committed a sin or killed someone based on a single witness or the owner's admission, and questions the case of a single witness where the owner is silent. The Gemara explains why both cases are necessary, distinguishing between the owner's potential loss and the general assumption about oxen.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one says 'your ox was mounted' and the owner is silent, the witness is believed.
A baraita is cited that similarly rules that an animal that committed a sin or killed someone is believed based on a single witness or the owner's admission.
The Gemara questions the case of a single witness in the baraita, arguing that if the owners admit it is redundant, so it must be a case where the owner is silent.
The Gemara explains why both cases are necessary, distinguishing between the owner's potential loss and the general assumption about oxen.

items.text: Dispute between Abaye and Rava about a wife's adultery
items.text_en: Dispute between Abaye and Rava about a wife's adultery
items.desc_en: A dilemma is raised: if a single witness says a man's wife committed adultery and the husband is silent, what is the law? Abaye says the witness is believed, while Rava says he is not, because matters of sexual prohibition require two witnesses.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a dilemma: if a single witness testifies that a man's wife committed adultery and the husband remains silent, what is the law?
Abaye rules that the single witness is believed, obligating the husband to divorce his wife.
Rava rules that the single witness is not believed, because matters of sexual prohibition (דבר שבערווה) require two witnesses.
The Gemara explains Rava's reasoning: this is a matter of sexual prohibition, which cannot be established with fewer than two witnesses.

items.text: Abaye's proof from the blind man and Mar Shmuel
items.text_en: Abaye's proof from the blind man and Mar Shmuel
items.desc_en: Abaye brings a story about a blind man who was late to Mar Shmuel's lecture. When the messenger arrived, he said the blind man's wife had committed adultery. Mar Shmuel told the blind man: if the messenger is credible to you, divorce her; if not, do not. Abaye interprets this as meaning if the messenger is not a robber (and thus credible), while Rava interprets it as requiring credibility like two witnesses.

sub.desc_en: Abaye introduces a story about a blind man who was late to Mar Shmuel's lecture, and the messenger reported that the blind man's wife had committed adultery.
Mar Shmuel tells the blind man: if the messenger is credible to you, divorce her; if not, do not.
The Gemara asks whether Mar Shmuel meant credibility based on the messenger not being a robber.
Rava explains that Mar Shmuel meant credibility like two witnesses, not merely that the messenger is not a robber.

items.text: Abaye's second proof: the story of King Yannai and the Pharisees
items.text_en: Abaye's second proof: the story of King Yannai and the Pharisees
items.desc_en: Abaye brings a lengthy story about King Yannai (Yannai) who, after conquering sixty cities, dined with the Sages. A heretic named Elazar ben Po'irah slandered the Pharisees, leading Yannai to kill all the Sages. The story illustrates that a single witness's testimony about a woman's capture (and thus her status) was accepted, supporting Abaye's position.

sub.desc_en: Abaye introduces a baraita about King Yannai's feast after conquering sixty cities, setting the stage for the story.

sub.text: Story of Elazar ben Po'irah's slander
sub.text_en: Story of Elazar ben Po'irah's slander
sub.desc_en: The heretic Elazar ben Po'irah slanders the Pharisees to King Yannai, advising him to test their loyalty by wearing the tzitz (frontlet) between his eyes.

Yehuda ben Gedidya tells Yannai to be content with the crown of kingship and leave the crown of priesthood to Aaron's descendants, claiming Yannai's mother was captured in Modi'im, which leads to the Sages being separated in anger.

sub.text: Elazar ben Po'irah's advice to kill the Sages
sub.text_en: Elazar ben Po'irah's advice to kill the Sages
sub.desc_en: Elazar ben Po'irah incites Yannai to trample the Sages, arguing that the Torah will remain available for anyone who wishes to learn.

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's comment and conclusion
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's comment and conclusion
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that heresy was immediately instilled in Yannai, leading to the killing of all Sages, until Shimon ben Shatach restored the Torah.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the Yannai story and Rava's response
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the Yannai story and Rava's response
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Yannai story: if two witnesses said she was captured and two said she was not, why believe one side? It concludes it was a case of one witness against two, and the single witness is believed when the accused is silent. Rava counters that it was a case of two sets of two witnesses, and the testimony was disqualified due to hazamah (perjury), as per Rav Acha bar Rav Minyomi.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the Yannai story is possible: if two witnesses said she was captured and two said she was not, why would the court rely on one side over the other?
The Gemara answers that it was a case of one witness against two, and the single witness is believed because the accused is silent.
Rava objects that it was actually two sets of two witnesses, and the testimony was disqualified due to hazamah (perjury), as per Rav Acha bar Rav Minyomi.

items.text: Alternative explanation and Rava's final statement
items.text_en: Alternative explanation and Rava's final statement
items.desc_en: An alternative explanation is offered based on Rabbi Yitzchak's teaching that a maidservant was substituted for her. Then Rava begins a new statement, which is cut off.

sub.desc_en: The gemara offers an alternative explanation based on Rabbi Yitzchak's teaching that a maidservant was substituted for her.
Rava begins a new statement, which is cut off at the end of the daf.

items.text: The dispute between Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva regarding a mikveh found deficient
items.text_en: The dispute between Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva regarding a mikveh found deficient
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah where a mikveh in Yavne was presumed full but found deficient. Rabbi Tarfon rules that all purifications performed using it are pure, based on the mikveh's presumptive status, while Rabbi Akiva rules them impure, based on the person's presumptive status of impurity. They debate using analogies to a priest serving at the altar who is later found to be a ben gerushah or ba'al mum. Rabbi Akiva argues that a mikveh is more like a ba'al mum because both are invalidated by a single witness and by a physical defect. Rabbi Tarfon then declares that anyone who separates from Rabbi Akiva separates from life.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the source for its discussion: a Mishnah citing Rabbi Shimon's account of a mikveh in Yavne that was presumed full but found deficient.

The Mishnah presents the core dispute: Rabbi Tarfon rules all purifications performed using the mikveh are pure based on the mikveh's presumptive status, while Rabbi Akiva rules them impure based on the person's presumptive impurity.
Rabbi Tarfon analogizes the mikveh to a priest serving at the altar who is later found to be a ben gerushah or ben chalutzah, whose service is valid.
Rabbi Akiva counters with an analogy to a priest serving at the altar who is later found to be a ba'al mum, whose service is invalid.
Rabbi Tarfon argues that the mikveh should be judged by which analogy it resembles, comparing it to both cases.
Rabbi Akiva argues that the mikveh is like a ba'al mum because both are invalidated by a single witness, unlike a ben gerushah who requires two witnesses.
Rabbi Akiva adds that the mikveh is like a ba'al mum because both are invalidated by a physical defect in themselves, unlike a ben gerushah whose defect comes from others.
Rabbi Tarfon declares that anyone who separates from Rabbi Akiva separates from life, ending the dispute.

items.text: Analysis of the analogy: How is a ba'al mum invalidated by a single witness?
items.text_en: Analysis of the analogy: How is a ba'al mum invalidated by a single witness?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a ba'al mum can be invalidated by a single witness, as stated in the Mishnah. It first suggests that the witness must be silent (not contradicted), but then notes that the same would apply to a ben gerushah. Abaye resolves this by explaining that the witness can be believed because he can be told to go and prove his claim, and the invalidation is in the person's body, not from others.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how a ba'al mum (blemished priest) can be invalidated by a single witness, and raises the objection that if the witness is contradicted, he is not believed.
The Gemara initially answers that the witness is believed because the ba'al mum remains silent and does not contradict him.

The Gemara objects that the same silence-based reasoning would apply to a ben gerushah (son of a divorced woman) or ben chalutzah (son of a halitzah-performed woman), yet the Mishnah distinguishes them, showing that silence alone is insufficient.

Abaye resolves that the witness is believed even when contradicted, because the ba'al mum can be told to go and prove his claim (the defect is in his own body), unlike a ben gerushah whose disqualification depends on others.

items.text: Scriptural sources for the validity of a ben gerushah and the invalidity of a ba'al mum
items.text_en: Scriptural sources for the validity of a ben gerushah and the invalidity of a ba'al mum
items.desc_en: The Gemara seeks the source for the rule that a ben gerushah or ben chalutzah may serve at the altar. Rav Yehudah cites a verse indicating that the priesthood continues for all descendants, even those who are disqualified. Shmuel's father and Rabbi Yannai offer alternative derivations. For a ba'al mum, the Gemara cites a verse indicating that the priest must be 'shalem' (whole), and Rav Nachman notes that the vav in 'shalom' is cut off, implying a defective priest is invalid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural source that a ben gerushah or ben chalutzah may serve at the altar.
Rav Yehudah in the name of Shmuel cites the verse 'וְהָיְתָה לּוֹ וּלְזַרְעוֹ אַחֲרָיו' to include both fit and unfit offspring in the priesthood.
Avuh deShmuel derives the same rule from the verse 'בָּרֵךְ ה׳ חֵילוֹ וּפֹעַל יָדָיו תִּרְצֶה', indicating that even the profane (disqualified) among the priests are accepted.

Rabbi Yannai derives the rule from the verse 'וּבָאתָ אֶל הַכֹּהֵן אֲשֶׁר יִהְיֶה בַּיָּמִים הָהֵם', explaining that it refers to a priest who was fit but became disqualified (a ben gerushah or ben chalutzah).
The Gemara asks for the scriptural source that a ba'al mum (blemished priest) may not serve at the altar.
Rav Yehudah in the name of Shmuel cites the verse 'לָכֵן אֱמֹר הִנְנִי נֹתֵן לוֹ אֶת בְּרִיתִי שָׁלוֹם', interpreting it to mean that the priest must be whole (shalem), not defective.
The Gemara objects that the verse actually reads 'שָׁלוֹם' (peace), not 'שָׁלֵם' (whole), so the derivation seems problematic.
Rav Nachman resolves the objection by noting that the vav in 'שָׁלוֹם' is written as a broken letter, hinting at the word 'שָׁלֵם' (whole).

items.text: Mishnah: Rules for determining the lineage of a child based on the validity of the parents' marriage
items.text_en: Mishnah: Rules for determining the lineage of a child based on the validity of the parents' marriage
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents four categories: (1) Where there are valid kiddushin and no transgression, the child follows the father. (2) Where there are valid kiddushin but a transgression, the child follows the defective parent. (3) Where there are no kiddushin with this man but there are with others, the child is a mamzer. (4) Where there are no kiddushin at all, the child follows the mother (e.g., a slave or gentile).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the first rule: where there are valid קידושין (betrothal) and no transgression, the child follows the father, giving examples of a priestess, Levite, or Israelite woman married to a priest, Levite, or Israelite.

The Mishnah states the second rule: where there are valid קידושין but a transgression, the child follows the defective parent, listing forbidden unions like a widow to a High Priest or a mamzeret to an Israelite.

The Mishnah states the third and fourth rules: where there are no קידושין with this man but there are with others, the child is a ממזר (mamzer); where there are no קידושין at all, the child follows the mother, as with a slave or gentile woman.

items.text: Gemara's opening question on the Mishnah's first clause
items.text_en: Gemara's opening question on the Mishnah's first clause
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon asks Rabbi Yochanan whether the Mishnah's first clause is a general rule, and begins to cite a counterexample, but the text cuts off.

sub.text: Rabbi Shimon's question to Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shimon's question to Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon asks Rabbi Yochanan whether the Mishnah's first clause is a general rule (כלל), and begins to cite a counterexample, but the text cuts off.

items.text: Gemara's challenge from the case of a convert marrying a mamzeret
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge from the case of a convert marrying a mamzeret
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the Mishnah's rule by citing a baraita where Rabbi Yossi rules that the child of a convert and a mamzeret is a mamzer, even though there is valid betrothal and no transgression. The Gemara initially assumes this contradicts the Mishnah, but then suggests the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that a convert may not marry a mamzeret, so there is a transgression.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the Mishnah by citing a baraita where Rabbi Yossi rules that the child of a convert and a mamzeret is a mamzer, despite valid betrothal and no transgression.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that a convert may not marry a mamzeret, so there is a transgression, and the child follows the defective parent.

items.text: First answer: the Mishnah's 'all cases' clause includes this
items.text_en: First answer: the Mishnah's 'all cases' clause includes this
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the Mishnah's phrase 'all cases' in the latter clause comes to include the case of a convert and a mamzeret, so the Mishnah does not contradict the baraita.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the Mishnah's phrase 'כל מקום' (in every case) in the latter clause comes to include the case of a convert and a mamzeret, resolving the contradiction with the baraita.

items.text: Alternative answer: the Mishnah is Rabbi Yossi, and 'which is that' excludes
items.text_en: Alternative answer: the Mishnah is Rabbi Yossi, and 'which is that' excludes
items.desc_en: Alternatively, the Gemara suggests the Mishnah is indeed Rabbi Yossi, and the phrase 'which is that' in the Mishnah comes to exclude the case of a convert and a mamzeret, meaning the child follows the father.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative answer: the Mishnah is indeed Rabbi Yossi, and the phrase 'איזו זו' (which is that) comes to exclude the case of a convert and a mamzeret, meaning the child follows the father.

items.text: Objection from the case of a ḥalal marrying an Israelite woman
items.text_en: Objection from the case of a ḥalal marrying an Israelite woman
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the Mishnah only lists 'which is that' for one case, it would exclude the case of a ḥalal marrying an Israelite woman, where the child follows the father despite valid betrothal and no transgression. The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Dostai ben Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that a ḥalal's child is a ḥalal.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the case of a ḥalal marrying an Israelite woman, where there is valid betrothal and no transgression, would be excluded by the Mishnah's 'איזו זו' (which is that) formulation, yet the child follows the father.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Dostai ben Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that a ḥalal's child is a ḥalal, so the child does not follow the father.

items.text: Objection from an Israelite marrying a ḥalala
items.text_en: Objection from an Israelite marrying a ḥalala
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects further from the case of an Israelite marrying a ḥalala, where the child follows the father. It answers that the Mishnah's 'all cases' in the first clause comes to include this case.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects from the case of an Israelite marrying a ḥalala, where the child follows the father, contradicting the Mishnah's rule.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah's phrase 'כל מקום' (in every place) in the first clause comes to include this case.

items.text: Why not list it explicitly?
items.text_en: Why not list it explicitly?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah does not list the case of an Israelite marrying a ḥalala explicitly. It answers that the Mishnah's list of women (priestess, Levite, Israelite, ḥalala) cannot include a ḥalala marrying a priest, as she is not fit for him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah does not list the case of an Israelite marrying a חללה (ḥalala) explicitly.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah's list (priestess, Levite, Israelite, חללה) cannot include a חללה marrying a priest, as she is not fit for him.

items.text: Challenge from Rabba bar bar Chana's ruling on an Egyptian
items.text_en: Challenge from Rabba bar bar Chana's ruling on an Egyptian
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises another challenge from Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan: a second-generation Egyptian who marries a first-generation Egyptian woman produces a third-generation child. This case has valid betrothal and no transgression, yet the child follows the defective parent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a challenge from Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan: a second-generation Egyptian who marries a first-generation Egyptian woman produces a third-generation child, which contradicts the mishnah's rule that the child follows the father in cases of valid betrothal without transgression.

items.text: Resolution: 'all cases' includes this, or 'which is that' excludes per Rav Dimi
items.text_en: Resolution: 'all cases' includes this, or 'which is that' excludes per Rav Dimi
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the Mishnah's 'all cases' in the first clause includes this case. According to Rav Dimi, who says the child is second-generation, the phrase 'which is that' excludes it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah's phrase 'all cases' in the first clause includes the case of a second-generation Egyptian marrying a first-generation Egyptian.
According to Rav Dimi, who holds the child is second-generation, the Mishnah's phrase 'which is that' excludes this case.

items.text: Challenge from Ravin's ruling on converts from nations
items.text_en: Challenge from Ravin's ruling on converts from nations
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises another challenge from Ravin citing Rabbi Yochanan: among nations, the child follows the father; but if they convert, the child follows the more defective parent. The Gemara answers that the Mishnah's 'which is that' excludes this case.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a challenge from Ravin's report citing Rabbi Yochanan: among nations, the child follows the father; but after conversion, the child follows the more defective parent.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah's phrase 'איזו זו' (which is that) excludes this case of converts from nations.

items.text: Summary of the resolution
items.text_en: Summary of the resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that if the Mishnah is Rabbi Yehuda, then 'all cases' in the first clause includes the case of an Israelite marrying a ḥalala and Rabba bar bar Chana's case, while 'which is that' excludes Rav Dimi's and Ravin's cases.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the earlier discussion by stating that if the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yehuda, then the phrase 'כל מקום' (every place) in the first clause includes the case of an Israelite marrying a חללה (ḥalala) and Rabba bar bar Chana's case, while the phrase 'איזו זו' (which is that) excludes Rav Dimi's and Ravin's cases.

items.text: Clarifying the redundant 'כל מקום' in the Mishnah
items.text_en: Clarifying the redundant 'כל מקום' in the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the purpose of the second 'כל מקום' in the Mishnah if it follows Rabbi Yosei's view. It answers that just as the first 'איזו זו' is paired with a second 'איזו זו' for stylistic symmetry, so too the first 'כל מקום' is paired with a second 'כל מקום'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yosei, the first 'כל מקום' already includes the case of a convert who married a mamzeret, so what does the second 'כל מקום' in the latter clause come to include?
The Gemara answers by analogy: just as the second 'איזו זו' in Rabbi Yehuda's version is only for stylistic symmetry, so too the second 'כל מקום' is merely a stylistic repetition of the first.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's principle on lineage of converts
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's principle on lineage of converts
items.desc_en: Ravin reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: Among gentiles, lineage follows the father; after conversion, lineage follows the more impaired parent.

sub.text: Ravin in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Ravin in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Ravin reports Rabbi Yochanan's principle: among gentiles, lineage follows the father; after conversion, lineage follows the more impaired parent.

items.text: Source for 'among gentiles follow the father'
items.text_en: Source for 'among gentiles follow the father'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the first part of Rabbi Yochanan's statement with a baraita: a gentile father and a Canaanite mother produce a child who can be acquired as a slave, derived from the verse 'וְגַם מִבְּנֵי הַתּוֹשָׁבִים'. However, a slave father and a gentile mother do not produce such a child, as the verse requires 'אֲשֶׁר הוֹלִידוּ בְּאַרְצְכֶם' – born in your land, not merely sojourning.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of Rabbi Yochanan's rule that among gentiles one follows the father, and cites a baraita that derives from the verse 'וְגַם מִבְּנֵי הַתּוֹשָׁבִים' that a child of a gentile father and Canaanite mother can be acquired as a slave.

The baraita explains that a child of a slave father and a gentile mother cannot be acquired as a slave, because the verse requires 'אֲשֶׁר הוֹלִידוּ בְּאַרְצְכֶם' – born in your land, not merely sojourning.

items.text: Clarifying 'after conversion follow the impaired parent'
items.text_en: Clarifying 'after conversion follow the impaired parent'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the second part of Rabbi Yochanan's statement: it refers to an Ammonite who married an Egyptian woman. The child's status follows the more impaired parent: if male, the child follows the father (Ammonite); if female, follows the mother (Egyptian).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what case the second part of Rabbi Yochanan's statement refers to, and rejects the possibility of an Egyptian man marrying an Ammonite woman because the Torah only disqualifies an Ammonite male, not female.
The Gemara answers that the case is an Ammonite man who married an Egyptian woman: if the child is male, it follows the father (Ammonite); if female, it follows the mother (Egyptian).

items.text: Source that betrothal does not take effect with relatives
items.text_en: Source that betrothal does not take effect with relatives
items.desc_en: The Gemara seeks the source for the Mishnah's rule that a woman who cannot be betrothed to a man (due to a prohibition) does not require a bill of divorce. Rabbi Yochanan and others derive from the verse 'וְהָיְתָה לְאִישׁ אַחֵר' that she goes to 'others' (strangers) and not to relatives.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of the Mishnah's rule that a woman who cannot be betrothed does not require a bill of divorce.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan (via Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba)
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan (via Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba)
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan and others derive from the verse 'וְהָיְתָה לְאִישׁ אַחֵר' that a woman who leaves her husband goes to 'others' (strangers) and not to relatives, implying that betrothal does not take effect with relatives.

items.text: Objection and resolution regarding the derivation
items.text_en: Objection and resolution regarding the derivation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba objects that the verse might exclude a son, not relatives. The Gemara responds that a son is already excluded by the verse 'לֹא יִקַּח אִישׁ אֶת אֵשֶׁת אָבִיו'. Further objections suggest the verse might distinguish between initial and post-facto situations, but the Gemara concludes that for a sister-wife, the rule applies even post-facto, and other relatives are derived from her.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba objects that the verse 'לְאַחֵר' might exclude a son, not relatives.
The Gemara responds that a son is already excluded by the verse 'לֹא יִקַּח אִישׁ אֶת אֵשֶׁת אָבִיו', so 'לְאַחֵר' must exclude relatives.
The Gemara objects that both verses might refer to a son, one לכתחילה (the ideal standard) and one בדיעבד (after the fact).
The Gemara answers that the לכתחילה (ideal standard) case is derived from the sister-wife (אחות אשה), where the prohibition is stronger.
The Gemara objects that both verses might refer to the sister-wife, one לכתחילה (the ideal standard) and one בדיעבד (after the fact).
The Gemara concedes that indeed both verses refer to the sister-wife, one for the ideal standard and one after the fact.

items.text: Deriving all forbidden relatives from the sister-wife
items.text_en: Deriving all forbidden relatives from the sister-wife
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to derive all forbidden relatives from the sister-wife through a logical analogy, but challenges arise regarding a married woman and a brother's wife, which have leniencies. Rabbi Yona (or Rav Huna) resolves by citing a verse that equates all forbidden relations to the sister-wife, establishing that betrothal does not take effect with any of them.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: we have derived the rule from the sister-wife, but from where do we derive it for all other forbidden relatives? It then attempts a logical analogy from the sister-wife.
The Gemara objects that the analogy fails for a brother's wife, which has a leniency (permission in the context of yibbum), unlike the sister-wife.
The Gemara further objects that the analogy fails for a married woman, who has a leniency (permission through divorce during the husband's lifetime), unlike the sister-wife.

sub.text: Rabbi Yona / Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yona / Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yona (or Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua) resolves by citing the verse 'כל אשר יעשה מכל התועבות האלה ונכרתו' (all who do any of these abominations shall be cut off), which equates all forbidden relations to the sister-wife, establishing that betrothal does not take effect with any of them.

items.text: Beginning of a new objection
items.text_en: Beginning of a new objection
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to raise a difficulty with the derivation, but the argument is cut off.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara begins to raise a difficulty with the derivation, but the argument is cut off.

items.text: Abaye's principle and Hezekiah's proof
items.text_en: Abaye's principle and Hezekiah's proof
items.desc_en: Abaye states that all agree a child from a niddah or sotah is not a mamzer. Hezekiah cites a verse to show that even during her niddah period, a husband's relations with his wife are considered a valid union.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Abaye's principle that all agree a child from a niddah or sotah is not a mamzer applies even to a niddah.
Hezekiah cites the verse 'וּתְהִי נִדָּתָהּ עָלָיו' to prove that even during her niddah period, relations with one's wife are considered a valid union (הֲוָיָה).

items.text: Gemara's question: why compare to sister-wife rather than niddah?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: why compare to sister-wife rather than niddah?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the earlier argument compared the case to a sister-wife (a prohibition) rather than to niddah (a permitted case). It answers that we compare to the stricter side.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the comparison is made to a sister-wife (אחות אשה) rather than to a niddah (נדה), which would yield a lenient result.
The Gemara answers that when there is a choice between a lenient and a stringent comparison, we compare to the stringent side (לחומרא מקשינן).

items.text: Rav Acha bar Yaakov's kal vachomer from yevamah
items.text_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov's kal vachomer from yevamah
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov proposes a kal vachomer: if a yevamah, who is only prohibited by a negative commandment, cannot receive kiddushin, then those liable for death or karet certainly cannot. The Gemara objects that this would also exclude other negative commandments.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov proposes a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument): if a yevamah (yibbum widow), who is only prohibited by a negative commandment (לאו), cannot receive kiddushin (betrothal), then those liable for death or karet (excision) certainly cannot.
The Gemara objects that Rav Acha bar Yaakov's kal vachomer would also exclude other negative commandments (שאר חייבי לאוין), which is not the case.

items.text: Rav Pappa's resolution from the verse
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's resolution from the verse
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa explains that the verse 'כי תהיין לאיש שתי נשים' explicitly discusses a case where kiddushin takes effect, referring to a beloved and hated wife, and the Torah says 'כי תהיין' – they become his through kiddushin.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa resolves the difficulty by citing the verse 'כי תהיין לאיש שתי נשים' (when a man has two wives), interpreting 'אהובה' and 'שנואה' as referring to marriages that are beloved or hated, and concluding that the verse establishes that kiddushin takes effect for חייבי לאוין (those liable for negative commandments).

items.text: Rabbi Akiva's position and Rabbi Simai's support
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's position and Rabbi Simai's support
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Akiva holds kiddushin does not take effect for those liable for negative commandments. The verse 'כי תהיין' is applied to a widow with a High Priest, as per Rabbi Simai, who says Rabbi Akiva only excludes that case from mamzerut.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Rabbi Akiva, who holds that kiddushin does not take effect for those liable for negative commandments, interprets the verse 'כי תהיין'.
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Akiva applies the verse to a widow with a High Priest, in accordance with Rabbi Simai.

The baraita cites Rabbi Simai, who states that Rabbi Akiva would render the child a mamzer from any forbidden union except a widow with a High Priest, because the verse 'לא יחלל' indicates he profanes but does not create mamzerut.

items.text: Rabbi Yeshevav's view and application to positive commandments
items.text_en: Rabbi Yeshevav's view and application to positive commandments
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers Rabbi Yeshevav, who says any union not permitted in Israel produces a mamzer. If he comes to exclude Rabbi Simai's case, it works; if he holds his own view, even positive commandments are included. The verse is then applied to a non-virgin with a High Priest, which is a positive commandment not universally applicable.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces Rabbi Yeshevab's view that any union not permitted in Israel produces a mamzer, and notes that if he comes to exclude Rabbi Simai's case, it works.
The Gemara asks: if Rabbi Yeshevab holds his own view and includes even positive commandments, how does he apply the verse?
The Gemara answers that the verse applies to a non-virgin with a High Priest, which is a positive commandment not universally applicable.

items.text: Rabbis' question and Rabbi Akiva's forced interpretation
items.text_en: Rabbis' question and Rabbi Akiva's forced interpretation
items.desc_en: The Rabbis ask why the verse is not applied to positive commandments. The Gemara explains that positive commandments do not fit the verse's context of two women from one nation. Rabbi Akiva is forced to interpret the verse in a strained manner.

sub.desc_en: The Rabbis ask why the verse is applied to negative commandments rather than positive commandments.
The Gemara explains that positive commandments do not fit the verse's context of two women from one nation.
The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Akiva is forced to interpret the verse in a strained manner, applying it to himself.

items.text: Source for Canaanite slavewoman not receiving kiddushin
items.text_en: Source for Canaanite slavewoman not receiving kiddushin
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source that a Canaanite slavewoman cannot receive kiddushin. Rav Huna cites the verse 'שבו לכם פה עם החמור' – a people comparable to a donkey.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source that a Canaanite slavewoman cannot receive kiddushin.
Rav Huna cites the verse 'שבו לכם פה עם החמור' – a people comparable to a donkey.

items.text: Source for the child of a non-Jewish mother being like her
items.text_en: Source for the child of a non-Jewish mother being like her
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where do we derive that the child of a non-Jewish mother is like her (i.e., non-Jewish)? It cites the verse 'the woman and her children shall be her master's' (Exodus 21:4) as the source.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks from where we derive that the child of a non-Jewish mother is like her, and cites the verse 'the woman and her children shall be her master's' (Exodus 21:4) as the source.

items.text: Source for a non-Jewish woman not being subject to kiddushin
items.text_en: Source for a non-Jewish woman not being subject to kiddushin
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where do we derive that a non-Jewish woman is not subject to kiddushin? It cites the verse 'you shall not intermarry with them' (Deuteronomy 7:3). It then asks: we have found that kiddushin does not take effect with her, but from where do we derive that her child is like her?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks from where we derive that a non-Jewish woman herself is not subject to betrothal, and then asks again from where we derive that her child is like her.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's answer
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's answer
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan says in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai: the verse 'for he will turn your son away from Me' (Deuteronomy 7:4) teaches that your son from a Jewish woman is called your son, but your son from a non-Jewish woman is not called your son, but rather her son.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan cites Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai, who derives from the verse 'כִּי יָסִיר אֶת בִּנְךָ מֵאַחֲרַי' (for he will turn your son away from Me) that only a son from a Jewish woman is called 'your son', but a son from a non-Jewish woman is called 'her son'.

items.text: Ravina's inference and the status of the child
items.text_en: Ravina's inference and the status of the child
items.desc_en: Ravina says: from this we learn that the son of your daughter from a non-Jew is called your son. The Gemara asks: does Ravina hold that a non-Jew or slave who has relations with a Jewish woman produces a mamzer? It answers: although the child is not fit (kosher), he is not a mamzer, but rather a 'pasul' (invalid).

sub.desc_en: Ravina infers from the earlier verse that the son of your daughter from a non-Jew is called your son.
The Gemara questions whether Ravina holds that a non-Jew or slave who has relations with a Jewish woman produces a mamzer.
The Gemara answers that although the child is not kosher (fit), he is not a mamzer but rather a pasul (invalid).

items.text: Extending the source to all nations
items.text_en: Extending the source to all nations
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the verse about 'turning away' is written regarding the seven Canaanite nations. From where do we derive this for other nations? It cites the verse 'for he will turn your son away' – to include all those who cause turning away (i.e., all idolatrous nations).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the verse 'כִּי יָסִיר' is written regarding the seven Canaanite nations, and asks from where we derive the same for other nations; it answers that the verse 'יָסִיר' includes all who cause others to stray.
The Gemara answers: the verse 'כִּי יָסִיר אֶת בִּנְךָ' (for he will turn your son away) includes all those who cause turning away, i.e., all idolatrous nations.

items.text: The Rabbis' alternative source
items.text_en: The Rabbis' alternative source
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: this works for Rabbi Shimon, who interprets the reason of the verse, but for the Rabbis, what is the reason? It answers: the verse 'and after that you may come to her and possess her' (Deuteronomy 21:13) implies that initially kiddushin does not take effect with her (the captive woman).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: this works for Rabbi Shimon, who interprets the reason of the verse, but for the Rabbis, what is the reason?

The Gemara answers: the verse 'וְאַחַר כֵּן תָּבוֹא אֵלֶיהָ וּבְעַלְתָּהּ' (and after that you may come to her and possess her) implies that initially kiddushin (betrothal) does not take effect with her (the captive woman).

items.text: Deriving the child's status from 'ki tihyena'
items.text_en: Deriving the child's status from 'ki tihyena'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: we have found that kiddushin does not take effect with her, but from where do we derive that her child is like her? It answers: the verse 'if a man has two wives... and they bear him children' (Deuteronomy 21:15) teaches that wherever we read 'ki tihyena' (if they are married), we read 've-yaledu lo' (and they bear him children), and wherever we do not read 'ki tihyena', we do not read 've-yaledu lo'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that we have found that betrothal does not take effect with her, but asks from where we derive that her child is like her.

The Gemara answers with the verse 'כִּי תִהְיֶיןָ לְאִישׁ... וְיָלְדוּ לוֹ' (when they are married to a man... and they bear children to him), establishing that wherever we read 'כִּי תִהְיֶינָה' (betrothal applies), we read 'וְיָלְדוּ לוֹ' (the child is his), and where betrothal does not apply, the child is not his.

items.text: Applying the same logic to a maidservant
items.text_en: Applying the same logic to a maidservant
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if so, the same should apply to a maidservant? It answers: indeed, that is the case. But then what is the purpose of the verse 'the woman and her children shall be her master's'? It is for that which was taught in a baraita.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if so, the same should apply to a maidservant (שפחה), but then answers that indeed it does, and asks why the verse 'הָאִשָּׁה וִילָדֶיהָ תִּהְיֶה לַאדֹנֶיהָ' is needed; it answers that it is for what was taught in a baraita.
The Gemara answers: indeed, that is the case.
The Gemara asks: if so, what is the purpose of the verse 'the woman and her children shall be her master's'?
The Gemara answers: it is needed for that which was taught in a baraita (as will be cited).

items.text: Opening Mishnah and Gemara's clarification
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and Gemara's clarification
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute between Rabbi Yosei HaGelili and the Sages regarding a man who says to his maidservant: 'You are free, and your child is a slave.' Rabbi Yosei holds the child follows the mother, while the Sages say his words stand. The Gemara asks what the scriptural basis is, and Rava explains it is according to Rabbi Yosei HaGelili.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the dispute: a man who declares his maidservant free and her child a slave — Rabbi Yosei HaGelili says the child follows the mother, the Sages say his words stand, citing the verse 'the woman and her children shall be her master's'.
The Gemara asks what the scriptural basis is for the Mishnah's positions.
Rava explains that the Mishnah's dispute is according to Rabbi Yosei HaGelili's position.

items.text: Mishnah: Rabbi Tarfon's proposal for mamzerim
items.text_en: Mishnah: Rabbi Tarfon's proposal for mamzerim
items.desc_en: Rabbi Tarfon states that mamzerim can become pure: a mamzer who marries a maidservant produces a child who is a slave; if the master frees the child, the child becomes free. Rabbi Eliezer disagrees, calling such a child a 'mamzer slave'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Tarfon states that mamzerim can become pure: a mamzer who marries a maidservant produces a child who is a slave; if the master frees the child, the child becomes free.
Rabbi Eliezer objects, calling such a child a 'mamzer slave'.

items.text: Gemara: Is Rabbi Tarfon's ruling lechatchilah or b'di'avad?
items.text_en: Gemara: Is Rabbi Tarfon's ruling lechatchilah or b'di'avad?
items.desc_en: The Gemara inquires whether Rabbi Tarfon permits marrying a maidservant initially (lechatchilah) or only after the fact (b'di'avad). It brings a proof from the Sages' objection that he only purified males, not females, and from the story of Rabbi Simlai's host, who was a mamzer. The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Tarfon speaks lechatchilah, and Rav Yehuda says Shmuel ruled the halakhah follows Rabbi Tarfon.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Rabbi Tarfon's ruling about mamzerim purifying themselves through a maidservant is meant לכתחילה (as an ideal initial action) or בדיעבד (only after the fact).

The Gemara brings a proof from the Sages' objection that Rabbi Tarfon only purified males, not females, and argues that if it were לכתחילה, a female mamzeret could also marry a slave, but a slave has no lineage concern.

The Gemara brings a story about Rabbi Simlai's host, who was a mamzer, and Rabbi Simlai told him that if he had come earlier, he would have purified his children, implying that the ruling is לכתחילה, not just after the fact.

The Gemara objects that if it were only after the fact, Rabbi Simlai would have advised the host to steal and sell himself as a Hebrew slave, but that is impossible because Hebrew slavery only applies when the Jubilee year is observed, so the story must prove that Rabbi Tarfon speaks לכתחילה.
Rav Yehuda reports that Shmuel ruled the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Tarfon.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning and the Sages' counter
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning and the Sages' counter
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar explains Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning: the verse 'לוֹ' (to him) indicates one follows the child's disqualification. The Sages argue that verse applies to an Israelite who marries a mamzeret. Rabbi Eliezer counters that just as 'לוֹ' overrides the principle of paternal lineage, it also overrides the principle that the child of a maidservant belongs to her master. The Sages respond that a child in a Canaanite maidservant's womb is like a child in an animal's womb.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah cites Rabbi Eliezer's ruling that the child of a mamzer who married a maidservant is a mamzer slave.
Rabbi Elazar asks for the reasoning behind Rabbi Eliezer's position.
Rabbi Elazar explains that Rabbi Eliezer derives from the verse 'לוֹ' (to him) that one follows the child's disqualification (mamzerut).
The Sages argue that the verse 'לוֹ' applies to an Israelite who marries a mamzeret, overriding the principle of paternal lineage (למִשְׁפְּחֹתָם לְבֵית אֲבֹתָם).

Rabbi Eliezer counters that just as 'לוֹ' overrides the principle of paternal lineage, it also overrides the principle that the child of a maidservant belongs to her master (האישה וילדיה תהיה לאדוניה).
The Sages respond that a child in a Canaanite maidservant's womb is like a child in an animal's womb, so the principle of maternal lineage does not apply.

items.text: Conclusion of the chapter
items.text_en: Conclusion of the chapter
items.desc_en: The Gemara marks the end of the chapter with the phrase 'הדרן עלך האומר' (we return to you, 'The one who says').

sub.desc_en: The Gemara marks the end of the chapter with the formulaic phrase 'הדרן עלך האומר' (we return to you, 'The one who says').

items.text: Mishnah: Ten genealogical classes from Babylonia
items.text_en: Mishnah: Ten genealogical classes from Babylonia
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists ten genealogical classes that ascended from Babylonia: priests, Levites, Israelites, halalim, converts, freed slaves, mamzerim, netinim, shetukim, and asufim. It specifies which classes may intermarry, and defines shetuki (one who knows his mother but not his father) and asufi (one found in the market, knowing neither parent). Abba Shaul called a shetuki a 'beduki' (examined).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the ten genealogical classes that ascended from Babylonia and defines the categories of shetuki and asufi.
Abba Shaul adds that the shetuki is called a 'beduki' (examined), implying his lineage was investigated.

items.text: Gemara: Why 'ascended from Babylonia'?
items.text_en: Gemara: Why 'ascended from Babylonia'?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah says 'ascended from Babylonia' rather than 'went to Eretz Yisrael.' It explains that the phrase teaches incidentally that the Temple Mount is higher than all of Eretz Yisrael, and Eretz Yisrael is higher than all other lands, as derived from the verse 'and you shall arise and go up to the place.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah uses the phrase 'ascended from Babylonia' (עלו מבבל) instead of 'went to Eretz Yisrael' (הלכו לארץ ישראל).

The Gemara answers that the Mishnah incidentally teaches that the Temple Mount is higher than all of Eretz Yisrael, and Eretz Yisrael is higher than all other lands, as derived from the verse 'and you shall arise and go up to the place.'
The Gemara begins to cite a baraita that supports the teaching about the relative heights of the Temple Mount and Eretz Yisrael, quoting the verse that establishes the Temple Mount's elevation.

items.text: Opening proof that Eretz Yisrael is higher than all lands
items.text_en: Opening proof that Eretz Yisrael is higher than all lands
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a verse to prove that Eretz Yisrael is higher than all other lands, using the verse from Jeremiah that speaks of bringing the people from the north and from all lands.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse from Jeremiah to prove that Eretz Yisrael is higher than all other lands, as the verse speaks of bringing the people from the north and from all lands.

items.text: Question on the Mishnah's wording and support for Rabbi Elazar
items.text_en: Question on the Mishnah's wording and support for Rabbi Elazar
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah says "עלו מבבל" (they ascended from Babylonia) rather than "עלו לארץ ישראל" (they ascended to Eretz Yisrael), and answers that it supports Rabbi Elazar's statement that Ezra did not ascend from Babylonia until he made it like pure flour and then ascended.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah uses the phrase 'עלו מבבל' (they ascended from Babylonia) instead of 'עלו לארץ ישראל' (they ascended to Eretz Yisrael).
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah's wording supports Rabbi Elazar's statement that Ezra did not ascend from Babylonia until he made it like pure flour and then ascended.

items.text: Dispute between Abaye and Rava on the Mishnah's reading
items.text_en: Dispute between Abaye and Rava on the Mishnah's reading
items.desc_en: Abaye and Rava dispute whether the Mishnah reads "עלו" (they ascended voluntarily) or "העלום" (they were brought up). The Gemara explains that they argue over Rabbi Elazar's statement: Abaye rejects it, while Rava accepts it. Alternatively, both accept it but disagree on whether Ezra separated them and they ascended on their own or he forced them up.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the dispute: Abaye says the Mishnah reads 'עלו' (they ascended voluntarily), while Rava says it reads 'העלום' (they were brought up).
The Gemara explains that Abaye and Rava dispute over Rabbi Elazar's statement that Ezra purified the community like fine flour before ascending.
The Gemara explains that Abaye rejects Rabbi Elazar's statement, while Rava accepts it.
Alternatively, both accept Rabbi Elazar's statement, but they disagree on whether Ezra separated them and they ascended voluntarily, or he forced them up.

items.text: Support for Abaye from Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel
items.text_en: Support for Abaye from Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel
items.desc_en: The Gemara supports Abaye's reading ("עלו") with Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel's statement that all lands are dough relative to Eretz Yisrael, and Eretz Yisrael is dough relative to Babylonia. It then questions how, according to Rava's reading ("העלום"), they would know the lineage of later generations, and answers that they knew only for that generation, not for later ones.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara supports Abaye's reading (עלו) by citing Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel's statement that all lands are dough relative to Eretz Yisrael, and Eretz Yisrael is dough relative to Babylonia.
The Gemara questions how, according to Rava's reading (העלום), they would know the lineage of later generations.
The Gemara answers that they knew only for that generation, not for later ones.

items.text: Scriptural support for Abaye and response to Rava
items.text_en: Scriptural support for Abaye and response to Rava
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a verse (Ezra 8:15) supporting Abaye's reading that they ascended voluntarily, as Ezra gathered them and found no Levites. For Rava's reading, it explains that while they were careful about those with blemishes, they were not careful about those who were fit.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara supports Abaye's position that they ascended voluntarily by citing the verse where Ezra gathered the people and found no Levites among them.

The Gemara explains that for Rava's reading that they were brought up, the Levites were careful about those with blemishes but not about those who were fit, so the verse's finding of no Levites refers to fit ones.

items.text: Proof that priests, Levites, and Israelites ascended
items.text_en: Proof that priests, Levites, and Israelites ascended
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a verse (Nehemiah 7:73) to prove that priests, Levites, and Israelites ascended from Babylonia.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse (Nehemiah 7:73) to prove that priests, Levites, and Israelites ascended from Babylonia.

items.text: Proof for chalals, converts, and freed slaves from Rabbi Yosei
items.text_en: Proof for chalals, converts, and freed slaves from Rabbi Yosei
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Yosei says that chazakah (presumption) is great, based on the story of the sons of Habayah, Hakotz, and Barzillai who were disqualified from the priesthood. The tirshata (Nehemiah) told them they would remain in their presumption, eating from kodshei hagvul (border sanctities) as they did in the exile.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where do we derive that חללים (disqualified priests), converts, and freed slaves ascended from Babylonia?

A baraita is cited where Rabbi Yosei states that chazakah (presumption) is great, proven by the story of the sons of Habayah, Hakotz, and Barzillai who were disqualified from the priesthood and told not to eat קדש הקדשים (most sacred offerings) until a priest with Urim and Tumim arises.

The Gemara explains that the tirshata (Nehemiah) told them they would remain in their presumption, eating from קדשי הגבול (border sanctities) as they did in the exile, thereby proving that חללים, converts, and freed slaves ascended.

items.text: Objection: If we elevate from terumah to yichusin, why were they eating terumah?
items.text_en: Objection: If we elevate from terumah to yichusin, why were they eating terumah?
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: according to the view that we elevate from terumah to yichusin (lineage), these people who were eating terumah should have been elevated! It answers that their presumption was weakened (they were suspect).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: according to the view that we elevate from terumah to lineage, these people who were eating terumah should have been elevated!
The Gemara answers: it is different there because their presumption was weakened (they were suspect).

items.text: Explanation of "great chazakah" regarding terumah
items.text_en: Explanation of "great chazakah" regarding terumah
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the greatness of the chazakah is that initially they ate rabbinic terumah, and eventually they ate biblical terumah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: If the previous explanation is rejected, then what is the meaning of 'great chazakah' in the baraita?
The Gemara answers: The greatness of the chazakah is that initially they ate rabbinic terumah, and eventually they ate biblical terumah.

items.text: Alternative explanation: They only ate rabbinic terumah, not biblical
items.text_en: Alternative explanation: They only ate rabbinic terumah, not biblical
items.desc_en: An alternative explanation: they always ate only rabbinic terumah, not biblical terumah. When we elevate from terumah to yichusin, it is from biblical terumah, not rabbinic. The greatness of the chazakah is that initially there was no concern for biblical terumah, but later, despite the concern, they still ate rabbinic terumah but not biblical.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative explanation: they always ate only rabbinic תרומה (terumah), not biblical; elevation to יוחסין (lineage) is only from biblical תרומה (terumah), not rabbinic.
The Gemara asks: If so, what is the greatness of the חזקה (presumption)?
The Gemara answers: The greatness is that initially there was no concern for biblical תרומה (terumah), but later, despite the concern, they still ate rabbinic תרומה (terumah) but not biblical.

items.text: Interpretation of the verse "they shall not eat from kodesh hakodashim"
items.text_en: Interpretation of the verse "they shall not eat from kodesh hakodashim"
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the verse that says they shall not eat from kodesh hakodashim, implying they may eat other things. It explains that the verse means they shall not eat anything called kodesh (holy) or anything called kodashim (sacrifices), citing verses to define these terms.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the verse that says they shall not eat from קודש הקדשים (the most sacred order), implying they may eat other things, including תרומה (priestly portion) by Torah law.

The Gemara explains that the verse means they shall not eat anything called קודש (holy) or anything called קדשים (sacrifices), citing verses to define these terms and citing Mar's statement about the portions separated from offerings.

items.text: מקור גרים וחרורים
items.text_en: Derivation of converts and freed slaves
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks from where we derive the categories of converts and freed slaves. Rav Chisda answers that the verse 'and all who separated from the impurity of the nations of the land' teaches this.
items.desc: הגמרא דורשת את הפסוק 'וכל הנבדל מטומאת גויי הארץ אלהם' כדי ללמוד שגרים וחרורים עלו מבבל, ומביאה את דברי רב חסדא.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks from where we derive the categories of converts and freed slaves.
sub.desc: רב חסדא דורש את הפסוק 'וכל הנבדל מטומאת גויי הארץ אלהם' כמקור לכך שגרים וחרורים עלו מבבל.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda answers that the verse 'and all who separated from the impurity of the nations of the land' teaches this.
sub.desc: רב חסדא מביא פסוק מספר עזרא להוכחה שגרים וחרורים נכללים בקהל, ומקשר את הפסוק לעניין.

items.text: Derivation of mamzerim
items.text_en: Derivation of mamzerim
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives the category of mamzerim from the verses about Sanballat and Tobiah, based on the principle that a gentile or slave who has relations with a Jewish woman produces a mamzer.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where do we derive the category of mamzerim (children of forbidden unions)?
The Gemara answers: It is derived from the verses about Sanballat and Tobiah, based on the principle that a gentile or slave who has relations with a Jewish woman produces a mamzer.

items.text: Objections to the derivation of mamzerim
items.text_en: Objections to the derivation of mamzerim
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises three objections: this derivation only works for one who holds that the child is a mamzer; perhaps Sanballat had no children; perhaps the children were born elsewhere and only later came to Judah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the derivation only works for one who holds the child is a mamzer, but what about one who holds the child is kosher?
The Gemara objects that perhaps Sanballat had no children at all.
The Gemara objects that perhaps the children were born elsewhere and only later came to Judah.

items.text: פרשנות שמות העולים
items.text_en: Alternative derivation from the returnees from Tel Melach
items.desc_en: The Gemara provides an alternative derivation from the verses about those who returned from Tel Melach, Tel Charsha, Cherub, Addon, and Immer, who could not prove their lineage. Rabbi Abahu offers two interpretations of the verse.
items.desc: הגמרא דורשת את הפסוק 'ואלה העולים מתל מלח תל חרשא' ומפרשת את השמות כרמזים למעשים פסולים, כולל ממזרות ואסופים, ומסיימת בדברי רבי אבהו על חשיבות ישראל.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces an alternative derivation from the verses about the returnees from Tel Melach who could not prove their lineage.
sub.desc: הגמרא מביאה פסוק אחר מספר עזרא על העולים מתל מלח ותל חרשא, ומפרשת שהם אנשים שמעשיהם דומים למעשה סדום, ושהאסופי נקרא כך שנאסף מהשוק; רבי אבהו דורש את השמות כרוּב ואדון.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abahu interprets that the Master said He intended Israel to be as precious as a cherub, but they made themselves like a leopard.

sub.text: Some say Rabbi Abahu's second interpretation
sub.text_en: Some say Rabbi Abahu's second interpretation
sub.desc_en: An alternative version states that Rabbi Abahu said the Master declared that even though they made themselves like a leopard, they are still as precious before Him as a cherub.

items.text: Rabba bar bar Chana on marrying an unsuitable woman
items.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chana on marrying an unsuitable woman
items.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana states that one who marries a woman not suitable for him is considered as if he plowed the entire world and sowed it with salt, as derived from the verse about Tel Melach.

sub.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana states that one who marries a woman not suitable for him is considered as if he plowed the entire world and sowed it with salt, citing the verse about Tel Melach.

items.text: Rav on marrying for money
items.text_en: Rav on marrying for money
items.desc_en: Rav states that one who marries a woman for money will have unworthy children, as derived from the verse 'they have begotten strange children'. The Gemara elaborates that the money will be lost within a month.

sub.desc_en: Rav states that one who marries a woman for money will have unworthy children, citing the verse 'they have begotten strange children'.
The Gemara elaborates that the money will be lost within a month, citing the verse 'now a month will devour their portions' and explaining that the loss occurs month after month.

items.text: עונש הפוסל ונושא אישה שאינה הוגנת
items.text_en: Elijah binds and God pierces the one who marries an unsuitable woman
items.desc_en: Rabba bar Rav Adda or Rabbi Salla quoting Rav Hamnuna states that Elijah binds and God pierces one who marries an unsuitable woman. A baraisa adds that Elijah writes and God signs: woe to one who disqualifies his seed, damages his family, and marries an unsuitable woman. Shmuel adds that one who disqualifies others is himself disqualified.
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה בשם רב המנונא שאליהו כופת את הנושא אישה שאינה הוגנת והקדוש ברוך הוא רוצעו, ומוסיפה שכל הפוסל פסול ואינו מדבר בשבח.

sub.text: Rabba bar Rav Adda / Rabbi Salla quoting Rav Hamnuna
sub.text_en: Rabba bar Rav Adda / Rabbi Salla quoting Rav Hamnuna
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar Rav Adda (or Rabbi Salla quoting Rav Hamnuna) states that Elijah binds and God pierces one who marries an unsuitable woman.
A baraita adds that Elijah writes and God signs a declaration of woe against one who disqualifies his seed, damages his family, and marries an unsuitable woman.
Shmuel adds that one who disqualifies others is himself disqualified, and he speaks through his own blemish.

items.text: Story of the man from Nehardea and Rav Yehuda
items.text_en: Story of the man from Nehardea and Rav Yehuda
items.desc_en: A man from Nehardea came to Pumbedita and insulted Rav Yehuda bar Yechezkel, who excommunicated him and declared him a slave. The man summoned Rav Yehuda to Rav Nachman's court. Rav Yehuda consulted Rav Huna, who advised him to go out of respect for the Nasi. Rav Yehuda then engaged in a series of verbal sparring with the man, each time citing a ruling of Shmuel to rebuke him.

sub.desc_en: A man from Nehardea came to the slaughterhouse in Pumbedita, insulted Rav Yehuda bar Yechezkel, and was excommunicated and declared a slave by Rav Yehuda.
The man summoned Rav Yehuda to Rav Nachman's court; Rav Yehuda consulted Rav Huna, who advised him to go out of respect for the Nasi.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda's question to Rav Nachman
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda's question to Rav Nachman
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda found Rav Nachman building a railing and challenged him with Shmuel's ruling that a community leader is forbidden to do work in front of three people; Rav Nachman replied he was only doing a small repair.

sub.text: Rav Nachman's verbal sparring with Rav Yehuda
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman's verbal sparring with Rav Yehuda
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman tested Rav Yehuda with a series of word choices (e.g., 'קרפטא' vs. 'ספסל', 'אתרונגא' vs. 'אתרוג'), and Rav Yehuda corrected each one, citing Shmuel's rulings on proper terminology.

sub.text: Rav Nachman's request and Rav Yehuda's response
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman's request and Rav Yehuda's response
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman asked for a female servant to pour a drink; Rav Yehuda cited Shmuel's ruling that one may not use a woman for service at all, whether adult or minor.

sub.text: Rav Nachman's request and Rav Yehuda's response
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman's request and Rav Yehuda's response
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman asked to send greetings to Yalta; Rav Yehuda cited Shmuel's ruling that a woman's voice is ervah, and when Rav Nachman suggested sending via a messenger, Rav Yehuda again cited Shmuel.

items.text: Opening question on greeting a woman
items.text_en: Opening question on greeting a woman
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the ruling that one may not inquire about a woman's welfare, citing Shmuel's absolute prohibition. The wife of the addressee sends a message to release his merchandise so he won't be considered an ignoramus.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling that one may not inquire about a woman's welfare, asking whether it is permitted through her husband.
Shmuel responds that one may not inquire about a woman's welfare at all, even through her husband.
The wife of the addressee sends a message to release his merchandise so he won't be considered an ignoramus.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's arrival and the summons
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's arrival and the summons
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda asks why the master (Rav) is there, and Rav explains he was summoned by a summons. Rav Yehuda denies sending it, but Rav produces the summons from his sleeve. Rav then asks Rav Yehuda to speak words of Torah to avoid accusations of flattery.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda asks Rav why he has come to his place.
Rav explains that Rav Yehuda sent him a summons.
Rav Yehuda denies sending any summons, claiming he does not even know Rav's foolishness.
Rav produces the summons from his sleeve and shows it to Rav Yehuda.
Rav asks Rav Yehuda to speak words of Torah so that people will not say the rabbis flatter each other.

items.text: Reason for excommunication
items.text_en: Reason for excommunication
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda explains that he excommunicated a man for causing pain to a rabbinic agent. Rav suggests that lashes would have sufficed, but Rav Yehuda responds that he did something even greater (excommunication).

sub.desc_en: Rav asks Rav Yehuda why he excommunicated a certain man.
Rav Yehuda explains that the man caused pain to a rabbinic agent.
Rav objects that lashes would have sufficed, as Rav himself administers lashes for such an offense.
Rav Yehuda responds that he did something even greater (excommunication) than lashes.

items.text: Reason for declaring him a slave
items.text_en: Reason for declaring him a slave
items.desc_en: Rav asks why Rav Yehuda proclaimed the man a slave. Rav Yehuda explains that the man habitually called others 'slaves', and one who disqualifies others is himself disqualified, as per Shmuel's principle. The Gemara questions whether Shmuel's statement warrants a public proclamation.

sub.desc_en: Rav asks Rav Yehuda why he publicly proclaimed that a certain man is a slave.

Rav Yehuda explains that the man habitually called others 'slaves', and cites the principle that one who disqualifies others is himself disqualified, as Shmuel said: he disqualifies with his own blemish.
The Gemara objects that Shmuel's statement only warrants suspicion, not a public proclamation of slave status.

items.text: The litigant from Nehardea claims Hasmonean descent
items.text_en: The litigant from Nehardea claims Hasmonean descent
items.desc_en: While they were speaking, the litigant from Nehardea arrived and told Rav Yehuda that he called him a slave, but he is from the Hasmonean royal house. Rav Yehuda responds with Shmuel's ruling that anyone claiming Hasmonean descent is a slave.

sub.desc_en: The litigant from Nehardea arrives and claims to Rav Yehuda that he is from the Hasmonean royal house, not a slave.
Rav Yehuda responds with Shmuel's ruling that anyone claiming Hasmonean descent is a slave.

items.text: Objection based on Rabbi Abba's ruling
items.text_en: Objection based on Rabbi Abba's ruling
items.desc_en: The litigant objects, citing Rabbi Abba's ruling that a Torah scholar who states a halakha before the fact is listened to, but not after. Rav Yehuda responds that Rav Mattana agrees with him.

sub.desc_en: The litigant objects, citing Rabbi Abba's ruling that a Torah scholar who states a halakha before the fact is listened to, but not after.
Rav Yehuda responds that Rav Mattana agrees with him, implying his ruling is not after the fact.

items.text: Rav Mattana's testimony and the story of the Hasmonean slave
items.text_en: Rav Mattana's testimony and the story of the Hasmonean slave
items.desc_en: Rav Mattana, who had not seen Nehardea for thirteen years, arrives and confirms Shmuel's ruling with a story: a Hasmonean maidservant climbed to a roof and declared that anyone claiming Hasmonean descent is a slave, then fell and died. A proclamation was made that she was a slave.

sub.desc_en: The narrator introduces Rav Mattana, who had not seen Nehardea for thirteen years, and notes that he arrived on that very day.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda's question to Rav Mattana
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda's question to Rav Mattana
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda asks Rav Mattana if he remembers what Shmuel said while standing with one foot on the bank and one foot on the ferry.
Rav Mattana answers that Shmuel said: Anyone who claims descent from the Hasmonean kingdom is a slave.
Rav Mattana provides the supporting story: only a Hasmonean maidservant remained, who climbed to a roof and declared that anyone claiming Hasmonean descent is a slave.
The narrator concludes that the maidservant fell from the roof and died, and a proclamation was made that she was a slave.

items.text: Aftermath in Nehardea and Rav Yehuda's threat
items.text_en: Aftermath in Nehardea and Rav Yehuda's threat
items.desc_en: Many ketubot were torn in Nehardea that day. As Rav Yehuda left, people followed to stone him. He threatened to reveal that there are two families in Nehardea, one pure and one impure, with a sign: impure is impure, pure is pure. They dropped their stones and a pile formed in the King's Canal.

sub.desc_en: The narrative reports that many ketubot were torn in Nehardea that day, and when Rav Yehuda left, people followed to stone him; he threatened to reveal the two families of Nehardea, causing them to drop their stones, which formed a pile in the King's Canal.

items.text: Various proclamations of lineage
items.text_en: Various proclamations of lineage
