items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in Pumbedita proclaims Ada and Yonatan as slaves, Yehuda bar Pappa as a mamzer, and Bati bar Toviya as not accepting a bill of freedom due to arrogance. Rava in Mehoza proclaims various professions as invalid. Rav Yehuda identifies Gova'ei as Gibeonites and Durnunita as Daraei Natinim. Rav Yosef says the Bei Kubei of Pumbedita are all slaves.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in Pumbedita proclaims Ada and Yonatan as slaves, Yehuda bar Pappa as a mamzer, and Bati bar Toviya as not accepting a bill of freedom due to arrogance.
Rava in Mehoza proclaims various professions (weavers, dyers, tailors, sailors, glassblowers) as invalid for lineage.
Rav Yehuda identifies Gova'ei as Gibeonites and Durnunita as Daraei Natinim (descendants of the Gibeonites).
Rav Yosef says that the Bei Kubei of Pumbedita are all slaves.

items.text: Pashhur ben Immer's slaves and the sign of a bold priest
items.text_en: Pashhur ben Immer's slaves and the sign of a bold priest
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says Shmuel stated that Pashhur ben Immer had 400 or 4000 slaves who all became mixed into the priesthood. Any priest with chutzpah is from them. Abaye says they all sit in the wall of Nehardea. Rabbi Elazar disagrees, saying not to suspect a bold priest, as per the verse 'And your people are like the quarrels of a priest'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports Shmuel's tradition that Pashhur ben Immer's 400 or 4000 slaves all became mixed into the priesthood, and any bold priest is from them.
Abaye adds that all these slaves now sit in the wall of Nehardea.
Rabbi Elazar disagrees, citing a verse to argue that one should not suspect a bold priest of being a descendant of slaves.

items.text: Punishment for marrying an unsuitable wife
items.text_en: Punishment for marrying an unsuitable wife
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avin bar Rav Adda says Rav stated that one who marries a woman not suitable for him, when the Holy One rests His presence, He testifies on all the tribes but not on him, as per the verse 'The tribes of God are a testimony for Israel'.

sub.text: Rabbi Avin bar Rav Adda citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rabbi Avin bar Rav Adda citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav states that one who marries an unsuitable wife will not have the Divine Presence testify on his behalf among the tribes.

items.text: The Shekhina rests only on yichus families
items.text_en: The Shekhina rests only on yichus families
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chama bar Chanina says the Shekhina rests only on well-born families in Israel, as per the verse 'At that time, says the Lord, I will be God to all the families of Israel' – not 'to all Israel'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chama bar Chanina states that the Shekhina rests only on well-born families in Israel, citing the verse that says 'to all the families of Israel' rather than 'to all Israel'.

items.text: The extra level of Israel over converts
items.text_en: The extra level of Israel over converts
items.desc_en: Rabba bar Rav Huna explains the verse 'And they shall be to Me a people' indicates an extra level for Israel over converts. For Israel it says 'I will be their God and they shall be My people', while for converts it says 'Who is this who pledged his heart to approach Me... and you shall be to Me a people and I will be to you God'.

sub.desc_en: Rabba bar Rav Huna explains that the verse 'And they shall be to Me a people' indicates an extra level for Israel over converts, as for Israel it says 'I will be their God and they shall be My people', while for converts it says 'Who is this who pledged his heart to approach Me... and you shall be to Me a people and I will be to you God'.

items.text: Converts are as difficult as a scab
items.text_en: Converts are as difficult as a scab
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chelbo says converts are as difficult for Israel as a scab, as per the verse 'And the convert shall join them and be attached to the house of Jacob' – 'attached' is used here and there regarding a scab.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chelbo states that converts are as difficult for Israel as a scab (סַפַּחַת), supporting this with a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) from the verse 'וְנִסְפְּחוּ' (and they shall be attached) used both for converts and for a skin affliction.

items.text: The Shekhina rests only on yichus families (repeated)
items.text_en: The Shekhina rests only on yichus families (repeated)
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chama bar Chanina repeats that the Shekhina rests only on well-born families in Israel, citing the verse 'At that time, says the Lord, I will be God to all the families of Israel'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chama bar Chanina states that the Shekhina rests only on well-born families in Israel, citing the verse 'At that time, says the Lord, I will be God to all the families of Israel'.

items.text: כוחו של כסף לטהר ממזרים
items.text_en: Purification of mamzerim through silver
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a verse about purifying the tribe of Levi, and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi derives that silver (money) purifies mamzerim. Rabbi Yitzchak explains that God performed an act of charity with Israel: a family that becomes assimilated is considered assimilated.
items.desc: החטיבה פותחת בדרשה על הפסוק מספר מלאכי, ולפיה הקב"ה יטהר את שבט לוי תחילה, ורבי יהושע בן לוי דורש שכסף (ממון) מטהר ממזרים, כלומר עשירים ממזרים מתערבים ומתקבלים בקהילה. רבי יצחק מסביר שזו צדקה שעשה הקב"ה עם ישראל: משפחה שנטמעה – נטמעה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by citing a verse about God purifying the tribe of Levi first, as it says He sits as a refiner and purifier of silver.
sub.desc: רבי יהושע בן לוי דורש שכסף מטהר ממזרים, שנאמר 'וישב מצרף ומטהר כסף', ומסביר ש'מגישי מנחה בצדקה' פירושו שצדקה עשה הקב"ה עם ישראל שמשפחה שנטמעה – נטמעה.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi derives from the verse that silver (money) purifies mamzerim (those of invalid lineage).
The Gemara asks: What is the meaning of the phrase 'presenters of a gift in righteousness' in the verse?
Rabbi Yitzchak explains that God performed an act of charity (צדקה) with Israel: a family that becomes assimilated is considered assimilated.

items.text: מחלוקת על מעלת הייחוס של בבל
items.text_en: The status of lands as dough for lineage
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says in the name of Shmuel that all lands are dough relative to Eretz Yisrael, and Eretz Yisrael is dough relative to Bavel. There were attempts to make Bavel dough for Eretz Yisrael, but Rabbi and Rabbi Pinchas opposed this, with Rabbi Pinchas using a clever ruse to escape.
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה את דברי רב יהודה בשם שמואל שכל הארצות עיסה לארץ ישראל וארץ ישראל עיסה לבבל. בימי רבי ביקשו לקבוע שבבל עיסה לארץ ישראל, ורבי התנגד. רבי חנינא בר חמא אישר את המסורת, ובימי רבי פנחס שוב ניסו, והוא נמלא על ידי אמירת דברים שנויים במחלוקת כדי להימלט.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports in the name of Shmuel that all lands are considered dough (עיסה) relative to Eretz Yisrael, and Eretz Yisrael is dough relative to Bavel.
In the days of Rabbi (Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi), they sought to make Bavel dough for Eretz Yisrael, but Rabbi objected and suggested they involve Rabbi Chanina bar Chama.

Rabbi Chanina bar Chama joined them and cited a tradition from Rabbi Yishmael beRabbi Yosei in his father's name, confirming that all lands are dough for Eretz Yisrael and Eretz Yisrael is dough for Bavel.

In the days of Rabbi Pinchas, they again sought to make Bavel dough for Eretz Yisrael; Rabbi Pinchas instructed his servants to carry him away on a litter after he made two statements, and he escaped, leaving the sages to investigate until danger forced them to desist.

items.text: העיקרון: משפחה שנטמעה נטמעה
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling and Abaye's support
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan says that the Temple (Heichal) is in our hands, but he cannot act because great people of the generation have become assimilated there. He follows Rabbi Yitzchak's principle that an assimilated family is considered assimilated. Abaye supports this with a baraita about families that were distanced or brought near by Ben Tziyon.
items.desc: רבי יוחנן אומר שבידינו לגלות את המשפחות הפגומות, אך אינו עושה זאת משום שגדולי הדור נטמעו בהן, וסובר כרבי יצחק שמשפחה שנטמעה נטמעה. אביי מביא ברייתא על משפחת בית הצריפה ובן ציון שריחק וקירב, ומסביר שרק משפחות ידועות ייחשפו על ידי אליהו, אבל משפחה שנטמעה כבר נטמעה.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that the Temple (Heichal) is in their hands, but he cannot act because great people of the generation have become assimilated there.
sub.desc: רבי יוחנן אומר בשבועה שבידיהם לגלות משפחות פגומות, אך אינו עושה זאת מפני שגדולי הדור נטמעו בהן.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Yochanan follows Rabbi Yitzchak's principle that an assimilated family remains assimilated.
sub.desc: רבי יוחנן אומר בשבועה שבידיהם לגלות משפחות פגומות, אך אינו עושה זאת מפני שגדולי הדור נטמעו בהן.

sub.desc_en: Abaye supports the principle by citing a baraita about the family Beit HaTzerifa in Transjordan.
sub.desc: אביי מביא ברייתא על משפחת בית הצריפה ובן ציון שריחק וקירב, ומסביר שרק משפחות ידועות ייחשפו על ידי אליהו, אבל משפחה שנטמעה נטמעה.

sub.desc_en: Abaye continues citing the baraita about another family that Ben Tziyon brought near.
sub.desc: אביי מביא ברייתא על משפחת בית הצריפה ובן ציון שריחק וקירב, ומסביר שרק משפחות ידועות ייחשפו על ידי אליהו, אבל משפחה שנטמעה נטמעה.

sub.desc_en: Abaye concludes that for a family that has become assimilated, it remains assimilated and is not to be exposed.
sub.desc: אביי מביא ברייתא על משפחת בית הצריפה ובן ציון שריחק וקירב, ומסביר שרק משפחות ידועות ייחשפו על ידי אליהו, אבל משפחה שנטמעה נטמעה.

items.text: מסירת שמות משפחות פסולות לתלמידים
items.text_en: Concealing families and the frequency of transmission
items.desc_en: A baraita states that there was another family that the Sages did not want to reveal, but they would transmit it to their children and students once a week, or twice a week. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak concludes that the correct view is once a week, as per a baraita about a nazirite vow.
items.desc: הברייתא מספרת על משפחה נוספת שלא רצו חכמים לגלותה, אך מוסרים את שמה לבנים ולתלמידים פעם בשבוע או פעמיים בשבוע. רב נחמן בר יצחק פוסק כמי שאומר פעם אחת בשבוע, על פי הברייתא על נזיר שלא יגלה משפחות.

sub.desc_en: A baraita reports that there was another family of flawed lineage that the Sages did not want to reveal publicly.
sub.desc: ברייתא מספרת על משפחה פסולה נוספת שחכמים לא רצו לגלותה, אך מוסרים את שמה לתלמידים פעם בשבוע או פעמיים בשבוע; רב נחמן בר יצחק מכריע כמי שאומר פעם אחת בשבוע, על פי הברייתא על הנזיר.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that the Sages would transmit the identity of that family to their children and students once a week, or some say twice a week.
sub.desc: ברייתא מספרת על משפחה פסולה נוספת שחכמים לא רצו לגלותה, אך מוסרים את שמה לתלמידים פעם בשבוע או פעמיים בשבוע; רב נחמן בר יצחק מכריע כמי שאומר פעם אחת בשבוע, על פי הברייתא על הנזיר.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak concludes that the correct view is that they transmitted it once a week.
sub.desc: ברייתא מספרת על משפחה פסולה נוספת שחכמים לא רצו לגלותה, אך מוסרים את שמה לתלמידים פעם בשבוע או פעמיים בשבוע; רב נחמן בר יצחק מכריע כמי שאומר פעם אחת בשבוע, על פי הברייתא על הנזיר.

sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak (citing a baraita)
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak supports his conclusion by citing a baraita that one who vows to reveal families of flawed lineage should become a nazirite and not reveal them, showing that such information should be kept secret.
sub.desc: ברייתא מספרת על משפחה פסולה נוספת שחכמים לא רצו לגלותה, אך מוסרים את שמה לתלמידים פעם בשבוע או פעמיים בשבוע; רב נחמן בר יצחק מכריע כמי שאומר פעם אחת בשבוע, על פי הברייתא על הנזיר.

items.text: Transmission of the Tetragrammaton and the Divine Name
items.text_en: Transmission of the Tetragrammaton and the Divine Name
items.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana says in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that the four-letter Name is transmitted once a week, with Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak supporting once a week based on the verse 'this is My name forever' (le'olam, read as le'alem). Rava wanted to teach it publicly but was stopped. Rabbi Avina resolves a contradiction between 'this is My name' and 'this is My remembrance'.

sub.text: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that the four-letter Name is transmitted to students once or twice a week.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak supports the view of once a week, citing the verse 'this is My name forever' (לְעֹלָם) which is written as לְעַלֵּם (to conceal).
Rava wanted to teach the Name publicly in the lecture hall, but an elder stopped him by citing the same verse that it is meant to be concealed.
Rabbi Avina resolves the apparent contradiction between 'this is My name' and 'this is My remembrance' by explaining that the Name is written with yod-hey but pronounced with alef-dalet.

items.text: The twelve-letter Name and the forty-two-letter Name
items.text_en: The twelve-letter Name and the forty-two-letter Name
items.desc_en: The Sages taught that initially the twelve-letter Name was transmitted to everyone, but when the insolent increased, it was given only to the modest priests, who would blend it into the melody. Rabbi Tarfon recounts hearing this. Rav Yehuda says in the name of Rav that the forty-two-letter Name is given only to the modest, humble, etc., and its keeper is beloved.

sub.desc_en: The baraita reports that initially the twelve-letter Name was transmitted to everyone, but when the insolent increased, it was given only to the modest priests, who would blend it into the melody.
Rabbi Tarfon recounts that he once ascended the platform and heard the High Priest blend the Name into the melody of the priests.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says in the name of Rav that the forty-two-letter Name is given only to the modest, humble, etc., and its keeper is beloved and inherits both worlds.

items.text: Presumption of lineage in different lands
items.text_en: Presumption of lineage in different lands
items.desc_en: Shmuel says in the name of Saba that Bavel stands in a presumption of fitness until known to be disqualified, while other lands stand in a presumption of unfitness until known to be fit. Eretz Yisrael follows its presumption. The Gemara questions a contradiction in the statement about Eretz Yisrael, and Rav Huna bar Tachlifa resolves it.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel in the name of Saba states the presumptions of lineage: Bavel is presumed fit until known to be disqualified, other lands are presumed unfit until known to be fit, and Eretz Yisrael follows its established presumption.

The Gemara points out an internal contradiction in the statement about Eretz Yisrael: the first clause implies that an unestablished person is fit, but the second clause implies that an unestablished person is unfit.

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Tachlifa citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Tachlifa citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Tachlifa in the name of Rav resolves the contradiction, asserting that there is no difficulty (the statement is consistent).

items.text: Distinction between marrying off and divorcing
items.text_en: Distinction between marrying off and divorcing
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a distinction: in one case we are concerned about lineage for marrying off a woman, in another for divorcing a woman from her husband.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a distinction between two contexts: one where lineage is checked for marrying off a woman, and another for divorcing a woman from her husband.

items.text: Rav Yosef's ruling on Babylonians
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's ruling on Babylonians
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef states that anyone whose conversation is in Babylonia may be married, but now that there are deceivers, we are concerned.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef rules that anyone whose conversation is in Babylonia may be married.
Rav Yosef adds that now that there are deceivers, we are concerned about lineage.

items.text: Ze'iri evades Rabbi Yochanan's marriage offer
items.text_en: Ze'iri evades Rabbi Yochanan's marriage offer
items.desc_en: Ze'iri avoids marrying Rabbi Yochanan's daughter, citing a mishna about ten lineages from Babylonia. Rabbi Elazar explains that Ezra purified Babylonia like fine flour.

sub.desc_en: The narrator describes how Ze'iri was evading Rabbi Yochanan's persistent offer of his daughter in marriage, until one day Rabbi Yochanan carried Ze'iri across a stream.
Rabbi Yochanan asks Ze'iri: 'Is our Torah fit but our daughters not fit? What is your reasoning?'
The Gemara suggests Ze'iri might have relied on the mishna that only ten lineages ascended from Babylonia, but rejects this because many others also remained.
The Gemara resolves that Ze'iri was actually relying on Rabbi Elazar's teaching that Ezra purified Babylonia like fine flour before ascending, implying only the purest remained.

items.text: Ulla's discussion with Rav Yehuda about lineage concerns
items.text_en: Ulla's discussion with Rav Yehuda about lineage concerns
items.desc_en: Ulla questions Rav Yehuda about not marrying off his son, citing verses about potential impurity from gentiles and sinners. Rabbi Avahu interprets verses about those who sleep on ivory beds as referring to those who exchange wives.

sub.desc_en: Ulla arrives at Rav Yehuda's house in Pumbedita, sees Rav Yehuda's son Rav Yitzchak grown and unmarried, and asks Rav Yehuda why he has not married off his son.
Rav Yehuda responds that he does not know from where to take a wife for his son, citing the verse about women violated in Zion and Judah as a source of potential lineage impurity.
Ulla objects that even if a gentile or slave who has relations with a Jewish woman produces a kosher child, the concern is from those described in the verse about those who sleep on ivory beds.

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's interpretation
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's interpretation
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina interprets the verse as referring to people who urinate naked in front of their beds, and Rabbi Avahu scoffs at this interpretation, questioning why such a sin would warrant exile at the head of exiles.
Rabbi Avahu offers his own interpretation: the verse refers to people who eat and drink together, bring their beds close, and exchange wives, thereby soiling their beds with semen that is not theirs.

items.text: Silence as a sign of lineage
items.text_en: Silence as a sign of lineage
items.desc_en: Ulla advises following silence, as the Westerners test by seeing who is silent first in a quarrel. Rav states that the silence of Babylonia is lineage, and clarifies that he tested by silence, not lineage.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda's son (Rav Yitzchak) to Ulla
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda's son (Rav Yitzchak) to Ulla
sub.desc_en: Rav Yitzchak asks Ulla what practical method to use for determining lineage.
Ulla advises following silence, citing the Western practice of observing who falls silent first in a quarrel as a sign of superior lineage.
Rav states that the silence of Babylonia is itself lineage, implying that silence is the test.
The gemara objects that Rav himself once tested people at the house of Bar Shafei Challa, implying it was a test of lineage, not silence.
The gemara rejects the objection, clarifying that Rav's test was about silence, not lineage, as he told them to check who is silent and who is not.

items.text: Quarrels indicate a blemish in lineage
items.text_en: Quarrels indicate a blemish in lineage
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quoting Rav and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi state that if two people or families quarrel, there is a blemish in one of them.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quotes Rav stating that if you see two people quarreling, there is a blemish of lineage in one of them, and they are not allowed to intermarry.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi extends the principle to families: if two families quarrel, there is a blemish in one of them, and they are not allowed to intermarry.

items.text: Metaphor for lands' lineage status
items.text_en: Metaphor for lands' lineage status
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa Sava in the name of Rav describes Babylonia as healthy, Meishon as dead, Media as sick, and Elam as dying, explaining the difference between sick and dying.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa Sava in the name of Rav presents a metaphor for the lineage status of lands: Babylonia is healthy, Meishon is dead, Media is sick, and Elam is dying, and explains the difference between sick and dying.

items.text: Boundaries of Babylonia for lineage
items.text_en: Boundaries of Babylonia for lineage
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel debate the boundaries of Babylonia, including rivers and locations. Abaye or Rav Yosef curses Rav for his opinion, and the Gemara clarifies the curse's scope.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks about the boundaries of Babylonia for lineage purposes, and Rav and Shmuel give their opinions regarding the upper and lower limits.
The Gemara asks about the lower boundary of the Tigris, and Rav Shmuel defines it as the lower Appameya, distinguishing between a fit and unfit location.
The Gemara asks about the upper boundary of the Euphrates, and Rav, Shmuel, and Rabbi Yochanan give their opinions, after which Abaye or Rav Yosef curses Rav.

The Gemara questions why only Rav was cursed and not Shmuel, and offers two answers: either the curse applies all the more to Shmuel, or the bridge of the Euphrates was downstream of Shmuel's boundary.

items.text: Abaye asks Rav Yosef about the boundary of the Euphrates
items.text_en: Abaye asks Rav Yosef about the boundary of the Euphrates
items.desc_en: Abaye asks Rav Yosef how far the Euphrates extends on one side, and Rav Yosef responds that the people of Pumbedita trace their lineage from Biram.

sub.desc_en: Abaye asks Rav Yosef how far the Euphrates extends on one side, given that the Persians have now diverted it.
Rav Yosef responds that the people of Pumbedita trace their lineage from Biram, implying the boundary is irrelevant for their lineage.

items.text: Rav Pappa and Rav Yosef dispute the boundary for lineage and for bills of divorce
items.text_en: Rav Pappa and Rav Yosef dispute the boundary for lineage and for bills of divorce
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa says the dispute about the boundary for lineage applies equally to bills of divorce, while Rav Yosef limits the dispute to lineage, but for bills of divorce all agree the boundary is the second bridge of the Arava.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa asserts that the dispute about the boundary for lineage applies equally to bills of divorce.
Rav Yosef limits the dispute to lineage, but for bills of divorce all agree the boundary is the second bridge of the Arava.

items.text: The boundaries of Chaveil Yama and the status of Kutim
items.text_en: The boundaries of Chaveil Yama and the status of Kutim
items.desc_en: Rami bar Abba defines Chaveil Yama as the blue thread of Bavel, and Shunya and Gubya as the blue thread of Chaveil Yama. Ravina adds Tzitzora. A baraita supports this. Rav Pappa notes that now Kutim have intermingled with them, but clarifies that it was a woman who asked them and they did not give her. He then explains that Chaveil Yama is the Perat of Borsif.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Abba defines Chaveil Yama as the blue thread of Bavel, and Shunya and Gubya as the blue thread of Chaveil Yama.
Ravina adds Tzitzora to the list of places within Chaveil Yama.
A baraita supports the definitions, with Chanan ben Pinchas listing Chaveil Yama as the blue thread of Bavel, and Shunya, Gubya, and Tzitzora as the blue thread of Chaveil Yama.
Rav Pappa notes that now Kutim have intermingled with them, but clarifies that it was a woman who asked them and they did not give her.
Rav Pappa explains that Chaveil Yama is the Perat of Borsif.

items.text: The status of Shut Meishot and the boundary of the Golah
items.text_en: The status of Shut Meishot and the boundary of the Golah
items.desc_en: A man claimed to be from Shut Meishot. Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha stood up and said Shut Meishot stands between the rivers. Abaye quotes Rabbi Chama bar Ukva quoting Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Chanina that between the rivers is like the Golah for lineage. Rabbi Yochanan says it is from Ihi deKira and above, but he also said up to the Ma'avarta of Gizma. Abaye resolves the contradiction by saying a strip of land extends out.

sub.desc_en: A man claimed to be from Shut Meishot, and Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha stood up and declared that Shut Meishot stands between the rivers.
The gemara asks: since it stands between the rivers, what is its halachic status?

sub.text: Abaye quoting Rabbi Chama bar Ukva quoting Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Chanina
sub.text_en: Abaye quoting Rabbi Chama bar Ukva quoting Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Chanina
sub.desc_en: Abaye reports a tradition that the area between the rivers is like the Golah (the diaspora) for purposes of lineage.
The gemara asks: where exactly is the boundary of this area?
Rabbi Yochanan says the boundary is from Ihi deKira and above.
The gemara objects: but Rabbi Yochanan also said the boundary is up to the Ma'avarta of Gizma, implying a different limit.
Abaye resolves the contradiction by explaining that a strip of land extends out from the main area.

items.text: The status of Chilazon and Nihavand as like the Golah
items.text_en: The status of Chilazon and Nihavand as like the Golah
items.desc_en: Rav Ika bar Avin quotes Rav Chananel quoting Rav that Chilazon Nihavand is like the Golah for lineage. Abaye tells them not to listen to him, as it was a yevamah who fell to him there. Rav Ika bar Avin responds that it is not his own statement but Rav Chananel's. They go and ask Rav Chananel, who confirms that Rav said this.

sub.text: Rav Ika bar Avin quoting Rav Chananel quoting Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Ika bar Avin quoting Rav Chananel quoting Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Ika bar Avin reports in the name of Rav Chananel citing Rav that Chilazon Nihavand is like the Golah for lineage.
Abaye warns the audience not to listen to Rav Ika bar Avin, claiming that the ruling is biased because a yevamah (a woman requiring levirate marriage) fell to him there.
Rav Ika bar Avin rejects Abaye's accusation, asserting that the statement is not his own but Rav Chananel's.
The people go and ask Rav Chananel, who confirms that Rav indeed said that Chilazon Nihavand is like the Golah for lineage.

items.text: Rabbi Abba bar Cahana's interpretation of the four exiles and the status of Mushkei and Mushkenei
items.text_en: Rabbi Abba bar Cahana's interpretation of the four exiles and the status of Mushkei and Mushkenei
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba bar Cahana interprets the verse about the exiles: Halach is Chilazon, Chavor is Hadyav, Nehar Gozan is Ginzak, and the cities of Madai are Chamadan and its companions, or Nihavand and its companions. Samuel identifies the companions as Karakh Mushkei, Chuskei, and Rumkei. Rabbi Yochanan says all are for disqualification. The Gemara initially thinks Mushkei is the same as Mushkenei, but Rabbi Chiya bar Avin quotes Samuel that Mushkenei is like the Golah for lineage, so they conclude Mushkei and Mushkenei are separate.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute involving Rabbi Abba bar Cahana, who interprets the biblical verse about the four exiles by identifying each place name with a specific location.
Samuel identifies the companions of the cities of Madai as the towns of Karakh Mushkei, Chuskei, and Rumkei.
Rabbi Yochanan declares that all these places are for disqualification of lineage.
The Gemara initially assumes that Mushkei is the same as Mushkenei, raising a contradiction.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiya bar Avin citing Samuel
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Avin citing Samuel
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Avin cites Samuel that Mushkenei is like the Golah for lineage, contradicting the assumption that it is disqualified.
The Gemara resolves that Mushkei and Mushkenei are two separate places, so there is no contradiction.

items.text: The three ribs in the mouth of the fourth beast
items.text_en: The three ribs in the mouth of the fourth beast
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan interprets the verse 'and three ribs were in its mouth between its teeth' as referring to Chilazon, Hadyav, and Netzivin, which sometimes swallow and sometimes spit out.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan interprets the verse 'and three ribs were in its mouth between its teeth' as referring to Chilazon, Hadyav, and Netzivin, which sometimes swallow and sometimes spit out.

items.text: The second beast like a bear refers to the Persians
items.text_en: The second beast like a bear refers to the Persians
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef teaches that the second beast like a bear refers to the Persians, who eat, drink, are clothed, grow hair, and have no rest like a bear. Rabbi Ami, when seeing a Persian riding, would say this is a moving bear.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse from Daniel describing a second beast like a bear.
Rav Yosef teaches that the bear-like beast refers to the Persians, who resemble a bear in eating, drinking, clothing, hair growth, and restlessness.
Rabbi Ami, upon seeing a Persian riding, would remark that this is a moving bear, reinforcing the comparison.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi asks Levi to show him various peoples
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi asks Levi to show him various peoples
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi asks Levi to show him Persians, and Levi says they resemble the soldiers of the house of David. He asks to see Chavarim, and Levi says they resemble angels of destruction. He asks to see Ishmaelites, and Levi says they resemble goats of the bathroom. He asks to see Torah scholars in Babylonia, and Levi says they resemble ministering angels.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi asks Levi to show him Persians, and Levi says they resemble the soldiers of the house of David.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi asks to see Chavarim, and Levi says they resemble angels of destruction.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi asks to see Ishmaelites, and Levi says they resemble goats of the bathroom.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi asks to see Torah scholars in Babylonia, and Levi says they resemble ministering angels.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's deathbed statements about Babylonian towns
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's deathbed statements about Babylonian towns
items.desc_en: When Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi was dying, he said: Humanya in Babylonia is entirely Ammonite; Masgarya is entirely mamzerim; Birka has two brothers who exchange wives; Birta deSatya has people who turned away from God, as they surrounded a fish pond with a net on Shabbat and fished, and Rabbi Achai bar Rabbi Yoshiya excommunicated them and they were destroyed; Akra deAgma has Ada bar Ahava.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi declares that Humanya in Babylonia is entirely Ammonite.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi declares that Masgarya in Babylonia is entirely mamzerim.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi declares that Birka in Babylonia has two brothers who exchange wives.

Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi declares that Birta deSatya in Babylonia has people who turned away from God, describing how they fished on Shabbat and were excommunicated by Rabbi Achai bar Rabbi Yoshiya and destroyed.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi declares that Akra deAgma in Babylonia has Ada bar Ahava.

items.text: The principle of righteous succession
items.text_en: The principle of righteous succession
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that when Rabbi Akiva died, Rabbi was born; when Rabbi died, Rav Yehuda was born, etc., teaching that a righteous person does not depart until another like him is created, as per the verse 'The sun rises and the sun sets'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that today Rabbi Yehuda sits in the bosom of Abraham and was born in Babylonia.
Mar teaches that righteous succession occurs: when Rabbi Akiva died, Rabbi was born, etc., citing the verse about the sun rising and setting and the lamp not going out before Samuel.

items.text: Interpretation of a verse about enemies
items.text_en: Interpretation of a verse about enemies
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda interprets the verse 'He has commanded His adversaries around Jacob' as referring to Humanya on the Euphrates.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda interprets the verse 'He has commanded His adversaries around Jacob' as referring to the city Humanya on the Euphrates.

items.text: The death of Pelatiah ben Benaiah: two interpretations
items.text_en: The death of Pelatiah ben Benaiah: two interpretations
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel debate whether Pelatiah's death was for good or evil. One view says it was good because he prevented sending a Jew to the king; the other says it was evil because he participated in idolatry in the Temple.

sub.desc_en: The gemara cites the verse about Pelatiah ben Benaiah's death and Ezekiel's cry.
The gemara reports that Rav and Shmuel debate whether Pelatiah's death was for good or for evil.
The view that it was good explains that Pelatiah prevented sending a Jew to the king, and the prophet laments that one who did good should die young.
The view that it was evil cites verses showing Pelatiah participated in idolatry in the Temple, and the prophet asks how one who did such evil could die peacefully.

items.text: Shmuel's view on Meshkeni and Meishon
items.text_en: Shmuel's view on Meshkeni and Meishon
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that Shmuel held the negative view, citing his statement that Meshkeni is like the exile for genealogical purity, and Meishon was not suspected of slavery or mamzerut, but priests there did not care about divorcées.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that Shmuel held the negative view, citing his statement that Meshkeni is like the exile for genealogical purity, and Meishon was not suspected of slavery or mamzerut, but priests there did not care about divorcées.

items.text: Alternative: Shmuel's view consistent with his own principle
items.text_en: Alternative: Shmuel's view consistent with his own principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that Shmuel might have held the positive view, consistent with his ruling that a master who abandons his slave frees him, based on the verse 'every slave of a man'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that Shmuel might have held the positive view, consistent with his own principle that a master who abandons his slave frees him, based on the verse 'every slave of a man'.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's statement and its application
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's statement and its application
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quotes Shmuel that Rabbi Meir's view is that all lands are suspect, but the Sages say all lands are presumed fit. Amemar permitted Rav Huna bar Natan to marry a woman from Mechuza, but Rav Ashi objected because the tradition was not taught in certain academies.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports in Shmuel's name that Rabbi Meir considers all lands suspect for genealogy, but the Sages hold all lands are presumed fit.
Amemar permitted Rav Huna bar Natan to marry a woman from Mechuza, applying the Sages' lenient view.
Rav Ashi objects that the lenient tradition was not taught in the academies of Rav Kahana, Rav Pappa, and Rav Zevid.
Despite the objection, Amemar did not accept Rav Ashi's challenge because he had heard the lenient tradition directly from Rav Zevid of Neharde'a.

items.text: Debate on the future purity of mamzerim
items.text_en: Debate on the future purity of mamzerim
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei says mamzerim and Netinim will be pure in the future, citing a verse; Rabbi Meir disagrees. Rav Yehuda rules in accordance with Rabbi Yosei, and Rav Yosef comments that without this ruling, Elijah would come and remove collars from them.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with a dispute: Rabbi Yosei says mamzerim and Netinim will be pure in the future, while Rabbi Meir says they will not be pure.

Rabbi Yosei cites the verse 'וְזָרַקְתִּי עֲלֵיכֶם מַיִם טְהוֹרִים וּטְהַרְתֶּם' (I will sprinkle pure water upon you and you will be purified) to argue that all impurity, including mamzerut, will be cleansed.
Rabbi Meir objects that the verse specifies 'מִכֹּל טֻמְאוֹתֵיכֶם וּמִכָּל גִּלּוּלֵיכֶם' (from all your impurities and from all your idols), excluding mamzerut.
Rabbi Yosei counters that the verse concludes 'אֲטַהֵר אֶתְכֶם' (I will purify you), implying purification even from mamzerut.
The Gemara asks: according to Rabbi Meir, the verse 'וְיָשַׁב מַמְזֵר בְּאַשְׁדּוֹד' (a mamzer will dwell in Ashdod) is understood, but how does Rabbi Yosei interpret it?
Rav Yosef explains that the verse is translated allegorically: Israel will dwell securely in their land, no longer resembling foreigners.
Rav Yehuda reports in the name of Shmuel that the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Yosei.
Rav Yosef remarks that without this ruling, Elijah would come and remove collars from them, implying that mamzerim would otherwise be permanently stigmatized.

items.text: Marriage of a convert to a mamzeret
items.text_en: Marriage of a convert to a mamzeret
items.desc_en: A baraita states that Rabbi Yosei permits a convert to marry a mamzeret, while Rabbi Yehuda forbids it. A convert, freed slave, and halal are permitted to marry a kohenet. The reason for Rabbi Yosei is that five 'congregations' are written.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that Rabbi Yosei permits a convert to marry a mamzeret, while Rabbi Yehuda forbids it, and adds that a convert, freed slave, and halal are permitted to marry a kohenet.
The gemara asks what is the reason for Rabbi Yosei's position.
The gemara answers that Rabbi Yosei's reason is that five 'congregations' are written in the verse, excluding converts from the prohibition.

items.text: דרשת 'קהל' לגבי גרים וממזרים
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's derivation of five קהלים and the alternative explanations
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yehuda derives five distinct קהל from the verse, including one for converts, while the Sages hold that converts are not called a קהל. Two alternative explanations are offered: one that the two prohibitions (mamzer with a שתוקי and a שתוקי with an Israelite) come from one קהל, and another that Rabbi Yehuda's reason is from the verse 'הקהל חקה אחת לכם ולגר הגר'.
items.desc: הגמרא דנה במקורות השונים לאיסור ממזר לבוא בקהל, ומבחינה בין קהל כוהנים, לויים וישראל. נחלקו רבי יהודה ורבי יוסי אם גר מותר בממזרת, כאשר רבי יהודה דורש 'קהל גרים' לאסור, ורבי יוסי סובר שאין גרים בכלל קהל. מובאות שתי תשובות אפשריות להבנת שיטת רבי יהודה.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yehuda's derivation
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yehuda's derivation
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yehuda derives five distinct קהל from the verse, including one for converts, while the Sages hold that converts are not called a קהל, and Rabbi Yehuda derives priests and Levites from one קהל, leaving one extra for converts.

The Gemara offers an alternative explanation: the two prohibitions (mamzer with a שתוקי and a שתוקי with an Israelite) come from one קהל, and the verse excludes only a definite mamzer from the definite קהל, but a doubtful mamzer is permitted.
The Gemara offers another alternative: Rabbi Yehuda's reason is from the verse 'הקהל חקה אחת לכם ולגר הגר', while Rabbi Yosei holds that the phrase 'חקה אחת' interrupts the context.

items.text: A convert, freed slave, and חלל are permitted to a priest's daughter
items.text_en: A convert, freed slave, and חלל are permitted to a priest's daughter
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a convert, a freed slave, and a חלל may marry a priest's daughter. This supports Rav's statement that fit women were not warned against marrying those disqualified from the priesthood.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that a convert, freed slave, and חלל (disqualified priest) may marry a priest's daughter, supporting Rav's statement that fit women were not warned against marrying those disqualified from the priesthood.

items.text: Rava's ruling on a convert marrying a priest or a mamzeret
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on a convert marrying a priest or a mamzeret
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira taught that a convert may marry a mamzeret, but was pelted with etrogim. Rava then taught that a convert may marry a priest's daughter, and later taught that a convert may marry a mamzeret, explaining that the convert may choose either. The halakha concludes that a convert is permitted to both.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira taught in Mehoza that a convert may marry a mamzeret, and the crowd pelted him with etrogim.
Rava questioned who would teach such a thing where converts are common, and then taught that a convert may marry a priest's daughter.
Rava later taught that a convert may marry a mamzeret, and when challenged, explained he gave them a choice: whichever they prefer.
The halakha concludes that a convert is permitted to marry both a priest's daughter and a mamzeret, the latter following Rabbi Yosei's view.

items.text: שתוקי ואסופי: דין תורה וגזירת חכמים
items.text_en: The status of a שתוקי: biblical law and rabbinic decree
items.desc_en: Rava states that by Torah law a שתוקי is fit, because the majority of people with whom the mother had relations are fit, and if the men came to her, each is considered separated from the majority. The Torah says only a definite mamzer is excluded, not a doubtful one. The rabbis decreed him unfit lest he marry his paternal sister, but the Gemara questions why this concern does not apply to a female שתוקי or a daughter of a שתוקי, and concludes it is a special stringency in lineage.
items.desc: רבא קובע ששתוקי כשר מדאורייתא, משום שרוב כשרים אצל האם, ואם האב בא אליה, כל הפורש מהרוב פורש. למרות זאת, חכמים פסלו שתוקי משום גזירה שמא ישא אחותו מאביו. הגמרא דוחה את הגזירה בטענה שאינה שכיחה, ומסבירה שהפסול הוא משום מעלה ביוחסין. כך גם לגבי אסופי, שכשר מדאורייתא אך נפסל בתקנת חכמים.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah defines a שתוקי as one who knows his mother but not his father.
sub.desc: רבא פותח בקביעה ששתוקי כשר מדאורייתא, ומנמק שרוב הכשרים אצל האם.

sub.desc_en: Rava states that by Torah law a שתוקי is fit, applying the principle of רוב (majority) and the rule that one who separates from a fixed group is considered as half-and-half.
sub.desc: רבא פותח בקביעה ששתוקי כשר מדאורייתא, ומנמק שרוב הכשרים אצל האם.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse 'לֹא יָבֹא מַמְזֵר' to prove that only a definite mamzer is excluded, not a doubtful one.
sub.desc: רבא מתרץ שהתורה פסלה רק ממזר ודאי, לא ספק, ולכן שתוקי כשר מדאורייתא.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the rabbis decreed a שתוקי unfit, and answers it is a decree lest he marry his paternal sister.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מדוע חכמים פסלו שתוקי, ומנמקת בגזירה שמא ישא אחותו מאביו.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the same concern should apply to a female שתוקי or the daughter of a שתוקי, and rejects the distinction as not being rare.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מדוע חכמים פסלו שתוקי, ומנמקת בגזירה שמא ישא אחותו מאביו.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the rabbis made a special stringency (מעלה) in matters of lineage, rather than a logical decree.
sub.desc: הגמרא מסבירה שפסול שתוקי הוא משום מעלה ביוחסין, לא משום גזירה.

items.text: The status of an אסופי: biblical law and rabbinic decree
items.text_en: The status of an אסופי: biblical law and rabbinic decree
items.desc_en: Rava states that by Torah law a foundling is fit, because the mother is presumed to be married to her husband, and the minority of betrothed women or husbands abroad is offset by unmarried women and those driven by hunger, making it a fifty-fifty case. The Torah excludes only a definite mamzer. The rabbis decreed him unfit lest he marry his paternal sister, but the Gemara questions why this does not apply to a female foundling or a daughter of a foundling, and concludes it is a special stringency in lineage.

sub.desc_en: Rava states that by Torah law a foundling (אסופי) is fit, because the mother is presumed to be married to her husband, and the minority of betrothed women or husbands abroad is offset by unmarried women and those driven by hunger, making it a fifty-fifty case.
The Gemara cites the verse 'לֹא יָבֹא מַמְזֵר בְּקָהָל ה (a mamzer shall not enter the assembly of the Lord)' to show that only a definite mamzer is excluded, but a doubtful one is permitted.
The Gemara asks why the rabbis decreed a foundling unfit, and answers that it is lest he marry his paternal sister.
The Gemara objects that if the concern is incest, then a male foundling should also be forbidden from marrying a female foundling, lest he marry his sister from either parent.
The Gemara rejects the objection, arguing that such a scenario is uncommon, just as the earlier objection about a female foundling was also uncommon.
The Gemara concludes that the rabbis decreed the foundling unfit as a special stringency in lineage (מעלה עשו ביוחסים).

items.text: Beginning of the discussion on a foundling found already circumcised
items.text_en: Beginning of the discussion on a foundling found already circumcised
items.desc_en: Rava bar Rav Huna begins a new topic: if one finds a child already circumcised, the Gemara will discuss its implications for lineage.

sub.desc_en: Rava bar Rav Huna opens a new topic: if one finds a child already circumcised, the Gemara will discuss its implications for lineage.

items.text: Signs that exclude a child from being an אסופי
items.text_en: Signs that exclude a child from being an אסופי
items.desc_en: The Gemara lists various signs that indicate a child was intentionally abandoned and thus is not an אסופי: being anointed, having kohl applied, having a weight placed on him, having a note or amulet hung on him. If hung on a palm tree, it depends if an animal could reach him. A latrine near the city or a synagogue frequented by many also affect the status.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma lists signs of intentional abandonment that exclude a child from being an אסופי (foundling): being anointed, having kohl applied, having a weight placed on him, having a note or amulet hung on him.
The Tanna Kamma adds a condition: if the child was hung on a palm tree, the status depends on whether an animal could reach him.
The Tanna Kamma further rules: a latrine near the city indicates abandonment, while a synagogue frequented by many indicates the child was not abandoned.

items.text: Amemar's distinctions regarding location
items.text_en: Amemar's distinctions regarding location
items.desc_en: Amemar rules that a child found in a fruit basket (פירא דסופלי) is an אסופי, but one found in a sharp place by a river (חריפתא דנהרא) is not. A child found in a place of peeling (פשרי) is an אסופי, while one found in the sides of the public domain (צידי רשות הרבים) is not, but one found in the public domain itself (רשות הרבים) is an אסופי.

sub.desc_en: Amemar opens by ruling that a child found in a fruit basket (פירא דסופלי) is an אסופי (foundling whose lineage is suspect).
Amemar rules that a child found in a sharp place by a river (חריפתא דנהרא) is not an אסופי.
Amemar rules that a child found in a place of peeling (פשרי) is an אסופי.
Amemar rules that a child found in the sides of the public domain (צידי רשות הרבים) is not an אסופי.
Amemar rules that a child found in the public domain itself (רשות הרבים) is an אסופי.

items.text: Rava's statement about famine years and its clarification
items.text_en: Rava's statement about famine years and its clarification
items.desc_en: Rava said that in famine years there is no concern of אסופי. The Gemara questions this: if it refers to the public domain, would they kill him in famine years? If it refers to the sides of the public domain, even without famine years it is not an אסופי. Rather, Rava's statement was said regarding a teaching of Rav Yehuda citing Rav: as long as the child is in the market, his parents are believed; if gathered from the market, they are not believed. Rava explains the reason: because a name of אסופי has gone out about him. And Rava adds: in famine years, even if gathered from the market, his parents are believed.

sub.desc_en: Rava states that in famine years, a found child is not subject to the halakhot of a foundling.
The Gemara asks to which specific case Rava's statement refers.
The Gemara objects: if Rava refers to the public domain, would a mother kill her child in famine years by leaving him there?
The Gemara objects: if Rava refers to the sides of the public domain, why mention famine years specifically? Even in non-famine years it is not a foundling.
The Gemara resolves that Rava's statement was said regarding Rav Yehuda's teaching: as long as the child is in the market, his parents are believed; once collected, they are not believed.
The Gemara asks for the reason why parents are not believed after the child is collected.
Rava explains: because a name of being a foundling has gone out about him.
Rava adds that in famine years, even after the child is collected from the market, his parents are believed.

items.text: Rav Chisda's principle: three are believed immediately
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's principle: three are believed immediately
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda states that three are believed immediately: an אסופי (the case already discussed), a midwife (חיה), and a woman who exempts her companions (פוטרת חברותיה). The midwife is believed to say which child was born first, as per a baraisa, with a dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages regarding a midwife who turned away. The woman who exempts her companions is from a Mishnah about three women sleeping in one bed; if one checks and is found impure, she is impure and the others are pure, provided she checked within the time of her fixed period.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda states that three people are believed immediately: an אסופי (foundling), a midwife, and a woman who exempts her companions.
The Gemara notes that the case of the אסופי (foundling) is the one already discussed earlier.
A baraita is cited: a midwife is believed to say which child was born first, with a dispute between the Sages and Rabbi Eliezer regarding a midwife who turned her face away.

The Gemara explains the case of the woman who exempts her companions: from a Mishnah about three women sleeping in one bed, with Rav Chisda's condition that she examined herself within the time of her fixed period.

items.text: Midwife's credibility for lineage and the challenge of an ערער
items.text_en: Midwife's credibility for lineage and the challenge of an ערער
items.desc_en: A baraisa teaches that a midwife is believed to say this child is a Kohen, Levi, Natin, or Mamzer, as long as no one challenged her (ערער). The Gemara questions what constitutes an ערער: if one person, but Rabbi Yochanan said an ערער requires at least two. An alternative answer distinguishes: Rabbi Yochanan's rule applies where there is a presumption of fitness, but where there is no such presumption, even one person is believed.

sub.desc_en: A baraisa teaches that a midwife is believed to state a child's lineage (Kohen, Levi, Natin, Mamzer) unless someone challenges her (ערער).
The Gemara asks what constitutes an ערער (challenge): if one person, but Rabbi Yochanan said an ערער requires at least two, so it must be two.
An alternative answer distinguishes: Rabbi Yochanan's rule applies where there is a presumption of fitness (חזקה דכשרות), but where there is no such presumption, even one person is believed.

items.text: Credibility of the seller when the item is in hand
items.text_en: Credibility of the seller when the item is in hand
items.desc_en: A seller is believed to say 'I sold to this one and not to that one' when the item is in his hand, but not if it is not in his hand.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that a seller is believed to say 'I sold to this one and not to that one' when the item is in his hand, but not if it is not in his hand.

items.text: אמינות דיין ומוכר
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the judge's credibility
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a judge can be believed to say he favored one litigant over another, and resolves that it applies only when the litigants are present; if not, he is not believed. It then asks why we cannot see who holds the document, and answers that the documents were torn, and suggests re-adjudicating, but that is only for a judge's error.
items.desc: הגמרא מבררת את גבולות האמינות של מוכר ושל דיין. במקרה שהמוכר קיבל כסף משני אנשים ואינו יודע מי נתן ברצון, הוא אינו נאמן. דיין נאמן רק כשבעלי הדין לפניו, ואם שטרי הזכות נקרעו ואין אפשרות לשפוט שוב (בשל שיקול דעת השופטים), אין סומכים על דבריו.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: let us see from whom the judge took the money, and explains that the case is where he took from both and it is unknown which was voluntary and which was coerced.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: מדוע צריך כלל את דין המוכר, הרי אפשר לראות ממי קיבל את הכסף?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that a judge is believed to say he favored one litigant, but only when the litigants are present; otherwise he is not believed.
sub.desc: הברייתא מביאה דין נוסף: דיין נאמן רק כשבעלי הדין לפניו.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: let us see who holds the document of judgment, and answers that the documents were torn.
sub.desc: הברייתא מביאה דין נוסף: דיין נאמן רק כשבעלי הדין לפניו.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: let them re-adjudicate, and answers that this is a case of a judge's error (שודא דדייני).
sub.desc: הגמרא מתרצת: מדובר במקרה שהמוכר קיבל כסף משניהם ואינו יודע מי נתן ברצון.

items.text: אמינות על בכור
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's statement on who is believed about the firstborn
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman lists three people believed about the firstborn: the midwife (immediately), the mother (for seven days), and the father (forever). This is derived from the verse 'he shall acknowledge' – he makes him known to others. Rabbi Yehuda adds that a man is believed to say 'this is my firstborn son' and similarly for a son of a divorced woman or a חלוצה, but the Sages disagree.
items.desc: רב נחמן מונה שלושה נאמנים על קביעת בכור: חיה (מיד), אם (שבעה ימים), ואב (לעולם). הברייתא דורשת 'יכיר' – האב מכירו לאחרים. רבי יהודה מרחיב אמינות זו גם לבן גרושה ובן חלוצה, וחכמים חולקים.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman lists three people believed about the firstborn: the midwife (immediately), the mother (for seven days), and the father (forever).
sub.desc: רב נחמן מונה שלושה נאמנים על קביעת בכור: חיה מיד, אם כל שבעה, ואב לעולם.

sub.desc_en: The baraita derives the father's belief from the verse 'יַכִּיר' (he shall acknowledge), meaning he makes him known to others.
sub.desc: רב נחמן מונה שלושה נאמנים על קביעת בכור: חיה מיד, אם כל שבעה, ואב לעולם.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda adds that a man is believed to say 'this is my firstborn son' and similarly for a son of a divorced woman or a חלוצה (a woman who performed חליצה).
sub.desc: רבי יהודה מרחיב אמינות האב גם לבן גרושה ובן חלוצה.

sub.desc_en: The Sages disagree and rule that the father is not believed for these declarations.
sub.desc: רבי יהודה מרחיב אמינות האב גם לבן גרושה ובן חלוצה.

items.text: אמינות האם לטהר את בנה – אבא שאול ורבן גמליאל
items.text_en: Abba Shaul's term 'Beduki' and its implications
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Abba Shaul called a שתוקי a 'בדוקי', meaning his mother is examined and believed when she says she was intimate with a fit man. This seems redundant with Rabban Gamliel's ruling, but the Gemara clarifies that Abba Shaul's ruling is more stringent: even where most men are unfit, she is believed. Rava rules the halakha follows Abba Shaul.
items.desc: הגמרא דנה בכינוי 'בדוקי' של אבא שאול לשתוקי. היא מבררת האם מדובר באמינות האם כשיטת רבן גמליאל, ומסיקה שאבא שאול מוסיף חידוש: האם נאמנת אפילו ברוב פסולים אצלה (כגון ארוסה). רבא פוסק כאבא שאול.

sub.desc_en: Abba Shaul calls a שתוקי (one whose father is unknown) a 'בדוקי' (examined one).
sub.desc: הגמרא פותחת בבירור כינויו של אבא שאול לשתוקי, ושואלת האם הכוונה לבדיקת האם כשיטת רבן גמליאל.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: What does 'בדוקי' mean?
sub.desc: הגמרא פותחת בבירור כינויו של אבא שאול לשתוקי, ושואלת האם הכוונה לבדיקת האם כשיטת רבן גמליאל.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that 'בדוקי' means his mother is examined and believed, which is already taught in a Mishnah according to Rabban Gamliel's ruling.
sub.desc: הגמרא פותחת בבירור כינויו של אבא שאול לשתוקי, ושואלת האם הכוונה לבדיקת האם כשיטת רבן גמליאל.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah where Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Eliezer rule that a pregnant woman is believed about the father's fitness, and Rav Yehuda reports Shmuel's ruling that the halakha follows Rabban Gamliel.
sub.desc: הגמרא פותחת בבירור כינויו של אבא שאול לשתוקי, ושואלת האם הכוונה לבדיקת האם כשיטת רבן גמליאל.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Abba Shaul's ruling is needed for two cases: one to permit her (the mother) and one to permit her daughter.
sub.desc: הגמרא מתרצת שאבא שאול בא להשמיע חידוש: האם נאמנת גם להכשיר את בתה, בניגוד לשיטת המכשיר בה הפוסל בבתה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that this explanation works only for the opinion that one who permits the mother disqualifies the daughter.
sub.desc: הגמרא מתרצת שאבא שאול בא להשמיע חידוש: האם נאמנת גם להכשיר את בתה, בניגוד לשיטת המכשיר בה הפוסל בבתה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: According to the opinion that permitting the mother also permits the daughter, what new teaching does Abba Shaul come to convey?
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: לשיטת המכשיר גם את הבת, מה חידש אבא שאול?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that Abba Shaul's ruling is more stringent than Rabban Gamliel's: even where most men are unfit, the mother is believed.
sub.desc: הגמרא מתרצת שאבא שאול עדיף מרבן גמליאל: הוא מכשיר אפילו ברוב פסולים אצלה, כגון ארוסה, ורבא פוסק כמותו.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that the halakha follows Abba Shaul.
sub.desc: הגמרא מתרצת שאבא שאול עדיף מרבן גמליאל: הוא מכשיר אפילו ברוב פסולים אצלה, כגון ארוסה, ורבא פוסק כמותו.

items.text: משנת תערובת הפסולים לקהל
items.text_en: Mishnah: Those forbidden to enter the congregation may marry each other
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that all those forbidden to enter the congregation (e.g., mamzerim, Netinim) may marry each other. Rabbi Yehuda forbids it. Rabbi Eliezer distinguishes: definite cases with definite cases are permitted, but definite with doubtful or doubtful with doubtful are forbidden; the doubtful categories are שתוקי, אסופי, and כותי.
items.desc: המשנה קובעת שכל הפסולים לקהל מותרים לבוא זה בזה, ורבי יהודה אוסר. רבי אליעזר מחלק: ודאים בודאים מותרים, אך ודאים בספיקות וספיקות בספיקות אסורים. הספיקות הם שתוקי, אסופי וכותי.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that all those forbidden to enter the congregation may marry each other.
sub.desc: המשנה פותחת בכלל שכל הפסולים לקהל מותרים לבוא זה בזה, ורבי יהודה אוסר.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda forbids such marriages.
sub.desc: המשנה פותחת בכלל שכל הפסולים לקהל מותרים לבוא זה בזה, ורבי יהודה אוסר.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer distinguishes: definite cases with definite cases are permitted.
sub.desc: רבי אליעזר מחלק בין ודאים לספיקות: ודאים בודאים מותרים, אך כל צירוף הכולל ספיקות אסור, ומפרט מהן הספיקות.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer rules that definite with doubtful, doubtful with definite, and doubtful with doubtful are all forbidden.
sub.desc: רבי אליעזר מחלק בין ודאים לספיקות: ודאים בודאים מותרים, אך כל צירוף הכולל ספיקות אסור, ומפרט מהן הספיקות.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer lists the doubtful categories: a שתוקי (whose father is unknown), an אסופי (foundling), and a כותי (Samaritan).
sub.desc: רבי אליעזר מחלק בין ודאים לספיקות: ודאים בודאים מותרים, אך כל צירוף הכולל ספיקות אסור, ומפרט מהן הספיקות.

items.text: בירור מחלוקות התנאים בתערובת הפסולים
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's categories
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions what 'all those forbidden' includes, since the first clause already permits mamzerim, Netinim, שתוקי, and אסופי to marry each other. It then asks what Rabbi Yehuda forbids, and suggests it cannot be definite with doubtful because Rabbi Eliezer's statement implies Rabbi Yehuda disagrees with that. It rejects the idea that Rabbi Yehuda forbids a convert with a mamzeret, since the Mishnah says 'all those forbidden to enter the congregation'. Rav Yehuda then begins to speak.
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה: המשנה כבר נשנתה? ומבררת על מי חל איסורו של רבי יהודה. היא דוחה אפשרויות ומסיקה שרבי יהודה אוסר גר בממזרת, אך המשנה לא עוסקת בגר. רב יהודה מתחיל להסביר.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'all those forbidden to enter the congregation' includes, noting that the first clause already permits mamzerim, Netinim, שתוקי, and אסופי to marry each other.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: מהי כוונת המשנה 'כל האסורין לבוא בקהל'? הרי כבר נשנה בראש הפרק שממזרים ונתינים שתוקים ואסופים מותרים לבוא זה בזה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Rabbi Yehuda forbids, and suggests it cannot be definite with doubtful because Rabbi Eliezer's statement implies Rabbi Yehuda disagrees with that.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה עוד: על מה חל איסורו של רבי יהודה? אם על ודאין בספיקין, הרי רבי אליעזר חולק ומתיר ודאין בודאין ואוסר ודאין בספיקין, מכלל שרבי יהודה לא סבירא ליה איסור זה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the idea that Rabbi Yehuda forbids a convert with a mamzeret, since the Mishnah says 'all those forbidden to enter the congregation'.
sub.desc: הגמרא דוחה אפשרות שרבי יהודה אוסר גר בממזרת, שהרי המשנה עוסקת ב'כל האסורין לבוא בקהל' ולא בגר.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda begins to speak, introducing a new statement.
sub.desc: רב יהודה מתחיל להסביר את מחלוקת התנאים במשנה.

items.text: Initial explanation of the Mishnah's principle
items.text_en: Initial explanation of the Mishnah's principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's statement refers to those forbidden to enter the congregation of priests, specifically a female convert under three years and one day, and not according to Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, who permits such a convert to marry a priest.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's principle refers to those forbidden to enter the congregation of priests, specifically a female convert under three years and one day, and not according to Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, who permits such a convert to marry a priest.

items.text: Refutation and counterexample
items.text_en: Refutation and counterexample
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the Mishnah refers to a female convert of three years and one day, even Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai would permit her to marry a priest, contradicting the Mishnah's exclusion. It then argues that if the Mishnah's leniency applies only to those forbidden to priests, then a female convert under three years, who is permitted to priests, would be forbidden to marry other forbidden individuals, but Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai permits her to marry them.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the Mishnah refers to a female convert of three years and one day, even Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai would permit her to marry a priest, contradicting the Mishnah's exclusion.

The Gemara argues that if the Mishnah's leniency applies only to those forbidden to priests, then a female convert under three years, who is permitted to priests, would be forbidden to marry other forbidden individuals, but Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai permits her to marry them.

items.text: Challenge to the general principle
items.text_en: Challenge to the general principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the general principle that those forbidden to enter the congregation of priests are permitted to marry each other, citing counterexamples: a widow, divorcee, ḥalala, and zonah are forbidden to priests yet forbidden to marry each other. It also notes a contradiction: a convert is permitted to marry a priestess and a mamzeret, yet the principle would imply otherwise.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the general principle that those forbidden to enter the congregation of priests are permitted to marry each other, citing counterexamples: a widow, divorcee, ḥalala, and zonah are forbidden to priests yet forbidden to marry each other, and a convert is permitted to marry a priestess and a mamzeret, contradicting the principle.

items.text: Second explanation by Rav Natan bar Hoshaya
items.text_en: Second explanation by Rav Natan bar Hoshaya
items.desc_en: Rav Natan bar Hoshaya reinterprets the Mishnah: it refers to anyone whose daughter a priest is forbidden to marry, specifically a male convert who married a female convert, and according to Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, they are permitted to marry each other. The Gemara objects that a ḥalāl who married an Israelite woman also has a daughter forbidden to a priest, yet such a couple is forbidden to marry each other, but this is resolved by limiting the rule to Rabbi Doste’s opinion.

sub.desc_en: Rav Natan bar Hoshaya reinterprets the Mishnah: it refers to anyone whose daughter a priest is forbidden to marry, specifically a male convert who married a female convert, and according to Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, they are permitted to marry each other.
The Gemara objects that a ḥalāl who married an Israelite woman also has a daughter forbidden to a priest, yet such a couple is forbidden to marry each other, contradicting the rule.
The Gemara resolves the objection by limiting the rule to Rabbi Doste ben Yehuda's opinion, which permits such unions.

items.text: Further challenges to the second explanation
items.text_en: Further challenges to the second explanation
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises additional objections: a ḥalāl who married a ḥalala has a daughter forbidden to a priest, yet they are forbidden to marry each other. It also notes a contradiction: a male convert who married an Israelite woman has a daughter permitted to a priest, yet they are permitted to marry each other, undermining the proposed rule.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that a ḥalāl who married a ḥalala has a daughter forbidden to a priest, yet they themselves are forbidden to marry each other, contradicting the proposed rule.

The Gemara raises a second objection: a male convert who married an Israelite woman has a daughter permitted to a priest, yet they themselves are permitted to marry each other, undermining the proposed rule.

items.text: Third explanation by Rav Nachman
items.text_en: Third explanation by Rav Nachman
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar Avuha explains that the dispute between the Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Yehuda concerns a mamzer from one's sister versus a mamzer from a married woman. The Tanna Kamma holds that even a mamzer from one's sister is a mamzer, while Rabbi Yehuda holds that only a mamzer from a married woman is a mamzer, not from one's sister.

sub.text: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar Avuha introduces the dispute between the Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Yehuda as concerning a mamzer from one's sister (ממזר מאחותו) versus a mamzer from a married woman (ממזר מאשת איש).
Rav Nachman explains that the Tanna Kamma holds even a mamzer from one's sister is a mamzer, while Rabbi Yehuda holds only a mamzer from a married woman is a mamzer, not from one's sister.

items.text: Supporting baraita on the definition of a mamzer
items.text_en: Supporting baraita on the definition of a mamzer
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Akiva defines a mamzer as anyone born from a union forbidden by 'lo yavo', Shimon HaTimni defines it as anyone liable for karet, and Rabbi Yehoshua defines it as anyone liable for court-imposed death. The halakha follows Shimon HaTimni.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the earlier dispute between the first Tanna and Rabbi Yehuda teaches us, and then cites a baraita to clarify.
The baraita cites Rabbi Akiva's definition of a mamzer as anyone born from a union forbidden by the verse 'לֹא יָבֹא' (a prohibited marriage into the congregation).
Shimon HaTimni defines a mamzer as anyone liable for כרת (karet, divinely imposed excision), and the baraita rules the halakha follows him.
Rabbi Yehoshua defines a mamzer as anyone liable for מיתת בית דין (court-imposed capital punishment).

items.text: Fourth explanation by Rava
items.text_en: Fourth explanation by Rava
items.desc_en: Rava explains that the dispute concerns an Ammonite or Moabite convert, and the Mishnah states that those forbidden to enter the congregation, such as an Ammonite or Moabite convert, are permitted to marry each other. The Gemara clarifies that even though Rabbi Yehuda forbids a convert to marry a mamzeret, this applies only to a convert who is eligible to enter the congregation, not to an Ammonite or Moabite convert who is not.

sub.desc_en: Rava explains that the dispute concerns an Ammonite or Moabite convert, and the Mishnah's rule that those forbidden to enter the congregation may marry each other applies to them.

The Gemara resolves the difficulty by clarifying that Rabbi Yehuda's prohibition of a convert marrying a mamzeret applies only to a convert eligible to enter the congregation, not to an Ammonite or Moabite convert.

items.text: Baraita on a nine-year-old boy and various unions
items.text_en: Baraita on a nine-year-old boy and various unions
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited: a nine-year-old and one day old Ammonite, Moabite, Egyptian, Edomite, Cuthean, Netin, ḥalāl, or mamzer who has relations with a priestess, Levite, or Israelite woman disqualifies her. Rabbi Yosei says that only one whose offspring is disqualified disqualifies, while Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel offers a differing opinion.

sub.desc_en: The baraita lists the categories of a nine-year-old boy (Ammonite, Moabite, Egyptian, Edomite, Cuthean, Netin, ḥalāl, or mamzer) who disqualify a priestess, Levite, or Israelite woman through relations.
Rabbi Yosei states the principle that only one whose offspring is disqualified (from the priesthood) disqualifies the woman he has relations with.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel offers a differing opinion (the baraita breaks off here, and his full statement is not recorded in this segment).

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states the principle: anyone whose daughter you may marry, you may marry his widow; anyone whose daughter you may not marry, you may not marry his widow.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the principle: anyone whose daughter you may marry, you may marry his widow; anyone whose daughter you may not marry, you may not marry his widow.

items.text: Gemara's question: Difference between Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Yosei
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Difference between Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Yosei
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains that the difference between Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Yosei is a second-generation Egyptian convert. Both derive their positions from the case of a High Priest with a widow, but Tanna Kamma focuses on the prohibition of intercourse, while Rabbi Yosei focuses on the disqualification of offspring, excluding a second-generation Egyptian whose offspring are not disqualified.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the first Tanna and Rabbi Yosei.
Rabbi Yochanan answers that the difference is a second-generation Egyptian convert, and both derive their positions from the case of a High Priest with a widow.
The first Tanna reasons by analogy to a High Priest with a widow: just as his union is forbidden and he disqualifies her, so anyone whose union is forbidden disqualifies his widow.

Rabbi Yosei reasons by analogy to a High Priest with a widow: just as his offspring are disqualified and he disqualifies, so anyone whose offspring are disqualified disqualifies, excluding a second-generation Egyptian whose offspring are not disqualified.

items.text: Difference between Rabbi Yosei and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
items.text_en: Difference between Rabbi Yosei and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
items.desc_en: Ulla explains that the difference between Rabbi Yosei and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel is a male Ammonite or Moabite convert. Rabbi Yosei disqualifies any lineage where the offspring is disqualified, while Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel requires that all offspring, including females, be disqualified, which excludes Ammonites and Moabites whose females are permitted.

sub.desc_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel repeats the Mishnah's principle.
The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between Rabbi Yosei and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.
Ulla answers that the difference is an Ammonite or Moabite convert, and both derive their positions from the case of a High Priest with a widow.
Rabbi Yosei reasons that just as a High Priest's offspring are disqualified and he disqualifies, so anyone whose offspring are disqualified disqualifies.

sub.text: Explanation of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's reasoning
sub.text_en: Explanation of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's reasoning
sub.desc_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel reasons that just as all of a High Priest's offspring are disqualified, so anyone whose all offspring are disqualified disqualifies, excluding Ammonite and Moabite converts whose female offspring are permitted.

items.text: Rav Chisda's statement on the widow of an עיסה
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's statement on the widow of an עיסה
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda states that all agree the widow of an עיסה (a doubtful lineage) is disqualified from the priesthood, even according to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's lenient principle. This excludes the testimony of Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira who deemed her fit due to a double doubt.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda states that all agree the widow of an עיסה (a doubtful lineage) is disqualified from the priesthood.
The gemara explains that even Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who is lenient in other cases, excludes the widow of an עיסה from his lenient principle, disqualifying her.
The gemara objects that Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira testified that the widow of an עיסה is fit for the priesthood, contradicting Rav Chisda's claim of universal disqualification.

The gemara resolves that the testimony of Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira is based on a double doubt (ספק ספיקא), which is treated leniently, but Rav Chisda's statement reflects the majority view that rejects such leniency in this case.

items.text: Rav's ruling and Shmuel's objection
items.text_en: Rav's ruling and Shmuel's objection
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quotes Rav that the halakha follows Rabbi Eliezer, but Shmuel objects, citing Hillel's teaching that all ten lineages from Babylon may intermarry.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports in Rav's name that the halacha follows Rabbi Eliezer.
Shmuel objects that Hillel taught that all ten genealogical classes from Babylonia may intermarry, contradicting Rav's ruling.

items.text: Contradiction between Rav and Shmuel on the status of a child from a betrothed woman
items.text_en: Contradiction between Rav and Shmuel on the status of a child from a betrothed woman
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction between Rav and Shmuel's positions on a child born to a betrothed woman who became pregnant. It explores multiple versions of their dispute, including whether the child is a mamzer or a shetuki, and whether he is permitted to marry a mamzeret. The Gemara resolves the need for multiple statements and offers alternative interpretations of shetuki.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction between Rav's and Shmuel's statements regarding the status of a child born to a betrothed woman who became pregnant.

The Gemara presents a first version of the dispute: Rav says the child is a mamzer permitted to marry a mamzeret, Shmuel says the child is a shetuki and forbidden to marry a mamzeret, and then the positions are reversed.
The Gemara asks why both versions of the dispute are necessary.
The Gemara explains that both versions are needed: one to teach Rav's leniency when most people are fit, and the other to teach Rav's stringency when most people are unfit.
The Gemara offers an alternative interpretation: Rav's 'mamzer' means forbidden to marry a daughter of Israel, and Shmuel's 'shetuki' means one who is silenced from the law of priesthood.

The Gemara objects that if the child is silenced from Israelite status, certainly he is silenced from priesthood, and then offers a different explanation: 'shetuki' means silenced from inheriting his father's property, unless he seized it.
The Gemara offers another explanation: 'shetuki' means 'checked' (beduki), where the mother is examined and believed if she says she was intimate with a fit man, following Rabban Gamliel's ruling.
The Gemara resolves that Shmuel's statement about Rabban Gamliel was necessary, because without it one might think the mother is not believed when most people around her are unfit.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's ruling on Kutites and the comparison to a convert
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's ruling on Kutites and the comparison to a convert
items.desc_en: A baraita states that Rabbi Elazar says a Kutite may not marry a Kutit. Rav Yosef explains that they are treated like a convert after ten generations, but Abaye objects that the cases are different. Rav Dimi reports that Rabbi Elazar holds like Rabbi Yishmael.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states that Rabbi Elazar rules a Kutite man may not marry a Kutite woman.
The gemara asks for the reason behind Rabbi Elazar's ruling.
Rav Yosef explains that the Kutites are treated like a convert after ten generations, citing a baraita about a convert's status with a mamzeret.
A baraita is cited: a convert is permitted to marry a mamzeret for ten generations, and thereafter forbidden; some say until idolatry is forgotten from him.
Abaye objects that the cases are not comparable: there the convert is old and the mamzeret is new, but here both Kutites are of equal status.
Rav Dimi reports that Rabbi Elazar actually holds like Rabbi Yishmael, providing an alternative basis for the ruling.

items.text: Initial statement of Rabbi Elazar's and Rabbi Yishmael's positions
items.text_en: Initial statement of Rabbi Elazar's and Rabbi Yishmael's positions
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that Rabbi Elazar holds like Rabbi Yishmael that Samaritans are lion-converts, and Rabbi Yishmael holds like Rabbi Akiva that a non-Jew or slave who has relations with a Jewish woman produces a mamzer.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that Rabbi Elazar holds like Rabbi Yishmael that Samaritans are lion-converts, and Rabbi Yishmael holds like Rabbi Akiva that a non-Jew or slave who has relations with a Jewish woman produces a mamzer.

items.text: Challenge to Rabbi Yishmael's position from a baraita
items.text_en: Challenge to Rabbi Yishmael's position from a baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the claim that Rabbi Yishmael holds like Rabbi Akiva, citing a baraita where Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Yishmael derives that a non-Jew or slave disqualifies a woman from kehuna, implying they are not considered to produce mamzerim. The Gemara argues that if Rabbi Yishmael held like Rabbi Akiva that the child is a mamzer, then certainly the act would disqualify the woman, so why need a separate derivation?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges whether Rabbi Yishmael actually holds like Rabbi Akiva, citing a baraita where Rabbi Yochanan in Rabbi Yishmael's name derives that a non-Jew or slave disqualifies a woman from kehuna via a verse, implying they are not considered to produce mamzerim.

sub.text: Supporting baraita (Rabbi Yochanan citing Rabbi Yishmael)
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita (Rabbi Yochanan citing Rabbi Yishmael)
sub.desc_en: The baraita explains the derivation: the verse applies only to one who can experience widowhood or divorce, excluding a non-Jew or slave who cannot.
The Gemara objects: if Rabbi Yishmael held like Rabbi Akiva that the child is a mamzer, then certainly the act would disqualify the woman, so why need a separate derivation?
