items.text: Revised attribution: Rabbi Elazar holds like both Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva
items.text_en: Revised attribution: Rabbi Elazar holds like both Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: The Gemara revises the initial statement: Rabbi Elazar holds like Rabbi Yishmael regarding Samaritans being lion-converts, and also holds like Rabbi Akiva that a non-Jew or slave produces a mamzer.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by revising the attribution: Rabbi Elazar holds like Rabbi Yishmael that Samaritans are lion-converts, and like Rabbi Akiva that a non-Jew or slave produces a mamzer.

items.text: Challenge to Rabbi Elazar's position from his own statement
items.text_en: Challenge to Rabbi Elazar's position from his own statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the revised attribution, citing Rabbi Elazar's own statement that Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel agree that a mamzer is only from a union forbidden as an ervah and punishable by karet, implying that a non-Jew or slave does not produce a mamzer.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the revised attribution by citing Rabbi Elazar's own statement that Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel agree that a mamzer is only from a union forbidden as an ervah and punishable by karet, implying that a non-Jew or slave does not produce a mamzer.

items.text: Resolution: Three disputes in the matter
items.text_en: Resolution: Three disputes in the matter
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradictions by citing a tradition from Ravin quoting Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba quoting Rabbi Yochanan (or alternative chains) that there are three disputes in this matter. Rabbi Yishmael holds Samaritans are lion-converts and the priests who intermingled were invalid, citing a verse interpreted as 'from the thorns of the people'. Rabbi Akiva holds Samaritans are true converts and the priests were valid, interpreting the same verse as 'from the choicest of the people', and explains that the Sages forbade them because they would perform levirate marriage with betrothed women.

sub.text: Tradition from Ravin quoting Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba quoting Rabbi Yochanan (or alternative chains)
sub.text_en: Tradition from Ravin quoting Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba quoting Rabbi Yochanan (or alternative chains)
sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a tradition from multiple chains that there are three disputes in this matter.
Rabbi Yishmael holds that Samaritans are lion-converts and the priests who intermingled were invalid, citing the verse interpreted as 'from the thorns of the people'.

Rabbi Akiva holds that Samaritans are true converts and the priests were valid, interpreting the same verse as 'from the choicest of the people', and explains that the Sages forbade them because they would perform levirate marriage with betrothed women.

items.text: Samaritans and their reliability in lineage
items.text_en: Samaritans and their reliability in lineage
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why Samaritans are considered suspect regarding lineage: they are not meticulous in the details of commandments, specifically the laws of betrothal and divorce. This is supported by a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer forbids Samaritan matzah for Passover due to their lack of precision.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what scriptural derivation the Samaritans use to justify releasing married women without a proper גט (bill of divorce), and explains their interpretation of the verse regarding a woman who sits outside.
The Gemara notes that Rabbi Akiva's position aligns with his own view that a mamzer can come from those liable for negative commandments.

sub.text: Yesh Omrim / Rav Idi bar Avin citing Rabbi Eliezer
sub.text_en: Yesh Omrim / Rav Idi bar Avin citing Rabbi Eliezer
sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents an alternative explanation that Samaritans are not meticulous in commandments, citing a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer forbids their matzah for Passover, while Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel notes they are meticulous in commandments they uphold.
The Gemara resolves the apparent contradiction by specifying that Samaritans are not meticulous specifically in the laws of קידושין (betrothal) and גירושין (divorce).

items.text: Mixed lineages among Samaritans
items.text_en: Mixed lineages among Samaritans
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman and Rava debate what types of individuals became mixed into the Samaritan population: Rav Nachman says it was a mamzer from one's sister and a mamzer from a brother's wife (both liable for karet), while Rava says it was a slave and a maidservant. Both agree the case was a real incident.

sub.text: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman says in the name of Rabbah bar Avuha that a mamzer from one's sister and a mamzer from a brother's wife were assimilated among the Samaritans.
The Gemara asks what Rav Nachman is teaching us — that there is a mamzer from those liable for karet?
The Gemara objects: if so, let him teach one example (of a mamzer from a sister) rather than two.
The Gemara resolves that the incident that took place was exactly that way, so both types were mentioned.
Rava says that a Canaanite slave and a Canaanite maidservant were assimilated among the Samaritans.
The Gemara asks: what is the prohibition due to — is it due to the maidservant (whose children are slaves)?
The Gemara objects: if so, let him teach one example (only the maidservant) rather than both slave and maidservant.
The Gemara resolves that the incident that took place was exactly that way, so both were mentioned.

items.text: Mishnah: Checking lineage for a kohen's wife
items.text_en: Mishnah: Checking lineage for a kohen's wife
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a man marrying a kohenet must check four mothers (eight total) on her side. For a Levite or Israelite woman, one more is added. It also lists those exempt from checking: those whose ancestors served at the altar, on the platform, or in the Sanhedrin, and those whose fathers were public officers.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that a man marrying a kohenet must check four mothers (eight total) on her side, and for a Levite or Israelite woman one more is added.
The Mishnah lists those exempt from checking: those whose ancestors served at the altar, on the platform, or in the Sanhedrin, and those whose fathers were public officers or charity collectors.
Rabbi Yosei adds that even the descendants of one who signed as a witness in the old court of Tzippori are exempt from investigation.
Rabbi Chanina ben Antigonos adds that even the descendants of one who was written in the army list of the king are exempt from investigation.

items.text: Gemara: Why check women but not men?
items.text_en: Gemara: Why check women but not men?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why we check women's lineage but not men's, answering that women's disputes are about forbidden relations (which would be known), while men's disputes are about lineage (which would be publicized). It then cites Rav that kosher women are not warned against marrying unfit men, and notes variant traditions about the number of mothers to check.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why we check women's lineage but not men's, and answers that women's disputes involve forbidden relations (עריות) which lack publicity, while men's disputes involve lineage (יוחסין) which becomes public.
The Gemara objects that the woman should also check the man, and supports Rav's statement that kosher women (כשרות) were not warned against marrying unfit men.
The Gemara notes variant traditions about the number of mothers to check: Rav Adda bar Ahava teaches twelve, and a baraita teaches sixteen.

items.text: Clarification of the Mishnah's 'another'
items.text_en: Clarification of the Mishnah's 'another'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's phrase 'another' refers to a pair, not an additional category, and suggests that the Mishnah might conflict with a prior statement, but resolves that it does not.

items.text: Two versions of Rav's statement on family presumption
items.text_en: Two versions of Rav's statement on family presumption
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quotes Rav: the Mishnah is Rabbi Meir's view, but the Sages say all families are presumed fit. A contradiction is raised from Rav Chama bar Gurya, and two versions of the resolution are presented.

items.text: No need to check those above the altar, platform, or Sanhedrin
items.text_en: No need to check those above the altar, platform, or Sanhedrin
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that those appointed to serve on the altar, the platform (duchan), or the Sanhedrin are presumed fit because they were already vetted, and cites verses supporting the Sanhedrin's purity.

items.text: Proof that Sanhedrin members must be without blemish
items.text_en: Proof that Sanhedrin members must be without blemish
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the verse refers to a physical blemish, and Rav Acha bar Yaakov and Rav Nachman cite verses showing that leaders must be like Moses, i.e., without defect.

items.text: Appointing from those whose fathers were public officers
items.text_en: Appointing from those whose fathers were public officers
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may appoint only from families whose fathers were public officers. The Gemara raises a contradiction with the rule that even a mamzer may judge monetary cases in Jerusalem, and resolves it.

items.text: Charity collectors may marry into priestly families
items.text_en: Charity collectors may marry into priestly families
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that charity collectors are presumed fit because their public dealings would expose any flaw, as they often quarrel with people and seize pledges.

items.text: Case of Rav Adda bar Ahava and Rav Beebi: appointing a convert
items.text_en: Case of Rav Adda bar Ahava and Rav Beebi: appointing a convert
items.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava, a convert, and Rav Beebi dispute who should lead the city. Rav Yosef rules that only one from 'among your brothers' may be appointed, but Rav Adda's mother is Jewish, so he qualifies. Rav Beebi, a Torah scholar, is advised to focus on Torah, while Rav Adda handles city affairs.

items.text: Practice in the West and Nehardea regarding converts
items.text_en: Practice in the West and Nehardea regarding converts
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Zeira and Rabbah bar Avuha would attend to converts, but in the West and Nehardea, they would not appoint even a minor official from among converts.

items.text: Rabbi Yose's statement and the soldiers of David's house
items.text_en: Rabbi Yose's statement and the soldiers of David's house
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yose says one may marry into a family that served in the army. Rav Yehuda quoting Samuel specifies this refers to David's soldiers. Rav Yosef cites a verse, and Rav explains the reason: their merit and their ancestors' merit assist them.

items.text: Challenges from converts in David's army: Zelek, Uriah, Ittai
items.text_en: Challenges from converts in David's army: Zelek, Uriah, Ittai
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how converts like Zelek the Ammonite, Uriah the Hittite, and Ittai the Gittite could be in David's army. It answers that they only lived there, but Ittai is a problem because Rav Nachman says he came and nullified the prohibition. The Gemara then cites Rav's statement about David's 400 children from captive women.

items.text: משנת הפתיחה: דיני חללה ופסולי כהונה
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the daughter of a male חלל is permanently disqualified from the priesthood. It then discusses cases of an Israelite marrying a חללה and a חלל marrying an Israelite woman, with opinions from Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, and Rabbi Yosi.
items.desc: המשנה פותחת בדין בת חלל זכר שפסולה לכהונה לעולם, ומבדילה בין מקרים שונים: ישראל שנשא חללה – בתו כשרה, חלל שנשא בת ישראל – בתו פסולה. מובאות דעות רבי יהודה ורבי אליעזר בן יעקב ורבי יוסי בנוגע לגרים ועבדים משוחררים.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that the daughter of a male חלל is permanently disqualified from the priesthood, and then rules on cases of an Israelite marrying a חללה and a חלל marrying an Israelite woman.
sub.desc: המשנה פותחת בדין בת חלל זכר שפסולה לכהונה לעולם, ומבדילה בין ישראל שנשא חללה שבתו כשרה לבין חלל שנשא בת ישראל שבתו פסולה.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda states that the daughter of a male convert is equivalent to the daughter of a male חלל and thus disqualified.
sub.desc: המשנה פותחת בדין בת חלל זכר שפסולה לכהונה לעולם, ומבדילה בין ישראל שנשא חללה שבתו כשרה לבין חלל שנשא בת ישראל שבתו פסולה.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov rules that the daughter of an Israelite who married a female convert is fit for the priesthood, and the daughter of a male convert who married an Israelite woman is also fit, but the daughter of a male convert who married a female convert is disqualified, and this applies to converts and freed slaves for ten generations until the mother is from Israel.
Rabbi Yosi adds that even a male convert who married a female convert has a daughter fit for the priesthood.

items.text: Gemara's question on 'forever'
items.text_en: Gemara's question on 'forever'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'forever' means in the Mishnah, suggesting it might be limited to three generations like the laws of Egyptians and Edomites, but the Mishnah teaches it is permanent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'forever' means in the Mishnah, suggesting it might be limited to three generations like the laws of Egyptians and Edomites.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah teaches the disqualification is permanent, not limited to three generations.

items.text: Source for Israelite marrying a חללה
items.text_en: Source for Israelite marrying a חללה
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon derives from a גזירה שווה that the disqualification applies only to males (priests) and not females. The Gemara then questions whether this would permit the daughter of a High Priest or granddaughter, and resolves the issues through textual analysis.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural source of the Mishnah's ruling that an Israelite who marries a חללה (woman disqualified from the priesthood) has a daughter who is fit for the priesthood.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan cites a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) between the verse 'וְלֹא יְחַלֵּל זַרְעוֹ' (he shall not profane his seed) and the verse 'לֹא יִטַּמָּא בַּעַל בְּעַמָּיו' (a husband shall not defile himself among his people), teaching that just as the latter applies only to males (priests), so too the former applies only to males, thus disqualifying only the priest's offspring, not the Israelite's.

The Gemara objects that if the disqualification applies only to males, then the daughter of a High Priest who married a חללה should be permitted to marry a priest, which contradicts the Mishnah's implication.
The Gemara answers that the verse says 'זַרְעוֹ' (his seed), not 'בְּנוֹ' (his son), so the disqualification extends to the priest's daughter as well, since 'seed' includes both sons and daughters.
The Gemara further objects that the granddaughter of a High Priest (daughter of his son) should be permitted, since she is not directly his 'seed' but his son's seed.
The Gemara answers that the verse 'לֹא יְחַלֵּל זַרְעוֹ' compares his seed to himself: just as his own daughter is disqualified, so too his son's daughter is disqualified.
The Gemara objects that the daughter of his daughter (great-granddaughter) should be forbidden, which would extend the disqualification too far.

The Gemara resolves that the גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) serves to limit the disqualification: it applies only to the priest's own seed (children and grandchildren through sons), not to further descendants, thus preventing the extension to the daughter of his daughter.

items.text: Redundancy in Mishnah
items.text_en: Redundancy in Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the case of a חלל marrying an Israelite woman seems redundant given the first clause, and explains it is mentioned because the Mishnah also taught the case of an Israelite marrying a חללה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah repeats the case of a חלל (disqualified priest) marrying an Israelite woman, since the first clause already stated that the daughter of a male חלל is permanently disqualified from the priesthood.

The Gemara explains that the redundancy is not a problem: because the Mishnah taught the case of an Israelite marrying a חללה (disqualified priest's daughter) in the first clause, it also taught the parallel case of a חלל marrying an Israelite woman in the second clause, for symmetry.

items.text: Rabbi Dostai ben Yehuda's opinion
items.text_en: Rabbi Dostai ben Yehuda's opinion
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah disagrees with Rabbi Dostai ben Yehuda, who holds that an Israelite woman purifies a חלל's offspring, based on the verse 'לֹא יְחַלֵּל זַרְעוֹ בְּעַמָּיו' meaning only with one nation (priesthood) does he profane, not with two (Israel and priesthood).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the Mishnah disagrees with Rabbi Dostai ben Yehuda, as cited in a baraita.

The baraita cites Rabbi Dostai ben Yehuda's opinion that an Israelite woman purifies a חלל's offspring, based on the verse 'לֹא יְחַלֵּל זַרְעוֹ בְּעַמָּיו' meaning only with one nation does he profane, not with two.

items.text: לימוד שהיא עצמה מתחללת מקל וחומר
items.text_en: Derivation that a חללה herself is disqualified
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from a קל וחומר that a woman who commits adultery becomes a חללה, and addresses a potential objection by citing the verse 'לֹא יְחַלֵּל' meaning one who was fit and became profaned.
items.desc: ברייתא דורשת מהפסוק 'לא יחלל זרעו' שגם האשה עצמה מתחללת, באמצעות קל וחומר מזרעו, ודוחה פירכא אפשרית. הגמרא מסבירה את הצורך ב'אם נפשך לומר' ומביאה את הלימוד מ'לא יחלל' – לא יחולל.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by citing the verse 'לֹא יְחַלֵּל זַרְעוֹ' (he shall not profane his offspring) and asks: from where do we derive that the woman herself (the חללה) is also disqualified? It then proposes a קל וחומר (a fortiori inference): if the offspring, who did not sin, is profaned, then she who sinned should certainly be profaned.
sub.desc: הברייתא פותחת בלימוד שהאשה עצמה מתחללת מקל וחומר מזרעו.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: the priest himself (the כהן) proves otherwise — he committed a transgression but is not profaned (he can return to service after divorcing her). The objection is rejected by noting that a male priest is never profaned in any case, whereas a woman is disqualified in all cases (e.g., by becoming a זונה).
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה שהכהן עצמו יוכיח שעבר עבירה ואינו מתחלל, ודוחה את הקל וחומר.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative resolution: the verse 'לֹא יְחַלֵּל' (he shall not profane) is interpreted as 'לֹא יְחוּלַּל' (shall not become profaned), referring to the woman who was initially fit and then became profaned — i.e., the חללה herself, not the offspring.
sub.desc: הגמרא מביאה את הלימוד מ'לא יחלל' – לא יחולל, שהאשה הכשרה מתחללת.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what is the meaning of 'if it is your wish to say' — i.e., what flaw in the original קל וחומר necessitated this alternative? It explains that one could refute the a fortiori argument by noting that the offspring is notable because his very formation was through a transgression.

The Gemara concludes: even if the a fortiori argument is refuted, the verse itself teaches that the woman who was fit and became profaned is the חללה, by reading 'לֹא יְחַלֵּל' as 'לֹא יְחוֹלֵל' (shall not cause to become profaned).

items.text: הגדרת חללה: נולדה מפסול כהונה
items.text_en: Definition of a חללה
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies the definition of a חללה: initially thought to be one born from disqualifying unions, but refined by Rav Yehuda and Rabba to mean one born from a union disqualified for the priesthood, and further specified by Rav Yitzchak bar Avin as a חללה whose primary status is from Torah law.
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה ברייתא המגדירה חללה כמי שנולדה מן הפסולים, ומקשה על כך מהמחזיר גרושתו. רב יהודה ורבה ורב יצחק בר אבין מבהירים שהכוונה למי שנולדה מפסול כהונה, ושיש חללה שאינה נולדה אלא נעשתה על ידי ביאה.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by defining a חללה (ḥalala) as any woman born from people of flawed lineage.
sub.desc: הברייתא פותחת בהגדרת חללה: כל שנולדה מן הפסולים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the baraita means by 'people of flawed lineage'.
sub.desc: הברייתא פותחת בהגדרת חללה: כל שנולדה מן הפסולים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if 'flawed lineage' means someone unfit for this particular man, then the case of a man who remarries his divorcée disproves it, since her children are fit.
sub.desc: הברייתא פותחת בהגדרת חללה: כל שנולדה מן הפסולים.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda refines the definition: a חללה is one born from a union disqualified for the priesthood.
sub.desc: רב יהודה מבהיר שהכוונה למי שנולדה מפסול כהונה, ומקשה על כך: הרי אלמנה, גרושה וזונה שלא נולדו מפסול כהונה נעשות חללות.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that this definition excludes women like a widow, divorcée, or זונה (zona) who become חללות without being born from such a union.
sub.desc: רב יהודה מבהיר שהכוונה למי שנולדה מפסול כהונה, ומקשה על כך: הרי אלמנה, גרושה וזונה שלא נולדו מפסול כהונה נעשות חללות.

sub.desc_en: Rabba further specifies that the baraita refers to a חללה who never had a moment of fitness, i.e., one born from a union disqualified for the priesthood.
sub.desc: רבא מתקן את ההגדרה: הכוונה לחללה שלא היה לה שעת הכושר כלל, כלומר שנולדה מפסול כהונה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the term 'mentioned' means in Rabba's statement.
sub.desc: רבא מתקן את ההגדרה: הכוונה לחללה שלא היה לה שעת הכושר כלל, כלומר שנולדה מפסול כהונה.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Avin explains that the baraita refers to a חללה whose primary status is from Torah law, i.e., one born from unions disqualified for the priesthood.
sub.desc: רבא מתקן את ההגדרה: הכוונה לחללה שלא היה לה שעת הכושר כלל, כלומר שנולדה מפסול כהונה.

items.text: חיוב מלקות על כהן גדול הבא על אלמנה
items.text_en: Liability for multiple forbidden relations
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses a baraita about liability for marrying multiple women of the same category (e.g., three widows) versus different categories, and questions why one is not liable for each individual case.
items.desc: ברייתא דנה בחיוב מלקות על כהן גדול הבא על אלמנה כמה פעמים, ומבדילה בין מקרה שבו היא נשארת באותו מעמד לבין מקרה שבו היא משנה מעמדה. הגמרא מתחילה לברר את המקרה של 'אלמנה אלמנה אלמנה' ושואלת אם מדובר בשלוש אלמנות שונות.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that if one marries three widows (or three divorcées) in sequence, he is only liable once.
sub.desc: הברייתא פותחת בדין כהן גדול הבא על אלמנה כמה פעמים, שחייב רק מלקות אחת, וכן על גרושה כמה פעמים.

sub.desc_en: The baraita contrasts: if one marries women from different forbidden categories in the correct order, he is liable for each; but if the women were disqualified in a different sequence, he is only liable once.
The Gemara questions why, in the case of three widows from different men, the man is not liable separately for each forbidden relation.

items.text: הבחנה בין גופים נפרדים לשמות נפרדים
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's case of one widow
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling that a man who has relations with one widow three times is liable only once. It distinguishes between separate bodies and separate names, and resolves that the case involves a woman who was the widow of Reuven, Shimon, and Levi, where the names are distinct but the body is the same.
items.desc: הגמרא דנה במקרה של הבא על אלמנה אחת שלוש פעמים, ומבחינה בין אם מדובר בגופים נפרדים (שלוש נשים) או בשמות נפרדים (אלמנת ראובן, שמעון ולוי). היא קובעת שצריך גופים נפרדים כדי לחייב על כל אחת, ולא שמות נפרדים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's case, noting that separate bodies and separate names would normally create multiple liabilities.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: אם מדובר בשלוש אלמנות שונות, הרי הגופים מוחלקים והשמות מוחלקים, ולכן ברור שחייב על כל אחת.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the case involves one widow with three relations, and if no warning was given, it is obvious that only one liability applies.
sub.desc: הגמרא מבהירה שהמדובר באלמנה אחת ושלוש ביאות, ואם לא התרו בו בין ביאה לביאה, פשוט שאינו חייב אלא אחת.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if warnings were given for each act, why is he liable only once? It cites the case of a nazir who drinks wine all day and is liable for each warning.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: אם התרו בו על כל ביאה וביאה, מדוע אינו חייב אלא אחת? והרי משנה בנזיר מחייבת על כל התראה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the case involves a woman who was the widow of Reuven, Shimon, and Levi, where the names are distinct but the body is the same, so only one liability applies.
sub.desc: הגמרא מתרצת: מדובר באלמנת ראובן שהיתה אלמנת שמעון ולוי, וקמ"ל שצריך גופים מוחלקים, וכאן אין.

items.text: איסור מוסיף ואיסור חל על איסור
items.text_en: Rava's explanation of the Mishnah's list using איסור מוסיף
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the Tanna can list 'widow, divorcee, ḥalala, zona' if he holds that a prohibition cannot take effect where another exists. Rava answers that the Tanna rejects איסור חל על איסור but accepts איסור מוסיף, explaining how each added status adds a new prohibition.
items.desc: הגמרא דנה בברייתא האומרת שכהן גדול הבא על אלמנה, גרושה, חללה וזונה חייב על כל אחת. רבא מסביר שהתנא אינו סובר 'איסור חל על איסור' אלא 'איסור מוסיף', כלומר כשנוספת איסור על אישה, היא מתווספת גם לגבי כהן גדול. לגבי זונה, רב חנא בר רב קטינא מסביר שהשם 'זונה' פוסל בישראל, ולכן נחשב איסור מוסיף.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Tanna's underlying principle regarding whether a prohibition can take effect where another exists, given the Mishnah's list of forbidden women.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: מהי שיטת התנא? אם איסור חל על איסור, היה צריך לחייב גם בסדר הפוך; ואם אין איסור חל על איסור, לא היה חייב אפילו בסדר זה.

sub.desc_en: Rava answers that the Tanna rejects the principle of איסור חל על איסור (a prohibition taking effect where another exists) but accepts איסור מוסיף (an added prohibition).
sub.desc: רבא מתרץ: התנא אינו סובר איסור חל על איסור, אך סובר איסור מוסיף, ולכן רק בסדר זה יש חיוב על כל אחת.

sub.desc_en: Rava explains how each status in the Mishnah's list adds a new prohibition through איסור מוסיף, starting from widow to divorcee to ḥalala.
sub.desc: רבא מפרט כיצד כל שלב מוסיף איסור: גרושה מוסיפה איסור לכהן הדיוט, חללה מוסיפה איסור אכילת תרומה, ובכך מתווסף איסור גם לכהן גדול.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what added prohibition exists in the case of a זונה (harlot) to justify its inclusion in the list.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת: מהו האיסור המוסיף בזונה, שהרי אין בה חידוש לעומת חללה?

sub.text_en: Rav Chana bar Rav Katina's answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Chana bar Rav Katina answers that the added prohibition is that the status of זונה disqualifies the woman from marrying an Israelite as well.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת: מהו האיסור המוסיף בזונה, שהרי אין בה חידוש לעומת חללה?

items.text: הברייתא על 'יקח' ו'לא יקח' ודעת רבי שמעון
items.text_en: Debate on the baraita about a High Priest with his sister-widow
items.desc_en: A baraita states that only those included in 'he shall take' are included in 'he shall not take', excluding a High Priest who has relations with his sister who is a widow. Rav Sheshet identifies the baraita as Rabbi Shimon's view that no prohibition takes effect on another, but an alternative explanation attributes it to the Rabbis, who hold that a light prohibition cannot take effect on a severe one.
items.desc: תני תנא קמיה דרב ששת ברייתא האומרת שכל שהיא ב'יקח' היא ב'לא יקח', פרט לכהן גדול הבא על אחותו אלמנה. רב ששת מקשה שהברייתא היא כרבי שמעון שאין איסור חל על איסור, אך ניתן להעמידה גם כרבנן אם האיסור הקל אינו חל על איסור חמור. יש גרסה אחרת שמעמידה כרבנן, ויש דחייה שאיסור כהונה שאני.

sub.desc_en: A Tanna recites a baraita before Rav Sheshet: all who are included in 'he shall take' are included in 'he shall not take', excluding a High Priest who has relations with his sister who is a widow.
sub.desc: התנא משמיע לפני רב ששת ברייתא הקובעת שכל האסור ב'לא יקח' הוא הנכלל ב'יקח', ופוטר כוהן גדול הבא על אחותו האלמנה.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet identifies the baraita as Rabbi Shimon's view that no prohibition takes effect on another, citing the case of eating neveila on Yom Kippur where Rabbi Shimon exempts, unlike the Rabbis who hold that a prohibition can take effect.
sub.desc: רב ששת מסביר שהברייתא היא כרבי שמעון, שאין איסור חל על איסור, ומביא ראיה מברייתא על האוכל נבילה ביום הכיפורים שפטור.

sub.desc_en: An alternative explanation suggests the baraita could even be the Rabbis, who hold that a severe prohibition takes effect on a light one, but a light prohibition does not take effect on a severe one.
sub.desc: הגמרא דוחה שניתן לומר שהברייתא כרבנן, שכן רבנן מודים שאיסור קל אינו חל על איסור חמור.

sub.desc_en: Another version states the baraita is the Rabbis, arguing that if it were Rabbi Shimon, who holds even a severe prohibition does not take effect on a light one, then a light prohibition on a severe one would certainly not take effect, making the baraita's exclusion unnecessary.
sub.desc: יש אומרים שהברייתא כרבנן, שאיסור חמור חל על קל אבל לא להיפך, ומדייקים שאם כרבי שמעון אין צורך במיעוט זה.

sub.desc_en: The gemara resolves that the baraita teaches that the prohibition of priesthood is unique and cannot be derived by a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument), so the exclusion is necessary even for the Rabbis.
sub.desc: הגמרא מיישבת שהברייתא אכן כרבי שמעון, וצריך להשמיענו שאיסור כהונה אינו שונה ואינו חל על איסור.

items.text: Rav Pappa's question to Abaye: Does an Israelite with his sister make her a ḥalala?
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's question to Abaye: Does an Israelite with his sister make her a ḥalala?
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks whether an Israelite who has relations with his sister, making her a zona, also makes her a ḥalala. Abaye answers that a ḥalala is only created through a prohibition related to priesthood, not through other prohibitions.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks Abaye whether an Israelite who has relations with his sister, making her a זונה (a woman forbidden to a priest), also makes her a חללה (a disqualified priestly woman), or whether a חללה is only created from a prohibition related to priesthood.
Abaye answers that a חללה is only created through a prohibition related to priesthood, not through other prohibitions like the one against relations with one's sister.

items.text: Rava's proof that a ḥalala is only from a priestly prohibition
items.text_en: Rava's proof that a ḥalala is only from a priestly prohibition
items.desc_en: Rava cites a baraita that derives from the Torah's mention of 'divorcee' that a ḥalala is only created through a prohibition unique to priesthood, and that 'zona' teaches that her offspring are profaned.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks for the source of the rabbinic principle that a ḥalala is only created through a prohibition unique to priesthood.
The baraita derives from the Torah's mention of 'divorcee' that a ḥalala is only from a priestly prohibition, and that 'zona' teaches that her offspring are profaned.
The gemara concludes that the term 'ḥalala' teaches that a ḥalala is only from a priestly prohibition, and 'zona' teaches that her offspring are profaned.

items.text: מסקנת רב אשי
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's halakhic conclusion
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi concludes that a priest who has relations with his sister is subject to the law of a ḥalala.
items.desc: רב אשי מתחיל לומר 'הילכך, כהן הבא על אחותו' ומסקנתו נקטעת באמצע, כנראה כדי להסיק שהיא נעשית זונה ולא חללה.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi rules that a priest who has relations with his sister is subject to the law of a חללה (profaned woman).
sub.desc: רב אשי מתחיל להסיק מסקנה לגבי כוהן הבא על אחותו, אך הקטע נקטע.

items.text: Opening statement on zonah and chalalah
items.text_en: Opening statement on zonah and chalalah
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that if a High Priest has intercourse with a widow, he makes her a zonah, but not a chalalah; if he then has intercourse with her again, he makes her a chalalah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that a High Priest who has intercourse with a widow makes her a zonah but not a chalalah, and if he repeats intercourse he makes her a chalalah.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's ruling on lashes for High Priest
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's ruling on lashes for High Priest
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says a High Priest who marries a widow is liable to two sets of lashes: one for 'lo yikach' and one for 'lo yechalel'. The Gemara questions why he is not also liable for 'lo yechalel zaro', and answers that it refers to a case where he did not complete intercourse.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda rules that a High Priest who marries a widow is liable to two sets of lashes: one for the prohibition 'לֹא יִקָּח' (he shall not take) and one for 'לֹא יְחַלֵּל' (he shall not profane).
The Gemara asks why the High Priest is not also liable for the prohibition 'לֹא יְחַלֵּל זַרְעוֹ' (he shall not profane his offspring).
The Gemara answers that the case is where he did not complete intercourse, so the offspring is not profaned.

items.text: Rava's objection and resolution regarding two names
items.text_en: Rava's objection and resolution regarding two names
items.desc_en: Rava raises an objection from a baraita that says a widow and divorcee is liable for two 'names', implying only two lashes total. The Gemara resolves that it means two names for each prohibition. The discussion continues with the case of a divorcee and a chalutzah, concluding that the baraita means he is only liable for one, but still two names.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects by citing a baraita that a widow and divorcee is lashed for two 'names', implying only two lashes total, contradicting the earlier position that multiple prohibitions apply.
The Gemara answers that the baraita means two names for each prohibition, not two total.
The Gemara resolves the apparent contradiction from the baraita's continuation about a divorcee and a chalutzah, explaining that he is only liable for one prohibition but still two names.

items.text: Clarification on chalutzah being rabbinic
items.text_en: Clarification on chalutzah being rabbinic
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a chalutzah is a rabbinic prohibition, citing a baraita that derives it from a verse. It concludes that it is rabbinic and the verse is merely an asmachta.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a chalutzah is only a rabbinic prohibition, citing a baraita that derives it from a verse.
The Gemara concludes that the prohibition of a chalutzah is rabbinic and the verse is merely an asmachta (support).

items.text: Abaye and Rava debate on when lashes apply
items.text_en: Abaye and Rava debate on when lashes apply
items.desc_en: Abaye holds that a High Priest who betroths a widow is liable for lashes, and if he has intercourse, he is liable again. Rava argues that he is only liable if he has intercourse, because the prohibition of 'lo yikach' is subsumed under 'lo yechalel'. They agree on exceptions: Abaye concedes in the case of remarrying a divorcee, and Rava concedes in the case of a High Priest with a widow without betrothal. Both agree that remarrying a divorcee without betrothal does not incur lashes.

sub.desc_en: Abaye states that a High Priest who betroths a widow is liable for lashes for the prohibition 'lo yikach', and if he has intercourse, he is liable again for 'lo yechalel'.
Rava argues that the High Priest is liable only if he has intercourse, because the prohibition 'lo yikach' is subsumed under 'lo yechalel'.
Abaye concedes that in the case of remarrying a divorcee, if he betrothed but did not have intercourse, he is not liable, because the Torah requires a marriage act (לקיחה) which is absent.
Rava concedes that a High Priest with a widow who had intercourse without betrothal is liable, because the verse 'lo yechalel' applies to the act of intercourse itself.
Both agree that remarrying a divorcee without betrothal does not incur lashes, because the Torah only prohibits marriage through the act of betrothal (דרך ליקוחין).

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's ruling on daughter of a male convert
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's ruling on daughter of a male convert
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda says the daughter of a male convert is like the daughter of a chalal. A baraita presents his reasoning through a series of analogies (binyan av) comparing a chalal, a High Priest with a widow, and an Egyptian first-generation convert, concluding that the common factor is that they are not part of the majority of the congregation, and thus their daughters are disqualified. The Gemara refines the argument, replacing the High Priest with an Egyptian first-generation convert, and notes that Rabbi Yehuda holds that a convert also disqualifies through his intercourse.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda rules that the daughter of a male convert is like the daughter of a חלל (a priest disqualified by forbidden marriage).

A baraita cites Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning: a kal vachomer (a fortiori) argument from a חלל (who comes from a fit seed) to a convert (who comes from a disqualified seed) concludes that the convert's daughter is also disqualified.

The Gemara objects that the kal vachomer is flawed: a חלל is created through a transgression, but a convert is not, so the analogy is not valid; the Gemara then introduces a High Priest with a widow as a counterexample that also disqualifies his daughter despite no transgression in his creation.
The Gemara objects further: a High Priest with a widow involves a transgression in his intercourse, so the analogy is still not perfect; a חלל can serve as a counterexample to that.

The Gemara resolves by constructing a בנין אב (common principle): the common factor between a חלל and a High Priest with a widow is that they are not part of the majority of the congregation (אינן ברוב הקהל), and thus the convert, who also is not part of the majority, has his daughter disqualified.
The Gemara objects that the common factor still has an element of transgression in both cases, which the convert lacks.

The Gemara replaces the High Priest with a widow with a first-generation Egyptian convert (מצרי ראשון) as a counterexample, since the Egyptian convert is not fit to enter the congregation, and a חלל serves as a counterexample to that.

The Gemara again constructs a בנין אב: the common factor between a חלל and a first-generation Egyptian convert is that they are not part of the majority of the congregation, and thus the convert's daughter is disqualified.

The Gemara objects that the common factor still involves disqualification through intercourse, and notes that Rabbi Yehuda holds that a convert also disqualifies through his intercourse, so he derives the law via a מה הצד (common element) from this reasoning.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov and Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai on converts
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov and Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai on converts
items.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's opinion on a convert, and Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai says a female convert under three years old is fit for the priesthood, citing a verse about Pinchas. The Rabbis interpret the verse as referring to slaves and maidservants.

sub.text: Baraita citation of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
sub.text_en: Baraita citation of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
sub.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's opinion on a convert.

sub.text: Baraita citation of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
sub.text_en: Baraita citation of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
sub.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's opinion that a female convert under three years old is fit for the priesthood, citing a verse about Pinchas.
The Rabbis object that the verse refers to slaves and maidservants, not to converts.

items.text: Exegetical basis for the differing opinions
items.text_en: Exegetical basis for the differing opinions
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that all the Tannaim derive their opinions from the same verse: 'Almanah ugerushah lo yikchu lahem lenashim ki im betulot mizera beit Yisrael'. Rabbi Yehuda requires the entire seed of Israel; Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov requires even partial seed; Rabbi Yosi requires those who were sown in Israel; Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai requires those who were sown in her virginity in Israel.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces that all the Tannaim derive their opinions from a single verse.
Rabbi Yehuda holds that the verse requires the entire seed of Israel.
Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov holds that even partial seed suffices.
Rabbi Yosi holds that the verse refers to those who were sown in Israel.
Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai holds that the verse requires those who were sown in her virginity in Israel.

items.text: Rav Nachman's question to Rava
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's question to Rava
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman addresses Rava, beginning a new discussion.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman addresses Rava, beginning a new discussion.

items.text: Gemara's question on the verse's inconsistency
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the verse's inconsistency
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a single verse can begin with the High Priest and end with an ordinary priest. The answer is given with a proof from a verse about Samuel, showing that Scripture can be split into two contexts.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a single verse can begin with the High Priest and end with an ordinary priest, and receives an affirmative answer that it is so.
The Gemara objects that Scripture cannot be written in such a split manner, and receives another affirmative answer.
The Gemara proves from the verse about Samuel that Scripture can be split into two contexts, where the lamp was in the sanctuary but Samuel slept in his own place.

items.text: Interpretation of 'from a priest'
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'from a priest'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the phrase 'from a priest' means from other priests, not from Israelites. A baraita supports this interpretation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the verse 'the widow who is a widow from a priest they shall take' implies only from a priest, not from an Israelite.
The Gemara answers that the verse means 'from the rest of the priests they shall take', i.e., from non-High-Priest priests.
A baraita supports this interpretation, stating that 'from a priest they shall take' means from the rest of the priests.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's opinion on who may marry the widow
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's opinion on who may marry the widow
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda limits the widow to those who can marry her daughter, consistent with his view that the daughter of a male convert is like the daughter of a חלל.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda states that the verse means they may take from those who marry into the priesthood.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yehuda follows his own principle that the daughter of a male convert is like the daughter of a male חלל (disqualified priest), so whoever you may marry his daughter you may marry his widow.

items.text: Rabbi Yossi's opinion and practical ruling
items.text_en: Rabbi Yossi's opinion and practical ruling
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yossi permits even a convert who married a convert woman. Rav Hamnuna and Rabbah bar bar Chanah rule like Rabbi Yossi. Since the Temple's destruction, priests have been stringent like Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov. Rav Nachman reports that one who consults is instructed like Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, but if already married, she is not removed.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yossi permits even a convert who married a convert woman to marry into the priesthood.
Rav Hamnuna reports in the name of Ulla that the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Yossi.
Rabbah bar bar Chanah also rules that the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Yossi.
Since the Temple's destruction, priests have been stringent and follow Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's stricter view.
Rav Nachman reports that one who consults is instructed like Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, but if already married, she is not removed, following Rabbi Yossi.

items.text: Mishnah: Declaring a child a mamzer
items.text_en: Mishnah: Declaring a child a mamzer
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a man who says 'this son of mine is a mamzer' is not believed. Even if both parents agree about a fetus, they are not believed. Rabbi Yehuda says they are believed.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who says 'this son of mine is a ממזר (illegitimate)' is not believed.
Even if both parents agree that the fetus in her womb is a ממזר (illegitimate), they are not believed.
Rabbi Yehuda says they are believed.

items.text: Gemara's explanation of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that 'even both' includes the mother, who is presumed to know, and even a fetus without a presumption of fitness, they are not believed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'even both of them' means.
The Gemara explains that it is not necessary to say that the father is not believed since he does not know for certain, but even the mother who knows for certain is not believed.

The Gemara further explains that it is not necessary to say that when there is a חזקה (presumption) of fitness they are not believed, but even for a fetus which has no such presumption they are not believed.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's proof and the debate with the Sages
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's proof and the debate with the Sages
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda derives from 'יַכִּיר' that a man is believed to declare his firstborn, and similarly for a son of a divorced woman. The Sages disagree. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak questions the Sages' use of the verse. The Gemara explains that the verse is needed for inheritance of after-acquired property, and for Rabbi Meir, for property acquired while dying.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that Rabbi Yehuda holds a man is believed to declare his son a firstborn or a son of a divorced woman.

A baraita is cited: Rabbi Yehuda derives from the verse 'יַכִּיר' (he shall recognize) that a man is believed to declare his firstborn, and similarly for a son of a divorced woman, while the Sages disagree.

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's question to Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's question to Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak asks Rava: for Rabbi Yehuda the verse 'יַכִּיר' is understood, but for the Sages who disagree, why is the verse needed?

The Gemara answers that the verse is needed for 'הכירא' (recognition) regarding the double portion of the firstborn, but then questions why a verse is needed since the father could simply give a gift.
The Gemara resolves that the verse applies to property acquired after the father's declaration, which he cannot give as a gift.

sub.text: Gemara's additional question for Rabbi Meir
sub.text_en: Gemara's additional question for Rabbi Meir
sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: for Rabbi Meir, who holds that one can transfer property not yet in the world, why is the verse needed? It answers: for property acquired while dying (גוסס), which cannot be given as a gift.

items.text: Mishnah: Conflicting betrothals by father and agent
items.text_en: Mishnah: Conflicting betrothals by father and agent
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses a case where a father authorizes an agent to betroth his daughter, but then betroths her himself. The validity depends on which betrothal occurred first. If unknown, the case is unresolved.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah begins: One who gave authority to his agent to betroth his daughter, and he himself went and betrothed her.
If his betrothal came first, his betrothal is valid; if his agent's betrothal came first, his betrothal is valid.
The Mishnah concludes with the case where it is not known which came first.

items.text: Mishnah: Cases of conflicting kiddushin
items.text_en: Mishnah: Cases of conflicting kiddushin
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents two cases: a man who sends two agents to betroth a woman, and a woman who sends an agent but betroths herself. In both, if the timing is unknown, both give a get, or one gives a get and one marries her.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the first case: a man who sends two agents to betroth a woman, and if the timing is unknown, both give a גט (bill of divorce) or one gives a גט and one marries her.
The Mishnah presents the second case: a woman who sends an agent but betroths herself, with the same ruling if the timing is unknown.

items.text: Gemara: Need for both cases
items.text_en: Gemara: Need for both cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the Mishnah needed to teach both cases: for the man, one might think only his kiddushin are valid because he is expert in lineage, but for the woman, one might think her kiddushin are not valid; conversely, for the woman, one might think she is careful, but for the man, he might not care.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that both cases are necessary, and explains that if only the father's case were taught, one might think his betrothal is valid because he is expert in lineage, but a woman's betrothal might not be valid.

The Gemara completes the reasoning: conversely, if only the woman's case were taught, one might think her betrothal is valid because she is careful, but the father might not care; therefore both cases are necessary.

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel
items.desc_en: A case is presented: a father betroths his daughter on the road, and she betroths herself in the city, and she is now a bogeret. Rav says she is a bogeret before us (so the father's kiddushin are invalid), while Shmuel says we suspect both kiddushin.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a case: a father betroths his daughter on the road, she betroths herself in the city, and she is now a bogeret (a young woman past the stage of na'arus).
Rav rules that she is a bogeret before us, so the father's kiddushin (betrothal) is invalid.
Shmuel rules that we suspect both kiddushin (betrothals) and require a get from each.

items.text: Clarifying the dispute: timing
items.text_en: Clarifying the dispute: timing
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the timing: if within six months of na'arus, Rav's ruling is obvious; if after six months, Shmuel's ruling contradicts his own statement that the only difference between na'arus and bagrus is six months. The Gemara resolves: it is on the very day the six months end. Rav assumes she was a bogeret all day, Shmuel says she only now developed signs.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks about the timing of the dispute: if within six months of na'arus, Rav's ruling is obvious; if after six months, Shmuel's ruling contradicts his own statement that the only difference between na'arus and bagrus is six months.
The Gemara resolves that the case is on the very day the six months end: Rav assumes she was a bogeret all day, while Shmuel says she only now developed signs.

items.text: Analogy to mikveh and rebuttal
items.text_en: Analogy to mikveh and rebuttal
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Shmuel from the case of a mikveh found deficient: all purifications performed retroactively are invalid. Shmuel distinguishes because there we can place the impure person in his presumptive state, but here we see her as a bogeret now. The Gemara counters that we could also place the mikveh in its presumptive state, but it is found deficient. The resolution: there are two factors against the mikveh, here only one against her.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Shmuel by citing the Mishnah of a mikveh found deficient, where all purifications performed retroactively are invalid.
Shmuel distinguishes the mikveh case because there we can place the impure person in his presumptive state (חזקה) and say he did not immerse.
The Gemara counters that we could also place the mikveh in its presumptive state and say it was not deficient, but it is found deficient now; similarly here she is a bogeret now.

The Gemara resolves that in the mikveh case there are two factors against the presumption (the impure person's presumptive state and the mikveh's deficiency), but here only one factor against her (her current bogeret status).

items.text: Analogy to a barrel of wine and resolution
items.text_en: Analogy to a barrel of wine and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Shmuel from a barrel of wine found to be vinegar: within three days it is certainly terumah, afterward it is uncertain. The Gemara notes a contradiction with the mikveh case. Rav Chanina from Sura resolves: the barrel case follows Rabbi Shimon, who treats even the mikveh as uncertain. For the Rabbis, the barrel would be retroactively tevel, but they distinguish because we can place the tevel in its presumptive state. The Gemara counters similarly, and the resolution is again that there are two factors against the wine, one against her.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Shmuel's position by asking why it differs from the case of a barrel of wine found to be vinegar.
The Gemara cites a baraita about a barrel checked for terumah that is later found to be vinegar: within three days it is certainly terumah, afterward it is uncertain.
The Gemara raises a contradiction between the barrel case and the mikveh case, questioning why one is certain and the other uncertain.
Rav Chanina from Sura resolves that the barrel case follows Rabbi Shimon, who treats even the mikveh case as uncertain.
The Gemara cites a baraita showing Rabbi Shimon's position that in the public domain the purifications are pure, and in the private domain they are suspended.
The Gemara objects that for the Rabbis, the barrel would be retroactively tevel, but they distinguish because we can place the tevel in its presumptive state.
The Gemara resolves that in the barrel case there are two factors against the wine, while in the woman's case there is only one factor against her.

items.text: Transition to Tannaic dispute
items.text_en: Transition to Tannaic dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the dispute between Rav and Shmuel may be parallel to a Tannaic dispute, setting up the next section.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the dispute between Rav and Shmuel may align with a Tannaic dispute, introducing the next section.

items.text: Tannaic dispute on burden of proof
items.text_en: Tannaic dispute on burden of proof
items.desc_en: The Mishnah's question 'Who extracts from whom?' is answered by Rabbi Yaakov and Rabbi Nathan with opposing rules: Rabbi Yaakov says the person claiming a change in status must bring proof, while Rabbi Nathan distinguishes based on current appearance.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah asks: who extracts from whom (in a case of disputed status)?
Rabbi Yaakov rules that the person claiming a change in status extracts without proof, but the others cannot extract from him without proof.
Rabbi Nathan distinguishes based on current appearance: if the person is healthy, he must bring proof he was a goses; if he is a goses, the others must bring proof he was healthy.

items.text: Rav and Shmuel aligned with the Tannaim
items.text_en: Rav and Shmuel aligned with the Tannaim
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests Rav follows Rabbi Nathan and Shmuel follows Rabbi Yaakov, but each Amora defends his position as consistent with both Tannaim by distinguishing the cases: Rav says Rabbi Yaakov's ruling applies only where property is at stake, not body status; Shmuel says Rabbi Nathan's ruling applies only where the default is health, not here.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that Rav follows Rabbi Nathan and Shmuel follows Rabbi Yaakov.
Rav defends his position, arguing that Rabbi Yaakov's ruling applies only where property is at stake (העמד ממון על חזקתו), not where body status is concerned.

Shmuel defends his position, arguing that Rabbi Nathan's ruling applies only where the default is health (כולי עלמא בחזקת בריאים קיימי), not here where the woman does not remove herself from her prior presumption.

items.text: Support from a baraita on kiddushin
items.text_en: Support from a baraita on kiddushin
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about a girl whose father betrothed her on the road and she betrothed herself in the city, and she is now a bogeret. One version says she is definitely a bogeret, another says we suspect both kiddushin. The Gemara initially suggests these correspond to Rav and Shmuel, but rejects this: both follow Shmuel, differing only on whether she contradicts herself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita presenting two versions about a girl whose father betrothed her on the road and she betrothed herself in the city and is now a bogeret: one says she is definitely a bogeret, the other says we suspect both kiddushin.
The Gemara asks whether the two versions correspond to Rav and Shmuel's positions.
The Gemara rejects the correspondence, explaining that both versions follow Shmuel, differing only on whether the girl contradicts herself.

items.text: Proof of dispute from a practical incident
items.text_en: Proof of dispute from a practical incident
items.desc_en: The Gemara argues that Rav and Shmuel must disagree, because Rav Yosef acted according to Rav and Shmuel was angry, calling him a 'big measure' compared to others' 'small measure'. The Gemara deflects that the case might have involved a contradictory claim.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rav and Shmuel could disagree, given that the Mishnah does not explicitly show a dispute, and suggests that the Amoraim also do not disagree.
The Gemara deflects the proof by suggesting that Rav Yosef's action might have involved a case where the woman contradicted herself (מכחשתו), so Shmuel's anger was not about the underlying dispute.

items.text: Halakhic ruling
items.text_en: Halakhic ruling
items.desc_en: Mar Zutra reports in the name of Ameimar that the halakha follows Shmuel, but Rav Ashi says it follows Rav, and the Gemara concludes the halakha follows Rav.

sub.desc_en: Mar Zutra reports Ameimar's ruling that the halakha follows Shmuel, but Rav Ashi says it follows Rav, and the Gemara concludes the halakha follows Rav.

items.text: Mishnah: Identification of wife and children
items.text_en: Mishnah: Identification of wife and children
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents cases of a man returning from overseas with his wife and children, detailing when he needs to bring proof about the woman and the children.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the first case: a man returning from overseas with his wife and children, stating that if he identifies the woman who left with him and her children, he needs no proof for either; if she died and he presents the children, he needs proof for the children but not for the woman.

The Mishnah presents the second case: if the man says he married a woman overseas, he must bring proof for the woman but not for the children; if she died, he must bring proof for both the woman and the children.

items.text: Gemara: Rabba bar Rav Huna and a baraita
items.text_en: Gemara: Rabba bar Rav Huna and a baraita
items.desc_en: Rabba bar Rav Huna comments that all cases involve the children clinging to her. A baraita adds details about large vs. small children and one vs. two women.

sub.desc_en: Rabba bar Rav Huna states that all cases in the Mishnah involve the children clinging to the woman.
A baraita adds details: for one woman, evidence is needed for the woman but not for the children, and for large children but not small ones; for two women, evidence is needed for all.

items.text: Resh Lakish's statement
items.text_en: Resh Lakish's statement
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish begins a statement, but the text cuts off.

sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish begins a statement, but the text cuts off, leaving the content incomplete.

items.text: מחלוקת על חזקת אמהות ליוחסין
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Rabbi Yochanan on presumptions in lineage
items.desc_en: Rav holds that the rule of relying on presumptions (חזקות) applies only to consecrated items of the border (קדשי הגבול), but not to lineage (יוחסין). Rabbi Yochanan argues it applies even to lineage.
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה מחלוקת בין חכמים לרבי יוחנן: האם חזקת ילדים הנכרכים אחר אישה מוכיחה שהיא אמם רק לעניין תרומה (קדשי הגבול) או גם לעניין יוחסין.

sub.desc_en: Rav states that the rule of relying on presumptions (חזקות) was taught only regarding consecrated items of the border (קדשי הגבול), but not regarding lineage (יוחסין).
sub.desc: הגמרא פותחת במחלוקת: חכמים מגבילים את חזקת האמהות לתרומה, ורבי יוחנן מרחיבה אף ליוחסין.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan argues that the rule applies even to lineage (יוחסין).
sub.desc: הגמרא פותחת במחלוקת: חכמים מגבילים את חזקת האמהות לתרומה, ורבי יוחנן מרחיבה אף ליוחסין.

items.text: שיטת רבי יוחנן: מלקין, סוקלין ושורפין על החזקות
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's general principle on presumptions
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan's view is consistent with his general principle: we flog, stone, and burn based on presumptions, but we do not burn terumah based on presumptions. The Gemara explains each clause: flogging follows Rav Yehuda's case of a presumed menstruant; stoning and burning follow Rabba bar Rav Huna's case of a boy and girl raised together; and a story from Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi illustrates stoning based on presumption.
items.desc: הגמרא מבארת שרבי יוחנן סובר שניתן להעניש על סמך חזקות: מלקין על חזקת נידה, סוקלין ושורפין על חזקת קורבה משפחתית (כמו במקרה מעשי של אישה ובנה שגדל עמה).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that Rabbi Yochanan's view is consistent with his general principle: we flog, stone, and burn based on presumptions (חזקות), but we do not burn תרומה (priestly portion) based on presumptions.
sub.desc: הגמרא פותחת בציטוט הכלל של רבי יוחנן: מלקין, סוקלין ושורפין על החזקות, אך אין שורפין תרומה על החזקות.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that flogging based on presumption follows Rav Yehuda's ruling: if a woman is presumed (הוּחְזְקָה) by her neighbors to be a menstruant (נִדָּה), her husband is flogged for relations with her.
sub.desc: הגמרא מביאה ראיה לדין מלקין על החזקות משיטת רב יהודה: בעלה של אשה שהוחזקה נידה בשכנותיה לוקה עליה משום נידה.

sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of stoning and burning
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that stoning and burning based on presumption follow Rabba bar Rav Huna's ruling: a boy and girl raised together in a house are stoned or burned for relations with each other based on the presumption of forbidden intimacy.
sub.desc: הגמרא מביאה ראיה לדין סוקלין ושורפין על החזקות משיטת רבא בר רב הונא: בני בית שגדלו יחד נסקלים ונשרפים זה על זה על סמך חזקת קורבה.

sub.text: רבי שמעון בן פזי בשם רבי יהושע בן לוי משום בר קפרא
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi in the name of Bar Kappara
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi reports a story in the name of Bar Kappara: a woman came to Jerusalem with a child on her shoulder, raised him, and he had relations with her; the court stoned them, not because he was certainly her son, but because he was constantly attached (כָּרוּךְ) to her, illustrating stoning based on presumption.
sub.desc: הגמרא מביאה מעשה כראיה נוספת: אישה שבאה לירושלים עם תינוק מורכב על כתפה, גדל ובא עליה, וסקלום בית דין על סמך חזקת קורבה.

items.text: מחלוקת על שריפת תרומה על סמך חזקת טומאה
items.text_en: Dispute on burning terumah based on presumption
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents the dispute between Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan regarding burning terumah based on presumptions. Reish Lakish holds that we do burn, while Rabbi Yochanan holds we do not. Their positions align with their respective views in the Mishnah about a child found near dough, where Rabbi Meir and the Sages disagree about the status of the dough.
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה מחלוקת בין ריש לקיש לרבי יוחנן: האם שורפין תרומה על סמך חזקת טומאה של ילד שנגע בעיסה. ריש לקיש סובר ששורפין, ורבי יוחנן חולק, והגמרא מקשרת זאת למחלוקת תנאים במשנה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the dispute between Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan regarding whether one burns terumah (priestly portion) based on presumptions (חזקות).
sub.desc: הגמרא פותחת במחלוקת בין ריש לקיש לרבי יוחנן בדין שריפת תרומה על סמך חזקת טומאה, ומקשרת זאת למשנה במסכת טהרות.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah about a child found near dough, where Rabbi Meir declares it pure and the Sages declare it impure, to show the underlying principles of Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan.
sub.desc: הגמרא פותחת במחלוקת בין ריש לקיש לרבי יוחנן בדין שריפת תרומה על סמך חזקת טומאה, ומקשרת זאת למשנה במסכת טהרות.

sub.text_en: Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan's statements
sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish, citing Rabbi Oshaya, rules that this case (the child near dough) is one where we burn terumah, while Rabbi Yochanan disagrees, saying this is not a presumption strong enough to burn terumah.
sub.desc: ריש לקיש בשם רבי אושעיא פוסק שזו חזקה ששורפין עליה תרומה, ורבי יוחנן חולק ואומר שאין זו חזקה לשרוף.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's definition of a valid presumption for terumah
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's definition of a valid presumption for terumah
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies what constitutes a valid presumption for burning terumah according to Rabbi Yochanan, citing a Mishnah about dough in a house with reptiles and frogs, where the majority determines impurity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what constitutes a valid presumption (חזקה) according to Rabbi Yochanan that would justify burning terumah.
The Gemara answers by citing a Mishnah about dough in a house with reptiles and frogs, where the majority determines impurity or purity.

items.text: Baraita supporting Rabbi Yochanan: two cases treated as if they have intent
items.text_en: Baraita supporting Rabbi Yochanan: two cases treated as if they have intent
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited in support of Rabbi Yochanan, stating that there are two things lacking intent (דעה לישאל) that the Sages treated as if they have intent: a child (the case already mentioned) and another case involving dough in a house with chickens and liquids.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited in support of Rabbi Yochanan, stating that there are two things lacking intent (דעה לישאל) that the Sages treated as if they have intent.
The Gemara asks: the child is the case we already mentioned, but what is the 'other' case?
The baraita answers: the other case is dough in a house with chickens and liquids, and they were found.

items.text: Blood spots in dough: dispute between Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi and Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Blood spots in dough: dispute between Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi and Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the Mishnah's ruling about blood spots in dough. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi limits the leniency to white liquids, while Rabbi Yochanan limits it to clear liquids, as a child's saliva is visible in them. The Gemara raises an objection about the dough absorbing the liquid.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that blood spots in dough are treated with uncertainty: one does not eat them but also does not burn them.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi limits the Mishnah's leniency to white liquids, because in red liquids a blood spot would be immediately noticeable.
The Gemara objects that perhaps the dough absorbs the red liquid, making the spot undetectable.
Rabbi Yochanan limits the leniency to clear liquids, where a child's saliva is visible, but not to cloudy liquids.

items.text: Mishnah: Laws of yichud with multiple individuals
items.text_en: Mishnah: Laws of yichud with multiple individuals
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a man may not seclude himself with two women, but a woman may seclude herself with two men. Rabbi Shimon allows a man to seclude with two women if his wife is with him. A man may seclude with his mother or daughter, even sleeping close, but when they are grown they sleep in separate garments.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the general rule: a man may not seclude himself with two women, but a woman may seclude herself with two men.
Rabbi Shimon adds an exception: a man may seclude himself with two women if his wife is with him, because his wife guards him.
The Mishnah concludes with the rule that a man may seclude himself with his mother or daughter, even sleeping close, but when they are grown they sleep in separate garments.

items.text: Gemara: Reason and scriptural source for yichud
items.text_en: Gemara: Reason and scriptural source for yichud
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the reason for the Mishnah's ruling: women's minds are light. It then cites Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Yishmael finding a hint for yichud in the verse 'If your brother, the son of your mother, entices you.' The Gemara clarifies that the verse teaches that a son may seclude with his mother but not with other forbidden relatives. Abaye explains the verse's plain meaning.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the reason behind the Mishnah's ruling that a man may not seclude himself with two women.
The Tanna of the school of Eliyahu answers that women's minds are light (frivolous), making them susceptible to seduction.
The Gemara asks for a scriptural source for the prohibition of ייחוד (seclusion).

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan cites Rabbi Yishmael that a hint for ייחוד is found in the verse 'If your brother, the son of your mother, entices you' (Deuteronomy 13:7).
The Gemara objects: does only a maternal brother entice, but not a paternal brother?
The Gemara resolves that the verse teaches that a son may seclude with his mother, but is forbidden to seclude with all other forbidden relatives (עריות).
The Gemara asks about the plain meaning (פשט) of the verse.

Abaye explains that the verse uses a לא מיבעיא (not only) formulation: not only a paternal brother who hates him would entice, but even a maternal brother who loves him might be listened to, so the Torah warns against him.

items.text: Debate about Abba Shaul's opinion on yichud during mourning
items.text_en: Debate about Abba Shaul's opinion on yichud during mourning
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers whether the Mishnah's leniency for a woman with two men aligns with Abba Shaul, who allows a man with two women during the first thirty days of mourning. It explains that during acute mourning, one's evil inclination is subdued. The Rabbis follow Rabbi Yitzchak, who holds that even during mourning the inclination is strong. Abba Shaul interprets the verse differently.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the Mishnah's leniency for a woman with two men contradicts Abba Shaul, who permits only one man with two women during the first thirty days of mourning.
The Gemara resolves that even according to Abba Shaul, the Mishnah's case is during acute mourning (אנינות), when the evil inclination is subdued.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of the Rabbis' view
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the Rabbis' view
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Rabbis follow Rabbi Yitzchak, who holds that even during mourning the evil inclination is strong.
Abba Shaul interprets the verse differently: it refers to one who complains about God's attributes, not to the strength of the evil inclination during mourning.

items.text: Exception for a single woman and the limit of trustworthiness
items.text_en: Exception for a single woman and the limit of trustworthiness
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a story supporting the Rabbis' view. Rav Yehuda says the Mishnah's leniency for a woman with two men applies only to upright men, but for licentious men even ten is insufficient. A story illustrates this. The Gemara attempts to support this from a baraita about two Torah scholars, but distinguishes them from ordinary people.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the Rabbis (who permit a woman with two men) justify their view, and cites a story of a woman who was brought out by two men.
Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav explains that the Mishnah's leniency for a woman with two men applies only to upright men, but for licentious men even ten is insufficient.
A story is told where ten men brought a woman out on a bed, illustrating that even a large group of licentious men cannot be trusted.
Rav Yosef supports this with a general observation: ten people will band together to steal a beam without shame from each other.
The Gemara attempts to support Rav Yehuda's view from a baraita that says two Torah scholars are appointed to accompany a woman, implying that ordinary people are not trusted.
The Gemara rejects the attempted support, distinguishing Torah scholars from ordinary people because scholars are aware of the severity of the prohibition.

items.text: Gemara's discussion on the Mishnah's ruling about yichud with a woman
items.text_en: Gemara's discussion on the Mishnah's ruling about yichud with a woman
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quoting Rav limits the Mishnah's leniency to a city, but on the road three people are needed lest one need to urinate and leave the other alone with the woman. The Gemara attempts to support this from a baraita about assigning two scholars to accompany a woman, but deflects that the two are witnesses, not protectors.

sub.desc_en: Opens with the end of the previous discussion about warning a sinner.
Rav Yehuda quoting Rav distinguishes between city and road: on the road, three are needed lest one leaves to urinate, causing yichud.
The Gemara attempts to support Rav's ruling from a baraita that assigns two scholars to accompany a woman, totaling three.
The Gemara deflects the support by explaining that the two scholars serve as witnesses, not protectors against yichud.

items.text: Story of Rav and Rav Yehuda on the road
items.text_en: Story of Rav and Rav Yehuda on the road
items.desc_en: Rav tells Rav Yehuda to lift his feet from before Gehinnom when a woman walks ahead of them, implying concern for yichud. Rav Yehuda questions this based on Rav's own ruling that it is fine for kosher people, and Rav clarifies that he meant people like Rabbi Chanina bar Papi and his colleagues.

sub.desc_en: The narrator sets the scene: Rav and Rav Yehuda are walking on the road, and a woman walks ahead of them; Rav tells Rav Yehuda to lift his feet from before Gehinnom.
Rav Yehuda questions Rav, pointing out that Rav himself ruled that for kosher people, such proximity is fine.
Rav clarifies that he did not mean people like himself and Rav Yehuda, but rather people like Rabbi Chanina bar Papi and his colleagues, who are truly kosher.

items.text: Rav's ruling on lashes for yichud and Rav Ashi's distinction
items.text_en: Rav's ruling on lashes for yichud and Rav Ashi's distinction
items.desc_en: Rav rules that we lash for yichud but do not prohibit the woman to her husband based on yichud alone. Rav Ashi limits this to yichud with an unmarried woman, but with a married woman we do prohibit, to avoid slander against her children.

sub.desc_en: Rav rules that we administer lashes for yichud (seclusion) but do not prohibit the woman to her husband based on yichud alone.
Rav Ashi limits Rav's ruling to yichud with an unmarried woman, but with a married woman we do prohibit, to avoid slander against her children.

items.text: Mar Zutra's practice and Rav Nachman's suggestion
items.text_en: Mar Zutra's practice and Rav Nachman's suggestion
items.desc_en: Mar Zutra would lash and announce the punishment. Rav Nachman from Parhatya suggests Rav Ashi do the same, but Rav Ashi responds that some hear of one case and not another.

sub.desc_en: Describes Mar Zutra's practice of flogging and publicly announcing the punishment for ייחוד (seclusion).
Rav Nachman from Parhatya suggests to Rav Ashi that he too should flog and announce the punishment.
Rav Ashi declines, explaining that some people hear of one case and not another, so the deterrent effect is inconsistent.

items.text: Rav's ruling on lashes for a bad report and Mar Zutra's practice
items.text_en: Rav's ruling on lashes for a bad report and Mar Zutra's practice
items.desc_en: Rav rules that we lash for a bad report, citing the verse 'Al banai ki lo tovah hashmu'ah'. Mar Zutra would place a strap on the offender's shoulder and recite the verse.

sub.desc_en: Rav rules that we lash for a bad report, citing the verse 'אַל בָּנָי' (Al banai) as support.
Mar Zutra would place a strap on the offender's shoulder and recite the verse 'אַל בָּנָי' (Al banai) as part of the punishment.

items.text: Exceptions to yichud: husband in town and public entrance
items.text_en: Exceptions to yichud: husband in town and public entrance
items.desc_en: Rabbah rules that if the husband is in town, there is no concern for yichud. Rav Yosef adds that an open entrance to the public domain removes concern. The Gemara relates that Rav Bibi visited Rav Yosef, and after the meal Rav Yosef ordered the ladder removed from under Rav Bibi, despite the husband being in town, because Rav Bibi's wife's friend was there and familiar with him.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah rules that when the husband is in town, there is no concern for ייחוד (seclusion with a married woman).
Rav Yosef adds that an entrance open to the public domain also removes concern for ייחוד.

sub.text: Story about Rav Bibi and Rav Yosef
sub.text_en: Story about Rav Bibi and Rav Yosef
sub.desc_en: The Gemara relates that Rav Bibi visited Rav Yosef, and after the meal Rav Yosef ordered the ladder removed from under Rav Bibi, despite the husband being in town, because Rav Bibi's wife's friend was there and familiar with him.

items.text: Rav Kahana's ruling on men outside and women inside, and Abaye's stringency
items.text_en: Rav Kahana's ruling on men outside and women inside, and Abaye's stringency
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana rules that if men are outside and women inside, there is no concern for yichud, but if men are inside and women outside, there is concern. A baraita teaches the opposite. Abaye concludes that since both opinions exist, he will act stringently.

sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana rules that if men are outside and women inside there is no concern for ייחוד (seclusion), but if men are inside and women outside there is concern.
A baraita teaches the opposite ruling, creating a contradiction with Rav Kahana.
Abaye concludes that since both opinions exist, he will act לכתחילה (stringently) and follow the stricter view.

items.text: Abaye and Rava's practices regarding yichud
items.text_en: Abaye and Rava's practices regarding yichud
items.desc_en: Abaye would dwell in a barrel (to avoid yichud), and Rava would dwell in a reed. Avin comments that a foot in the sandal is a foot (meaning a precaution is a precaution).

sub.desc_en: Reports that Abaye would dwell in a barrel and Rava would dwell in a reed to avoid yichud.
Avin comments that a foot in the sandal is a foot, meaning a precaution is a precaution.

items.text: Story of the captive women and Rav Amram the Pious
items.text_en: Story of the captive women and Rav Amram the Pious
items.desc_en: Captive women were brought to Neharde'a and taken to Rav Amram the Pious's house. They removed the ladder from before them. As one passed, a light fell on her face, and Rav Amram lifted the ladder alone, but at the midpoint he cried out 'Fire at Amram's house!'
