The rabbis came and said he shamed them, but he said it is better to be shamed in this world than in the next. He adjured the evil inclination to leave, and it left like a pillar of fire, and he said 'See, you are fire and I am flesh, and I am greater than you.'

sub.desc_en: The story opens: captive women were brought to Neharde'a, taken to Rav Amram the Pious's house, and the ladder was removed; when a light fell on one woman's face, Rav Amram lifted the ladder alone and began to ascend.

At the midpoint, Rav Amram cried out 'Fire at Amram's house!', the rabbis came and he explained it is better to be shamed in this world than in the next; he adjured the evil inclination to leave as a pillar of fire, declaring 'You are fire and I am flesh, and I am greater than you.'

items.text: Stories of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Akiva mocking sinners
items.text_en: Stories of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Akiva mocking sinners
items.desc_en: Rabbi Meir used to mock sinners. One day Satan appeared as a woman on the other side of a river, and Rabbi Meir took a rope and crossed. At the midpoint, Satan left him, saying that if not for the heavenly proclamation to be careful with Rabbi Meir and his Torah, he would have made him pay. Similarly, Rabbi Akiva mocked sinners, and Satan appeared as a woman on a palm tree; he climbed halfway and Satan left him with a similar warning.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Meir used to mock sinners; one day Satan appeared as a woman across a river, and Rabbi Meir took a rope bridge and crossed.
At the midpoint, Satan left him, warning that without the heavenly proclamation to be careful with Rabbi Meir and his Torah, he would have made him pay.
Similarly, Rabbi Akiva mocked sinners; one day Satan appeared as a woman on a palm tree, and Rabbi Akiva grabbed the tree and began climbing.
At the midpoint, Satan left him with a similar warning about the heavenly proclamation regarding Rabbi Akiva and his Torah.

items.text: Story of Pleimo and Satan on Yom Kippur eve
items.text_en: Story of Pleimo and Satan on Yom Kippur eve
items.desc_en: Pleimo used to say daily 'An arrow in the eye of Satan'. One Yom Kippur eve, Satan appeared as a poor man and asked for bread, then complained that everyone is inside while he is outside, and then that everyone is at the table while he is alone. They brought him to the table, and he sat and filled himself with boils and sores and did disgusting things. Pleimo said to him... (the segment ends mid-sentence).

sub.desc_en: Introduces Pleimo's daily habit of saying 'An arrow in the eye of Satan'.
Relates that one Yom Kippur eve, Satan appeared as a poor man and Pleimo gave him bread.
Satan complains that on this day everyone is inside while he is outside.
Pleimo brings him inside and gives him bread; Satan then complains that everyone is at the table while he is alone.
Pleimo seats him at the table; Satan then covers himself with boils and pus and does disgusting things.
Pleimo begins to speak to the pauper, but the segment ends mid-sentence.

items.text: Story of Pelimo and the Satan
items.text_en: Story of Pelimo and the Satan
items.desc_en: Pelimo is accused of killing a man, hides in a latrine, and the Satan follows him. When Pelimo sees the Satan distressed, he reveals himself and the Satan asks why Pelimo said a certain curse. Pelimo advises him to say 'May the Merciful One rebuke the Satan' instead.

sub.desc_en: Pelimo is given a cup, spits into it, the man chokes and dies, and people say Pelimo killed a man.
Pelimo flees to a latrine, the Satan follows and falls before him; Pelimo asks why the Satan said a certain curse.
The Satan asks how he should phrase the curse, and Pelimo advises him to say 'May the Merciful One rebuke the Satan' instead.

items.text: Story of Rabbi Chiyya bar Ashi and his wife
items.text_en: Story of Rabbi Chiyya bar Ashi and his wife
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Ashi would pray to be saved from the evil inclination. His wife, thinking he had separated from her, tested him by disguising herself as a harlot. He succumbed to temptation, but later realized it was his wife and fasted until his death.

sub.desc_en: Introduces Rabbi Chiyya bar Ashi's habit of praying to be saved from the evil inclination every time he prostrates.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Ashi's wife (internal thought)
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Ashi's wife (internal thought)
sub.desc_en: His wife overhears his prayer and wonders why he prays for protection from the evil inclination, given that he has already separated from her for many years.
Describes the wife's test: she disguises herself as a harlot, approaches him in the garden, and he succumbs to temptation, fetching her a pomegranate from the top of a branch.
Upon returning home, he confesses the incident to his wife, who reveals she was the disguised woman; he insists he intended a transgression, and fasts until his death.

items.text: Rabbi Akiva's exposition on inadvertent sin
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's exposition on inadvertent sin
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about a woman who vowed to be a nazirite, her husband annulled it without her knowledge, and she violated her vow. Rabbi Akiva weeps over the verse, arguing that if one who intended to eat pork but ate lamb needs atonement, how much more so one who intended to eat pork and ate pork. A similar exposition is given regarding one who intended to eat fat but ate forbidden fat.

sub.desc_en: The baraita introduces the case of a woman who vowed to be a nazirite, her husband annulled it without her knowledge, and she violated her vow, setting up the context for Rabbi Akiva's exposition.
Rabbi Akiva weeps over the verse and argues that if one who intended to eat pork but ate lamb needs atonement, how much more so one who intended to eat pork and ate pork.
Rabbi Akiva gives a parallel exposition regarding one who intended to eat fat but ate forbidden fat, arguing that the verse's requirement for atonement applies even more strongly to intentional sin.
Isi ben Yehuda adds that over this matter all who mourn should mourn, emphasizing the severity of inadvertent sin.

items.text: Yichud with mother and sister
items.text_en: Yichud with mother and sister
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a person may be secluded with his mother. Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav Asi adds that one may be secluded with his sister and live with his mother and daughter. Shmuel objects, saying it is forbidden to be secluded with any forbidden relatives, even with an animal.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a person may be secluded with his mother.
Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav Asi adds that one may be secluded with his sister and live with his mother and daughter.
Shmuel objects, asserting that it is forbidden to be secluded with any forbidden relatives, even with an animal.

items.text: Reconciling the Mishnah with Shmuel's ruling
items.text_en: Reconciling the Mishnah with Shmuel's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from the Mishnah that permits seclusion with mother and daughter against Shmuel's ruling. Shmuel deflects by citing a baraita that forbids seclusion with other relatives without witnesses. The Gemara concludes that the dispute is between Tannaim, citing Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Tarfon who were cautious even with their own daughters and daughters-in-law.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from the Mishnah that permits seclusion with mother and daughter against Shmuel's ruling that forbids seclusion with all forbidden relatives.
Shmuel deflects by citing a baraita that forbids seclusion with other relatives without witnesses, implying the Mishnah's leniency is limited to mother and daughter.

The Gemara concludes that the dispute is between Tannaim, citing Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Tarfon who were cautious even with their own daughters and daughters-in-law, and the story of a student who scoffed and later stumbled with his mother-in-law.

items.text: Stories of sages avoiding seclusion with animals
items.text_en: Stories of sages avoiding seclusion with animals
items.desc_en: Abaye would distance himself from all animals, Rav Sheshet would move them away. Rav Chanan from Nehardea visited Rav Kahana and saw him studying with an animal standing before him, and questioned him about Shmuel's ruling. Rav Kahana replied that he was not aware of it.

sub.desc_en: The gemara reports that Abaye would distance himself from all animals, even from a single animal.
The gemara reports that Rav Sheshet would move the animal away from him.

sub.text: Story of Rav Chanan and Rav Kahana
sub.text_en: Story of Rav Chanan and Rav Kahana
sub.desc_en: Rav Chanan from Nehardea visited Rav Kahana, saw him studying with an animal standing before him, questioned him about Shmuel's ruling, and Rav Kahana replied that he was not aware of it.

items.text: Rava's ruling on yichud with multiple women
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on yichud with multiple women
items.desc_en: Rava rules that a man may be secluded with two yevamot, two tzarot, a woman and her mother-in-law, a woman and her stepdaughter, and a woman and a minor girl who knows the taste of intercourse but does not submit to it.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that a man may be secluded with two yevamot, two tzarot, a woman and her mother-in-law, a woman and her stepdaughter, and a woman and a minor girl who knows the taste of intercourse but does not submit to it.

items.text: Age of a minor for yichud
items.text_en: Age of a minor for yichud
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the age at which a minor girl or boy is considered a potential object of desire for yichud. Rav Adda bar Rav Uzza in the name of Rav Asi says a girl of nine years and a day, a boy of twelve years and a day. Others say a girl of twelve and a boy of thirteen. Rafram bar Pappa in the name of Rav Chisda adds that this applies only if she is not embarrassed to stand naked before him; if she is embarrassed, it is forbidden because the evil inclination has already clothed her.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: At what age does the Mishnah's rule about a minor sleeping in the same garment apply?

sub.text: Rav Adda bar Rav Uzza citing Rav Asi
sub.text_en: Rav Adda bar Rav Uzza citing Rav Asi
sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Rav Uzza in the name of Rav Asi gives the ages: a girl of nine years and a day, a boy of twelve years and a day.
Others say the ages are higher: a girl of twelve years and a day, a boy of thirteen years and a day, citing the verse about physical maturity.

sub.text: Rafram bar Pappa citing Rav Chisda
sub.text_en: Rafram bar Pappa citing Rav Chisda
sub.desc_en: Rafram bar Pappa in the name of Rav Chisda adds that the lenient ages apply only if she is not embarrassed to stand naked before him; if she is embarrassed, it is forbidden.
The Gemara explains the reason: the evil inclination has already clothed her, meaning she is a potential object of desire.

items.text: Story of Rav Acha bar Abba and his granddaughter
items.text_en: Story of Rav Acha bar Abba and his granddaughter
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Abba visited his son-in-law Rav Chisda and sat his granddaughter on his lap. Rav Chisda questioned him, citing Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav that one should not betroth his daughter when she is a minor, and Shmuel that one should not use a woman for service. Rav Acha bar Abba replied that he follows a different version of Shmuel's statement.

sub.desc_en: The narrative opens with Rav Acha bar Abba visiting his son-in-law Rav Chisda and placing his granddaughter on his lap.
Rav Chisda challenges Rav Acha bar Abba, citing Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav that one should not betroth a minor daughter, and Shmuel that one should not use a woman for service.
Rav Acha bar Abba replies that he follows a different version of Shmuel's statement, implying leniency.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Restrictions on teachers and shepherds
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Restrictions on teachers and shepherds
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that an unmarried man should not teach children, nor should a woman teach children. Rabbi Elazar adds that even a man whose wife is not with him should not teach. Rabbi Yehuda prohibits an unmarried man from herding animals or sleeping under the same blanket with another unmarried man, while the Sages permit it.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with a general principle and then lists restrictions: an unmarried man should not teach children, nor a woman; Rabbi Elazar adds a man whose wife is not with him; Rabbi Yehuda prohibits an unmarried man from herding animals or sharing a blanket with another unmarried man, while the Sages permit it.

items.text: Gemara: Reason for the Mishnah's restrictions
items.text_en: Gemara: Reason for the Mishnah's restrictions
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah prohibits an unmarried man from teaching. It suggests it is not due to suspicion of pederasty, as Jews are not suspected of that, but rather because of the mothers of the children. Similarly, a woman should not teach because of the fathers.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the reason for the Mishnah's restriction on an unmarried man teaching children.
The Gemara rejects the possibility that the concern is about the children themselves, citing a baraita that Jews are not suspected of bestiality or homosexuality.
The Gemara explains that the concern for an unmarried man is due to the mothers of the children, and for a woman teacher due to the fathers.

items.text: Clarification of Rabbi Elazar's statement
items.text_en: Clarification of Rabbi Elazar's statement
items.desc_en: A dilemma is raised: does Rabbi Elazar refer to a man who has no wife at all, or one whose wife is not with him? The Gemara resolves it with a baraita: even one who has a wife but she is not with him should not teach.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question about Rabbi Elazar's statement: does 'who has no wife' mean he has no wife at all, or that his wife is not with him?
The Gemara resolves the question by citing a baraita that explicitly includes a man whose wife is not with him.

items.text: Support for Rabbi Yehuda's ruling
items.text_en: Support for Rabbi Yehuda's ruling
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited where the Sages told Rabbi Yehuda that Jews are not suspected of bestiality or homosexuality, challenging his prohibition. This implies the Gemara questions his reasoning.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited where the Sages tell Rabbi Yehuda that Jews are not suspected of homosexuality or bestiality, challenging his restriction.

items.text: Second Mishnah: On trades and seclusion with women
items.text_en: Second Mishnah: On trades and seclusion with women
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one whose business is with women should not seclude himself with them, and a man should not teach his son a women's trade. Rabbi Meir advises teaching a clean and easy trade and praying to God, as wealth comes from merit. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar argues that if animals are sustained without effort, humans should be too, but sin disrupts this.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one whose business is with women should not seclude himself with them, and a man should not teach his son a women's trade.
Rabbi Meir advises teaching a clean and easy trade and praying to God, as wealth comes from merit, not from the trade itself.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar argues that if animals are sustained without effort, humans should be too, but sin disrupts this.

items.text: Abba Guryan's list of undesirable trades
items.text_en: Abba Guryan's list of undesirable trades
items.desc_en: Abba Guryan of Tzaydan says in the name of Abba Gurya that one should not teach his son to be a donkey driver, camel driver, potter, sailor, shepherd, or shopkeeper, as their trades are thievery. Rabbi Yehuda adds in his name that most donkey drivers are wicked, most camel drivers are upright, most sailors are pious, and the best of doctors goes to Gehinnom, the best of butchers is a partner of Amalek.

sub.desc_en: Abba Guryan lists trades to avoid teaching one's son (donkey driver, camel driver, etc.) as they lead to banditry; Rabbi Yehuda adds that most donkey drivers are wicked, most camel drivers are fit, most sailors are pious, and the best of doctors go to Gehinnom.

sub.text: Rabbi Yehuda in the name of Abba Gurya
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda in the name of Abba Gurya
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda adds in Abba Gurya's name that most donkey drivers are wicked, most camel drivers are upright, most sailors are pious, the best of doctors goes to Gehinnom, and the best of butchers is a partner of Amalek.

items.text: Rabbi Nehorai's praise of Torah study
items.text_en: Rabbi Nehorai's praise of Torah study
items.desc_en: Rabbi Nehorai says he would abandon all trades and teach his son only Torah, as one enjoys its fruits in this world and the principal remains for the world to come. Other trades fail in sickness or old age, but Torah protects in youth and provides hope in old age, as verses and Abraham's example show.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Nehorai declares he would abandon all trades and teach his son only Torah, because one enjoys its fruits in this world while the principal remains for the world to come.
Rabbi Nehorai contrasts Torah with other trades: when a person falls ill, ages, or suffers and cannot work, he starves.
Rabbi Nehorai states that Torah protects from all evil in youth and gives hope in old age.
Rabbi Nehorai cites verses: in youth, 'those who hope in the Lord shall renew strength' (Isaiah 40:31); in old age, 'they shall still bring forth fruit in old age' (Psalms 92:15).

Rabbi Nehorai supports his claim with Abraham, who observed the entire Torah before it was given, as the verse says 'because Abraham obeyed My voice and kept My charge, My commandments, My statutes, and My laws' (Genesis 26:5).

items.text: Gemara: On trades that involve women and the 'clean and easy' trade
items.text_en: Gemara: On trades that involve women and the 'clean and easy' trade
items.desc_en: The Gemara lists trades that involve frequent contact with women, such as goldsmiths and weavers, and notes that such people are not appointed as king or high priest due to the lowliness of their trade. It then discusses the 'clean and easy' trade, with Bar Kappara teaching that one should teach his son such a trade, and Rav Yehuda begins to specify what it is.

sub.desc_en: A baraita lists trades involving frequent contact with women (e.g., goldsmiths, weavers) and states that such people are not appointed as king or high priest, not because they are disqualified but because their trade is lowly.
A second baraita lists ten negative traits associated with the 'גָרָע' (a specific lowly trade), including arrogance, stinginess, and being suspected of sexual immorality, theft, and murder.
Bar Kappara teaches that one should always teach his son a 'clean and easy' trade, and the Gemara asks what that trade is.
Rav Yehuda begins to specify the identity of the 'clean and easy' trade, but the text cuts off at this point.

items.text: Opening phrase
items.text_en: Opening phrase
items.desc_en: The daf opens with a brief Aramaic phrase, 'The mistake of the students,' which serves as a heading or transition from the previous discussion.

sub.desc_en: The gemara opens with the Aramaic phrase 'The mistake of the students,' serving as a heading or transition from the previous discussion.

items.text: Rabbi's statement on trades
items.text_en: Rabbi's statement on trades
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi teaches that no trade disappears from the world; one should be happy if their parents have a noble trade and lament if they have a base one. He uses analogies to perfumers and tanners, and to having sons versus daughters.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited in which Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi states that no profession disappears from the world, praising those whose parents have a noble craft and lamenting those whose parents have a degraded one, and similarly regarding perfumers vs. tanners and male vs. female children.
Rabbi illustrates with the analogy of perfumers and tanners: the world needs both, but one is fortunate to be a perfumer and unfortunate to be a tanner.
Rabbi adds a second analogy: the world needs both males and females, but one is fortunate to have sons and unfortunate to have daughters.

items.text: Rabbi Meir's advice on trade and prayer
items.text_en: Rabbi Meir's advice on trade and prayer
items.desc_en: Rabbi Meir advises teaching a child a clean and easy trade, and praying to God, for wealth and poverty come not from the trade but from God, as Scripture says.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Meir teaches that a person should always teach his son a clean and easy craft, pray to the One who truly owns wealth, and cites the verse 'לי הכסף ולי הזהב' (Mine is the silver and Mine is the gold) to show that wealth comes from God, not from the craft itself.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's kal vachomer
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's kal vachomer
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar argues from nature: since animals like deer, lions, and foxes are sustained without toil, humans created to serve God should certainly be sustained without toil, but sins disrupt this.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar argues from the fact that wild animals (deer, lions, foxes) are sustained without toil, even though they were created only to serve him, that he who was created to serve his Master should certainly be sustained without toil — but his sins have spoiled his livelihood, as the verse 'עונותיכם הטו' (Your sins have diverted) states.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar resolves the kal vachomer by explaining that human sins disrupt the ideal: 'your sins have turned aside' (Isaiah 59:2), causing the loss of effortless sustenance.

items.text: Rabbi Nehorai's praise of Torah
items.text_en: Rabbi Nehorai's praise of Torah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Nehorai declares he would abandon all trades and teach only Torah, because trades only sustain in youth, while Torah sustains in both youth and old age, citing verses from Isaiah and Psalms.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Nehorai declares that he would abandon all worldly crafts and teach his son only Torah, because every craft supports a person only in youth but leaves him starving in old age, whereas Torah sustains a person in both youth and old age, citing verses from Isaiah and Psalms.
He explains that any trade only sustains a person in youth, but in old age he is left in hunger.
He contrasts that Torah stands by a person in both youth and old age, providing a future and hope.
He cites verses: for youth, 'those who hope in the Lord will renew their strength' (Isaiah 40:31), and for old age, 'they will still bear fruit in old age' (Psalms 92:15).
